title: cluster/session: three relay envelopes still double their opaque payload — the ByteArray-through-CBOR sites outside :kuilt-raft
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**#2746 gave `:kuilt-raft`'s opaque payloads byte-string framing. Three envelopes *outside* that
module still wrap opaque bytes through a codec without `alwaysUseByteString`, so they double every
payload byte outside CBOR's short range — and one of them wraps the very Raft frames #2746 just
halved.**

Found by the cross-module survey #2160 called for. #2746's fix is deliberately scoped to `raftCbor`
(a codec option, not a `@ByteString` annotation, precisely to bound its blast radius), so it cannot
reach these by construction.

## The three sites

| Field | Codec | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| `RaftRelay.bytes` — `kuilt-cluster/…/RaftRelay.kt:44`, codec at `:62` | `Cbor { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }` | "the opaque, already serialised Raft RPC" (its own KDoc) |
| `RoutingEnvelope.payload` — `kuilt-cluster/…/RoutedUnicastRouter.kt:228`, codec at `:231` | same | the opaque payload routed to one player |
| `RelayEnvelope.payload` — `kuilt-session/…/RelayEnvelope.kt:108`, codec at `:132` | same | the opaque payload on the session relay topology |

For reference, the codecs that already do this correctly: `:kuilt-otel`, `:kuilt-otel-otlp`,
`:kuilt-otel-tap` and now `:kuilt-raft`.

## Why `RaftRelay` is the sharp one — the expansion compounds

`RoutedRaftTransport.kt:281` and `RaftRelayHub.kt:185` wrap an **already-encoded Raft frame** as
`RaftRelay.bytes`. So on the learner/relay lane the two expansions multiply:

| | Raft frame | after relay wrap |
|---|---|---|
| before #2746 | 2× | **4×** |
| after #2746 | 1× | **2×** |
| with this issue fixed | 1× | **1×** |

#2746 halves the relayed lane, but the second halving is still on the table — and the relay lane is
the whole point of the two-tier cluster topology, so it is

title: heddle test: the under-ack arm's frequency floor is bought with 1,200 runs because the trials are not independent
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #2673 / PR #2744, filed because that PR bought its frequency floor with **sample size rather than design**, and its own measurements say so.

## What #2744 established

Reaching `PerEdgeSafety(e1)` in `EntitlementLedgerConservationTest`'s under-ack arm is a **chaotic tail event**, not a smooth function of the generator's knobs:

- Driven to their maximum (coin always, `delta = base`) at 80 runs, `prefixSafety` moves **1 → 1** — `underAcks` 67→123 and residual 435→1484, yet the end-of-run margin on `e1` gets *shallower* (−17 → −9).
- At 400 runs the counter is **non-monotone** in the knobs: a ¾ coin gives 3, *below* baseline.
- Doubling the inner step count (`repeat(60)` → 120) is **counterproductive** — `prefixSafety` fell to 0, because the breach is a transient that later honest delegation across `e1` washes out.

So bias buys ~2–3×; only sample size makes the count stable. #2744 landed **1,200 runs** to get a floor of `>= 10` against a measured 22 (worst of seven re-seeded trajectories: 14).

## The cost

**~+49 s of CI wall-clock across the two native targets** (`macosArm64` treatment test 2.013 s → 26.11 s, measured both ends). Accepted deliberately: 600 runs re-seeds to **3, 7, 13, 18**, so its floor would have to sit at ~2 — the knife edge #2673 declined in the first place.

That is a defensible trade, but it is paying wall-clock forever for a *reachability* property, and there are two cheaper shapes nobody has priced.

## Option A — independent per-run seeds (cheap, probably sufficient)

The arm threads **one** `Random(0x1783C0DE)` through all 1,200 runs, so run *k* depends on runs 0..*k*−1. Consequences:

- Raising the count **re-walks every run** rather than appending, which is why the s

title: A second collector of a Spool-backed incoming STEALS frames, and nothing reds
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Falling out of #2735 (the #2106 fix). That PR made `RoutedRaftTransport.incoming` a
`Spool<RaftEnvelope>` — `Channel.receiveAsFlow()` — instead of `merge(inner.incoming, relayed)`
over a `SharedFlow`. Correct for the defect, and it changes what a **second** collector does:

| | second collector gets | how it presents |
|---|---|---|
| before | its own copy (`SharedFlow` fans out) | duplicate delivery — loud, and Raft's §8 dedup absorbs it |
| after | **half the frames** (`receiveAsFlow` is a competing receiver) | frames vanish from the engine at random — silent |

The engine would simply stop seeing an arbitrary subset of `AppendEntries`/`RequestVote`: a
cluster that elects slowly, replicates unevenly, and reproduces nowhere.

**Nothing reds if a second collector appears.** The single-collection requirement is stated in prose
on `RaftTransport.incoming` ("The engine collects this flow for the node's entire lifetime. Do not
collect it from application code.") and in ADR-034, and nothing in-tree violates it today —
`RaftEngine` is the sole collector, and `ConsensusPlacement.federatedCore` / `buildClusterClient`
each hand the transport to exactly one `RaftNode`. That is a property held by convention with no
mechanism, which is the shape this track has been closing all day.

This is the general form, not a `RoutedRaftTransport` quirk: `Spool` is the repo's sanctioned
single-receiver buffer and **every** `Seam.incoming` is one, so the same silent-theft failure is
available at every fabric. `Spool`'s KDoc says "collect once"; nothing enforces it.

## Design question

What should a second collection *do*? Candidates, none obviously right:

1. **Refuse it** — `Spool.incoming` latches a `collected` flag and the second

title: LogTapAdmission cannot express a symmetric mesh — two offering peers both get Verifier and deadlock
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`LogTapAdmission` splits cleanly into an offering role and a pulling role. That works for the two topologies it was built for — loopback (`Open`) and a one-directional reach pull (host `Verify`, puller `Present`) — and **structurally cannot express a symmetric mesh**, where every peer both offers and pulls.

## The mechanism

`LogTapAdmission.kt:49-62`:

```kotlin
internal fun LogTapAdmission.offeringRole(): GateRole? = when (this) {
    is LogTapAdmission.Open    -> null
    is LogTapAdmission.Verify  -> GateRole.Verifier(token, clock, random)
    is LogTapAdmission.Present -> error("LogTapAdmission.Present is for the pulling side; an offering tap needs Verify or Open")
}

internal fun LogTapAdmission.pullingRole(): GateRole? = when (this) {
    is LogTapAdmission.Open    -> null
    is LogTapAdmission.Present -> GateRole.Prover(code)
    is LogTapAdmission.Verify  -> error("LogTapAdmission.Verify is for the offering side; a pulling client needs Present or Open")
}
```

Every offering side gets `Verifier`. So when two peers both offer with `Verify`, **both are verifiers, neither is a prover, and neither can ever prove.** There is no value of `LogTapAdmission` that makes a symmetric pair converge: `Open` admits everyone, `Verify` deadlocks, and `Present` errors on the offering path.

## How it was found — the positive control, not the test

A worker on fireworks-compose #3238 was gating a mesh-ride log tap and wrote a test giving both the hub and a peer `Verify`. The test passed. **Its positive control then failed: the *correct* code timed out too.**

That is what makes this worth filing rather than shrugging at. The harness produces a timeout for *any* failure to converge, so "wrong code times out" is satisf

title: kuilt-raft: onChangeMembership's settled-Simple guard has no reachable emit trajectory — keep it, delete it, or find the trajectory
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RaftEngine.onChangeMembership`'s last guard —

```kotlin
val current = state.membershipState
if (current !is MembershipState.Simple) {
    deferred.completeExceptionally(MembershipChangeInProgressException(MembershipRefusal.UnsettledJointConfig))
    return
}
```

— appears to have **no reachable emit trajectory**. Found while implementing #2032 (PR #2736), which
gave it the name `MembershipRefusal.UnsettledJointConfig`; the value is declared there and
deliberately left **unclaimed by any test**, with its KDoc saying so. This issue is where that
decision gets revisited rather than quietly inherited.

## The derivation, and the premise it rests on

`membershipState` always reflects the **last config entry**, so on a leader `Joint` means the last
config entry is a `Joint` (or, with the log compacted, the snapshot's config is). Then:

- **uncommitted** → the guard above it (`lastConfigIndex > currentCommitIndex`,
  `UncommittedConfigEntry`) refuses first;
- **committed** → a `Simple(C_new)` was already appended above it *in the same call that committed
  it* — `onConfigCommitted`'s Joint branch — or, on election, by `finalizeInheritedCommittedJoint`,
  which also covers the compacted case (`jointIndex = snapshotIndex`, and
  `commitIndex >= snapshotIndex` always). So the guard sees a `Simple`.

**The load-bearing premise** is that a leader's `membershipState` is written *only* by its own
`appendConfigEntry`. The other four `recomputeMembership()` sites — the `init` restore,
`finalizeInstalledSnapshot`, and `onAppendEntries`' truncate and append arms — all run on a
**Follower**, because `demoteToFollowerOnLeaderContact` fires **unconditionally** at the top of
`onAppendEntries` (and `onInstallSnapshot`) before an

title: kuilt-nw: NwCrossProcessProbeTest self-skips as PASS on a Mac with the dylib — the #2621 defect on a capability gate
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2621 fixed the three `-P`-gated probes that self-skipped as PASS and added
`forbidRuntimeSelfSkippingProbe` to make that shape unwritable. One instance of the same defect is
**outside** both the fix and the guard, and was found while enumerating for it.

## The site

`kuilt-nw/src/jvmTest/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/nw/NwCrossProcessProbeTest.kt`, both `@Test`s:

```kotlin
if (!bridgeUnavailable) return // macOS-with-dylib: real-radio path, skip
```

The gate is a **capability** (`NwNativeLib.jvmAvailability()`), not a `-P` flag. On a Linux runner
the bridge is `Unavailable`, the guard falls through, and the assertions run. **On a Mac with
`libkuilt.dylib` on the classpath they return early and the test reports `passed` having asserted
nothing** — the identical reporting defect #2621 is about, one gate-kind over.

Two reasons it was left alone rather than swept in:

- It is not `-P`-gated, so it is outside #2621's definition of done.
- `forbidRuntimeSelfSkippingProbe` structurally cannot see it: the guard keys on `getenv(` and
  non-JDK `System.getProperty(`, and there is neither here. That limit is stated in the guard's own
  header, so this is a known gap rather than a missed one.

## Why it matters more than it looks

`apple-nightly.yml` runs `:kuilt-nw:jvmTest` **on a real macOS host** (#2487) precisely so the bridge
is present. That lane already carries a step asserting the bridge suite "reports a non-zero run count
with zero skips" — but a self-skip is not a skip, so these two rows satisfy that assertion while
proving nothing. The two mechanisms that would catch it (`skipped` in the XML, and a run-count
assertion) are both defeated by the same early `return`.

title: conformance: LWWRegister's no-op ceiling now catches #2158's shape by only 2.9 points (was 7.3) — the detection band narrowed with #2087
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`VacuityFloorSelfTest.everyBindingWhoseCeilingCatchesDeadRetirementBreachesIt` (via
`bindingsWhoseCeilingCatchesDeadRetirement`) asserts that `LWWRegister`'s no-op ceiling **reds** on
#2158's crippled shape — retirement dead off replica 0. That is the ceiling's only live catch: the
binding's healthy rate is far below it, so nothing else can make it fire.

#2087 narrowed the band that detection sits in, from 7.3 points to **2.9**.

## Measured

`VacuityBreakdownProbe`, seeds `0..15` (the window `generatorIsNotVacuous` runs), shipped
`EVERY_REPLICA` arm:

| | before #2087 | after #2087 | ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|
| healthy (`AS_BOUND`) | 6.6% | **0.0%** | 13% |
| crippled (`DEAD_OFF_REPLICA_ZERO`) | 20.3% | **15.9%** | 13% |
| detection margin | 7.3 pts | **2.9 pts** | |

## Why it narrowed, and why it is not a regression to undo

The healthy rate falling to zero is the *intended* outcome. Before #2087 `LWWRegister.set` assigned,
so a write at a losing tag still changed the register; after it, such a write is dropped, and three
**absolute** timestamp bands became no-ops on 44.0% of steps. The generator was re-aimed to offset
its bands by `nextRoundBase(state.timestamp)`, which makes every op strictly dominate the state it is
applied to — so no draw can be discarded, and the healthy rate is now **structurally** 0.

The same ascent also removes some of the crippled arm's waste, which is why 20.3% fell to 15.9%. Both
numbers moved for the same reason; the ceiling did not move at all.

## The risk

At 2.9 points, an ordinary future tweak to this generator — band sparsity, the round size, the parity
rule, the offset — could drop the crippled rate below 13%. `VacuityFloorSelfTest` would then go
**quietly green whil

title: kuilt-raft: record the exact (actor-loop) propose-envelope measurement rejected in #2156, and when to revisit it
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Not a defect — a recorded alternative, deliberately not taken, with a reopen trigger.** Filed so the analysis survives outside #2728's PR body.

## What was decided

#2156 made `checkProposeFitsTransport` measure the `AppendEntries` envelope rather than trust a flat `HEADER_BUDGET`. The measurement is **conservative, not exact**: the probe charges `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_INDEX` / `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM` / `Long.MAX_VALUE` for every `Long` in the envelope, because the entry's real `index` and `term` do not exist at that call site — they are assigned on the actor loop, and the gate runs before it on the caller's coroutine.

Cost: **~70 B** of over-reserve on a young log. Measured — the envelope is ~199 B at a simulation's magnitudes and the probe charges 270 for a 24-character auto id.

## The alternative

Move the measurement to the **actor loop**, where `index`, `term` and the real `dedupKey` are all known, and complete the caller's `CompletableDeferred` exceptionally with `PayloadTooLarge` before `state.log += entry`. The caller still gets a typed, actionable failure; it arrives through the deferred rather than synchronously. That is exact — no pessimism, and no data race on `myClientId` either, since the actor loop owns it.

## Why it was rejected

**The conservative probe's limit is stable over the node's lifetime; the exact one is not.** Charging the widest admitted values makes the reserve a function of this node's `ClientId` alone, so the published limit is a constant a caller can read once and cache. An actor-loop measurement makes it **drift with log position**: `index` and `term` widen through CBOR's size steps (1 → 2 → 3 → 5 → 9 bytes) as the log grows, so a command accepted yesterday is refused today with no

title: crdt-test: RetirementReAssertion.subject is mandatory in arity and optional in content — a blank one passes
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Residual from [#2184](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2184), measured rather than
suspected while closing it.

`RetirementReAssertion.subject` carries **no constraint**: a blank string passes every arm of
`QuiltedConformanceSuite.samplesReAssertAfterRetirement`. `RetirementSubjectSelfTest.aBlankSubjectPassesToo`
asserts that, so it is a standing receipt rather than a claim.

## Why that is worse than it looks

#2184's whole argument for calling the sibling-referencing-predicate hole *unreachable by accident*
is that the mandatory `subject` field makes such a predicate **conspicuous in review**:

> It is also **not reachable by accident** — you would have to write a predicate referencing the
> sibling samples, which the mandatory `subject: String` field already makes conspicuous in review.

A blank `subject` defeats exactly that. The field is mandatory in *arity* and optional in *content*,
so the stated mitigation is weaker than the issue claims — and the machine never reads the field at
all, so nothing but a reviewer's eye is left.

## Why it was not fixed in the same PR

`RetirementReAssertion` is a `public` class in `:kuilt-conformance`'s `commonMain`, so
`require(subject.isNotBlank())` in its `init` changes a published constructor's contract. Every
in-tree binding would pass it today (13 of 13 name a concrete subject), but a downstream consumer
subclassing `QuiltedConformanceSuite` would start throwing at construction. That is a deliberate
call, not a drive-by.

## Precedent for making it

This repo already treats a blank reason as itself a violation for its `// ALLOW-` escape hatches —
`ALLOW-bareSeamState`, `ALLOW-ise`, `ALLOW-hashOrderedDraw`, `ALLOW-realDispatcher` and
`ALLOW-staleCitation`

title: kuilt-primitives routes to symbols newer than consumers' pins — the skill has no way to state a minimum version
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**#2572 fixed the skill being *behind* the library. That fix created the opposite drift: the skill is now ahead of what consumers can resolve, and it has no way to say so.**

## Measured in fireworks-compose today

`.claude/skills/kuilt-primitives/SKILL.md:54` routes agents to `Flow.pumpIn(scope, onFailure, name) { … }` (`us.tractat.kuilt.core`, `:kuilt-core`) — the route #2572 added.

fireworks-compose pins `kuilt = "0.7.0-dev.1371"`. That artifact **does not contain it**:

```
$ unzip -l …/kuilt-core-jvm/0.7.0-dev.1371/…/kuilt-core-jvm-0.7.0-dev.1371.jar | grep -c PumpInKt
0
```

`PumpIn.kt` landed on kuilt `main` in `149ec6c1` on **2026-09-04** — after dev.1371 was cut. The daily sync carried the *route* down within a day; the *symbol* arrives only when a consumer bumps its pin, which is a separate and much larger decision.

## Why this is worse than a compile error

It surfaced when a dispatched worker on fireworks #3238 followed the route, found the symbol absent, and had to improvise — it used an explicit `CancellationException` rethrow instead and flagged the mismatch in its report. That is the good outcome, and it depended on the worker being briefed to stop and report rather than to self-correct.

The bad outcome is the one #2541 already named: **drift here fails open.** A worker that reads a route it cannot satisfy does not go red — it hand-rolls the primitive the skill exists to prevent, which is exactly the interception #2572 was filed to restore. So the ahead-drift silently re-opens #2572 for every consumer whose pin predates the symbol, and nothing anywhere goes red.

title: conformance: LatticeLawHarness cannot see a mutator that moves its replica DOWN the lattice — 'changed' is the only bit it records
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The gap

`LatticeLawHarness` records one bit per generator step:

```kotlin
steps += Step(chosen.kind, changed = latest[r] != before)
```

`changed` is the *only* thing any vacuity metric reads (`noOpSteps`, `effectiveRetireSteps`). So a
step that moved the replica **down** the lattice — `after != before` **and** `before.piece(after) ==
before` — is counted as a perfectly healthy, effective step. Nothing in the harness, in
`VacuityReport`, or in `VacuityFloorSelfTest` can tell it apart from a step that moved up.

Grep receipt: `before.piece`, `piece(after)` and `piece(before)` appear nowhere in
`LatticeLawHarness.kt`.

## Why it matters — it already hid a live defect

`LWWRegisterConvergenceTest` drew from three **absolute** timestamp bands while `LWWRegister.set`
assigned. Every draw that landed below the state's current tag pushed that replica strictly down the
lattice. That is #2087, happening inside the conformance suite, on most seeds, for as long as the
binding has existed — and every floor stayed green, because a down-move looks exactly like an
up-move to `changed`.

It only became visible when #2087's fix turned those same draws into **no-ops**, at which point the
no-op ceiling reddened immediately (44.0% against a 13% ceiling). The metric that caught it is the
one that measures the *absence* of the defect's replacement, not the defect.

## What a fix looks like

A `Step` also carrying `inflationary = before.piece(after) == after`, and either a floor
(`downMoveSteps == 0` by default) or an outright `check`. Two things to settle first, which is why
this is filed rather than done:

1. **Is it true of every binding today?** Not measured. Most alphabet ops are written as
   `state.piece(state.someDelta

title: kuilt-raft: a ConfigPayload entry can exceed the batch bound with no gate to refuse it — boundedBatch's always-send-one clause has a second entrance
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`boundedBatch` deliberately sends a single entry that does not fit, alone, rather than emitting an empty batch — the KDoc argues that correctly: a zero-entry frame degrades into a heartbeat the follower *acks*, so the leader would spin with no log line naming why. It names the residual case as "the budget shrinking after the entry was already committed", and says that has no fix at either site.

**There is a second way into that path that the KDoc does not name, and it does not require the budget to move: a config entry.** `LogEntry.config` is a `ConfigPayload` — a `ClusterConfig` of consumer-supplied `NodeId`s — and a membership-change entry is minted internally by `addServer`/`removeServer`, so it never passes `checkProposeFitsTransport`. Nothing bounds its size at any gate.

Measured cost of a `ConfigPayload` alone (see #2720 for the full table, measured on the `InstallSnapshot` envelope which carries the identical field): 5 voters × 20-char ids is 267 B simple and 382 B joint; 5 voters × 36-char uuid ids is 552 B joint. A **joint** config carries two `ClusterConfig`s, and every membership change transits one.

So on a transport with a small budget, a config entry can exceed `budget - HEADER_BUDGET` on its own, be sent alone by the always-send-at-least-one clause, and be dropped at `SeamRaftTransport.sendTo` — permanently, because unlike an application command there is no proposer to refuse and no retry with something smaller. §6 adopts config entries **on append**, so a follower that never receives one never adopts the new membership, and the leader's own commit quorum is computed against a configuration its followers do not hold.

Not necessarily a fix — possibly just an honest bound a

title: crdt-test: Histogram, DDSketch and GCounterDouble have no cross-target golden vector
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

[#1979](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1979) adds four `CanonicalMapSerializer` sites —
`Histogram.buckets`, `DDSketch.positive`, `DDSketch.negative`, `GCounterDouble.counts` — and binds
all three types to `LatticeLawSuite`. That closes the **within-target** axis: every merge
permutation now encodes identically on each target.

It does **not** close the cross-target one. `CanonicalGoldenVectorTest` holds checked-in CBOR byte
strings for ten zoo types and none of these three is among them, so nothing asserts that a JVM peer
and a Kotlin/Native peer agree on their bytes. That file's own KDoc says the rule: *"Adding a type
to that family does not inherit a pin from this file — add a vector."*

`MetricCatalog` (`:kuilt-otel`) embeds both `GCounterDouble` and `DDSketch`, and it goes over
`:kuilt-otel-tap`'s wire, so the two axes are not academic for these types.

## Why it was split out

`CanonicalGoldenVectorTest.kt` was being edited concurrently by another worker while #1979 was in
flight, so #1979 deliberately did not touch it and corrected the claim in `CanonicalDigest.kt`
instead (it read *"covering every `Canonical*Serializer` site"*, which stopped being true).

## What to add

Three vectors, built the way the file's KDoc requires — replicas contributing **different** slices,
merged in a deliberately non-sorted order, multi-entry (a single-entry map has one iteration order
and pins nothing). Then extend the mutation table in that KDoc with the four new rows, measured by
commenting out one annotation at a time.

title: kuilt-test: FakeSeam retains the caller's ByteArray in broadcasts/directed — the #2546 shape one field over
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2546 fixed `FakeSeam`'s roster being **retained rather than copied** (`_peers =
MutableStateFlow(initialPeers)` held the caller's own `Set` instance, so a `MutableSet` could be
edited out from under the seam after the constructor's `require` had passed). The same
retained-not-copied shape is one field over, and #2546 deliberately did not widen scope to it.

`broadcast` and `sendTo` store the caller's `ByteArray` by reference:

```kotlin
_broadcasts.add(payload)                 // FakeSeam.broadcast
_directed.add(peer to payload)           // FakeSeam.sendTo
```

The getters copy the **list** but not the arrays it holds:

```kotlin
public val broadcasts: List<ByteArray> get() = _broadcasts.toList()
public val directed: List<Pair<PeerId, ByteArray>> get() = _directed.toList()
```

So a caller that reuses one buffer sees the fake rewrite its own history:

```kotlin
val buf = byteArrayOf(1, 2, 3)
seam.broadcast(buf)
buf[0] = 9
seam.broadcasts[0]   // {9, 2, 3} — a frame that was never sent
```

## Why this is a judgement call rather than an obvious bug

A real fabric serializes at send time, so the frame that went on the wire is `{1, 2, 3}` and the fake
reports `{9, 2, 3}` — it describes something production did not produce, which is the permissive-fake
direction this family keeps closing (#2432 / #2443 / #2536 / #2546). Buffer reuse is also a normal
thing for a consumer to do, so this is reachable without doing anything strange.

Against: a defensive `copyOf()` per send costs an allocation on every `broadcast` in every consumer's
test suite, and every in-tree call site passes a freshly built array, so nothing in this repo can
observe the difference. The `broadcasts`/`directed` KDoc already promises only that ea

title: FlakyLifecycleSeam: the delegate-peers collector is still an unlocked check-then-write
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while landing #2633 (PR #2713), which swept `FlakyLifecycleSeam`'s **`SeamState`** onto a `SeamStateGate`. That closes the lost-terminal-`Torn` race on any dispatcher. It does **not** touch the seam's other flow, and the argument for leaving that one alone is the same "cannot lose a write *here*" that #2633 rejected.

`FlakyLifecycleSeam`'s delegate-peers collector is still an unlocked check-then-write:

```kotlin
delegate.peers.collect { delegatePeers ->
    if (stateGate.state.value is SeamState.Woven) _peers.value = delegatePeers
}
```

On a multi-threaded dispatcher: the collector reads `Woven`, is preempted, `tear()` collapses `_peers` to `{selfId}` and latches `Torn`, then the collector resumes and writes the full delegate roster. The seam is then `Torn` while `peers` names remotes — the exact contract violation `TestFakePeersCollapseOnTearTest` and #1854 exist to pin.

## Why this is not just a reopen of #71

[#71](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/71) is this window, closed COMPLETED via #87. Two things about how it closed are worth recording rather than re-deriving:

- #87's comment says the ordering fix (`_state` written before `_peers`) **eliminates** the window. It narrows it — the class's own KDoc has said "**narrowing**" ever since, in the same commit. The ordering only helps when the collector's *read* happens after the state write; a collector preempted before that still lands late.
- The derived-source fix (#76) was tried first and reverted: `combine(...).stateIn(...)` makes `peers` propagation asynchronous, which reddened `LifecycleContractTest` / `ResilienceSoakTest` on the **Android unit-test target**, and removing the collector outright reddened `CompositeResilienceTest`,

title: crdt: Gauge.observe shares #2087's shape under a delta-mutator contract — decide whether it adopts the join too
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #2087, which decided **Option 2 — make `LWWRegister.set`/`unset` inflationary** and
scoped itself to `LWWRegister`. Its closing instruction was: *"Check whether `MVRegister` and `Gauge`
share the shape. If they do, say so and file separately rather than widening this PR."* Checked —
this is the answer.

## `MVRegister` — **does not** share the shape. No action.

`MVRegister.set` mints a fresh dot (`causal.context.nextDot(replica)`) rather than taking a caller
timestamp, and returns `Causal(DotFun(d↦v), context + d)`. The new dot always dominates and the
result's context is a superset of the input's, so `X.piece(m(X)) == m(X)` holds by construction:
the causal join drops `X`'s old dot (it is in `m(X)`'s context) and keeps the new one. There is no
losing-tag domain to be in.

## `Gauge` — **does** share the shape, but under a different contract

`Gauge.observe` is `Gauge(LWWRegister.tagged(replica, timestamp, value))` — the bare observation,
with no join against what the gauge already holds. So `gauge.observe(r, losingTs, v)` sits strictly
below `gauge`, which is exactly #2087's `m(X) < X`.

**What makes it a separate call rather than the same bug.** `LWWRegister.set` promised nothing about
absorption, which is why #2087 landed on it. `Gauge.observe`'s KDoc has always prescribed the
opposite:

> Returns a new state carrying just this tagged observation; absorb it with `piece`
> (`gauge = gauge.piece(gauge.observe(replica, ts, v))`) so an older-timestamp observation never
> overwrites a newer one.

That is a *delta-mutator* contract. The down-move is the documented return value, not an accident,
and every in-tree caller follows the prescription. #2087's PR therefore preserved `observe`
byte-for-byte

title: dial cancellation-cleanliness is documented but unpinned — no in-tree fabric can demonstrate the resume-into-cancellation window
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #2587, which fixed the three *reachable* leak sites in `handshakeLink`. This is the
fourth site named there, and the only one that could not be fixed — because it cannot be
**demonstrated**, and the deliverable is the fixture, not the assertion.

## The window

`dial` is a caller-supplied `suspend (…) -> Connection`. If the dialing coroutine is cancelled **as
`dial` resumes**, the continuation takes the cancellation instead of the connection: the conn exists
inside the caller's transport, and no handle ever reaches kuilt. Nothing on kuilt's side can close
it, because kuilt's ownership provably cannot begin before `dial` returns.

#2587 added the contract clause (`assembleVoterMesh`'s `@param dial`, echoed on
`superviseVoterReconnection`): *`dial` must be cancellation-clean — if cancelled at any point, every
transport resource it opened is closed before the `CancellationException` propagates.* It is
**documented, not enforced**, and unpinned.

## Why no in-tree fabric can demonstrate it

The window is **zero-width in every harness**:

- `InMemoryVoterFabric.dial` has no suspension point at all — `openLink()` is a non-suspending
  `connectionPair()`, and `InMemoryConnectionSource.offer` is a `trySend` on a `Channel.UNLIMITED`.
- `SeverableInMemoryVoterFabric.openLink` `awaitCancellation()`s **before** `connectionPair()` while
  severed, so no conn is ever created and there is nothing to leak.
- `WebSocketVoterMesh`'s dial has no guard, and its window is non-zero only over a real socket.

So the in-memory fabrics are *accidentally* immune rather than compliant — the
reference-implementation-hides-the-gap shape `CLAUDE.md` records, and the reason #2587 left this
open rather than shipping an assertion

title: Two different libkuilt.dylib libraries export the same kuilt_protocol_version symbol — after #2705 the ABI check can no longer tell them apart
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Latent, not currently biting. Surfaced by #2705 (`:kuilt-multipeer` slice of #1430) and **parked deliberately** — filing it with an explicit reopen trigger rather than fixing it inside an unrelated PR.

## The shape

`:kuilt-multipeer` and `:kuilt-nw` each build a **separate** macOS dylib, both named **`libkuilt.dylib`**, and each exports the **same** cdecl symbol:

```
kuilt-multipeer/src/macosMain/.../bridge/Bridge.kt:25   @CName("kuilt_protocol_version")
kuilt-nw/src/macosMain/.../bridge/Bridge.kt:25          @CName("kuilt_protocol_version")

Each JVM side loads by that name and gates on the version it reads back:

**Today the two versions differ (1 vs 2), so the ABI check accidentally discriminates the two libraries.** If the wrong `libkuilt.dylib` were ever on the load path, the version mismatch would catch it — by luck, not design.

**#2705 raises multipeer's protocol to 2** (it must: `mc_runtime_create` grew a `selfId` parameter). Both libraries then report **2**, and that accidental protection is gone. A wrong-library load would pass the ABI gate and fail later, somewhere else, as a missing-symbol or wrong-behaviour error that names neither module.

Nothing collides today: the two modules do not share a test classpath, and each resolves its own dylib from its own module's resources. The fix is not a one-liner — it means either distinct library names (`libkuilt-multipeer.dylib` / `libkuilt-nw.dylib`) or distinct symbol prefixes (`kuilt_mc_protocol_version` / `

title: kuilt-multipeer: policy and dispatcher must land together — a policy knob alone is unwitnessable
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up from #2705 (the `:kuilt-multipeer` slice of #1430), which shipped `selfId` alone — 1 of the 4 universal knobs.

## What was found

`policy` **is** traceable to a real consumer: the `Spool` in both multipeer seams. But **neither factory forwards one**, so every multipeer seam is pinned to `DeliveryPolicy.Reliable` — the identical defect `:kuilt-nearby` and `:kuilt-websocket` (#2686) each had.

## Why the knob was added and then removed again

Both seams also **hardcode `Dispatchers.Default`** for the delivery drain. So a lossy-policy assertion made through a woven seam *races that drain* rather than observing it — the test cannot reliably witness the policy taking effect.

That makes `policy` alone unshippable on this fabric, for the reason this epic exists:

> An argument whose arrival no test can witness is indistinguishable, to a reader, from one that never arrives.

A `policy` parameter that compiles, is forwarded, and cannot be demonstrated to change behaviour is only marginally better than one that is ignored — and it *looks* identical in review. `:kuilt-nearby`'s note on this epic already records shipping a partial knob set as a legitimate outcome.

## What to do

**Land `policy` and `dispatcher` together**, not separately:

1. Thread `dispatcher` through both seams, replacing the hardcoded `Dispatchers.Default` on the delivery drain.
2. Thread `policy` to the `Spool` in both seams.
3. Then a test can inject a test dispatcher, drive the drain deterministically, and **witness** a non-default policy dropping frames. That test is the point of the exercise — without it, step 2 alone should not be merged.

title: build: DetektCatalogScanner / AgpCatalogScanner match their alias as a SUBSTRING, so a prefixed neighbour is a false GREEN
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced by #2700 and deliberately left out of its scope.

Three catalog scanners live in the root `build.gradle.kts`. All three find their plugin alias, read its `version.ref`, and resolve that ref in the `[versions]` block. **One anchors the alias to the start of a line; two do not.**

`KotlinCatalogScanner` (#2700), with the reasoning at the regex:

```kotlin
// ANCHORED to the start of a line, unlike the two sibling scanners. Without `(?m)^\s*` the
// alias is matched as a SUBSTRING, so a differently-prefixed neighbour (`xkotlin-gradlePlugin`)
// would satisfy it and this guard would confirm itself against an entry the build never
// applies — a green, which is the failure mode that matters here.
val entry = Regex(
    """(?m)^\s*kotlin-gradlePlugin\s*=\s*\{[^}]*module\s*=\s*""" + ...
```

`DetektCatalogScanner` and `AgpCatalogScanner` open with the bare alias:

```kotlin

"""android-gradlePlugin\s*=\s*\{[^}]*module\s*=\s*"com\.android\.tools\.build:gradle"[^}]*""" + ...
```

Both guards are built around *"an unconfirmed probe must fail rather than pass"* — each `error`s loudly when its scanner returns `null`, precisely so a catalog respelling cannot silently disarm it. Not an `error` — a **green**.

title: conformance: payloadBudgetObligationIsTrackedWhenUnpublished reads the HOST only, so a joiner that publishes no budget is a silent skip
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #2601, whose 15 rows are now all converted. This is the one obligation the sweep left role-asymmetric for a reason that still needs a decision.

## The hole

`payloadBudgetObligationIsTrackedWhenUnpublished` reads `host.maxPayloadBytes` only:

```kotlin
connectedPair { host, _ ->
    if (host.maxPayloadBytes == null) { /* require a gap URL */ } else { /* require it cleared */ }
}
```

`maxPayloadBytes` is declared on `Seam`, so a role-split fabric publishes it **twice, from two implementations** — a `LinkSeam` joiner forwards its connection's `maxFrameBytes` while a `MeshSeam` host folds every ply's. A joiner that publishes nothing is therefore a **silent skip** of both payload obligations, and nothing declares it. That is #2601's own named failure mode, one end over, and `payloadOfExactlyTheBudgetIsCarried`'s KDoc says so explicitly while deferring the fix as "its own change".

## Why it was deferred rather than done

The accountability hook is one value per harness, not per end:

```kotlin
public open fun payloadBudgetGap(): String? = CapabilityGaps.PAYLOAD_BUDGET
```

It binds in **both** directions — publish a number and the gap must be cleared; publish nothing and it must be set. So a harness whose host publishes and whose joiner does not cannot satisfy a per-end check against one hook: the gap must be simultaneously blank and non-blank. Two ways out, both real changes:

1. **Assert the two ends agree** about whether they publish. Cheap, one line — but it makes this row depend on a symmetry claim `Seam` does not make. #2681 refused it on exactly that ground, and that refusal looks right: nothing in the contract says a role-split fabric's two ends must name the same ceiling, or both name one.

title: ci: #408's cold-build heap fix was never confirmed sufficient on the real runner — and the exit-143 fingerprint does not identify its own cause
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**#408's fix has been assumed sufficient for three months and nobody ever filed the receipt it asked for.** Its own record says:

> **Sufficiency on the real runner is pending empirical confirmation** (a catalog-cold-build PR is the test). If it still trips: drop to 2.5 GB, or do the structural fix — split the native/wasm compile+test into its own job so daemon heaps don't co-reside.

That confirmation was never filed, and **#320 — the tracking issue that held the durable options — was closed on 2026-06-14, the same day the fix landed.** So the open question has had no live home since. This issue is that home.

## What is actually unconfirmed

#408 dropped the CI daemon-heap floor 8 GB → 6 GB via CLI `-D` overrides (`org.gradle.jvmargs`/`kotlin.daemon.jvmargs` at `-Xmx3g`), keeping `gradle.properties` at 4 GB for local dev. The **mechanism** was proven by a controlled experiment — two `-Xmx4g` heap-committing JVMs in a 7 GB cgroup are OOM-killed every run, `-Xmx2–2.5g` pairs survive every run. What was never established is **sufficiency on the real 16 GB runner**, because the local box cannot reproduce the full peak (arm64 Mac runs neither the x86_64 K/N compiler, nor `wasm-opt`, nor headless Chrome).

A controlled experiment proves a mechanism is *possible*. It does not show the remedy is *enough*.

## And the fingerprint does not identify the cause — this is the part that makes it worth measuring rather than assuming

The recorded tells are exit 143 (not 137), `The runner has received a shutdown signal`, and **every remaining step skipped including `if: always()` ones**, because the VM is reaped whole. Those cleanly separate *"the job died"* from *"a step failed"*, and the `if: always()` tell works even whe

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by the `:kuilt-webrtc` slice of #1430 (PR #2694), which recorded the exemption verdicts but deliberately did **not** fix this — closing it means adding parameters to a public constructor, which is an API decision.

## The gap

`WebRTCPeerLinkFactory.weave(rendezvous)` — the `Loom` contract entry point — takes no timeout and calls `connect` without one, so **every weave is pinned at `DEFAULT_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS` (30 s)**.

The only public surface that can widen it is `openWithServerRoleResult(...)` (`WebRTCPeerLinkFactory.kt:174`), which also demands a `WebSocketSignalingChannel` — so a caller who just wants a longer deadline has to abandon the `Loom` interface to get one.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`DeliveryPolicy` cannot reach a `WebSocketSeam`. `identified()` accepts one — it is what governs the
seam's inbound `Spool` capacity and overflow — but the WebSocket path never passes it:

host and join paths to those two looms — can choose a lossy/bounded inbox. `grep -rn DeliveryPolicy kuilt-websocket/src`
returns only `KtorMeshClientLoom`.

layer over. It blocks the `policy` knob for the `:kuilt-mdns` slice of #1430, which omits the
parameter rather than shipping one nothing reads (PR forthcoming), and will block `:kuilt-websocket`'s

title: release: nothing detects a breaking public-API change — the `!` marker missed one of the two known breaks, and it was spelled `fix:`
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Nothing in this repo detects a breaking public-API change. The only signal is the `!` conventional-commit marker, applied by hand — and on the one population where we know the ground truth, **it missed half the breaks, and the one it missed is spelled `fix:`**.

## The measurement

#2608 identified, by hand, the two breaking changes sitting unshipped on `main`. Checked against the commit log from `v0.7.3` to `main` (205 commits):

| break | subject | `!` marker? |
|---|---|---|
| `e2682b12` | `feat(heddle)!: … delete AttachmentRecord.initialVirtualTime` | **yes** |
| `aec97e3f` | `fix(crdt): JsonCrdt.set/remove return a Patch, so one write ships one key` | **no** |

```
$ git log v0.7.3..origin/main --oneline | grep -cE '^[0-9a-f]+ [a-z]+(\([^)]*\))?!:'
1
$ git merge-base --is-ancestor aec97e3f v0.7.3 ; echo $?
1     # unshipped
```

Recall of the marker on the known population is **1 of 2**. And the miss is the bad direction: `aec97e3f` changes a public return type (`JsonCrdt` → `Patch<JsonCrdt>`), so every call site must change, while its prefix is `fix:` — the prefix a reader trusts most.

It was found only because a human was auditing #1752's decision comment during a backlog sweep. That is not a detector.

## Why it bites here specifically

- A **minor** bump is a deliberate human call (`CLAUDE.md`), and **patch is correctly the documented default** for pre-1.0 externals. So the failure mode is not "someone forgets" — it is "someone does exactly the documented thing" and ships a break as a patch.

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #2592 / #2671, filed so a deliberately-declined strengthening is tracked rather than forgotten.

## What changed

#2671 made `EntitlementLedgerConservationTest`'s seeded generator impose its own total order at the draw, so the same seed now walks the same trajectory on every target. A side effect: `prefixSafety` reads **1 on every target**, where before it was 0 on the JVM and 1 on Kotlin/Native.

Two in-tree comments asserted that old asymmetry as the *justification* for preferring a bound over a frequency floor. #2671 rewrote both, since they became false the moment the walk was pinned.

## The declined strengthening

With the trajectory pinned, a **frequency floor** — asserting `prefixSafety >= 1` **alongside** the bound — is now available. It closes a vacuity the bound cannot see: it would fail if the under-ack arm ever stopped reaching the case at all.

It was **not** taken, for a good reason: the arm fires at exactly **1 in 80 runs**. At that rate `>= 1` is a knife edge that any unrelated generator tweak reds, and a floor that reds for unrelated reasons gets weakened or deleted within a month — which leaves the property worse off than not having asserted it.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`SeamRoom.leave` gates its `AdmitMessage.Goodbye` on `_role.value == SessionRole.Joiner` ([`SeamRoom.kt:3374`](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/kuilt-session/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/session/SeamRoom.kt)), so a **host** leaving deliberately broadcasts nothing and goes straight to `seam.close(CloseReason.Normal)`. `NwSeam.close` puts nothing in-band either (`:2179-2201`) — it disconnects each `connId`, so the peer observes an error, not a close.

Every joiner therefore learns of a *deliberate* host departure the same way it learns of a crashed radio: `Partitioned` → `WindowOpened` → the full `heartbeatConfig.reconnectWindow` → `HostLost(WindowExpired)`.

Three things make this unfixable from the consumer side:

- `JoinerResumeMachine.runReconnect` opens that window **unconditionally** (`:459,470`). The string `CloseReason` does not occur in that file.
- `handleFarewell` refuses a `Farewell` naming the host **by design** — *"host departure is transport-level … never a roster eviction"* (`SeamRoom.kt:1646`).
- `MembershipEvent` gives a consumer nothing to key on, so it cannot distinguish a deliberate departure from a dropped radio and shorten the wait itself.

The asymmetry looks deliberate — #1292 built the joiner→host `Goodbye` and host→joiners `Farewell` pair and stopped there — so this is a **feature request, not a regression report**. Two shapes seem available:

- a host-authoritative `Farewell`-alike naming the host, admitted by `handleFarewell` and surfaced as a new terminal `MembershipEvent` (`HostLeft`) distinct from `HostLost`; or
- carrying `LeaveReason` / `CloseReason` in-band on the seam close, so `runJoinerTornWatcher` can go terminal without opening a window at all.

title: kuilt-deal: a malformed reveal is now dropped with the sender in scope and no trace — attribution lost, and the module has no logger at all
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #2650 / #2664, filed so a deliberate trade is tracked rather than silently accepted.

## The trade

#2664 moved `FairRandomMessage.Reveal`'s width check onto the wire type, which is right. A consequence is that a wrong-width reveal is now **dropped in the collector** instead of raising `CommitmentViolation`.

That part is an improvement on its own terms: the `CommitmentViolation` it replaced passed an **empty `actualHash`**, and on this path the commitment typically *does* verify — the whole re-split attack is that `(33, 15)` hashes to the same value as `(32, 16)`. So the old exception named the wrong check and carried no evidence. Dropping a frame beats reporting a fabricated diagnosis.

## What is lost, and one claim worth correcting

The PR describes this as unavoidable — *"the type refuses to materialise, so the handler has no peer to accuse."* That is true of **`awaitAllReveals`**, but not of the drop site. In `FairRandom.roll`'s collector the sender is bound on the line **above** the `try`:

```kotlin
val sender = swatch.sender ?: return@collect
val msg = try { swatch.decode(Cbor, FairRandomMessage.serializer()) }
          catch (_: IllegalArgumentException) { return@collect }
```

So the identity of the peer that sent a malformed reveal **is** in scope, and is discarded. `:kuilt-deal` has no logger in `commonMain` at all, so the drop leaves no trace of any kind — a peer probing the protocol with malformed reveals is indistinguishable from a peer with a flaky link, and from one that simply withheld.

For a module whose subject is *cryptographically fair* dealing, losing attribution for a malformed frame is a real, if second-order, downgrade.

title: core: a mux channel view's close() has no wire representation, so a survivor keeps advertising a peer it can no longer deliver to
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Isolated while landing #2372's fix (a channel view owns its own `SeamState`/`peers`). That fix makes a closed view honest **locally**; this is the half it leaves standing, and it is now the whole of what stops `MuxServerLoomConformanceTest` declaring `reportsPeerLoss = true`.

## The gap

A `MuxSeam`/`NamedMux` channel view's `close()` is a **local unsubscribe with no wire representation**. Nothing is emitted, so the remote end cannot observe it — a room hub deregisters a spoke only when the underlying link tears (`RoomHubSeam.deregister`, driven from `MuxServerLoom`'s per-connection read-loop teardown), and `RoomFanoutIsolationConformanceSuite.aDepartedClientLeavesEveryRoomItJoined` departs by closing the client's **base seam** for exactly that reason.

So after a client closes its `table-7` channel:

- the client's own view is correct — `Torn`, roster `{ selfId }`, sends refused (#2372);
- the **hub** still advertises that client in `table-7`'s `peers`, and `sendTo` it still "succeeds": the frame reaches the client's live base connection, is demuxed to the closed view's spool, and is dropped.

That is the lie `Seam.peers`' KDoc forbids — *"a peer in `peers` must be addressable by `sendTo`"* — and it is exactly what `SeamCapabilities.reportsPeerLoss` names.

## Measured

On `fix/2372-channelview-owns-its-state`, with the fix in and `reportsPeerLoss = false` dropped from `MuxServerLoomConformanceTest`:

```
31 tests completed, 1 failed
survivorStopsAdvertisingADepartedPeer   UncompletedCoroutinesError (wedge to the ceiling)
```

The Torn **precondition** now passes — #2372 fixed that half, and the diagnosis it was added for is spent. What wedges is the obligation itself: `host.peers.combine(host.state) { … }.

title: kuilt-primitives' description is 1,254 tokens — the largest single eager-context item in any consuming repo
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## Measurement

Auditing eager context in `fireworks-compose` on 2026-09-05 (`~/.claude/bin/claude-context-audit`),
a skill's `description:` frontmatter loads into **every session and every subagent** — only the body
is lazy. Ranked by that cost:

```
   1254 tok  skill:kuilt-primitives      <-- larger than any agent in the setup
    572 tok  skill:fgn-primitives
    408 tok  skill:hanab-primitives
```

Total eager budget in that repo was 8,319 tok. **The three `*-primitives` skills are 2,234 of it —
27%** — and they are the one part a consuming repo cannot fix: they are vendored caches, and a local
edit is silently reverted by `sync-vendored-skills.yml`. It has to be fixed here.

For scale: trimming *nine agent descriptions* in that repo saved ~2,500 tok. `kuilt-primitives`
alone is half of what that whole exercise recovered.

## The tradeoff — this is not simply "make it shorter"

The description is long *because* it is a trigger-phrase list, and that is what makes the skill
auto-invoke instead of sitting unused. Issues #2541 and #2572 were both about the skill **failing to
route**, and the cure was more coverage. Cutting it blindly re-opens exactly those.

So the question is not "can it be shorter" but **"is the marginal trigger phrase still buying
routing accuracy, or is the tail dead weight?"** Cheap way to find out: the skill fires on a
*substring* match against task language, so near-duplicate phrases that share a stem
(`"reconnect"` / `"reconnect grace window"` / `"hold the seat open"`) may be carried by one entry.

## Suggested approach

1. Group the trigger list by stem and keep one representative per distinct concept.
2. Move anything that is *explanatory* rather than *triggering* into the body —

title: Roster read-then-write sweep: ManagedSeam.close collapses outside its lock, and mdns PeerRoster has no lock at all
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

The sibling-fabric sweep #2626 asked for, run in #2653. Three hits beyond the two fixed there; **#2648 is one of them and is already filed**, so this covers the other two.

## 1 — `ManagedSeam.close()` (`:kuilt-cluster`) — the strongest

Collapses the roster **outside** `lock`, and relies on `relayJob.cancel()` to stop in-flight emissions. Its own comment asserts that the cancel is sufficient.

That assertion is the claim **#1879 records as false** — `cancel()` without a `join()` returns before the cancelled body has necessarily stopped running, so an emission already in flight can land after the collapse. The comment is therefore not just unproven; it is contradicted by an issue already in the tree.

## 2 — `PeerRoster` (`:kuilt-mdns`)

An unsynchronised `var` read-modify-write with **no lock at all**. Different family from the other hits — there is no tear-time collapse here — so it is not a #1816 ordering bug, but it is an unguarded shared mutable read-modify-write in a module that is not single-threaded.

Read and found correct: `MeshSeam`, `RoomHubSeam`, `CompositeSeam`, `LinkSeam`, `NearbySeam`, `TieredSeam`, `WebRTCPeerLink`. Recording the negative result so the next sweep starts from a bounded set rather than re-reading all of them.

title: #1803 remedy 2 prescribes a FOLD for the roster race; the measurement says it needs a LATCH — five fabrics hand-roll one today
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1803's Shape A remedy 2 names a `FoldedStateFlow` as the general remedy for the roster twin of the `state` race, and #2626 repeated that framing. **#2653 measured it, and a fold is the wrong shape.**

## The measurement

`BridgePeerLink`, 20 000 forced races per arm:

| mutation | clobbers |
|---|---|
| unfixed (`main`) | 14 327 |
| **lock only** — `collapsed` marker removed | **14 718** |
| **marker only** — lock removed | **315** |
| both | **0** |

**The lock is almost irrelevant; the marker does the work.** The dominant case is not an interleaving at all — it is a transport callback arriving *entirely after* teardown, binding into the freshly-cleared registry and recomputing the same roster from scratch. There is no read-then-write to make atomic there, so no fold, and no CAS, can see it.

And atomicity would not even close the interleaved 1.6%: the collapse writes `setOf(selfId)`, frequently the value the flow **already holds**, so a concurrent `compareAndSet` *succeeds* against it instead of retrying.

## What the general remedy actually is

A **`RosterGate`** carrying a *latch* — the roster analogue of `SeamStateGate`, not of a fold. It cannot simply reuse `SeamStateGate`, and it cannot key its guard on `state`: `Seam.peers` requires the collapse be published **before** `Torn` is observable, so in the window between collapse and latch the seam is not yet `Torn` and a publish landing there would resurrect the roster. That is exactly why every implementation needs a *separate* marker.

**Five fabrics hand-roll that marker today** — `NearbySeam`, `TieredSeam`, `RoomHubSeam`, and now `BridgePeerLink` + `MCSessionLink` (#2653). That is the same "N fabrics hand-rolled the same latch" count that justified ma

title: kuilt-deal: FairRandomMessage.Reveal's fixed widths are enforced in the handler, not the wire type
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

A fourth instance of #1822's class, found while wiring the `WireCodecConformanceSuite` TCK (see #1822 remedy 1). Not a live bug — and the fix is **not** a one-liner, which is why it is filed rather than folded in.

## The shape

`FairRandomMessage.Reveal(secret: ByteArray, nonce: ByteArray)` ([`FairRandom.kt:305`](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/kuilt-deal/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/deal/FairRandom.kt)) has no `init`, so `Cbor.decodeFromByteArray<FairRandomMessage>` happily produces one with a 31-byte `secret`. The widths **are** enforced — but in the handler, `awaitAllReveals` (`FairRandom.kt:200`), one call site away from the type:

```kotlin
if (msg.secret.size != SECRET_BYTES || msg.nonce.size != NONCE_BYTES) { … }
```

That is precisely the asymmetry #1822 calls generative: the invariant holds because *this* consumer remembers it, not because the wire type does. The comment beside it states the threat correctly (the commitment is `SHA-256(secret ‖ nonce)` with no length framing, so a re-split preimage lets a peer contribute a different secret post-commit).

`Commit.hash` is **not** a hit: it has no documented fixed width, and a wrong-width hash simply fails `contentEquals` against the locally computed one.

## Why this is not a one-line move to `init { require(...) }`

`FairRandomTest.wrong_length_reveal_isRejected` builds its malicious reveal by giving the **local** `FairRandom` a 33-byte `fixedSecret` and letting it encode. Put the check in `Reveal`'s constructor and the *sender* throws before the frame exists, so Bob never receives it — the test stops exercising the receiver it was written to exercise, while still passing. That is "removing vacuity can remove detection".

So

title: kuilt-nw: NwSeam.close latches Torn BEFORE collapsing peers — the exact ordering violation Seam.peers' KDoc predicts the TCK cannot see
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`Seam.peers`' contract (#1816) requires the roster collapse be published **"before, or atomically with, latching `Torn`"**, so a consumer woken by the terminal state already observes the collapse. `NwSeam.close` does the opposite.

## The window

`kuilt-nw/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/nw/NwSeam.kt`

```
2185:  if (!latchTorn(reason)) return        // latchTorn: lock.withLock { _state.value = Torn(reason); spool.close() }
2186:  val targets = lock.withLock {
  …
2199:      _peers.value = setOf(selfId)      // the collapse — a SECOND, LATER lock acquisition
```

`latchTorn` (`:2238-2250`) publishes `Torn` and **never touches `_peers`** — it only *logs* it (`peers-were=${_peers.value…}` at `:2243`, which is itself the tell that the roster is still populated at that moment). The collapse happens at `:2199`, after `latchTorn` has returned and released the lock.

`_peers` is a plain `MutableStateFlow(setOf(selfId))` (`:449-450`) with `_peers.update { it + remoteId }` on peer-add — not a derived/latching flow — so on a live seam with a remote it genuinely reads `{self, remote}` at the moment `Torn` is published. A collector on `state.first { it is Torn }` that resumes between the two lock acquisitions reads the pre-close roster off a torn seam.

**Scope: the explicit `close()` path only.** The other `latchTorn` caller is the self-driven last-peer-drop, where `_peers.update { it - peer }` has already reduced the roster to `{ selfId }`. That path is fine.

## Why nothing caught it — and this was foreseen, in writing

`Seam.peers`' own KDoc (`Seam.kt:104-111`) says it:

title: plies still collapses on TieredSeam, RoomHubSeam and GossipSeam
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2634 fixed `plies` for **mux channel views** (`MuxBase.kt:121` now forwards `delegate.plies`), which
is what #2393 named. Three other decorators still collapse it, and were out of that issue's scope.

| Decorator | Why it collapses | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| `GossipSeam` | trivial pass-through of the wrapped seam's map | **easy — just do it** |
| `RoomHubSeam` | has no delegate `Seam` at all; it fans out through per-connection `OutboundSender`s, so there is no single map to forward | needs the same treatment `maxPayloadBytes` got in #2634 — a member on the sender interface, folded by the hub |
| `TieredSeam` | **two** delegates, so `PlyId`s from the two tiers can collide | **needs a design call** — see below |

## The `TieredSeam` design question

`plies: StateFlow<Map<PlyId, SeamState>>` is keyed by `PlyId`. A tiered seam wraps two independent
seams which may each report a ply under the same `PlyId`, so a naive union either silently drops one
or reports a state for a key that means two different things to two different peers. The options are
roughly: namespace the keys (changes what a `PlyId` *is* to a caller that reads it), report only the
active tier's map (loses the standby, which is arguably the interesting half), or leave it collapsed
and say so in KDoc.

Not obvious, and it is a contract decision rather than an implementation detail — hence
`needs-design` rather than `ready`.

## Why this is filed separately

#2393's title names mux channel views specifically, and #2634 discharged that. Leaving the residual
inside a closed issue is the *"a listed sub-problem with no recorded resolution"* rot — the next
reader reopens it expecting code, or worse, assumes `plies` is fixed everywhere because #2393 cl

title: Seam decorators publish a payload budget they do not enforce (the other half of #2058)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2634 closed the **publishing** half of #2058: a mux channel view, `TieredSeam`, `CompositeSeam`,
`RoomHubSeam`, `GossipSeam` and `PerPeerSeam` now all derive `maxPayloadBytes` from what they wrap
instead of reporting `null`. **None of them enforces the number it publishes.**

## The gap

A decorator publishes `wrapped − itsOwnFraming`. It then hands the send straight down, so the refusal
comes from the seam **underneath**, measured against *that* seam's budget. Consequences:

- An over-budget send is still refused, so nothing is silently truncated or dropped — good.
- But `PayloadTooLarge.budgetBytes` **over-reports by exactly the framing the decorator reserved.** A
  caller that sizes to the reported number, gets a refusal, and reads the exception's budget is told
  a number larger than the one it was promised.
- A payload between the decorator's published budget and the underlying seam's actual ceiling is
  **delivered**, not refused — which is defensible (`Seam.maxPayloadBytes`' KDoc already says the
  number is a promise, not the refusal threshold) but means the decorator's number is unenforced in
  both directions.

This is milder than the failure `Seam.maxPayloadBytes`' "Publishing IS enforcing" section describes —
the refusal is synchronous and the send never reports success — but it is not the contract.

## ⚠ Why this is filed rather than left as a KDoc note

`Seam.kt` currently says *"The **enforcing** half stays open under #2069."* **#2069 is CLOSED** — it
was about `maxPayloadBytes` having no TCK coverage, a different gap, and it was closed before #2634
landed. So the citation added by #2634 points at a closed issue for work nobody is tracking.

That is the same defect #2419 had (citing closed #15

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`SeamConformanceSuite.midSessionDeathDeclarationIsHonest()` exists to stop a harness declaring an
obligation it does not actually discharge. **It does not detect the case it most needs to.**

## The gap

Found while converting the four harnesses in #2637 (part of #1442). Each conversion was
revert-checked by neutering its injection rig — making `injectMidSessionDeath` do nothing while still
returning `true`. In all four:

- `incomingCompletesOnInjectedMidSessionDeath` **red**, as it must.
- `midSessionDeathDeclarationIsHonest` stayed **green**.

Its `Proven` arm only checks that the hook returned `true`. A rig that returns `true` while severing
nothing is precisely the shape #1442's body warns about — *"an override that returns `true` while
injecting something the seam does not notice converts a visible, tracked gap into an invisible false
green, strictly worse than the state it replaces"* — and the meta-test written to catch it passes.

The obligation test does catch it today. That is worth being precise about: this is not a live false
green, it is **a guard that is not carrying the weight its name claims**. The risk is a future
harness whose obligation is skipped or weakened for some unrelated reason, leaving the honesty check
as the only thing standing — at which point it certifies a claim it never verified.

`Proven` cannot be verified from inside the suite by observing the hook's return value, because that
value *is* the thing under suspicion. The information has to come from the rig. #2637's four

title: capability-probes membership is pinned only by a name, and one member already breaks the property
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2636 graduated `SeamStateGateLatchCapabilityConcurrencyTest` into `capability-probes` and, while
classifying all 13 probes, established the property the gate is really drawn on: a member must hold
**no wall-clock budget of its own**. Determinism is necessary but not sufficient — a probe waiting on
`state.first { it is Torn }` or a timed barrier reds when the runner starves *however* deterministic
the defect it guards.

That property is now written in the job header. **Nothing enforces it, and one current member
already violates it.**

## 1 · The gate's membership rests entirely on a name

`capability-probes` selects `--tests "*CapabilityConcurrencyTest"`. So:

- Renaming a probe out of the pattern silently removes it from the merge gate. Nothing reds.
- A **new** `*CapabilityConcurrencyTest` joins the gate automatically, carrying whatever wall-clock
  budget it likes. Nothing reds.

The second is not hypothetical — see below. A gate whose membership is a string convention will
drift, and the drift is invisible in exactly the direction that hurts: a starving member blocks
merges repo-wide, and a departed member goes back to landing regressions green.

## 2 · `ScopedCloseableCloseOnceCapabilityConcurrencyTest` already violates it

Gating since #2305. It parks on a `CyclicBarrier.await(30s)` and asserts `completedRounds == ROUNDS`,
so **a starved runner can red it and block a merge** — the precise failure mode #1158 rejected
option 3 to avoid.

Its structural twin `DelayedWovenSeamCloseOnceConcurrencyTest` (`:kuilt-conformance`) has the same
barrier, the same 30 s, and the same rig assertion, and is deliberately **non**-gating. The two
halves of the split disagree about the same shape.

title: Put the lost-terminal-Torn property in ci-required via a SeamConformanceSuite fixture hook
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #1803 / #2620. The gap: **nothing in `ci-required` pins the lost-terminal-`Torn` fix for any fabric.**

Every probe in this family (`:kuilt-core`, `:kuilt-nearby`, and now `:kuilt-multipeer` via #2620) lives behind `-Pconcurrency.stress.tests=true` on a **non-blocking** job. Each carries the same stated reason, and it is correct as far as it goes:

> a single-threaded test cannot distinguish the check-then-act from the gate, because the check-then-act is *correct* when nothing runs between the read and the write — which is exactly what a test dispatcher guarantees.

That is true **for the unhooked production shape**: firing a transport callback *after* `close()` is green under both the old and the new code, so a sequential test discriminates nothing.

## But it is not fundamental — `NearbySeam` already disproves it

`NearbySeamStateLatchConcurrencyTest` reproduces this class **deterministically**, in one iteration, because that site happens to evaluate a **test-supplied** predicate inside the window (`_state.value is Weaving && session.any { … }` — `&&` is short-circuit, so the roster iteration runs after the read and before the write, and a trap set blocks there). The window is reachable when *something in it* is test-controlled.

title: kuilt-multipeer: BridgePeerLink's roster publish races its own teardown, so a Torn seam can advertise a lost peer
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`BridgePeerLink`'s roster publish is a read-then-write that races its own teardown, so a `Torn` seam
can end up advertising a peer it has already lost — the #1816/#1851 collapse-on-tear invariant, one
flow over from the `state` flow #1803 Shape A just fixed.

## The window

`kuilt-multipeer/src/jvmMain/…/BridgePeerLink.kt:167`

```kotlin
_peers.value = registry.peers + selfId
```

`registry.peers + selfId` is evaluated, then stored. `tearDown` concurrently does
`registry.clear(); _peers.value = setOf(selfId)`. A promoter that evaluates the expression to
`{self, remote}` and is preempted through a **complete** teardown then stores that stale roster over
the collapsed one — leaving a seam whose `state` is `Torn` and whose `peers` still names a peer that
is gone.

Same shape as the `state` race PR #2620 just closed with `SeamStateGate`, on the sibling flow. This is
`FoldedStateFlow` territory — Shape A remedy 2 in #1803 — not something `SeamStateGate` covers.

**Two probes already stand on exactly this window and assert the opposite in prose.**
`BridgePeerLinkStateLatchConcurrencyTest.kt:737-742` and its Apple twin assert only `state`, while
their failure message states as established fact that *"`incoming` has completed and `peers` has
collapsed"*. Nothing checks the second clause, and the race above can make it false.

cheapest moment to record it: whoever takes `FoldedStateFlow` gets a probe that already drives the

title: kuilt-test: FakeSeam.weave() un-tears a torn seam, so any consumer test resting on terminality is vacuous
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`FakeSeam.weave()` writes `Woven` unconditionally, so a torn `FakeSeam` can be **un-torn** — a
transition the real `Seam` contract forbids, and the one `SeamStateGate` exists to make impossible.

```kotlin
/** Transition state from [SeamState.Weaving] to [SeamState.Woven]. */
public fun weave() {
    _state.value = SeamState.Woven
}
```
`kuilt-test/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/test/FakeSeam.kt:138-140`

The KDoc says *"from [SeamState.Weaving]"*. Nothing enforces that. `tear()` twelve lines below **is**
guarded — `if (_state.value is SeamState.Torn) return` (`:157-158`) — so the two halves of the same
state machine disagree about whether `Torn` is terminal.

## Why it matters — it makes consumer tests vacuous, not just the fake wrong

`Torn` is terminal on every real seam; that is the invariant `SeamStateGate` was written to hold and
that #1803's Shape A is about. A test that uses `FakeSeam` to verify *"this component leaves a torn
seam torn"* cannot fail against a component that un-tears it, because the fake permits the very
transition under test. The assertion is satisfied by a fake that would not notice the defect.

**43 files construct a `FakeSeam`.** I have not audited which of them rest on terminality — that
audit is the bulk of this issue, and the count is a ceiling, not a claim.

## The tell, which is reusable

**One arm of the pair guards and the other does not.** That asymmetry — not the missing guard in
isolation — is what identifies the bug: `tear()` is idempotent and defended, `weave()` is neither, and
nothing in the type says why they differ. The same tell surfaced the same night in #2614, where
`ContractDiffers` asserted its rig fired and its sibling `NotConstructible` asserted nothin

`WebRTCPeerLinkFactory.buildLink` mints

title: Quilter.close() cancels in-flight broadcasts, so a write-then-close loses the frame
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`Quilter.close()` cancels the replicator's scope. `Quilter.apply` hands the outgoing frame to a `launch`
on that same scope (`broadcastDelta` → `getScope().launch`), so **a write immediately followed by a
`close()` cancels its own broadcast before it leaves.** There is no way for a caller to know whether the
frame went out.

## Where it bites

The natural teardown shape — *publish a departure notice, then release the seam* — is exactly the shape
that loses the notice:

```kotlin
quilter.apply(departingPresence)   // queues a broadcast on the replicator's scope
quilter.close()                    // cancels that scope, and the queued broadcast with it
```

Found in `tractat-us/fireworks-compose`
[#3192](https://github.com/tractat-us/fireworks-compose/issues/3192) (PR
[#4836](https://github.com/tractat-us/fireworks-compose/pull/4836)), where per-fabric presence replicators
are closed on peer detach. The consumer confirmed the mechanism by decompiling `broadcastDelta` rather
than inferring it. Symptom for a user: a peer that left cleanly can linger as present on its own fabric's
peers until a reconnect/presence window expires — a ghost peer, from a *deliberate* leave.

## The workaround we have, and why it is not good enough

A `yield()` between the write and the `close()`, which lets the queued broadcast be dispatched first. It
is honest about being best-effort and the loss is bounded to that Room's peers — but **a `yield()` used
as a synchronisation primitive is a race**: it yields once, and guarantees nothing if the broadcast needs
more than one dispatch (any suspension inside the send). It is also precisely the shape that turns into an
intermittent test failure later.

Any one of these,

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The gap

`ExporterHealth` — `accepted` / `failed` / `consecutiveFailures` / `lastFailure` / `recoveryFailed` / `dropped` / `refused`, plus `isDead` — exists only on `WarpLogRecordExporter`. It was added by #1860, where a device silently stopped accepting telemetry and stayed that way for hours with nothing written and nothing logged: the export result is returned, but on the logging path every caller discards it, so the exporter had no way to say it had died.

`WarpSpanExporter` and `WarpMetricExporter` have the same shape and the same problem. A consumer asking **"is this device's telemetry landing?"** can answer it for logs and not for spans or metrics.

#2593 was the log-noise defect on those two exporters, and its brief proposed giving them a health surface and keying the log dedup on `ExporterHealth.consecutiveFailures` — reusing production state so the dedup key would not be a test-only instrument.

That is the design #2586 **removed**, and it is worth writing down so it is not re-derived a third time. Keying the report on the streak was itself the bug (#2237): a streak counts *every* failure while only the store path reports one, so a member of the difference opens the streak first and the outage is reported **zero** times rather than once — the log then points at the wrong subsystem while `health.lastFailure` quietly carries the store's exception. `WarpLogRecordExporter.failure`'s KDoc now says "do not merge the two back together."

body:

Follow-up to #2591, which #2602 (`f6db2711`) closed. That PR made the joiner-roster obligation real *and* made the remaining exposure visible — this issue is the exposure.

`SeamConformanceSuite` now asserts the joiner's `peers`, and each of the 21 harnesses declares a `JoinerRosterOrigin`. - `WebRTCConformanceTest`
- `MDNSConformanceTest`

So #2591 is fixed for the harnesses that can express it, and **still open in substance for four shipped fabrics.** `FilledByConstruction` is honest about this — it is a declaration, not a suppression — but a declaration does not catch a regression.

title: heddle: one departed donor with a residual carried row freezes the generation move for every peer on that edge
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2577 makes `relocationPatch` refuse a generation move when a **still-uncancelled carried row**'s donor is absent from the fence's acks (`EntitlementLedger.unackedCarriedDonors`). Refusing is the right call — a recoverable misassignment beats an unrecoverable one — but its cost is not recorded anywhere, and it is a *fairness* cost, which is the thing this module exists to prevent.

title: heddle: witness() does not copy transferRelocIn, so carried credit spends unwitnessed — fixing it crosses the plane-ownership boundary
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Deliberately not fixed in #2577.** Raised by review, examined, and left for a human call because
the obvious fix violates an ownership rule the design rests on.

## The observation

`EntitlementLedger.witness()` copies `transfers[pathKey]` but **not** `transferRelocIn`. So a
recipient whose credit arrived purely by a carried hand-off (the case #2366 added) spends without a
witness.

#2577 makes this newly reachable for a **single-hop** transfer, which the surrounding KDoc claims is
covered. Before that PR, carried credit could not exist, so the gap was unreachable in that shape.

## Why the obvious fix is not obviously right

Extending `witness()` to copy `transferRelocIn` means a **data-plane patch republishing a
control-plane-owned counter family**. That inverts the ownership rule the whole #1691 argument rests
on: the control plane owns relocation families, and the data plane does not write them. Fixing the
symptom here buys a consistency win at the cost of the invariant that keeps the two planes
separable.

`issuedRelocIn` is already unwitnessed for exactly this reason, so the current behaviour is
*consistent* with the existing treatment rather than an oversight — it is the reachability that
changed, not the rule.

## Consequence if left as-is

A transient false `PerEdgeSafety` conflict on a **lagging replica** whose holdings are funded by
carried credit — it looks momentarily net-negative until the carrying patch arrives. That is inside
the documented eventually-consistent class: it self-heals on delivery, and it is a *diagnostic*
surface, never a safety gate. Nothing admits work it should not, and no quantity is lost.

So this is a report-quality issue, not a correctness one — which is precisely why i
