title: test: a seeded generator that walks a HashSet is not reproducible across targets — a JVM-only measurement can be false on native
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The hazard

**A seeded property generator is only cross-target reproducible if its trajectory never depends on
iterating a hash-ordered collection.** `Random(seed)` is portable; `HashSet`/`HashMap` iteration
order is not — bucket layout differs between the JVM and Kotlin/Native, so the *same seed* walks a
*different trajectory* on each target.

The consequence is the nastiest kind: **a measurement taken on one target is silently invalid for
the others**, and nothing announces it.

## How it surfaced — a near-miss on #2577

While fixing #2366, a worker examined a tolerance in `EntitlementLedgerConservationTest` that
accepts `PerEdgeSafety(e1)` in the under-acked arm. Measured on the JVM it was **inert**:
`prefixSafety == 0` across 80 runs / 76 under-acks, identical with the #2366 carry disabled. That is
a clean, well-run measurement and the obvious conclusion is "the tolerance is dead — remove it and
pin zero."

They reverted it, and `:kuilt-heddle:build` **reddened on `iosSimulatorArm64`**, where the same
seeded generator does reach the case (breach 17, residue 36).

The mechanism is in `EntitlementLedger.allEdges()`:

```kotlin
records.keys + lifecycle.keys + allEdgeCounters().flatMapTo(HashSet()) { it.keys }
```

The generator walks `allEdges()` / `allReplicas()`, so an explicit `HashSet` decides the order in
which edges are visited, and JVM and K/N disagree. Same seed, different walk, different reachable
states.

**Had the worker only run `jvmTest` — the documented fast inner loop — they would have landed a
zero-pin that is false on three of six targets, with an 80-run measurement backing it.**

title: conformance: SeamConformanceSuite asserts peers.size >= 2 on the HOST only — a fabric whose joiner never learns its peer is conformant
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The gap

`SeamConformanceSuite.runPeersReportsSelfIdAndAtLeastTwo` asserts three things:

```kotlin
assertTrue(host.selfId in host.peers.value, "host peers must include its own selfId")
assertTrue(joiner.selfId in joiner.peers.value, "joiner peers must include its own selfId")
assertTrue(host.peers.value.size >= 2, "peer set must have ≥2 after join")
```

The `>= 2` is asserted on the **host only**. There is no `joiner.peers.value.size >= 2`.

So a fabric whose **joiner never learns its counterparty at all** — `peers` stuck at `{selfId}`
forever — passes the TCK. `Seam.peers` is symmetric by contract (`Seam` is "one peer's *symmetric*
view of a session"; there is no client/server split at this layer), and the suite checks it in one
direction.

## This is not hypothetical — it hid a shipped defect

Found while reviewing #2588. On `main`, `NearbyLoom.joinSession` wrote only
`endpointPeers[endpointId] = remotePeerId`; it never put the host's `PeerId` into any roster flow.
The joiner's `peers` was populated *only* by `NearbySeam`'s constructor folding in
`sharedPeers.value` — which, in the single-process fake harness, already contained the host's id
because both ends shared one `NearbyLoom`.

Take the coincidence away — two devices, two looms — and a real Nearby joiner:

- reports `peers == {selfId}` forever, violating the `Seam.peers` contract;
- never leaves `SeamState.Weaving`, so `state.first { it is Woven }` hangs;
- and never completes `incoming` on a remote disconnect, because `disconnectLoop`'s tear is gated
  on `_state.value is Woven`.

Three shipped symptoms on a shipped fabric, and the TCK was green throughout — because the
assertion that would have caught it is written on the host.

title: singleCollection's republish buffer ignores the caller's DeliveryPolicy, so a lossy policy is only honoured at the seam
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

A `DeliveryPolicy` chosen by a fabric consumer bounds the **seam inbox** and nothing below it.
Both 2-peer and N-peer paths wrap each `Connection` in `singleCollection` before reading the
preamble, and that wrapper takes its own policy which **neither caller passes**:

```kotlin
// Handshaking.kt
val single = conn.singleCollection(dispatcher)      // policy defaults to Reliable

// MeshSeam.kt handshakeLink
val single = conn.singleCollection(dispatcher)      // same
```

`singleCollection`'s republish `Spool` is therefore always `DeliveryPolicy.Reliable` —
`DEFAULT_CAPACITY` = 256, `SUSPEND`. So `DeliveryPolicy(capacity = 1, overflow = DROP_OLDEST)`
delivers what it promises at the seam (verified by `HandshakingPolicyTest`) while up to 256
frames still queue one hop below it.

## Why this is a question and not obviously a bug

Two readings, and the right one is not settled:

1. **The policy names the seam's inbox.** That is what `identified`'s and `Spool`'s KDoc say,
   and the split is pre-existing and consistent across both fabrics. Nothing is broken.
2. **The policy is a memory bound the caller asked for.** A consumer picking a capacity-1 lossy
   inbox for a memory-constrained peer is asking for a *bound*, and a fixed 256-deep buffer one
   layer down defeats most of it. Under reading 2 the wrapper should inherit the policy.

Reading 2 has a real cost: `singleCollection`'s spool carries the **preamble** as well as data,
so a lossy policy applied there could drop frames a handshake depends on, and a `FAIL` policy
would tear links down during normal burst traffic. It probably wants a *derived* policy
(the caller's capacity, `SUSPEND` overflow) rather than the caller's verbatim, which is a design
call rather

title: withLogContext: on Apple/wasmJs a scope resuming beside a sibling still reads the sibling's attributes — #1659 survives on iOS
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`withLogContext` (#1659, landing in #2564) fixes cross-session log attribution on **JVM/Android**, where `LogContextElement : ThreadContextElement` re-establishes the binding on every coroutine dispatch. On **iOS/macOS and wasmJs** the binding is a plain `@ThreadLocal` slot set imperatively, and the original defect survives in a narrower but still-live form — **on the consumer's primary platform, under the dispatcher an iOS app normally uses.**

## The surviving sequence

One thread `T` (an iOS app on `Dispatchers.Main` is exactly this), two concurrent sessions:

1. **A** enters — `merged_A = {sess:A}`, `slot = {sess:A}`. A suspends inside its block.
2. **B** enters on `T` — `merged_B = currentLogContext() + attrs = {sess:A} + {sess:B}`, `slot = {sess:B}`. B suspends.
3. **A resumes on `T` and logs** — reads `slot`, which is `{sess:B}`. **A's line is stamped with B's session id.**

That is #1659's reported defect, reached by a different route. The identity-guarded restore in `WithLogContext.apple.kt` correctly prevents *corruption* (it writes back only if the slot still holds the exact instance it set), but it cannot prevent a **read** by an unrelated scope that resumes while a sibling is mid-block.

**Second effect, same step 2:** `merged_B` inherits every key A bound that B does not itself set. B's own keys win on collision, so `session.id` is right for B — but a key only A set leaks into B's records. `withLogContext`'s contract says attributes are "merged over any enclosing binding"; on Apple the "enclosing" binding may be a concurrent **sibling** rather than a lexical parent.

## Why it is still worth having shipped

Strictly better than the status quo it replaces. The process-global `CaptureConfig.attrib

title: SeamConformanceSuite gap hooks cannot express "inapplicable by design" — 9 of #1442's 16 routers are not gaps, and the framing invites re-introducing tear-on-death
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`SeamConformanceSuite`'s gap hooks are `String?` — **two** states, a tracking URL ("not implemented yet") or `null` ("proven"). There is no way to say **"this obligation does not apply to this fabric, by design."** So every by-design inapplicability is filed as an unimplemented gap, and the umbrella it points at can never close.

```kotlin
public open fun midSessionDeathGap(): String? = CapabilityGaps.MID_SESSION_DEATH
```

## Evidence: 9 of #1442's 16 routers are not gaps

The refreshed #1442 inventory (from #2566) splits its 16 routers by blocker. Only **5** are genuine gaps — 4 convertible, 1 needing `TcpLoom` plumbing. The other **9 are by-design**:

title: CompositeSeam has no seam-level failure channel, so a dead reconcile pump can only be absorbed
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`CompositeSeam`'s only failure signal is `onPlyFailure`, and `PlyReconcileException` carries a
`PlyId`. That is right for every failure that *belongs* to a ply — and leaves one that does not.

**The gap.** The reconcile pump collects `desired`, the `StateFlow<List<Pair<PlyId, Loom>>>` the
**consumer** hands to `CompositeLoom`. A throw from that flow ends the pump: the composite never
attaches or detaches another ply for the life of the seam. Guarding it is what stops the process
abort (#1788 / #1803, landed as `pumpIn`), but the guard has nowhere honest to report to —
`CompositeSeam.absorbDesiredFailure` is deliberately empty, because inventing a `PlyId` would be a
false report on the consumer's own logger, and `:kuilt-core` is logger-free by contract.

**Why it was absorbed rather than escalated, and why that is defensible today.** A dead `desired`
pump leaves the composite running its current ply set forever, which is behaviourally identical to a
`StateFlow` that simply stops emitting — an in-contract state a consumer may produce deliberately.
Contrast a *ply's* pumps, where a dead pump leaves the composite folding a value it believes is live;
those report `Phase.PUMP_ENDED`.

**What this issue is for.** Whether the composite should have a seam-level failure channel — a
`CompositeLoom(onSeamFailure = …)`, or a widening of `onPlyFailure`'s payload so a ply-less failure is
representable — so that "reconciliation is over" is *reported* rather than inferred from a composite
that has quietly stopped following its desired set. It is a public-API decision, which is why it was
not folded into the guard PR.

- Is "reconciliation is over" a failure the composite should also *act* on (te

body:
**Scoped as a sub-issue of #1822** (owner's call, 2026-08-30). #1822 is the epic for enforcing
documented wire fields structurally — "a codec TCK, not a lint rule" — and golden vectors for wire
types are the same problem approached from the other side. Designing them together avoids shipping
two overlapping mechanisms. Do not dispatch this independently of #1822.

_🤖 Status prepended by Claude on behalf of @keddie._

---

> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

A `@Serializable` type that rides the wire between peers can gain, lose or reorder a field and **no test in this repo will notice**, as long as both sides of the test use the same serializer. That is the shape of every round-trip test we have for `:kuilt-heddle`.

## The concrete instance

`EntitlementLedgerTest.roundTripsThroughJson` encodes with a serializer and decodes with **the same** serializer. It proves the type is self-consistent *at one version*. It is structurally incapable of detecting a cross-version break, because there is no second version in the test.

That matters because `EntitlementLedger` is the **Quilter gossip payload** — it is what peers merge — and it contains `MintRecord`. #1751 adds a required field to `MintRecord`. Old→new decode throws `MissingFieldException`; new→old hits an unknown key. A mixed-version mesh cannot merge at all, and the entire in-tree suite stays green through it.

Discovered while reviewing [#2547](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2547). It was caught by a human-directed review reading the serializer, **not** by any gate — which is the actual problem here. The next one will not be reviewed by someone who happens to be thinking about wire compatibility.

title: conformance: availabilityReturnsAKnownVariant is a tautology — the only property reading Loom.availability() cannot fail
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`SeamConformanceSuite.availabilityReturnsAKnownVariant` is a **tautology**. It cannot fail, for any fabric, ever — and it is the *only* conformance property that reads `Loom.availability()`.

## The assertion

`kuilt-conformance/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/conformance/SeamConformanceSuite.kt`, property (6):

```kotlin
assertTrue(
    availability is FabricAvailability.Available ||
        availability is FabricAvailability.Unavailable ||
        availability is FabricAvailability.Unknown,
    "availability() must return Available, Unavailable, or Unknown, got $availability",
)
```

And `FabricAvailability` is a sealed interface with **exactly those three members**:

```kotlin
public sealed interface FabricAvailability {
    public data object Available : FabricAvailability
    public data class Unavailable(public val reason: String) : FabricAvailability
    public data class Unknown(public val reason: String) : FabricAvailability
}
```

So the predicate is `true` by construction for every non-null value the type can hold. There is no implementation — correct, broken, or malicious — that reds it. The failure message it carries (`got $availability`) can never be printed.

Sealing is what makes it vacuous, and sealing is also what makes the property unnecessary: the compiler already guarantees exhaustiveness. This is not a case of "no current implementation reaches the failure" — the failure is **unreachable in principle**.

## Why it matters more than one dead assertion

Every fabric in the repo subclasses `SeamConformanceSuite`, so this reads on a results page as ~N green conformance checks of `availability()`. It is the entire conformance coverage of that surface, and it is worth nothing. Found whi

On the **dropped** peer, a consumer saw `MembershipEvent.Resumed` roughly **3 s after dropping** — before any real reconnect could have completed. - every `Partitioned` / `WindowOpened` / `Resumed` / evict event with its `at=` field (the record write-time is not the event time),

title: conformance: selfDialIsRejected's roster arm is structurally vacuous on any fabric that recomputes peers as <bound> + selfId
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced by the review of [#2532](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2532) (#2445). Confirmed by static trace, not conjecture.

## The gap

`SeamConformanceSuite.selfDialIsRejected` checks two complementary shapes: **(a)** the self-dial does not perturb the roster (`peersBefore == peers`), and **(b)** the self-dial's own frame does not echo back. On `MCSessionLink`, **shape (a) is structurally impossible to violate**, so that arm is permanently vacuous — it cannot fail for any implementation of this fabric.

Mechanism: `_peers.value` is only ever written as

```kotlin
_peers.value = registry.peers + selfId
```

`selfId` is **unconditionally folded in** rather than bound. So a self-dial that wrongly reaches `registry.bind(selfId, …)` still yields a roster byte-identical to `peersBefore`. `connectedPair`'s `monitorSelfAlwaysInPeers` monitor is blind for the same reason.

Measured on #2532: reverting its **guard 1** (the `if (peerId == selfId) return` in `session:peer:didChangeState:`) leaves **the entire TCK green** — `selfDialIsRejected` passes with a self-peer bound. Only shape (b) reds, and only because of that PR's *second*, independent guard. A single `MCSessionLinkSelfDialTest` supplies the one observable that moves: the `state` of a link that has met nobody.

## Why it generalises

Two properties of the suite, either of which alone defeats an arm:

1. **Any fabric that recomputes its roster as `<bound> + selfId`** defeats the `peersBefore == peers` arm, for the reason above. That spelling is not unique to `:kuilt-multipeer` — it is the natural way to honour `Seam.peers`'s "the initial value is `{ selfId }` — this peer is included from the moment a `Seam` is created" invariant.

title: spike/harness.sh pattern-kills devicectl, reaping concurrent agents' device runs
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`spike/harness.sh` reaps processes by command-line pattern, twice:

```sh
29: pkill -f "devicectl device process launch" 2>/dev/null; sleep 1; : > "$H"; : > "$J"
49: pkill -f "devicectl device process launch" 2>/dev/null
```

`pkill -f` matches **every** process on the machine whose command line contains that string —
not just the ones this script started. Several agent workers build and run device harnesses on
one box concurrently, so this reaps *siblings'* `devicectl` launches too.

The damage is nasty because it lands somewhere else and looks like something else. The victim
sees its own device run die mid-suite: a truncated log, a missing report block, a one-off that
will not reproduce. The honest reading of that evidence is "my change broke the device path" or
"the harness is flaky", and both are wrong. It attacks **verification** specifically.

This is the process-level twin of a shared-scratch-path collision, and it is the same class as
#2461 (a browser outliving its build) seen from the other side: #2461 is cleanup that does not
happen, this is cleanup that reaches too far.

## Fix shape

Scope teardown to the script's **own** spawned processes:

```sh
xcrun devicectl device process launch … >> "$H" 2>&1 &
HOST_PID=$!
…
trap 'kill "$HOST_PID" "$JOIN_PID" 2>/dev/null' EXIT
```

The script already backgrounds both launches, so `$!` is available at both call sites and no
new machinery is needed. `--terminate-existing` (already passed) covers the "stale app still
running on the device" case that the line-29 `pkill` appears to be there for, so that one may
just be deletable.

Found while fixing #2461; not fixed there to keep that PR to one concern.

title: kuilt-test: FakeSeam's constructor accepts a roster without selfId — the live-path twin of #2432
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`FakeSeam`'s constructor still accepts an `initialPeers` that does not contain `selfId`:

```kotlin
FakeSeam(selfId = PeerId("alice"), initialPeers = setOf(PeerId("bob")))   // accepted
FakeSeam(selfId = PeerId("alice"), initialPeers = emptySet())             // accepted
```

Both are states no conforming seam reaches. `Seam.peers`' KDoc is explicit that the roster *always*
includes this peer's own id, from construction onward — it is the same paragraph #1816 and #2432 are
about, one clause earlier.

## Why it matters

Two contract behaviours read wrong against such a fake, in the direction that makes a consumer test
pass while describing something production cannot produce:

- **`peers.value.size > 1`** is the contract's documented sentinel for "at least one remote is

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by [#2528](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2528) (#2481) in `NwSeamConcurrencyTest` and fixed **there only**. The same shape sits in five sibling probes and two other places.

## The trap

`kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException` typealiases to `java.util.concurrent.CancellationException`, which **extends `IllegalStateException`**. Measured, not inferred:

```
$ java  // IllegalStateException.class.isAssignableFrom(java.util.concurrent.CancellationException.class)
CancellationException isa IllegalStateException: true
```

`CLAUDE.md`'s exception-discipline section is thorough about `runCatching`, bare `catch (Throwable)` and the `ensureActive()` discriminator, but **every example is a broad catch**. Nothing warns that a *narrow, specific, apparently-safe* catch of `IllegalStateException` has the same effect. That is why this passed review repeatedly.

title: conformance: the filename TCK's case-folding arm is gated only nightly — a folding filesystem in build-jvm would gate it per-PR
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced by #2521 (the `DurableStoreFilenameConformanceSuite`). **Deliberately sized low — read the "why this is smaller than it looks" section before picking it up.**

## The gap

Every `ci-required` job is `ubuntu-latest`, including `build-native`. So on a PR:

- the **JVM/Android** binding of the filename TCK runs on ext4 → takes the **case-sensitive** arm;
- the **Apple** binding does not execute at all (arm64 Darwin binaries cannot run on Linux — that skip is `apple-nightly.yml`'s stated reason for existing).

The suite's case-folding arm — `theLegacyOverlapACaseFoldingFilesystemExposesIsExactlyTheDocumentedOne`, which asserts that `StoreKey("config")` really does reach a planted `Config` — therefore runs **only** on `apple-nightly.yml` (macOS, `cron: 0 7 * * *`, off the required gate). A regression there **merges**, and the nightly catches it within about a day.

The suite documents this honestly; the question is whether to close it.

## The shape of a fix

A **vfat loop image** needs no special kernel features and is case-insensitive/case-preserving, which models APFS well enough for this. It is also sufficient: encoded names are `[a-z0-9-]` plus `%`, and every planted legacy name in the suite (`Config`, `otel_logs`, `spans`) is vfat-legal.

## Why this is smaller than it looks

**The high-risk half is already gated on every PR.** `StoreKeyFilenameTest.distinctKeysEncodeToFilenamesThatDifferEvenIgnoringCase` decides the folding question from **encoded strings**, needs no filesystem at all, and runs on every target on every PR. So an **encoder** regression — the thing #2506 actually was — cannot reach `main` today.

title: otel: WarpOtlpBridge.drain reports Success while a signal fails permanently, and discards every cause on Failure
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced while reviewing #2520. Pre-existing and independent of it — that PR removed one *trigger* for this, not the mechanism.

## Two gaps, both in `drain`'s return expression

`kuilt-otel/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/otel/WarpOtlpBridge.kt:63`

```kotlin
return if (anyAttempted && anyFailed && spansSent == 0 && logsSent == 0 && metricsSent == 0) {
    DrainResult.Failure(IllegalStateException("WarpOtlpBridge: all attempted signals failed to drain"))
} else {
    DrainResult.Success(spansSent = spansSent, logsSent = logsSent, metricPointsSent = metricsSent)
}
```

**1. A partial failure returns `Success`.** `anyFailed` is computed, then discarded unless *every* signal sent zero. So spans succeeding while metrics fail **permanently** yields `Success(spansSent = N, metricPointsSent = 0)` — and the caller cannot distinguish that from "there were no metrics to send". A signal can fail on every drain forever and nothing above ever learns.

**2. `Failure` discards the causes.** Up to three distinct exceptions are caught, each logged, then collapsed into one `IllegalStateException` with a fixed message, no `cause` and no suppressed exceptions. The one place the actual diagnosis exists is a `debug` log line.

## What is *not* wrong here

The `debug` level is deliberate and the reasoning in the comment above the span arm is sound: an unreachable collector is this bridge's **normal** state, the transport exception's type and message carry the whole diagnosis, and attaching the trace makes a routine offline drain a candidate for the process's first symbolication — a one-time cost that collapses under load on Apple targets (#1596). **Do not "fix" this by raising the log level.** The gap is that the *result ty

title: Should Room.leave defend against a Seam that mints a CancellationException from close?
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up from #2501, which added a `TeardownFault` knob to `FaultySeam` so a teardown can be made
slow or made to fail. `TeardownFault.Fails` deliberately **rejects** a `CancellationException` cause
(`require` in its `init`). This issue is the question that rejection defers.

## The facts

- **`Seam.close` already carries the no-minting obligation** — [`Seam.kt:337`](../blob/main/kuilt-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/core/Seam.kt#L337), #1826. A conforming `Seam` never mints a `CancellationException` from `close`.
- **`SeamRoom.leave` calls `seam.close(...)` unguarded** — [`SeamRoom.kt:3414`](../blob/main/kuilt-session/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/session/SeamRoom.kt#L3414). So a minted cancellation propagates straight through `leave` and *cancels* the caller rather than failing it: no handler runs, no stack trace, and every obligation behind the call is skipped. That is the maximally-silent #1834 shape.
- **Both `RoomHost` implementations already hand-write `catch (Throwable)` around `leave`** — [`RoomHost.kt:105-110`](../blob/main/kuilt-session/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/session/RoomHost.kt#L105), [`KtorRoomHost.kt:141-146`](../blob/main/kuilt-websocket/src/jvmAndAndroidMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/websocket/KtorRoomHost.kt#L141) — precisely because a library cannot assume a consumer honours the contract. So the defence is already being paid for, twice, by hand, one level up.

## The question

Should `Room.leave` (concretely: `SeamRoom.leave`'s `seam.close(...)` call) **defend against a
`Seam` that violates `Seam.close`'s contract** by converting a callee-minted `CancellationException`
into a plain failure — `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` as the discriminator,

title: store: legacy-orphan disjointness holds only up to case folding — a new key can adopt an old key's file on APFS
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2506 landed in #2511 with **no migration**: files under the old lossy names stay on disk, and the
new safe set (`[a-z0-9-]`) is chosen so a new key can never pick one up. That argument was proved
under string equality — but on a **case-insensitive filesystem** (APFS by default, also exFAT/NTFS)
case folding, not `==`, decides whether two names are one file. There the guarantee holds only *up
to case*.

The residual overlap is exactly the case-variants of keys both schemes leave alone:

- consumer once stored `StoreKey("Config")` → legacy file `Config`, now orphaned (accepted);
- consumer later adds a **new, never-written** `StoreKey("config")` → encodes to `config`;
- on APFS that **is** the file `Config` → the new key's first read returns the old key's bytes.

Reproduced outside the JVM: plant a file `Config` in a temp dir on an APFS volume, read `config`,
get the bytes.

**Nothing kuilt ships is exposed** — every key it stores contains a `.`, so every one of them moves.
This is consumer-facing only, and only for a consumer whose old key was inside `[A-Za-z0-9-]`.

Documented in `encodeStoreKeyName`'s KDoc and `kuilt-store/module.md`, and *measured* rather than
left unstated: `noKeyAdoptsADifferentKeysLegacyFilenameEvenOnACaseFoldingFilesystem` asserts the
overlap set **equals** the enumerated case-variant pair, so an overlap of any other shape reds.

Closing it outright means forcing an escape into **every** encoded name (e.g. always escaping the
first character), so no encoded name can ever equal a legacy one. That was deliberately not taken in

`Seam`, `Room`, `RaftStorage`, `Bolt` and `CommutativeScheme` all have published conformance suites. **`DurableStore` does not** — despite having four implementations (`InMemoryDurableStore`, `FileChannelDurableStore`, `NSFileManagerDurableStore`, `IndexedDbDurableStore`) and, since #2506, a shared addressing contract they must all honour.

title: store: a malformed StoreKey name throws only on the file backends — validate at StoreKey construction instead
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced by the review of #2511 (fixes #2506). #2511 ships the documentation half; this is the structural half, held back because it changes a public type's contract.

## The split

#2511's shared filename encoder rejects a name it cannot encode losslessly — a lone surrogate, say, which a consumer can produce by slicing a string mid-pair. That is the right call: the previous scheme quietly folded it to `_`, and fail-loud beats silent corruption.

But the rejection lives in the **encoder**, which only the two file-backed stores call. So:

| Backend | `StoreKey("\uD800")` |
|---|---|
| `FileChannelDurableStore` (jvm/android) | throws `IllegalArgumentException` |
| `NSFileManagerDurableStore` (apple) | throws `IllegalArgumentException` |
| `InMemoryDurableStore` | accepted |
| `IndexedDbDurableStore` (wasmJs) | accepted |

**The same `StoreKey` passes in a test and throws in production.** `InMemoryDurableStore` is what most tests use, so the natural development path never sees the rejection — the failure is deferred to the first real device, and the platform where it fires is not the platform where it was written.

It is also undiscoverable. `encodeStoreKeyName` is `internal`, so its `@throws` never reaches Dokka; nothing on the public surface says a key name can be refused, or which names.

## Fix

Validate at construction — `StoreKey.kt:12` is a `@JvmInline value class`, which supports `init`:

```kotlin
init { require(/* encodable */) { … } }
```

That makes the invalid state unrepresentable rather than backend-conditional: every backend and every platform refuses the same names, at the point the name is written rather than at first `write`, and the encoder's own throw becomes unreachable defence-in-depth.

title: otlp: OtlpHttpEdge keys its sent-set on base.hashCode(), so two endpoints can share one dedup set
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Pre-existing and independent of #2506/#2511 — surfaced while reviewing that work. Distinct from #2512, which is about those keys *moving*; this is about two different endpoints *colliding* on the same key.

## The defect

```kotlin
private val spanKey = StoreKey("otlp.sent.spans@${base.hashCode()}")
private val logKey = StoreKey("otlp.sent.logs@${base.hashCode()}")
private val metricKey = StoreKey("otlp.sent.metrics@${base.hashCode()}")
```
<sub>`kuilt-otel-otlp/.../OtlpHttpEdge.kt:83-85`</sub>

`base` is the collector base URL. `String.hashCode()` is a 32-bit non-cryptographic hash with trivially constructible collisions, so **two `OtlpHttpEdge`s pointing at different collectors can share one sent-set.**

Consequences, both silent:

- **Under-delivery** — endpoint B skips spans it never sent, because A recorded them. This is data loss at a collector, and nothing surfaces it: the edge believes it deduplicated correctly.
- **Cross-endpoint interference** — the `maxSentIds` cap is applied to the merged set, so a busy endpoint evicts a quiet one's ids and each corrupts the other's notion of what it has sent.

Under-delivery is the one that matters. #2512's failure mode duplicates; this one drops.

## Why the hash is there at all

Presumably to keep the key a short, filename-safe token — a real constraint when the store's filename encoding was lossy. **#2511 removes that constraint**: `StoreKey` names are now encoded losslessly, so a key may contain the URL verbatim (`:`, `/` and all) and still address a distinct file. The workaround can retire with the thing it was working around.

## Options

1. **Use `base` verbatim** — `StoreKey("otlp.sent.spans@$base")`. Now correct-by-construction, and the key is legible on

title: otlp: the #2506 filename re-encoding orphans the sent-set, so the first run after upgrade re-POSTs already-sent telemetry
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #2506 / #2511. Not a defect in that PR — a consequence of the "no migration" decision that is worth recording rather than discovering in a bill.

## What happens

`OtlpHttpEdge` persists its producer-local dedup sets under three keys:

```kotlin
private val spanKey = StoreKey("otlp.sent.spans@${base.hashCode()}")
private val logKey = StoreKey("otlp.sent.logs@${base.hashCode()}")
private val metricKey = StoreKey("otlp.sent.metrics@${base.hashCode()}")
```
<sub>`kuilt-otel-otlp/.../OtlpHttpEdge.kt:83-85`</sub>

Every one of those names contains `.` and `@`, so **all three move** under #2511's encoder — `.` is outside the `[a-z0-9-]` safe set by design. With no migration, the legacy files are orphaned and the new names are absent.

A miss is not distinguished from an empty set:

```kotlin
private suspend fun readIdSet(key: StoreKey): Set<String> {
    val bytes = store.read(key) ?: return emptySet()
```
<sub>`OtlpHttpEdge.kt:159-160`</sub>

So on the first run after upgrading past #2511, the edge believes it has sent nothing and **re-POSTs every span/log/metric still in the buffer that it had already delivered**. One-time, bounded by the buffer, and it duplicates at the collector rather than losing anything.

## Why it is worth a ticket rather than a shrug

title: kuilt-bolt: PosixMappedBolt's caught-up CleanTail short-circuit is pinned by nothing
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while landing #2337 (PR #2499), from the same measurement — recorded rather
than fixed there, because it is a different claim from the one that PR measures.

`PosixMappedBolt.replay` short-circuits a **caught-up** resume:

```kotlin
val firstUnpruned = views.indexOfFirst { !skippable(it, scope) }
if (firstUnpruned < 0) return@flow emit(CleanTail)
```

Every segment skippable means the cursor is at or past the archive's end, so the
replay answers `CleanTail` having read nothing. `MappedBolt` has the same
short-circuit, and its KDoc argues it is what keeps the pruning contract from
depending on the archive's **length**: without it a cursor at the end always reads
the last two segments, and damage below the cursor gets reported or not according
to how far from the tail it happens to sit. A consumer polling an unchanged,
unrepaired archive would then see `Truncated` today and `CleanTail` after two more
rolls, over bytes that never moved.

**On the JVM that argument is pinned; here it is not.**
`MappedBoltPruningTest.aCaughtUpResumeAnswersTheSameWhereverTheDamageIs` sweeps the
damage position and asserts both the verdict and a zero byte count. There is no
Apple twin.

## The measurement

Under the `firstUnpruned = 0` mutation on `appleMain` — which disables the
short-circuit as a side effect of disabling the pruning — the whole of
`macosArm64Test` is **156 tests across 14 classes, and exactly one fails**: the new
`PosixMappedBoltPruningTest`, on its two byte-count assertions. All three
`BoltConformanceSuite` subclasses stay green, and so does `PosixMappedBoltTest`. So
nothing anywhere exercises a caught-up resume over an archive with damage below the
cursor on this backend.

Port `aCaughtUpResume

title: MeshSeam: buildMesh's construction-time dedup still closes its losers abruptly
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2474 gave `Mesh.addLink`'s two dedup arms a graceful drain: the displaced loser stays open, keeps a read loop, is sent an in-band `GOODBYE`, and is closed only at drain end, with a per-peer ordering hold behind it. `buildMesh`'s **construction-time** dedup (`kuilt-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/core/fabric/MeshSeam.kt`, the `losers.forEach { closeBestEffort(it.conn) }` line) was deliberately left on the old abrupt path, with the reason in a comment beside it.

## Why it was left

A drain needs a seam to attribute the drained link's frames to, and at that point there is none — `MeshSeam` is constructed on the last line of `buildMesh`. Doing it properly means handing the losers to the constructor and starting their drains from `init`, where the ordering hold cannot be armed before the winners' read loops start (`armOrderingHold` suspends on `stageMutex`, and `init` cannot).

## The residual, stated precisely

No peer has been published locally at construction, so there is **no local publish-then-swap window**. What is lost is the **remote's** window: if the remote deduped first and wrote into the link before we got here, those frames die at our close. That is narrower than the `addLink` case #2474 fixed, and narrower still because it needs a caller that hands `buildMesh` two connections to one peer — which no in-tree caller does today (`VoterMesh`, `MuxServerLoom`/`hostedOverlay` and `GameHosted` all start empty and grow via `addLink`).

## What "fixed" would look like

Either (a) thread the losers into `MeshSeam`'s constructor plus a non-suspending arm-hold path usable from `init`, or (b) decide the arm is genuinely unreachable for every supported construction shape and say so in code — with some

title: Build guard: forbid a suspend call inside withLock — the violation compiles today and no test dispatcher can reach it
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`NwSeam` states the rule in its own KDoc: "**No `suspend`/`api.*` call ever runs under the lock** —
targets are snapshotted under the lock, then sent/disconnected/delivered outside it"
(`kuilt-nw/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/nw/NwSeam.kt:166-171`, lock at `:326`).

Nothing enforces it, and nothing can detect a violation at runtime in this repo's test suite:

- `kotlinx.atomicfu.locks.withLock` is `inline` with a non-`crossinline` block, so a `suspend` call
  inside it **compiles silently** when the enclosing function is `suspend`.
- Under a `StandardTestDispatcher` — which is every `:kuilt-nw` test — a coroutine that suspends
  while holding the lock resumes on the *same* thread, so the illegal unlock never happens. The
  defect is structurally unreachable.
- On a real multi-threaded dispatcher the resumption can land on a different thread and the unlock is
  performed by a non-owner. The only thing that has ever run this code that way is the real-transport
  conformance suites, and only probabilistically (#2466).

Same argument applies wherever else the repo uses a `reentrantLock` around code that may grow a
suspend call — this should be repo-wide, not `:kuilt-nw`-only.

## The detector

A lexical root-build guard in the existing `forbid*` family (`forbidBareRunCatching`,
`forbidProductionDispatcherInTests`, `forbidCancellationRethrowAroundBound`,
`forbidCoroutineLaunchInPropertyInitializer`, …), wired into `check`: scan production `src/*Main/**`
for a `withLock { … }` / `synchronized(…) { … }` body containing a call the scanner can see is
suspending — pragmatically, `api.`, `.send(`, `.emit(`, `delay(`, `withContext(`, `withTimeout(`,
`.first(`, `.collect(`, or a call to a known `suspend` member o

title: MeshSeam: port kuilt-nw's D+ displacement drain — ordering hold + in-band GOODBYE
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`MeshSeam` has the same double-dial displacement shape as `:kuilt-nw`, and #2457 decided that fabric's fix: **D+** — on losing the dedup, drain the loser rather than cancelling it, terminated by an in-band `GOODBYE`, with a bounded receiver-side ordering hold. Port the same design here once #2425 lands.

## What is actually broken here — narrower than `NwSeam`'s

Verified while reviewing #2457, and worth stating precisely so this isn't over-scoped:

- The displaced loser is **not** read-abandoned today. `addLink` launches the winner's `readLoop` and leaves the loser's alive (`MeshSeam.kt:583`), and the loop delivers until the connection's flow ends (`MeshSeam.kt:669-685`).
- `closeBestEffort(existing.conn)` (`MeshSeam.kt:582`) goes through `Connection.close`, which on a framed-TCP impl is an **orderly** release that flushes and FINs.

So on a well-behaved `Connection`, `MeshSeam` **already drains to EOF**. The two real gaps are:

1. **No ordering hold.** `Seam.incoming` promises frames "in send order" (`Seam.kt:207-219`). Loser-link frames can be delivered *after* winner-link frames, because cross-link ordering is not a TCP guarantee.
2. **No guarantee for a `Connection` impl whose close is abrupt.** The drain is a property of the impl, not of `MeshSeam`, so it is unpinned — nothing reds if an impl starts cancelling.

## Scope

- `MeshHello` gains the same frame-type/version discrimination as `NwHello` (#2425 slice 1).
- The displacement arm (`admitOrReject`, `MeshSeam.kt:612`) sends `GOODBYE` before close.
- Receiver-side ordering hold, keyed on the goodbye, same shape as `NwSeam`'s: **buffer-and-continue, never suspend** — both links' bytes arrive through one loop, so suspending it deadlocks against the ver

title: crdt: a nested JsonCrdt write still ships the whole rebuilt subtree — needs a path-addressed mutator
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #2111, which fixed the **top level** only: `JsonCrdt.set`/`remove` now return a
`Patch<JsonCrdt>` built from `ORMap`'s minimal delta, so a write's frame no longer grows with the
number of keys in the document (measured 12,416 b → 177 b at 1,000 keys).

## What is still O(subtree)

A write *inside* an existing `JsonNode.Object` or `JsonNode.Array` has no mutator of its own. The
obvious spelling rebuilds the enclosing node and hands it to `set` at the top:

```kotlin
val profile = (doc["profile"] as JsonNode.Object).map
doc.set("profile", JsonNode.Object(profile.piece { it.put(replica, "email", leaf) }))
```

The frame is one key — that part is now flat — but that key's value is the **whole rebuilt subtree**.
Measured at 12,507 b → 127,553 b across a 100- vs 1,000-field subtree (10.2×), by
`JsonCrdtDeltaMutatorLawTest.aNestedWritesFrameGrowsWithTheRebuiltSubtree`.

## The mechanism already exists — the API does not

The minimal nested frame is expressible today: hand `set` the nested `ORMap`'s **own delta** instead
of the rebuilt map.

```kotlin
doc.set("profile", JsonNode.Object(profile.put(replica, "email", leaf).delta))
```

That is flat — 262 b at both sizes — and reads back as the same document.

**But it is not the same write, and that is the interesting part.** The rebuild parks the whole
merged subtree on the outer tag it mints; the nested delta parks only the field written. The
difference is invisible until a concurrent `remove` retires the *other* replica's outer tag: what
survives is whatever the surviving tag was carrying, so the rebuild keeps the entire subtree and the
cheap spelling keeps one field. Both behaviours are defensible. Pinned by
`JsonCrdtDeltaMutatorLawTest.theCheapNeste

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

The `:kuilt-nw` real-transport conformance suites detect whole classes of defect **only under CPU contention**. On a quiet runner they go green with a real bug present. That is a false-negative gate, and it has already cost us once.

## The measurement

While fixing #2462 (a null-deref `NwSeam` shipped from a property-initialiser launch), the same defect was measured against the same suite at two load levels, with load controlled by spinners and sampled immediately before each run:

| suite | box load | reds |
|---|---|---|
| `NwBridgeLoopbackConformanceTest` (JVM) | **5.3–5.7** | **0/6** |
| `NwBridgeLoopbackConformanceTest` (JVM) | 16.6–28.4 | **6/6** |
| `NwLoopbackConformanceTest` (K/N) | 26.3–29.4 | 3/6 |

Same tree, same defect, opposite verdicts. **A green run of these suites is not evidence the defect is absent** — it is evidence the runner was quiet.

## Why this is not #2386

#2386 is the **false-positive** direction: a real 30 s wall-clock Bonjour deadline that a loaded build trips on its own. Annoying, but it fails *loudly* and nobody ships a bug because of it.

This is the **false-negative** direction, and it is the dangerous one: CI goes **green** while the defect is present. #2462 reached `main` through review and a full green CI run precisely this way, and was found ~1 h later by an unrelated worker whose box happened to be loaded.

## Why it happens, and what is *not* the fix

These suites drive **real** transports — real Network.framework + TLS-PSK, the real dylib, real dispatchers, real wall-clock. That is the point of them; they are the only thing exercising the actual transport. **They cannot be made deterministic without ceasing to be what they are**, so "fix the flakiness" is the wrong

title: A coroutine launched from a property initialiser should be a build failure (follow-up to #2462)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2462 was a coroutine launched from a **property initialiser** that read a property declared 840
lines below it. Kotlin initialises in declaration order, so the body dereferenced a `null` backing
field — NPE on the JVM, SIGSEGV on Kotlin/Native — from inside a `launch {}`, where nothing catches
it. It shipped, and every `runTest` suite stayed green because a `StandardTestDispatcher` defers the
body past construction.

#2464 fixed the instance structurally (all of `NwSeam`'s launches moved into one `init { }` block
last in the class body) and pinned it with an eager-dispatcher test. **Neither generalises.** The
audit on that PR found the same *shape* — a coroutine started from a property initialiser — at eight

property in its class. Nothing rejects the next one.

`forbidCoroutineLaunchInPropertyInitializer`, wired into `check` alongside the existing
`forbidProductionDispatcherInTests` / `forbidTightRunTestTimeout` guards: scan production
`src/*Main/**/*.kt` for a **class-member property initialiser** whose right-hand side contains
`launch(` / `launch {` / `async(` / `async {`, and fail with the fix ("start it from an `init { }`
block placed last in the class body, or from an explicit `start()`").

Deliberately the blunt rule rather than the precise one. The precise question — *does the launched
body transitively read a property declared after the launch?* — needs a call graph, and the tool that

`NwSeam`'s new wedge watchdog launches a coroutine that reads a field declared **840 lines below the

private val silenceJob: Job = scope.launch { inboundSilenceLoop() }

private val watchdogWake = MutableStateFlow(0L)

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`wasmJsBrowserTest` launches a headless Chrome via Karma. When the build ends abnormally, the Karma **server** dies but the Chrome **process tree it spawned survives** — reparented to `launchd` (`ppid=1`), holding memory indefinitely. Found two independent leaks alive on the dev box today, days old.

## Receipts (sampled 2026-08-17 ~23:40 ET)

```
PID    PPID  ETIME        RSS     COMMAND
24276  1     05-19:04:38  245 MB  Google Chrome --user-data-dir=…/T/karma-90394940 --headless …
84858  1     03-20:47:17  225 MB  Google Chrome --user-data-dir=…/T/karma-86243439 --headless …
```

Both had `ppid=1`, `%CPU 0.0`, and **zero ESTABLISHED sockets**. Nothing was listening on Karma's port:

```
$ lsof -nP -iTCP:9876 -sTCP:LISTEN
(no output)
```

Their working directories name this repo and module:

```
24276 -> …/kuilt/.claude/worktrees/agent-a35ad116e986b7cb5/build/wasm/packages/kuilt-kuilt-conformance-test
84858 -> …/kuilt/.claude/worktrees/agent-ab0f42de5b4553558/build/wasm/packages/kuilt-kuilt-conformance-test

Neither `agent-a35ad116e986b7cb5` nor `agent-ab0f42de5b4553558` still appears in `git worktree list` — **the worktrees were swept while their Chrome kept running**, so the browser outlived not just the build but the checkout it was testing.

The two roots run **different Chrome builds** — `151.0.7922.110` and `151.0.7922.138` — so they leaked in separate events days apart. The oldest survived ~6 days. title: kuilt-nw: the inbound-silence watchdog cannot fire on the #2425 wedge — that link carried a heartbeat every ~1 s
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2451 merged `nw.seam.inbound-silent` to make the #2425 formation wedge legible, and its cadence is explicitly timed against that wedge — the WARN is tuned to land "STRICTLY INSIDE the ~8 s bound a consuming application applies to formation today (#2425)".

But #2425's byte ledger refutes the premise the trigger rests on. **The wedged link was not silent**, so the watchdog cannot fire on it.

## The arithmetic

- `processFrame` increments `cs.inboundFrames` for **every** data frame on a resolved connection (`NwSeam.kt:566`). Heartbeats are data frames; nothing filters them.
- `sweepInboundSilence` resets `cs.silentSweeps = 0` whenever `inboundFrames` moved since the last sweep (`NwSeam.kt:1339-1342`).
- `SILENT_SWEEPS_TO_WARN = 2` at `DEFAULT_INBOUND_SILENCE_PROBE = 3 s` ⇒ the WARN needs **~6 s with zero inbound frames**.

An arrival every ~1 s means `silentSweeps` never reaches 2. The issue body says it outright: the link "carried kuilt's own liveness protocol and nothing else."

## Why it slipped through

The ledger landed between #2451's review round and its merge. Its *"both ends deduped onto the same link"* half **was** absorbed — that is the `dialled=` field's KDoc. Its *"742 bytes traversed, every one acknowledged"* half was not, and that is the half the silence trigger depends on.

## Scope

Any link carrying periodic traffic at an interval shorter than the probe — i.e. every deployment with kuilt heartbeats running. The watchdog detec

title: Six seams' sendTo consults a roster that does not collapse on a local tear, so their Torn guard is the only thing refusing the send
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Fallout from measuring #2448 / #2453. `Seam.sendTo`'s two refusals are meant to be independent: the `Torn` check states a fact about **this seam**, the roster lookup states one about the **addressee**. In six impls the second is inert on a torn seam, so the first is load-bearing alone.

## Measured, not argued

Deleting each impl's `sendTo` Torn guard and reading which conformance assertion reds:

| impl | rig verdict |
|---|---|
| `LinkSeam`, `MeshSeam`, `RoomHubSeam`, `CompositeSeam`, `TieredSeam`, `NwSeam`, `MCSessionLink` | 🔴 `PeerNotConnected` — roster collapsed, lookup refuses |
| **`InMemoryLoom`, `ControllableSeam`, `GossipSeam`, `NearbySeam`, `BridgePeerLink`, `WebRTCPeerLink`** | 🔴 **on `assertFailsWith` — the send COMPLETES** |

The roster `sendTo` reads is not the one the tear collapses:

- **`GossipSeam`** — `sendTo` is pure delegation to its base; it has no `Torn` check of its own, so it inherits whatever the base does.
- **`WebRTCPeerLink`** — tests `resolvedRoster()`, recomputed as `setOf(selfId, senderIdDeferred.await())` from an already-completed deferred. `tear()` collapses `_peers`, which `sendTo` never reads.
- **`NearbySeam`**, **`BridgePeerLink`** — same shape via their own lookups.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than noting

A seam whose roster lookup cannot refuse has **one** guard between a caller and a silent delivery onto a dead session. `Seam.peers`' own KDoc argues the collapse obligation (#1816) *from* `sendTo` — "a remote

title: kuilt-nw: RealNwApi.send cannot fail, so a frame written to a dead connection vanishes silently and NwSeam's send-failure eviction is dead code
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RealNwApi.send` has no failure path. Two independent swallow points:

1. a send to a **closed or unknown `connectionId`** returns **silently** via `log.debug`, rather than throwing;
2. `nw_connection_send`'s **completion error** is also `log.debug`-only and is never propagated.

`NwApi.send`'s own KDoc says an implementation "MAY throw synchronously to signal an immediately-known failure (e.g. an unknown/closed `connectionId`) — `NwSeam` treats a throw as a cue to evict that connection." On this fabric it never does.

## Consequence: the eviction path is dead code

`NwSeam.sendTo` and `NwSeam.broadcast` both wrap the send in `.onFailure { … → removeByConn(connId) }`. On `:kuilt-nw` that branch is **unreachable**. So:

- a frame written to an already-dead connection is **silently discarded** — `Seam.sendTo` returns normally, and the caller is told nothing;
- the send-failure route to evicting a dead connection never fires, leaving `connectionClosed` / `connectionStates` as the only teardown authorities.

## Field evidence

In the 2026-08-17 session this is what made a formation wedge **silent**. During a double-dial dedup swap, **182 bytes** were written onto a connection the remote peer had already destroyed. Nothing anywhere recorded a failure — not a warn, not an error, not a metric — and the frame was never retried. The session then sat for 8 s and tore down. See #2425 for the full two-sided byte ledger.

## Why this is worth its own issue

- It is **independent of #2425's ordering bug.** Fixing the publish-then-swap window removes *this* instance; it does not give the fabric a failure path, so the next lost write is equally invisible.
- It makes **"no send error in the log" evidence of nothing** on this

title: A re-forming seam blames the addressee too: after an eviction NwSeam is Weaving, so sendTo answers PeerNotConnected for a link that died locally
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2448 / #2453 tighten `sendOnTornSeamThrows` so a **`Torn`** seam can no longer report a torn `sendTo` as `PeerNotConnected`. This is the second instance of the same misattribution, and the tightening cannot reach it — because the seam is not `Torn`.

## The shape

`NwSeam` answers a peer eviction with `Woven → Weaving`, not `Torn` — #1513's deliberate "peer loss is recoverable, re-form don't tear". So on the eviction path:

- `evictPeerLocked` removes the peer from `registry` and `_peers`, and sets `SeamState.Weaving` when it was the last remote;
- `sendTo`'s only state guard is `check(_state.value !is SeamState.Torn)` — which passes;
- the `registry` miss falls straight through to `throw PeerNotConnected(peer)`.

The eviction that got us here can be a **purely local** failure. `evictPeerLocked` is reached from three places, and on the real Apple transport only two of them fire:

| path | real on `RealNwApi`? |
|---|---|
| `connectionClosedLoop` — a `failed`/`cancelled` connection state | ✅ yes — and per `RealNwApi.send`'s KDoc this is how eviction happens *at all* in production |
| `removeByConn` from the #1478 path-loss **grace expiry** | ✅ yes |
| `removeByConn` from `sendTo`/`broadcast`'s **send-failure** handler | ❌ **no** — `RealNwApi.send` is documented fire-and-forget and never throws, so this branch is dead weight against reality |

The addressee may be perfectly healthy and entirely unaware in every one of these.

```

```

title: OSLogAppender: INFO maps to OS_LOG_TYPE_INFO, which never persists — state-transition logs are unreadable post-hoc on Apple devices
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`OSLogAppender` (and the capture passthrough delegate on Apple targets) maps kotlin-logging levels to os_log types as INFO → `OS_LOG_TYPE_INFO` and DEBUG → `OS_LOG_TYPE_DEBUG`. Apple keeps `OS_LOG_TYPE_INFO` in a memory ring and suppresses `OS_LOG_TYPE_DEBUG` unless streaming — neither persists to the unified log store. Only WARN (`OS_LOG_TYPE_DEFAULT`) and ERROR (`OS_LOG_TYPE_ERROR`) survive to a later `log collect` / sysdiagnose.

Consequence for consumers that follow the usual convention (info = state transitions, debug = per-event): **every state-transition line an app logs at info is unreadable after the fact on a real device, by construction.** A post-hoc unified-log pull from a field device shows only warn/error — a handful of lines — while the app's actual narrative was written and discarded. When the durable-store channel is unavailable (store dead, or only a sysdiagnose from a remote device is available), there is no second channel.

Proposal: map INFO → `OS_LOG_TYPE_DEFAULT` so state transitions persist, keeping DEBUG → `OS_LOG_TYPE_DEBUG` (ring-only) as the volume valve. Alternatively, make the level→type mapping a constructor parameter on `OSLogAppender` with this as the default (or opt-in), so consumers choose their persistence boundary.

Volume: measured in a real consumer under active multiplayer use, info-level output runs ~11 lines/min — negligible against the unified log store's capacity and rotation.

Cheapest possible change is two enum arms in the mapping; the configurable form is a small constructor addition.

title: conformance: sendOnTornSeamThrows is satisfied by PeerNotConnected, so a seam that blames the peer for its own death passes
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`SeamConformanceSuite.sendOnTornSeamThrows` asserts:

```kotlin
assertFailsWith<IllegalStateException>("sendTo on a Torn seam must throw") {
    host.sendTo(joiner.selfId, byteArrayOf(2))
}
```

**`PeerNotConnected` extends `IllegalStateException`** (`kuilt-core/…/PeerNotConnected.kt:9`). So a fabric whose torn `sendTo` reports `PeerNotConnected` — *blaming the addressee for the seam's own death* — satisfies this assertion. The property is weaker than it reads, **for every fabric**, and nothing in the suite distinguishes the two outcomes.

## How this surfaced

Found while landing #2444 ([#2447](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2447)). The Apple `MCSessionLink` had exactly this defect. Per-guard revert measurement on `macosArm64`:

| reverted | `sendOnTornSeamThrows` |
|---|---|
| `broadcast` guard only | 🔴 red |
| **`sendTo` guard only** | 🟢 **stays green** |

So the TCK caught the broadcast half and was blind to the addressed half. What caught the addressed half was a **fabric-local** test asserting the throwable's identity (`MCSessionLinkTornSendTest.sendToOnAClosedLinkReportsTheTearNotAMissingPeer`). #2447 documents the limitation in the suite comment but deliberately does not change the assertion, because tightening it is a cross-fabric change with its own blast radius.

The distinction is not cosmetic. `PeerNotConnected` means "that peer is absent from `peers`" — a statement about the *addressee*, which a caller may reasonably respond to by re-resolving the roster and retrying a different peer. A torn seam reporting it sends the caller chasing a peer that was never the problem, and hides the fact that this seam is dead and must be replaced. On a retrying transport

body:

Found by binding `ControllableSeam` to `SeamConformanceSuite` for #2441 — the first time anything drove that seam through the contract.

## The gap

`ControllableSeam.peers` **is** the loom's shared registry, handed straight through:

```kotlin
override val peers: StateFlow<Set<PeerId>> = loom.peersState
```

and `close()` removes this peer from that registry (`loom.remove(selfId)`). So a torn seam's roster is `registry − selfId` — it keeps advertising every remaining remote **and** has dropped its own id. Both halves of the #1816 obligation fail at once.

title: conformance: bind the four bindable-but-unbound seams, shrinking #2437's opt-out list
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

[#2437](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2437) landed the guard that *enumerates* seam-harness coverage. `docs/seam-harness-coverage.md` now names **20 of 34** production `Seam` implementations as having no conformance harness, each with a written reason. **This issue is the follow-through: bind the ones that are bindable today.**

Four rows are classified **bindable-but-unbound** — nothing structural prevents a harness, they simply never got one:

| Seam | Note |
|---|---|
| `ResumableChannel` (`MuxClientLoom`) | publishes a `selfId` **frozen** across a heal — worth pinning precisely because that is unusual |
| `ControllableSeam` (`ControllableLoom`) | `:kuilt-test`; already `Loom`-produced, so binding should be cheap |
| `FakeSeam` | `:kuilt-test`; **see the caveat below** |
| `MCSessionLink` | `appleMain`; `MultipeerConformanceTest` is `jvmTest` and covers `BridgePeerLink` only, so the Apple link's guards rest on inspection plus `appleTest` unit tests (#2430, #2435) |

Each row moved from opt-out to a real harness shrinks the list and buys every *future* `Seam` obligation for free on that fabric — which is the whole point of the suite.

## Why this is separate from #2439

[#2439](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2439) covers the seams that are **not produced by any `Loom`** (`ManagedSeam`, `PeerlessSeam`, the `PerPeerSeam` family, `TokenGatedSeam`, `RawIncomingProxy`, …). Those need a design call first — `SeamConformanceSuite` drives seams *through* a `Loom`, so covering them means splitting the suite's single-seam half out or writing adapter `Loom`s. That is `needs-design`.

The four above need no such call. Keep the tracks separate so the cheap work is not blocked behind the design one.

title: conformance: bind ManagedSeam (and the unwoven decorators) to the single-seam half of SeamConformanceSuite
body:

A decorator that is never woven — `ManagedSeam`, `PerPeerSeam`, `RoomChannelSeam`, `TokenGatedSeam`, `MeteredSeam` and the rest of #2437's "not produced by any `Loom`" bucket — cannot be handed to it without either a fake `Loom` wrapper per decorator or a split of the suite into the obligations that need a *pair* and the obligations that need only *a seam*.

The second is probably the right cut, and it is a design question rather than a mechanical wiring job — which is why #2436 scoped it out rather than growing.

## What "done" looks like

- The portable, single-seam obligations of `SeamConformanceSuite` are reachable without a `Loom` pair (roster invariants, self-send refusal, payload budget, close idempotence).
- `ManagedSeam` is bound to them, and the

title: ManagedSeam.swap overwrites peers with the BACKING seam's roster, dropping its own selfId
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`Seam.peers` says: *"Live set of peers currently connected. **Includes [selfId]**"*, and its initial-value invariant makes `peers.value.size > 1` the documented sentinel for "at least one remote is connected". `ManagedSeam` honours that until the first `swap`, then stops.

```kotlin
// kuilt-cluster/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/cluster/ManagedSeam.kt
fun swap(newSeam: Seam) {
    …
    lock.withLock {
        current = newSeam
        _peers.value = newSeam.peers.value   // ← the backing seam's roster, verbatim
    }
    …
}
```

…and the per-swap tracker keeps it that way: `launch { seam.peers.collect { _peers.value = it } }`.

The backing seam's roster names **the backing seam's** `selfId`, not this one. `ManagedSeam.selfId` is a *constructor parameter* — the client's stable id, deliberately unchanged across reconnects, and by design **not** the fabric-minted id of whichever server seam is currently swapped in. So after the first swap, `ManagedSeam.peers` does not contain `ManagedSeam.selfId` at all.

## Why nothing catches it

`SeamConformanceSuite` has a continuous monitor for exactly this — `monitorSelfAlwaysInPeers` asserts `selfId ∈ peers` on every emission of a live seam, added by #1490 after the #1466 self-eviction bug. `ManagedSeam` is not a `SeamConformanceSuite` subclass, so nothing runs it. This is the #1871 shape (the matrix enumerates *harnesses*, not *seams*) rather than a missing property.

## How it surfaced

Found while landing #2428: `ManagedSeamSelfSendTest` asserts `selfId ∈ peers` as the precondition that makes the self-send refusal distinct from `PeerNotConnected`, and it red-lit post-swap. That test samples the precondition **pre**-swap with a comment pointing here, so it st

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Status (2026-08-17): the hypothesis below is REFUTED, and the fix this issue suggested would not have worked.** Investigated in [#2442](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2442); that PR's body carries the full evidence. The original text is kept below for the record.

## What was established

**There is no route-installation window.** In Ktor 3.5.2 (this repo's version), `EmbeddedServer.start()` loads modules **before** starting the engine, and does so blockingly: `createApplication()` runs inside `applicationInstanceLock.write { }` and only then does `engine.start(wait)` run; module loading goes through `avoidingDoubleStartup { runBlocking { … } }`, and both loader modes complete before returning. `KtorServerLoom.init` installs its route synchronously. So the connector cannot be bound while the routing table is empty.

That also resolves the tension this issue flagged: the `lateinit var serverLoom` succeeding is **not** evidence of a narrower window — it is evidence there is no window.

Measurement agrees: a probe dialling from the earliest observable instant got `101` on every attempt — 150 iterations idle, 150 under load 10.6→23.7 (the reported 18–27 band), 300 sequential, plus 200 iterations of the full dial path under load 19→30. Zero 404s.

"Poll a plain HTTP GET until it stops returning 404" never observes a 404 on a *healthy* kuilt WebSocket route. Measured status taxonomy against a live `KtorServerLoom`:

| Request | Status |
|---|---|
| right path + upgrade headers | **101** |
| right path, **no** upgrade headers | **400** |
| POST to the path | **405** |
| **wrong path** | **404** |
| after `stop()` | connection refused |

> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`FakeSeam`'s constructor can build a state no conforming seam can reach: `initialState = SeamState.Torn(…)` together with an `initialPeers` containing a remote.

title: kuilt-webrtc: WebRTCPeerLink has two unguarded tear paths, so a locally-closed seam can report CloseReason.RemoteRequested
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`WebRTCPeerLink` has **two** tear paths and no single-shot guard between them, so whichever runs second overwrites the first's `CloseReason`. `SeamState.Torn` is documented terminal (`Seam.kt:26,38`), and consumers branch on `CloseReason` to decide whether to reconnect.

**Updated 2026-08-17 — there are two directions, not one. The second needs no race at all**, and it is why the `closed`-flag fix is insufficient. Found while implementing this in [#2438](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2438).

| # | Scenario | Result before the fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | local `close(Normal)` | → `Torn(RemoteRequested)`. `facade.close()` → `dataChannel.close()` → `onclose` completes the deferred the `init` tear coroutine is parked on, *inside* `facade.close()` — so `finally { scope.cancel() }` is too late. **Timing-dependent.** |
| 2 | `close(Normal)` after the peer already vanished | → `Torn(Normal)`, overwriting the earlier `Torn(RemoteRequested)`. `close` consults only `closed`, and the remote path **never sets it** (`closed` is written solely at `:191-192` inside `close`). **No timing involved — a plain sequential overwrite.** |

## Why `closed` is not the fix

Honouring `closed` from the remote path repairs row 1 and leaves row 2 untouched, because in row 2 the *first* tear is the remote one, which never sets `closed`. The guard has to sit on the single write both paths share.

## The fix taken

A local single-shot early-return in the shared `tear`:

```kotlin
private fun tear(reason: CloseReason) {
    if (_state.value is SeamState.Torn) return
    _peers.value = setOf(selfId)
    _state.value = SeamState.Torn(reason)
}
```

`SeamStateGate` (`kuilt-core/…/SeamStateGate.kt:85`) is the repo's proper single-shot pr

title: conformance: no SeamConformanceSuite property asks whether two peers pointed at one session can collide on a discovery name
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Generalises #2416 past `:kuilt-nw`. Belongs to the #2247 family ("a conformance property is only as
strong as the weakest failure the reference implementation can reach"), and specifically to that
issue's **second** question — *which declaration does nothing consume?* — because today there is no
declaration here at all.

## The gap

#2416 was: under `Rendezvous.New` every `:kuilt-nw` peer advertised the **same** Bonjour instance
name, identity came from the TXT `PeerId`, and the dial went to the *name* — which mDNS re-resolves at
connect time. A dial armed for peer X could land on another device, or on self. It took two iPhones
30 cm apart to find, and the fix is ADR-005 (#2423).

Nothing in `SeamConformanceSuite` asks a fabric the question that would have caught it:

> **When a consumer points two peers at one session, can those peers collide on whatever name your
> discovery layer resolves — and if so, does formation still converge?**

Any fabric that discovers peers by a consumer-chosen name can have this. `:kuilt-nw` is simply where
it was found first; `:kuilt-nearby` and `:kuilt-multipeer` have naming layers too. The nine current
`SeamCapabilities` flags (`reportsPeerLoss`, `terminatesIncomingOnClose`, `staysTornAfterClose`,
`throwsOnSendToTorn`, `supportsSendTo`, `securesTransport`, `meshDelivery`, `reportsLiveCapability`,
`collapsesPeersOnTear`) are all about the *seam's* behaviour once formed. None is about how peers are
**found**, so a discovery-layer defect has no home in the TCK.

structurally unreachable, no property was written, the suite stayed green, and `

title: kuilt-nw: under Rendezvous.New the dial target is a shared Bonjour NAME while identity is the TXT PeerId — the two can resolve to different devices
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Design resolved 2026-08-15 — see [ADR-005](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/docs/adr-005-per-peer-bonjour-instance-name.md) (merged in #2418).** Option 2 was chosen, in the form
**bare `selfId.value`** — the option analysis further down is retained as history but its costing of
option 2 as "the most invasive" was wrong; see "What the investigation changed" below. Implementation
is in flight; this issue stays open until validated on the two-phone reproducer.

## The problem

Under `Rendezvous.New` every peer advertises the **same** Bonjour instance name (the shared session
name). Discovery identity and dial target are keyed on **different things**, and they can diverge:

- **Identity** comes from the TXT record — `readPeerIdFromTxt(result)` keys the discovered
  `NwEndpoint.id` (`RealNwApi.kt:1266`), and the pre-dial self-filter keys on that
  (`NwLoom.kt:383-411`). This part is correct.
- **The dial** goes to the stored browse *endpoint object* — a **named Bonjour service**, which mDNS
  **re-resolves at connect time**.

So the loom can correctly identify peer `X` from TXT and then dial a *name* that resolves to a
different device — including itself — because within the pre-rename collision window both devices
hold the same instance name. mDNS conflict resolution renames one to `… (2)` only afterwards.

title: verifyDocCitations scans gitignored .superpowers/, so a local full build fails on SDD scratch
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`verifyDocCitations` collects markdown via an `allMarkdown` file tree that does not exclude
`.superpowers/`. That directory is **gitignored** — it is where the subagent-driven-development
workflow keeps its ledger, task briefs, per-task reports and review packages.

Consequence: anyone running a full local `./gradlew build` while an SDD workflow has run in that
checkout gets a `verifyDocCitations` failure on the workflow's own scratch artifacts. **CI never sees
it**, because the files are not committed — so it presents as "the build is broken on my machine
only", which is the most expensive shape a false red can take.

## Fix

Add `**/.superpowers/**` to the `allMarkdown` exclude list (`build.gradle.kts:1149`).

Not `citationExempt` — exemption implies the files were considered and excused. These are scratch in
a gitignored directory and should never enter the scan at all.

## A related footgun worth fixing in the same pass

The scan **trims and does not skip fenced code blocks**, so a markdown file that *quotes* a citation
marker inside a code fence is itself treated as an offender. That makes any post-mortem, design note,
or issue write-up that shows an example citation into a build failure — and the natural fix (paraphrase
instead of quoting) degrades the document.

`verifyModuleTable` already skips fenced blocks (that is why a fenced example row does not register as
a module row). `verifyDocCitations` should do the same.

## How it was found

While landing the discovery-departures branch. The worker had to move a report file aside to complete
its verification runs, then restore it — so the local failure is still reproducible exactly as before.

title: multipeer: departures() on appleMain and jvmMain only emits while discoveries() is collected
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by binding `:kuilt-multipeer` to `DiscoverySourceConformanceSuite` (the TCK added alongside
#1917 / #1903 / #2400). Both actuals **free-ride on `discoveries()`** — a consumer collecting
`departures()` alone receives nothing, forever.

- **appleMain:** `departures()` is `factory.lostPeerHandles`, written only by the `BrowserDelegate`
  that `startBrowsing` installs — and only `discoveries()` calls `startBrowsing`.
- **jvmMain:** `departures()` is a `SharedFlow` fed by the JNA peer-lost callback, registered inside
  `discoveries()`' own `callbackFlow`.

So a lone `departures()` collector never opens a browse session at all.

## Why this was invisible

`discoveryRoster` does `events.merge()` over both feeds, so the canonical consumer always collects
both and the coupling never shows. This is the same defect #1917 fixed on `kuilt-mdns` jvmMain, and
the same property caught it: `departuresEmitsWithNoConcurrentDiscoveriesCollector`.

Notably, appleMain was recorded as **the one correct implementation** in the survey that opened this
work — correct only because nobody had checked it.

## Two obligations fail, not one

`departuresEmitsWithNoConcurrentDiscoveriesCollector` **and** `anArrivalIsNeverReportedAsADeparture`
(which stages an arrival, so it needs a session too). Key-equality and cancellation both pass.

## Current state on `main`

Both failures are **pinned** in the TCK bindings with `assertFailsWith`, matched on the message that
names the cause — so whoever fixes the coupling gets a red telling them to remove the pin. Each
binding also ships a ref-counted-session control that passes every obligation on the same fixture,
which is what makes these reds a statement about the backend rather than about the

> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while reviewing the #2400 `departures()` work. **This is a use-after-free, not a ghost** —
filing separately from #2407 / #2408 because the failure mode is memory corruption.

`ServiceDelegate` sets itself as the delegate of every `NSNetService` the browser finds, and asks
it to resolve:

```kotlin
sink.onFound(didFindService.name()) {
    didFindService.setDelegate(this)
    didFindService.resolveWithTimeout(RESOLVE_TIMEOUT_S)   // 5 s
}
```

`NetServiceBrowseSession.stop()` clears the **browser's** delegate. Nothing clears the
**services'** delegates, and nothing cancels a resolution already in flight.

The chain:

1. `NSNetService.delegate` is `assign`/unowned — Objective-C takes no strong reference to a Kotlin
   `NSObject` subclass, so the delegate's lifetime is decided entirely by Kotlin/Native's GC.
2. `resolveWithTimeout` schedules the service on a run loop, which retains **the service** for up
   to 5 s — past `browser.stop()`.
3. After teardown the session becomes unreachable, so the `ServiceDelegate` it holds becomes
   collectable, and its Objective-C counterpart is deallocated.
4. The still-live `NSNetService` then calls `netServiceDidResolveAddress:` or
   `netService:didNotResolve:` through a pointer to freed memory.

**Why this is ordinary rather than exotic:** the trigger is cancelling a discovery flow within ~5 s
of a peer appearing — i.e. a user backing out of a lobby screen while it is still finding peers.
Not a contrived race. What makes it intermittent is only step 3: it needs a GC inside that window.
That makes it a rare, unreproducible crash rather than a rare, harmless one.

**Fix (cheap and local):** have `ServiceDelegate` keep the services it attached to, and in
`stop()` cal

title: mdns: NSD resolutions are serialised per browser instance, not per NsdManager
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up from the #1903 / #2400 `departures()` work (see also #2407).

`NsdManager.resolveService` handles one resolution at a time, and below API 31 a second
concurrent one fails with `FAILURE_ALREADY_ACTIVE`. `minSdk` here is 24.

`NsdManagerBrowser` serialises resolutions through a queue scoped to **the browser instance**
— one per `MDNSServiceDiscoverer`. That covers the case the departures fix introduced: both
feeds of one discoverer are separate browse registrations over one browser.

**It does not cover two `MDNSServiceDiscoverer`s over the same injected `NsdManager`** (two
service types being the obvious reason to have two). Those get two queues and no serialisation
between them, so a resolution can be lost to `FAILURE_ALREADY_ACTIVE` — and a service whose
resolution is lost has no knowable peer id, so it can neither be emitted by `discoveries()` nor
removed by `departures()`. That is a permanent ghost: exactly the bug #1903 existed to fix,
re-entering by a different door.

**Why it was left open rather than keyed to the manager.** A process-global
`Map<NsdManager, …>` would retain the manager for the life of the process; an Android
system-service manager is obtained per-`Context` and holds one, so that is a `Context` leak with
no eviction point. A weak-keyed variant avoids the leak but buys one increment only — it still
cannot serialise against another process, and the true scope of the platform limit (per client,
per process, or device-wide) is unverified. Trading a leak for a doc fix seemed the worse deal.

Mitigation shipped meanwhile: `onResolveFailed` now logs its error code, so the failure is
observable rather than silent.

**Options**
1. Weak-keyed, synchronized `Map<NsdManager, Serialiser>
