title: mdns jvmMain: discoveries() blocks up to 6s per unresolved service on JmDNS's single dispatch thread
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while fixing #1917. `departures()` was fixed there; `discoveries()` was deliberately left alone
under a behaviourally-identical constraint, and is now the only remaining instance.

`MDNSServiceDiscoverer.discoveries()`' `serviceAdded` calls the **2-argument**
`jmdns.requestServiceInfo(event.type, event.name)`. In jmdns 3.6.3 all four overloads funnel into
`resolveServiceInfo` + `waitForInfoData(info, SERVICE_INFO_TIMEOUT)`, where
`SERVICE_INFO_TIMEOUT = DNSConstants.ANNOUNCE_WAIT_INTERVAL * 6L` = **6000 ms**.

Why that matters more than it looks: `JmDNSImpl.updateRecord` submits `serviceAdded` **and**
`serviceRemoved` to a single `newSingleThreadExecutor` (`JmDNSImpl:336`). So a cached-but-unresolvable
service blocks that one thread for 6 s, and every other event — including the departures this feed
now finally emits — queues behind it.

`addServiceListener` also delivers cached `serviceAdded` synchronously on the **caller's** thread, so
a collector's own coroutine dispatcher can take the 6 s too.

## Fix

The same one #1917 took for `departures()`: `jmdns.requestServiceInfo(event.type, event.name, false, 0L)`.
`loops = timeout / 200` clamps to a minimum of 1, so `0L` yields exactly one ≤200 ms poll.
`resolveServiceInfo` dispatches the query **before** the wait, and resolution arrives via the async
`serviceResolved` callback — the (ignored, `void`) return value was never the mechanism. No
correctness trade.

## Why it was not folded into #1917

That PR was constrained to keep `discoveries()` behaviourally identical, so the reviewer and I kept
the change scoped. Latency behaviour on the shared executor is a real behaviour change and deserves
its own PR with its own verification — in particular a re-run o

title: otel-logging: nothing enforces that a capture edge routes through resolveAtEdge
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #1993 (fixed in #2402). Recording what that fix is now unpinned on.

`LogCapture.resolveAtEdge` is the single funnel where edge-resolved fields are stamped — the active
trace (#1034), the attribute bag (#1630) and now the event time (#1993). Three separate bugs, all the
same shape: a value that must be read on the logging thread was instead read on the drain.

Each time, the fix was to move the read into `resolveAtEdge`. But **nothing makes an edge call it.**
`NormalizedLogEvent`'s edge-resolved fields are nullable with defaults, so a new capture edge that
constructs one directly compiles cleanly and silently gets drain-time values for all three.

This has already happened once: per #1630's own commit message, the log4j2 appender "had already
fallen into" the did-you-remember-to-call-`resolveTrace()` trap before the funnel consolidated them.

## Why it keeps recurring

The funnel is a **convention**, not a mechanism. The type system cannot tell a `NormalizedLogEvent`
that went through the edge from one that did not, because the difference is `null` vs non-`null` on
fields that are legitimately nullable for source-compatibility.

## Shapes worth considering

- A distinct type for the post-edge event (`ResolvedLogEvent`) that only `resolveAtEdge` can mint,
  so `LogCapture.capture()` cannot accept an unresolved one. Strongest, most invasive.
- Make the fields non-nullable on a private constructor and force construction through the funnel.
- A conformance suite for capture edges asserting each one stamps all three fields on the caller
  thread — cheapest, and it would have caught all three historical bugs. Fits the house pattern
  (`SeamConformanceSuite`, and the new `DiscoverySourceConformanceSuite

title: iosMain MDNSServiceDiscoverer never implements departures(), so Bonjour consumers accumulate ghost peers
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Third instance of the same class as #1903 (androidMain) and #1917 (jvmMain, implemented-but-broken).

`kuilt-mdns`'s **iosMain** `MDNSServiceDiscoverer` never overrides `PeerDiscoverySource.departures()`,
so it silently takes the interface default `emptyFlow()`. Its browser delegate already *receives* the
leave signal and drops it on the floor:

```kotlin
// MDNSServiceDiscoverer.kt:93-98 — iosMain
@ObjCSignatureOverride
override fun netServiceBrowser(
    browser: NSNetServiceBrowser,
    didRemoveService: NSNetService,
    moreComing: Boolean,
) {}
```

Structurally identical to androidMain's `onServiceLost(info: NsdServiceInfo) {}` — the signal
exists, is delivered by the platform, and is simply not forwarded.

## Why it was not caught

`PeerDiscoverySource` has **no conformance suite**, and `departures()` defaults to `emptyFlow()`, so
an implementation that omits it is invisible at the call site and in CI. Four of the five
`PeerDiscoverySource` implementations in the repo emit no departure; only `kuilt-multipeer`
appleMain is correct.

## Constraint on the fix

The removal event carries only the service **name** — `NSNetService` here is unresolved, so
`TXTRecordData()` is unavailable. The peer id is knowable only from state built on the resolve path
(`netServiceDidResolveAddress`), keyed on `sender.name()`.

## Related

- #1903 — androidMain, same omission.
- #1917 — jvmMain, implements it against data the goodbye packet does not carry.
- Downstream: [fireworks-compose#3871](https://github.com/tractat-us/fireworks-compose/issues/3871).

title: kuilt-nearby: nearbyLoom() registers a process-lifetime BroadcastReceiver with no route to release it
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found in review of #2395 (#1543, the Nearby live-capability lane). The blocking finding from that
review is fixed there; this is the part that needs its own PR because it is a **public API**
decision.

## The leak

`nearbyLoom(context, …)` constructs `GmsNearbyApi(context)` internally and stores it in
`NearbyLoom.api`, which is private with no accessor. `NearbyLoom` has no `close()`. So
`GmsNearbyApi.close()` — which unregisters the `AndroidRadioObserver`'s `BroadcastReceiver` — is
**unreachable through the documented Android entry point**, and every `nearbyLoom()` call
permanently registers another receiver.

One instance is harmless (it sits on the application context, so there is no shorter-lived object to
leak into). N is not: an app that builds a loom per session or per screen accumulates registrations
until `registerReceiver` throws `IllegalStateException: Too many receivers, total of 1000,
registered for pid` — a hard ActivityManager limit. Each leaked observer also keeps re-polling
`isGooglePlayServicesAvailable` on the main thread at every Wi-Fi transition.

## Why it was not fixed in #2395

The natural fix is to make registration lifetime-bound to collection rather than to construction:

```kotlin
override val radioState: StateFlow<NearbyRadioState?> = callbackFlow {
    val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() { … }
    appContext.registerReceiver(receiver, filter)
    send(read())
    awaitClose { appContext.unregisterReceiver(receiver) }
}.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(), null)
```

That needs a `CoroutineScope`, and **`GmsNearbyApi(context: Context)` has none**. Adding one means a
required parameter on a public constructor *and* on `nearbyLoom()` — it cannot be defaulted, beca

title: mDNS cross-platform discovery matrix (Apple × Android × JVM) — untracked since the transport-mdns extraction
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`:transport-mdns` now lives here (extracted from `fireworks-compose` in tractat-us/fireworks-compose#1595), but the cross-platform discovery matrix that used to gate it did not come with it. As of 2026-08-15 the five matrix issues in `fireworks-compose` (#1082–#1086) are closed as outliving their container, and their doc — `docs/lan-transport-mdns-matrix.md` — is frozen there as a historical record. **That leaves cross-platform mDNS discovery untracked anywhere.** This issue is the replacement.

## What needs covering

The advertiser↔browser pairs, since a working advertiser on one platform proves nothing about a browser on another:

| Advertiser | Browser | Note |
|---|---|---|
| JVM/macOS | JVM/macOS | Baseline; cheapest to automate |
| JVM/macOS | iOS (`NSNetServiceBrowser`) | Apple cross-layer |
| iOS (`NSNetService`) | JVM/macOS | Apple cross-layer, reverse |
| iOS | iOS | Same-LAN pair |
| Android (`NsdManager`) | Android | Same-LAN pair |
| Android | iOS / JVM | Cross-OS |
| iOS / JVM | Android | Cross-OS, reverse |

The historical matrix doc in `fireworks-compose` is the reference for which cells were previously proven and which never were — read it rather than re-deriving.

## Why it matters

Consumers pick a transport on the assumption that discovery is symmetric. Any unproven cell is a silent "two devices on the same LAN never see each other" for the users who happen to be on that OS pair, which reads as a product bug rather than a transport gap.

## Note for consumers

One known consumer-side gap is tracked separately and is **not** this issue: tractat-us/fireworks-compose#4245 — that app still wires `MdnsAdvertiser.NoOp` on Android, so it never advertises regardless of what this library supports.

title: kuilt-core: mux channel views drop the per-ply breakdown — plies collapses a multi-ply CompositeSeam to a single synthetic Sole entry
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Sibling of #2058 (decorators dropping the payload budget), found while fixing #1546.

`MuxBase.ChannelView` does not override `Seam.plies`, so it takes the interface default:

```kotlin
public val plies: StateFlow<Map<PlyId, SeamState>>
    get() = MappedStateFlow(state) { mapOf(PlyId.Sole to it) }
```

`ChannelView.state` delegates to the base seam, so over a multi-ply `CompositeSeam` the view
reports a single synthetic `{ Sole: <rolled-up state> }` and the **per-ply breakdown is lost**. A
consumer holding a mux channel view cannot tell a 3-ply composite from a single-ply fabric.

## Why nothing reds on it

The `Seam.plies` contract invariant — *"`state.value` equals the rollup of `plies.value.values`
under 'any ply Woven ⇒ Woven'"* — still **holds**, trivially: one entry whose value *is* `state`.
So this is silent information loss that no existing assertion can see, the same shape as the
capability defect fixed in #1546 (where the view reported the `Unknown` floor while the base
answered confidently).

## Scope note

Both public muxers are affected, since both are one `MuxBase`: `MuxSeam.channel(tag)` and
`NamedMux.channel(name)`. Nested mux-over-mux sites (e.g. `GameNode.kt:715-718` nests a `NamedMux`
inside a mux channel) would forward transitively once each layer delegates.

Unlike #2058's `maxPayloadBytes`, a plain passthrough looks correct here — the plies of the base
*are* the plies carrying the channel; multiplexing does not add or remove a transport path. Worth
confirming that reading before implementing.

title: kuilt-nw: deleting NwSeam's double-dial dedup entirely reds nothing — a surviving duplicate link is unobservable through the Seam contract
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up from #2309 / #2384, and a **measured** gap rather than an inferred one.

## The measurement

Deleting `NwSeam.resolveIdentity`'s duplicate-link dedup outright — both connections kept in `conns`, neither disconnected, no tombstone — reds **nothing**: all 186 tests in `:kuilt-nw:jvmTest` stay green, including `NwSeamTest.doubleDialCollapsesToOneConnectionWithExactlyOnceDelivery`, which is the one in-tree test named for this behaviour.

It is not an unexecuted mutation. A counting probe placed in that branch fires **42 times** across `NwMeshConformanceTest`'s 6 tests, so the double-dial really happens on `FakeNwRadio` and the dedup decision really runs — it just has no observable consequence any test reads.

## Why nothing sees it

`NwSeam.broadcast` and `sendTo` both fan out over `registry` — one connection per peer — so a *surviving* duplicate link carries no application frames. It is a wasted socket, not a duplicating one. That is why:

- #2384's new `MeshConformanceSuite.broadcastIsDeliveredExactlyOnceToEveryPeer` does **not** close this. It closes the *observable* #2309 named (duplicate delivery), which is reachable through other causes — and it does red on rows 1 and 2 of that PR's receipt.
- Reading `Seam.peers` cannot close it either: a `Set<PeerId>` is unchanged by a second link. That was #2309's original finding.

So the cost of a dedup regression today is invisible: leaked file descriptors, a doubled TLS handshake per pair, and an endpoint the redial loop keeps re-settling — none of it observable through the `Seam` contract.

Not a `Seam`-contract property — the contract cannot see connections. Candidates, in rough order of cost:

title: heddle: no relocation test moves a rung carrying BOTH leaf and roll-up charge — the 'former leaf gains a child' shape
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while closing #2367 (PR #2382).

## The half neither ladder can reach

`EntitlementLedgerConservationTest` now drives two relocation ladders — one on a **leaf-inbound**
edge (`g1 → g3`, #2365) and one on a **prefix** edge (`root → g1`, #2382). Between them every
relocation family is written. But a single move still only ever carries **one** of `lsp`/`rsp`:

- an edge carries `leafSpent` exactly when it is some path's **final** edge;
- a final edge is never a strict prefix, so it never carries `rollupSpent`.

So `sp = lsp + rsp` in `relocationPatch` is never evaluated with both terms non-zero, and the
per-edge writes (`LEAF_RELOC_OUT` and `ROLLUP_RELOC_OUT` on the same `(edge, replica)` slot,
`LEAF_RELOC_IN` and `ROLLUP_RELOC_IN` on the same live slot) are never exercised together.

## The topology that reaches it is the one the design names

`EntitlementLedger`'s KDoc says the `leafSpent`/`rollupSpent` split is what "keeps the conservation
identity topology-independent even when **a former leaf later gains a child**", and `spendCaptured`
exists for exactly that reshape. That is the shape:

1. `h2` is a leaf; a spend there charges `leafSpent(f2)` where `f2` is `h2`'s inbound edge;
2. `prepare` + `activate` an `h2 → h3` edge, so `h2` stops being a leaf;
3. a spend at `h3` now charges `rollupSpent(f2)` as well.

`f2` then carries both, and re-homing it moves a non-zero `lsp` **and** a non-zero `rsp` in one
patch. Neither current ladder can produce it, because `records` is grow-only and `isLeaf` reads
every record regardless of lifecycle — the child edge has to appear **mid-run**, which needs a
topology of its own rather than the shared static one.

title: kuilt-core: a refused dispossession attempt on RoomHubSeam is silent — no signal a deployment can alarm on
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2380 makes `RoomHubSeam` refuse an unattested link that claims a live attested peer's id (#2357). The refusal is **silent**, so a deployment under active attack cannot tell — a refused dispossession attempt is indistinguishable from a peer that never connected.

## Why silent was right *there*

Not an oversight, and not something the fix could have chosen differently:

- **`kuilt-core` is logger-free by contract**, so "just log it" is not available.
- **Throwing is worse than silence.** `deliver`'s only caller is `MuxServerLoom.readLoop`, a per-connection read loop inside `rawSeam.incoming.collect { }`. A throw tears that loop down and escapes into a launched coroutine on the loom's scope — potentially taking more than the offending connection with it.
- **Silence is the established convention** for a room-level denial: an authorizer rejection is silent in exactly the same way, and the refusal is deliberately byte-identical in shape to one.

## Why it is still a gap

A security control that cannot report having fired is a control you cannot alarm on, tune, or prove is working in production. Note the contrast with the mesh, which raises `LinkRejectedException` for a policy rejection — the per-link signal `hostedOverlay`'s accept pump absorbs and debug-logs, precisely so kuilt-core stays logger-free while the *consumer* still learns. The room hub has no equivalent, and neither does its plain authorizer denial.

The nearest signal a deployment gets today is indirect and ambiguous: its `RoomAuthorizer` is invoked for a frame that never registers. That is what #2380's test uses as a rig, but it cannot distinguish a refused dispossession from an ordinary authorizer denial.

title: kuilt-core: an unattested link can still take an attested peer's id on a Mesh (dispossession) — the hub's #2357 fix cannot transfer
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #2357, which is fixed for `RoomHubSeam` in #2380. The mesh half is **not** fixed there, deliberately, and this records why and what is left.

## The behaviour

An unattested link that claims a live attested peer's `PeerId` can take that id on a `Mesh`. It wins the canonical-nonce dedup tiebreak roughly half the time (and an attacker can simply redial until it does), `links[alice]` becomes its connection, and the victim's link is **closed**. Pinned as live behaviour by `MeshAdmissionTest.controlSpoofedLinkWinsDedupLotteryUnderAcceptAll`.

The roster stays honest about it — `attestedPrincipals` is derived from the live link set, so after the takeover the peer is reported **unattested**, which is accurate: the connection the host verified is gone. #2380 pins that with `unattestedDuplicateWinningDedupIsReportedUnattested`, after trying and reverting the tempting half-fix (having the survivor inherit the displaced link's principal), which would have made the roster assert a verification for a connection the host verified as nothing — a fail-open, strictly worse than reporting the downgrade truthfully.

So this is **dispossession**, not erasure. It is a different defect from the one #2357 fixed on the hub, and it is louder: the victim's link dies rather than being silently shadowed.

## Why the hub's fix does not transfer

`RoomHubSeam` refuses the claimant outright because a mux hub holds *two live links for one id at once* and can therefore choose. A mesh cannot:

- Duplicate links are collapsed by a tiebreak that is a **pure function of the two nonces**, precisely so both ends derive the same survivor with no coordination.
- Attestation is **local knowledge**. A veto based on it would have each end

title: kuilt-conformance: RoomConformanceSuite pins that a resume refusal is terminal, but not WHICH RejectCode — the verdict→code mapping is enforced by one implementation's unit tests
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2378 (closing #2364) made a resume rejection carry its `RejectCode`, so a joiner can finally tell "the grace window elapsed" from "that token was invalid". The split between host verdicts and joiner outcomes is now enforced by the compiler, and *terminality* is enforced by `RoomConformanceSuite` — which asserts a cross-room token's refusal is non-retryable without pinning which code it is.

What nothing enforces is **the mapping itself**. `SeamRoom.handleResume` turns a `HostVerdict` into a `RejectCode` in four hand-written pairs. Swap two of them — answer `ResumeWindowExpired` for a token that was actually foreign, say — and it compiles, and reds **nothing** in the conformance suite. It would red `RoomResumeTest`'s new arms, but those are the reference implementation's own unit tests: a second `RoomFactory` inherits none of them.

So the guarantee a consumer actually acts on — *this specific code means this specific thing happened* — rests on one implementation's unit tests, which is precisely the shape #2247 is about. A backend that mapped every verdict to one plausible-looking terminal code would pass the TCK and silently hand consumers a wrong retry decision.

Secondarily: `WindowClosed`'s joiner-side meaning ("we never asked the host") rests on prose. A future path that completed a flight with `WindowClosed` *after* the host answered would red nothing.

**Shape of the fix** — a conformance property per verdict, driven through a harness hook that puts the host into each of the four states and asserts the code the joiner receives. title: heddle: the control plane cannot observe the transfer tangle it must refuse — FenceState.relocations carries no transfer rows
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while implementing #2366 option 2 (PR #2376).

## The shape

#2366's containment refuses a generation move whose strand carries transfer rows. The guard reads `transfers[PathKey.of(s)]` on `relocationPatch`'s **receiver** — and in production that receiver is `FenceState.relocations`:

```kotlin
// ControlPlane.kt
return when (val move = fence.relocations.relocationPatch(liveEdge, finals)) {
```

`FenceState.relocations` accumulates only the relocation patches the control plane has itself authored, so it carries **no `transfers` rows, ever**. The guard is sound and deterministic there — it simply never fires. The H5 control plane therefore still publishes the corrupting move, and the data plane still merges it.

Pinned, not assumed: `EntitlementLedgerReconcileTest.theAbandonedRowsSilentlyReassignTheRecipientsEntitlementToTheDonor` derives the patch from `EntitlementLedger.ZERO` — the exact production shape — and asserts the corruption still lands.

## Why it can't be patched where it stands

- Reading the gossip-merged data plane would break §6.3/§5.4.3: the derived patch must be a deterministic function of the committed log prefix, and `EntitlementLedgerReconcileTest.break2_theMagnitudeIsNoLongerReadFromAProposerViewAtAll` pins exactly that.
- The projection is topology/lifecycle-only, so it has no rows either.
- Nothing in `SlotFinals` carries a transfer.

## The available fix

`transfers[pathKey][donor]` is **single-writer** at the donor, and once `s` is retired it is no longer any group's live inbound, so no new transfer can land on `PathKey.of(s)`. The rows are frozen at retire time on exactly the same argument that makes `SlotFinals` declarable — so a peer can declare its own transfer row final i

A generation move relocates **three** quantities — net inflow (`issuedRelocIn`), leaf charge
(`leafRelocIn`/`Out`) and roll-up charge (`rollupRelocIn`/`Out`). The new property drives a ladder of

title: heddle: a generation move abandons the strand's transfer rows, silently reassigning a recipient's entitlement to the donor
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while putting relocation into the randomized conservation property (#1894, PR #2365).

## The shape

`transfers` is keyed by `PathKey.of(edge)` — the **generation's** id, not the child group. A generation
move re-homes the counter families onto the live edge but leaves the transfer rows on the dead
generation's path key, where `holdings` no longer reads them. The recipient's credit and the donor's
debit both vanish, so the donor silently recovers what it gave away.

Reproduced on current `main` (`root →e1→ g1 →e3→ g3`, g3 a leaf; mint 100 to alice):

```
alice delegates 100 across e1, 60 across e3, transfers 40 to bob at g3
before:  alice@g3 = 20   bob@g3 = 40
relocateFromConvergedView(g3)   →   Moved
after:   alice@g3 = 60   bob@g3 = 0
validate() = []
```

- **Conservation is blind.** `Σ_r transferNet(pathKey, r) = 0`, so abandoning a whole path key's rows
  is sum-preserving. The identity `minted == Σ holdings + Σ effLeafSpent` holds exactly, and the new
  randomized relocation property in #1894 stays green through it.
- **`validate()` is silent.** No pocket goes negative (the recipient lands on `0`, not below), no edge
  goes per-edge-unsafe, nothing is retired undrained.
- **The documented guard does not cover it.** `relocationPatch`'s KDoc names the transfer tangle —
  "a replica left net-negative on `s` … would need its transfer rows moved too. Out of scope ⇒

  the strand. A recipient who merely holds transferred credit has no slot on the edge at all, is
  absent from `replicasOnEdge`/`baseFinalsOn`, and the move proceeds.

title: kuilt-session: the cookbook tells consumers to branch Room.resume on two values it can never return, and WindowClosed silently means "refused for any reason"
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kuilt-session/src/commonSamples/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/session/AgentCookbookSamples.kt` tells a
consumer to branch `room.resume(token)` on **two values that surface can never return**:

```kotlin
when (room.resume(token)) {
    ResumeResult.Success -> Unit
    ResumeResult.WindowClosed -> Unit
    ResumeResult.WindowNotYetOpen -> Unit   // ← unreachable
    ResumeResult.TimedOut -> Unit
    is ResumeResult.TokenInvalid -> Unit    // ← unreachable
}
```

## Verified, not inferred

`Room.resume`'s reachable range from the joiner is **`{Success, WindowClosed, TimedOut}`**.

| Step | Receipt |
|---|---|
| `TokenInvalid` is a **host** verdict, not a joiner one | `SeamRoom.kt:1452` calls `ctrl.tryResume(...)` to build an `AdmitMessage.Reject`; `SeamRoom.kt:1466` asserts outright that *"tryResume must not return TimedOut: it is a joiner await outcome, **not a host verdict**"* |
| It reaches the joiner as a reject **code**, not a result | `SeamRoom.kt:1461-1462` — `is ResumeResult.TokenInvalid -> AdmitMessage.Reject("resume-token-invalid: …", RejectCode.ResumeTokenInvalid)` |
| The joiner collapses **every** reject to one value | `JoinerResumeMachine.kt:336` — `d?.complete(ResumeResult.WindowClosed)`, unconditionally, whatever the `code` |

That collapse is **deliberate** and documented — it keeps the retry loop alive across the
window-not-yet-open race — so this is not a bug in `rejectFlight`. The defect is that the cookbook
advertises a discrimination the API does not offer.

## Why it matters more than a dead branch

The sample's comments assign meanings the values do not carry:

- `WindowClosed -> // grace window elapsed — re-join fresh`

But `WindowClosed` is *also* what a consumer gets for **wrong session**

title: kuilt-deal: SraScheme's domain check admits p-1, a fixed point of every key it generates
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Turned up while adding the secrecy floor to `CommutativeSchemeConformanceSuite` (#2313). Latent —
not reachable through `encodePlaintext` — but it is a gap in the check that is *supposed* to keep
plaintexts away from encryption fixed points, and the check's own KDoc claims otherwise.

## The gap

`SraScheme.requireInDomain` admits any `value` with `2 <= value < PRIME`, so it admits `p-1`.

`p-1 ≡ -1 (mod p)`, so for **every** key this scheme generates:

```
encrypt(p-1, e) = (-1)^e mod p = p-1     because generateKey forces e odd
strip(p-1, d)   = (-1)^d mod p = p-1     because d·e ≡ 1 (mod p-1) with p-1 even, so d is odd too
```

`p-1` is therefore a universal fixed point: a card encoding to it is layered by every player and
still readable by all of them. It is the only one besides `0` and `1` — `p` is a safe prime, so the
subgroup orders are `1, 2, q, 2q`, and `p-1` is the unique order-2 element. `requireInDomain`
already excludes `0` and `1`; it stops one short.

`encodePlaintext`'s KDoc says the marker guarantees the encoded value "is never the 0 or 1
encryption fixed point", which is true and now reads as if the set were exhaustive.

## Severity: low, and why

- **Not reachable via `encodePlaintext`** — it prepends `0x01`, so the high byte is `0x01` while
  `p-1`'s is `0xFF`. A deck built the documented way cannot produce it.
- **Not reachable via a later layer** — an intermediate ciphertext equals `p-1` with probability
  ~`1/p`.
- **Reachable via the public API**, which is the actual complaint: `SraScheme.encrypt` is `public`
  and accepts any in-domain `ByteArray`, and the domain check is the only thing standing between a
  consumer and a value that hides nothing.

## Fix

One clause in `requireInDoma

title: kuilt-core: an unattested peer claiming an attested peer's PeerId displaces it — roster entry erased, unicast hijacked
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while implementing #2316 (attestation provenance). **Reproduced, not theorised** — probe output below.

## What happens

An **unauthenticated** connection that self-asserts an already-attested peer's `PeerId` silently
takes that peer's place in a `RoomHubSeam`:

```
PROBE: after alice   -> {alice=verified-alice}, peers=[server, alice]
PROBE: after mallory -> {},                     peers=[server, alice]
```

alice joins over a link the host verified as `Principal("verified-alice")`. mallory then dials a
**second, concurrent** link — alice's is never dropped — carrying **no** principal and announcing
`PeerId("alice")` in its `MeshHello`. Result:

1. `attestedPrincipals` loses alice's entry entirely (`RoomHubSeam.deliver`: `principal == null` ⇒
   `principals.remove(connPeerId)`). Any consumer reading the roster now sees alice as unattested.
2. `registered[alice]` is now **mallory's** `OutboundSender`, so `room.sendTo(alice, …)` delivers to
   the impostor. `MuxServerLoom.admit` likewise overwrites `connRecords[alice]`.
3. alice stays in `peers`, so nothing observable says a takeover occurred.

No credential is needed — only knowledge of the peer id, which is not a secret (it is the
self-asserted preamble field every peer broadcasts).

## Why nothing catches it

- `PrincipalAttestationConformanceSuite.rosterUpdatesPrincipalOnReconnect` **mandates** the
  displacement: it requires a second link presenting the same `PeerId` with a different principal to
  supersede the first. The harness cannot distinguish "alice reconnecting" from "someone else
  claiming alice's id", so the suite makes the overwrite obligatory. Noted as an open question in

title: docs: uncited code snippets are verified by nothing — a Pattern/Tag parameter rename left four that would not compile
body:
🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`Pattern` and `Tag` used to take a `displayName`; it is `sessionName` now. Four doc snippets never followed:

| Site | Wrote | Real |
|------|-------|------|
| `docs/usage.md:45` | `Pattern(displayName = "alice", maxPeers = 4)` | `sessionName` |
| `docs/usage.md:103` | same | `sessionName` |
| `docs/usage.md:165` | `WebSocketAdvertisement(displayName = "alice")` | `sessionName` |
| `docs/extending-fabrics.md:238` | `override val displayName: String` | `sessionName` |

None would compile. The last one is the sharpest: it is presented as a quote of `TcpAddress`, complete with a `// kuilt-tcp/src/…/TcpAddress.kt:11-17` line reference, and the field it quotes has said `sessionName` since the rename. `docs/usage.md` is one of the two in-repo sources the README points readers at.

#2352 fixes the four instances. This issue is the class.

## Why nothing caught it

We have three snippet-verification mechanisms and all three are opt-in per block:

- `@sample` — compiled as `commonTest`, and `verifySampleLinks` (#2259) proves the tag resolves. Strongest, but only reaches KDoc.
- `<!-- verbatim from <path>#<symbol> -->` — `verifyDocCitations` (#1792) checks the block still matches its source character-for-character.
- `<!-- condensed from … -->` — path and symbol must resolve; content never checked again.

A block with **no marker at all** is checked by nothing, and that is most of them:

| Surface | ```` ```kotlin ```` blocks | carrying a citation |

title: build: kuilt-deal and kuilt-deal-test cite a karma.config.d/timeouts.js that no longer exists
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Two build files tell a reader to look in a file that does not exist.

`kuilt-deal/build.gradle.kts:6-10` and `kuilt-deal-test/build.gradle.kts:3-6` both say the wasmJs
Mocha/Karma limits are:

> Both limits are raised in `karma.config.d/timeouts.js` (the Gradle `useMocha` DSL does not reach
> the wasmJs browser test task).

There is no `karma.config.d/` in either module, or anywhere in the tree. The config is **generated**
by the `kuilt.kmp-library` convention plugin — `GenerateKarmaTimeouts`
(`build-logic/src/main/kotlin/kuilt.kmp-library.gradle.kts:164-167`) writes it per-module into
`build/karma-config.d/timeouts.js`. Note the directory name differs too: `karma-config.d`, hyphen,
under `build/`.

## What is still true, so the fix stays narrow

- The `2s` figures are **accurate** — Mocha's default per-test timeout and Karma's ~2 s ping, both
  named in `GenerateKarmaTimeouts.kt:31-34`.
- The parenthetical is **accurate** — `useMocha { timeout }` really does target the wasmJs *node*
  task, not the browser one (`GenerateKarmaTimeouts.kt:11`).

Only the **location** claim is wrong. Don't rewrite the rest.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than shrugging at

The failure mode is not "a stale path". It is that a reader who goes looking, finds nothing, and
reasonably concludes **the timeouts are not actually raised** — then either re-adds a hand-maintained
`karma.config.d/` beside the generated one, or starts debugging a wasmJs timeout that is already
handled. The comment was correct when written; the config moved into the convention plugin and the
comment did not follow. That is the ordinary way a citation rots.

Noticed while working #2311 and deliberately left out of that PR to keep the diff off #2313's line

title: kuilt-deal: an empty validPlaintexts() silently switches off two CommutativeScheme TCK properties
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while landing #2343 (part of #2247, audit slice C).

`CommutativeSchemeConformanceSuite.validPlaintexts()` is a `public open fun` with a non-empty
default. It is also a free knob, and its empty setting switches two properties off silently:

- `encryptThenStripRecoversPlaintext` — `for (m in validPlaintexts())` over an empty list asserts
  nothing and passes.
- `encryptionIsCommutative` — same shape, same result.

Measured on the #2343 branch by overriding `validPlaintexts()` to `emptyList()` in
`SraSchemeConformanceTest` and running `:kuilt-deal-test:jvmTest --rerun-tasks`: four properties
error on `.first()` (`NoSuchElementException` — a red, but an illegible one), the new
`encryptionIsCommutativeAcrossPeerInstances` reds on its own explicit non-empty check, and those two
go **green over an empty loop**.

Nobody has overridden it to empty, so nothing is broken today. The point is that the suite does not
notice: a downstream scheme whose valid domain is expressed by an override that happens to compute
empty loses two properties with no signal.

## Remedy

One assertion, at the top of each property that loops (the cross-peer property already carries it):

```kotlin
assertTrue(messages.isNotEmpty(), "validPlaintexts() is empty, so this property asserts nothing")
```

Better still, hoist it so a subclass cannot reach any property with an empty domain — but the
per-property check is the cheap version and is what #2343 uses.

Small and mechanical; kept separate from #2343 (cross-peer commutativity) and #2313 (the
security-bearing properties) so each lands on its own.

title: kuilt-bolt: PosixMappedBolt prunes a resume prefix with nothing proving it was skipped rather than read
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`PosixMappedBolt` prunes a segment prefix on a `FromOffset` resume — `PosixMappedBolt.kt:526-531`
computes `firstUnpruned` and starts the emit loop there. **Nothing proves it.**

The JVM twin is proven, and thoroughly: `MappedBoltPruningTest.aResumeReadsFarLessThanThePrefixItPrunes`
counts **bytes read off the segment files**, uses a `ReplayScope.All` control arm so a saving cannot
be an artefact of a small denominator, and carries a mutation receipt (returning `0` from
`MappedBolt.firstSegmentToRead` — the pre-#2236 behaviour — takes the resume from 7,431 bytes to
25,327 and reds assertions 3 and 4).

The Apple side has no equivalent. `git grep fileBytesRead` hits `MappedBolt.kt` and
`MappedBoltPruningTest.kt` and nothing else; `kuilt-bolt/src/appleTest/` holds only
`PosixMappedBoltConformanceTest` and `PosixMappedBoltTest`.

## Why this is worth an issue rather than a shrug

Every *correctness* property is shared — the conformance suite runs on all three backends, so
`PosixMappedBolt` cannot silently return wrong frames. What is unguarded is the **saving**: a
`PosixMappedBolt` that read every segment whole and then filtered would pass the entire TCK, because
a conformance property can only ask what a replay *said*, never what it touched. That is the
`MappedBoltPruningTest` KDoc's own argument for existing, applied to the backend it does not cover.

And this is precisely the #2240 shape: **two independently-written backends shipping the same defect
because the shared suite could not reach it.** #2236 was a real regression on the JVM side; there is
no reason to believe the Apple implementation is immune, and no test that would tell us.

title: kuilt-bolt: the reserved event-time key slot has no tracking issue
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

The bolt frame format **reserves a key slot that nothing tracks**. Epic #2210 put event-time
indexing out of scope with the words *"the frame reserves a key slot; the index is a follow-up"* —
the slot shipped, the follow-up was never filed.

## What is actually in tree

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `kuilt-bolt/.../BoltFrame.kt:54` | `public val key: String?` on `Archived` |
| `kuilt-bolt/.../BoltFrame.kt:45` | KDoc: *"the reserved key slot — always `null` in format version `BOLT_FORMAT_VERSION`. The slot exists so event-time indexing can be layered on later without a format change."* |
| `kuilt-bolt/.../BoltFrame.kt:157` | `private const val NO_KEY: Int = -1` |
| `kuilt-bolt/.../BoltFrame.kt:373`, `:435` | the sentinel written and read on the wire |

So the slot is real, costs a wire int per frame, is public API, and is documented as permanently
`null`.

## Why this needs an issue rather than a comment

**A reserved-but-untracked format slot is the thing a later reader deletes as dead weight.** The
KDoc explains what it is *for*, but nothing records that the follow-up is wanted, so the honest
reading available to a future sweep is "public nullable field that is always null, plus a sentinel
branch on both the read and write paths, delete it." Removing it is a **format-version bump** and a
breaking change to `Archived`; keeping it is free. The asymmetry is the argument for writing the
intent down somewhere a backlog sweep will find it.

There is no reachability claim here and nothing is blocked — `ReplayScope.Arrived` already indexes
on *arrival* time, which is what every current consumer wants. This tracks the deferred half:
indexing on **event** time, the time the ops actually happened, which arrival order

title: build: androidMain production source has no detekt task, so Android-only public API ships unlinted
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while landing the `:kuilt-nearby` slice of #1430 ([PR #2333](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2333)), whose whole deliverable — the top-level `nearbyLoom(...)` factory — lives in `kuilt-nearby/src/androidMain/` and is therefore **never linted**.

## The gap

`kuilt.detekt-kmp` builds `detektAll` from a type-resolved `detektJvmMain` (into which it folds `commonMain` and each **intermediate** source set, per #1021) plus three test tasks — `detektJvmTest`, `detektAndroidDebugUnitTest`, `detektAndroidReleaseUnitTest`.

**`androidMain` is none of those.** For a module whose Android code is a *leaf* Android-target source set rather than a shared `jvmAndAndroidMain` intermediate, its production source is folded nowhere and has no detekt task of its own. `detektAll` reports success without analysing a line of it.

Note the shape of the miss: the two Android tasks that *are* configured are both **UnitTest** variants. There is no `detektAndroidDebug`/`detektAndroidRelease` **main** counterpart, so Android *test* source is covered while Android *production* source is not — the opposite of the priority you would choose deliberately.

## Why it matters more than a lint gap

The rules this repo actually relies on need type resolution — `UnsafeCallOnNullableType` and the nullability family. #2263 is the receipt that they catch real defects only where type resolution runs, and `androidMain` is where the platform-specific `expect`/`actual` implementations live: exactly the code most likely to carry a `!!` or a platform-type round-trip. `:kuilt-nearby` is the clearest case (the entire Google Nearby binding is `androidMain`), and any `#1430` slice that adds a platform-gated factory lands it unlinted by constructio

title: gradle/libs.versions.toml: the atomicfu comment says 'locks API only' — 23 main sources use the atomic-field API
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while fixing #2305 (`ScopedCloseable`'s close-once guard needed `atomic(false)` + CAS).

## The stale claim

`gradle/libs.versions.toml:34-35`:

```toml
# atomicfu — multiplatform reentrant lock (locks API only; the runtime artifact is
# sufficient — the gradle plugin's bytecode transform is for atomic *fields*, not locks):
```

"locks API only" is false. `git grep` finds **23 files under `*Main/`** importing
`kotlinx.atomicfu.atomic` — including `MuxBase` inside `:kuilt-core` itself.

The *second* half of the comment is the part that is actually load-bearing and still true: only the
runtime artifact is applied (no atomicfu Gradle plugin), so the bytecode transform that unboxes atomic
fields on JVM does not run. That is a real and deliberate trade — it just is not the same statement as
"we only use the locks API".

## Why it is worth correcting

It reads as *"the atomic-field API is not available here"*, which is the opposite of true, in a repo
whose `CLAUDE.md` **bans** `limitedParallelism(1)` confinement-as-mutex and directs contributors to
"explicit, local primitives — atomicfu `reentrantLock` … or `kotlinx.atomicfu` atomics". A contributor
who reads the catalog comment before reaching for `atomic()` will conclude it is off the table and
reach for the banned pattern instead. That is a comment steering people toward the thing the project
forbids.

## Deliberately not fixed inline

The #2305 worker found this and left it alone on purpose: **touching the version catalog invalidates
the whole build cache**, and this repo has a recorded cold-build OOM on catalog PRs (runner exit 143),
where the lever is the 8 GB daemon-heap floor rather than `--max-workers`. A two-line comment fix is
not worth a cold fu

title: kuilt-core: a throwing onClose() leaks the coroutine tree — the latch is already set, so ownJob.cancel() never runs and no retry is possible
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Noticed while fixing #2305 (`ScopedCloseable`'s close-once guard). **Pre-existing and unchanged by that
PR** — the same hole exists before and after — so it is filed separately rather than folded in.

## The defect

`ScopedCloseable.close()` is, in shape:

```kotlin
if (!_closed.compareAndSet(expect = false, update = true)) return
onClose()
ownJob.cancel()
```

If `onClose()` throws, `ownJob.cancel()` **never runs** — but the latch is already set. So:

- the coroutine tree under `ownJob` is never cancelled and leaks;
- every subsequent `close()` returns immediately at the latch, so **there is no retry**; and
- the object is now permanently in a state that is neither open nor closed.

The latch is claimed *before* the work it guards is known to have succeeded, which makes the failure
unrecoverable rather than merely unsuccessful.

## Why it matters more than it might look

`ScopedCloseable` has **ten** subclasses in-tree — `Quilter`, `DealSession`, `RgaGcCoordinator`,
`MovableTreeGcCoordinator`, `FugueGcCoordinator`, `MuxServerLoom`, `LogTapHost`, `LogTapClient`,
`MetricTapHost`, `MetricTapClient`. Several `onClose()` bodies close *other* `ScopedCloseable`s, so a
throw partway through a hook leaves a partially-torn-down object graph with no way to finish the job.

This is also adjacent to the repo's own cleanup rule (`CLAUDE.md`): inside a `NonCancellable` shield,
best-effort teardown wants one `try`/`catch (failure: Throwable)` **per** cleanup item, precisely so
one failure cannot skip the remaining closes. `ScopedCloseable.close()` is the same hazard one level
up — a failing hook skips the cancel.

title: crdt: a consumer cannot write the sound segment-retirability predicate against Fugue
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found reviewing #2298 (which closes #2223 by making `Fugue.compactedIds` public).

#2223 fixed one instance of an asymmetry. The class behind it is still open: **a consumer cannot write the sound segment-retirability predicate against `Fugue` at all.**

## The predicate, and why `Fugue` can't express it

`WarpLogRecordExporter.contentOf` is the worked example, and it needs two things from a segment:

```kotlin
if (segment.compactOpCount > 0) SegmentContent.Pinned
else SegmentContent.Ids(segment.sequence.toSet() + segment.tombstones)
```

The `compactOpCount > 0` gate comes first and is load-bearing. `Rga.compactOpCount`'s KDoc says why it is not `compactedIds.isNotEmpty()`: that projection is blind to a `Compact` carrying an empty positions map, and "may I delete this?" must not be decided by a predicate with a false-negative case. Dropping a segment that holds a `Compact` revokes "once compacted, always compacted" — a peer that never received the compaction re-admits the purged elements on the next `piece`.

On `Fugue` **none** of the three inputs is reachable: no `compactOpCount`, no `opCount`, no public `sequence`, no public `tombstones`, and `ops` is `internal`. The only sound route is an O(ops) walk of `OpLogCrdt.operations()` + `classify` — which works, and which #2298's KDoc now directs readers to, but it is a walk per query where `Rga` gets a cached read.

## What to decide

Not "mechanically mirror the three members". `Rga`'s three each have a named consumer:

- `compactOpCount` / `opCount` — the otel exporter's segment budget and retirability gate (#2187).
- `tombstones` — `WindowPolicy.byCount` via `RgaGcCoordinator`; the windowing path is `Rga`-only today, since `Fugue` has no `dropWindow`/`compac

title: handshaking() drops DeliveryPolicy, so no stream fabric can honour a policy knob
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`identified(conn, selfId, remoteId, dispatcher, policy)` takes a `DeliveryPolicy` and hands it to `LinkSeam`'s inbox `Spool`. `handshaking(conn, selfId, dispatcher)` — the in-band identity negotiation every **stream** fabric goes through — does not, and calls `identified(...)` without it, so the inbox of any handshaking-built seam is hard-wired to `DeliveryPolicy.Reliable`.

## Why it surfaced

#1430 step 3 says to "forward `policy` to the Ktor/TCP/Nearby top-level factories (the Seam layer already accepts it)". That is true of `identified` and **false of `handshaking`**, which is the only layer `:kuilt-tcp` goes through:

```kotlin
// kuilt-tcp/.../TcpLoom.kt — weave()
return handshaking(tcpConnection(socket, ioDispatcher), selfId, seamDispatcher)
```

So the `:kuilt-tcp` slice of #1430 ships **no** `policy` parameter: an argument accepted there could not reach the seam, and a silently-ignored argument is exactly what got option (a) rejected on #1430.

## Fix

Add a trailing `policy: DeliveryPolicy = DeliveryPolicy.Reliable` to `handshaking` and forward it to `identified`. Purely additive — `handshaking` is a top-level function with no implementors, and every call site today passes three positional arguments.

Who gains the knob: `TcpLoom.weave` (and thus the `:kuilt-tcp` factories), the `connectionPair`-based test helpers in `:kuilt-test`, and any third-party stream fabric built per `docs/extending-fabrics.md`.

Test home: `kuilt-core/src/commonTest/.../fabric/HandshakingTest.kt` — a non-default policy through `handshaking` must be observable on the returned seam's inbox (e.g. a capacity-1 `Overflow.FAIL` spool overflows where `Reliable` backpressures).

Then the TCP factories gain `policy` in canonical pos

title: The release job's README-coords PR can stall indefinitely — its workflow run needs manual approval
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## What happened

`v0.7.3` was tagged today. The `maven-central` job auto-opened #2297 (`docs: update README
coordinates to 0.7.3`) as `app/github-actions`. It then sat with **zero checks for 20 minutes** —
`ci-required` never even appeared, so auto-merge could not fire.

The cause is not a CI failure. The `pull_request` run existed but its conclusion was
**`action_required`** — GitHub held the workflow pending manual approval because the PR author is a
bot, and **no jobs ran at all**. Approving it (`gh api -X POST
repos/tractat-us/kuilt/actions/runs/<id>/approve`) released it immediately.

## Why it matters more than it looks

This is the last step of a release, and it fails **silently and open-endedly**: nothing is red,
nothing is failing, the PR simply never progresses. Anyone watching for a failure sees none.

It is also intermittent, which is why it has not been noticed:

| Release | PR | Author | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.7.3 | #2297 | bot | stalled until manually approved |
| 0.7.2 | #1883 | bot | merged same day |
| **0.7.1** | **#1394** | **bot** | **created 07-11, merged 07-18 — 7 days** |
| 0.7.0 | #1169 | keddie | merged same day (human-authored, no gate) |
| 0.6.0 | #615 | bot | merged same day |

#1394's seven-day gap is very likely this same stall, unnoticed at the time.

## Options

1. **Settings fix (cheapest):** Actions → General → *Approval for running workflows from
   collaborators/bots*. If the repo currently requires approval for bot-authored PRs, exempting them
   removes the gate entirely. Worth checking what the setting actually is before assuming.
2. **Don't open a PR at all.** The README version line is release-managed, not hand-edited — the job

title: kuilt-conformance: LatticeLawSuite encodes but never decodes — a lossy-but-deterministic serializer satisfies every lattice law
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice C). `LatticeLawSuite` was the strongest suite in my slice — `VacuityFloors`
and `generatorIsNotVacuous` already answer #2247's question for the *generator*. One seam is left.

## The gap

`LatticeLawHarness` **encodes** and never **decodes**.

- `encoded(state)` — `kuilt-conformance/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/conformance/lattice/LatticeLawHarness.kt:165`
- Every use compares two encodings against each other (`:264-265`, `:336-337`, `:746`, `:759`).

Replicas in the harness hand each other **in-process objects**. In production `Quilter` sends
encoded deltas over a `Seam` and the receiver decodes them. So a `Quilted` whose serializer is
**lossy but deterministic** — drops a field, collapses a dot context, omits tombstones — satisfies
every law in the suite: associativity, commutativity, idempotence, LUB, and the byte law (both
bracketings encode through the same lossy path, so the bytes match). On the wire the receiver
decodes a state missing the omitted part, and a removed element resurrects on the next merge.

That is exactly the #2247 shape: the harness makes the failure structurally impossible, so nobody
wrote the property for it.

The shipped types *are* covered, by hand: per-type round-trip tests in `kuilt-crdt/commonTest`
(e.g. `FugueTest.kt`, `MovableTreeTest.kt`) and `CanonicalGoldenVectorTest`, which includes
`thePreFloorGoldenStillDecodesToTheSameValue`. So there is no open hole today.

The problem is the **obligation**. `LatticeLawSuite` is what a new CRDT subclasses — every
`*ConvergenceTest` under `kuilt-conformance/src/commonTest/.../lattice/` — and it hands the new
binding zero wire-round-trip requirement. `Cano

title: kuilt-warp: loadRejectsModuleWithOversizeInitialMemory's fixture also violates the no-max rule, so it cannot attribute the rejection
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice C). A test that cannot fail for the reason its name gives.

## The gap

`WasmRuntimeConformanceSuite.loadRejectsModuleWithOversizeInitialMemory`
(`kuilt-warp-test/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/warp/test/WasmRuntimeConformanceSuite.kt:132`)
asserts only `assertFailsWith<WasmLoadException>`. Its fixture violates **two** rules at once.

`OVERSIZE_INITIAL_MEMORY` (`WasmKernelFixtures.kt:89`) encodes memory limits as
`0x05, 0x03, 0x01, 0x00, 0x20` — section 5, flags `0x00` (**no max declared**), min `0x20` = 32
pages. So it is simultaneously the no-max violation that `loadRejectsModuleDeclaringMemoryWithNoMax`
tests and an oversize initial. An implementation that never checks the initial size still throws
`WasmLoadException` via the no-max guard, and this test stays green.

Contrast the neighbouring `loadRejectsModuleWithImports` (`:109`), whose KDoc explicitly reasons
"the capability violation is the only possible rejection" and then **asserts the message**. This
one does neither.

## The fixture's KDoc makes a claim the test does not check

> Rejected on the initial size (checked before the max/no-max guards on every impl).

That happens to be true right now — `ChicoryWasmRuntime.kt:199` and `BrowserWasmRuntime.kt:116`
both check initial first — but it is a statement about implementation ordering that nothing
enforces. Reorder either guard and the comment silently becomes false while the suite stays green.

## Note: the property may be structurally unisolatable

The wasm spec requires `min <= max` for limits validity, so any module with `initial > 16` and an
explicit max also has `max > 16` and trips the oversize-max guard. There is no fixture that
isolates the initial check.

title: kuilt-deal: the scheme TCK's security-bearing properties all pin the benign branch — verify* is accept-only and uncalled, and nothing asserts ciphertext != plaintext
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice C). Two properties in `CommutativeSchemeConformanceSuite`, both of which
a degenerate scheme passes.

## 1. `verifyAcceptsHonestTransitions` pins the accept branch of a predicate nobody calls

`kuilt-deal-test/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/deal/test/CommutativeSchemeConformanceSuite.kt:114`
asserts `verifyEncrypt`/`verifyStrip` **accept** an honest transition. There is no property that
they **reject** a forged one.

Both shipped schemes return `true` unconditionally — `SraScheme.kt:36-38`,
`XorKeystreamScheme.kt:47-49`. And a repo-wide grep for `verifyEncrypt|verifyStrip` finds **zero
production call sites**: `DealSession` computes proofs (`DealSession.kt:127`, `:195`, `:235`) and
applies remote ops through `deck.applyRemote(...)` without ever verifying one.

So the suite's only cheat-detection property pins the one branch of a predicate that is
(a) unconditionally true in every implementation and (b) never consulted by production. This is the
corollary from #2247 in its strongest form: *forcing a predicate always-true proves it is
CONSULTED, never SUFFICIENT* — here it is not even consulted.

`XorKeystreamSchemeConformanceTest`'s KDoc advertises "honest-transition verification" as covered
contract, which reads as more than it is.

## 2. Nothing asserts the ciphertext differs from the plaintext

No property states `encrypt(m, k) != m`. A scheme whose `encrypt` is the identity for *some* key
passes everything: round-trip inverts, commutativity holds trivially, strip-order is free, and
`distinctKeysProduceDistinctCiphertexts` (`:80`) compares **two** keys — so a degenerate key `a`
alongside a healthy key `b` still yields different ciphertexts and the test is green.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice B). Small, latent, and a three-line fix — filed because the sibling suite in the same package already has the guard and this one does not.

## The unenforced floor

`QuiltedConformanceSuite.samples()`'s KDoc: *"[samples] must return at least **three distinct** values for the associativity and absorption checks to be meaningful."*

Nothing asserts it. All four laws quantify over `samples()`, so a binding returning `listOf(x)` — or `listOf(x, x, x)` — passes `pieceIsIdempotent`, `pieceIsCommutative`, `pieceIsAssociative` and `pieceIsLeastUpperBound` having compared one value with itself.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice C). The `CommutativeScheme` analogue of the Bolt finding: the TCK
cannot reach the failure, and neither can the integration harness.

`CommutativeSchemeConformanceSuite` calls `newScheme()` **once per test** and draws every key from
that single instance:

- `encryptionIsCommutative` — `kuilt-deal-test/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/deal/test/CommutativeSchemeConformanceSuite.kt:50`
- `multiLayerDealRecoversPlaintextRegardlessOfStripOrder` — same file, `:62`

- `SraScheme` — `PRIME` is a `companion object` constant, so every instance shares the group.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

title: conformance: RoomFanoutIsolationConformanceSuite tests only the egress half — a non-member's frame ENTERING a room is unasserted
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice A).

## The gap

`RoomFanoutIsolationConformanceSuite` exists to pin **structural per-room isolation**. All four of its properties test isolation in the **egress** direction only — a broadcast originating at the *server room seam* must not reach a non-member:

- `broadcastOnRoomReachesOnlyRoomMembers:149` — `serverRoom7.broadcast(payload)`
- `perRoomPeersReflectsOnlyRoomMembers` — roster shape only
- `closingOneRoomDoesNotAffectSibling:239` — `serverRoom9.broadcast(cPayload)`
- `rejectedConnectionIsStructurallyExcluded:280` — `serverRoom7.broadcast(payload)`

Client-side sends appear only as registration signals (`muxA.channel("table-7").broadcast(byteArrayOf())`) and **nothing ever asserts where a client's frame lands**. Two obligations are therefore missing:

1. **Ingress from a non-member.** A `NamedMux` client multiplexes many channels over one connection, so a client admitted to `table-7` can put a frame on the `table-9` channel at will. Nothing asserts it is dropped — neither from `table-9`'s fanout nor from `serverRoom9.incoming`.
2. **Ingress from a *rejected* peer.** `rejectedConnectionIsStructurallyExcluded` asserts only that the rejected client receives zero frames and is absent from `peers`. It never asserts that the rejected client's own frame fails to reach the room's members or the hub's own `incoming` — which is the direction an authorizer exists to stop.

## Why nobody wrote them

`MuxServerLoom`'s design makes both unrepresentable in the reference: *"A connection joins a room when its first frame arrives on that room's channel AND `authorizer` grants admission"* ([`MuxServerLoom.kt:22`](../blob/main/kuilt-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/core/MuxServerLo

body:

title: kuilt-core: ScopedCloseable._closed is an unguarded var, so onClose() can run twice under a concurrent close()
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found auditing `CloseableLifecycleConformanceSuite` for #2247. A production defect in `:kuilt-core`, not a test gap — but the reason it survives is a test gap, which is why it belongs to that audit.

## The defect

`ScopedCloseable` (`kuilt-core/.../ScopedCloseable.kt`) guards its close with a plain field:

```kotlin
private var _closed = false

final override fun close() {
    if (_closed) return
    _closed = true
    onClose()
    ownJob.cancel()
}

title: kuilt-conformance: RaftStorageConformanceSuite never round-trips LogEntry's isNoOp/config/dedupKey, SnapshotMeta.config, or a snapshot overwrite
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice B). Sibling of the reopen gap; this one needs no new fixture, only assertions.

## Three records the TCK stores and never reads back

**1. `LogEntry` has six fields. The suite only ever writes three.** Every entry in `RaftStorageConformanceSuite` is built as `LogEntry(index = …, term = …, command = …)`, leaving `isNoOp = false`, `config = null`, `dedupKey = null` in all ~20 constructions. `grep -rn "isNoOp\|dedupKey\|ConfigPayload" kuilt-conformance/` returns **zero hits**.

| dropped | consequence |
|---|---|
| `isNoOp` | the §5.4.2 election no-op restores as application data and is delivered to `RaftNode.committed` — the app applies a command nobody proposed |
| `config` | a §6 config entry restores as a normal entry, so it is **not adopted on append** (the cardinal §6 rule) — the node comes back under the wrong cluster membership |
| `dedupKey` | §8 client-serial dedup is lost — a client command is re-applied after restart |

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2247 (audit slice B). The `RaftStorage` analogue of #2240.

## The gap

`RaftStorage`'s own KDoc opens: *"Durable state that a Raft node must persist to **survive restarts**… All writes must be synchronised to stable storage before the corresponding RPC reply is sent."* That is the entire reason the interface exists.

`RaftStorageConformanceSuite` has exactly one abstract member — `newStorage()`, documented to return a **fresh, empty** instance. Every read-back in all 24 properties is off the *same live object* that just took the write. Nothing in the suite ever obtains a second handle onto the same medium.

- an adapter that buffers every write in a `HashMap` and flushes on `close()` — or never — passes **100%** of the suite;
- an adapter whose write is an `INSERT` with no `COMMIT` passes;
- an adapter on `NSUserDefaults` without `synchronize()` — the shape `RaftStorage.saveTermAndVotedFor`'s KDoc warns about **by name** — passes.

`InMemoryRaftStorage` (`kuilt-raft/.../InMemoryRaftStorage.kt`) is the only implementation in the tree and the only subclass of the suite. title: kuilt-session: the lobby's became-host/heartbeat signals are pinned to the host as of awaitRoom entry
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Two residual gaps in `SeamElectionLobby.awaitRoom`, both surfaced (and deliberately left) while landing #1483 / PR #2287. Neither is a regression from that PR — one is pre-existing, one is a known limit of the discriminator it added.

## 1. The lobby heartbeat watches the host as of `awaitRoom` **entry**, forever

`SeamElectionLobby.awaitRoom` passes `coElectorLostSignal(setOf(host.value))` — `host.value` is read **once**, when the call starts. In a 3+-peer lobby where the elected host `H` leaves and a *different* peer `H2` (not self) becomes host:

- the promotion signal does not fire (`electHost(peers) != selfId`);
- the heartbeat detector keeps monitoring `H`, which is gone;
- if `H2` then goes **silent-but-present** (the #1478/#1480 condition — `peers` still lists it, `state` stays `Woven`), nothing detects it and `awaitRoom` suspends past the freeze/commit window.

The same read makes the signal outright vacuous when `host.value == selfId` at entry: `watched = monitored - selfId` is empty, so `coElectorLostSignal` takes its `awaitCancellation()` branch for the whole call.

Fix shape: make the signal track `host` reactively — restart the per-peer detector when `host` changes, and suspend rather than go permanently vacuous while `host == selfId`.

## 2. A lobby **constructed after** the host left is indistinguishable from weave-in

#1483's discriminator is history: `awaitRoom` reports `BecameHost` only once the lobby has observed some *other* peer as the elected host. That history is lobby-scoped (recorded from `electLobby` time), which covers the read-`host.value`-then-call-`awaitRoom` window.

title: Three more unshielded best-effort teardowns have the #1834 shape — mDNS accept loop, voter redial, joiner resume
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1834 was fixed in `MeshSeam` (#1845) and the rule restated in `CLAUDE.md` (#2285). Doing that restatement
I swept production `*Main` sources for the same shape and found it live elsewhere. The shape is
`runCatchingCancellable` guarding a **teardown** call (`close`/`leave` — none of which carry a

title: RoomConformanceSuite: a fabric that never admits burns 60s per case and fails with UncompletedCoroutinesError instead of naming the roster it saw
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RoomConformanceSuite` guards most of its cases with a **suspending** roster wait:

```kotlin
val hostRoster = host.roster.first { it.size == 1 }
val joinerRoster = joiner.roster.first { it.isNotEmpty() }
```

If the fabric under test never admits, that predicate is never satisfied, nothing times out, and
the case burns the whole `runTest` wedge backstop before failing with no information about what
went wrong. Measured, by breaking `SeamRoom.admitPeer` so the joiner is never added to the
roster and running `InMemoryRoomConformanceTest.membersAppearUnderTheirOwnMemberName`:

```
TEST: membersAppearUnderTheirOwnMemberName[jvm]  time= 60.383
TYPE: kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncompletedCoroutinesError
  After waiting for 1m, the test body did not run to completion
```

60 s, and the message names neither the room, the roster it did see, nor the assertion that was
about to run. This is the same disease as #1823 — the diagnosis is deleted exactly in the broken
state — by a different mechanism, and it is worse: this is the TCK an implementor runs against a
brand-new fabric, i.e. precisely the population whose fabric does not admit yet. A suite of 13
cases mostly guarded this way is a multi-minute silence.

`CLAUDE.md` already names the fix shape for the Raft sim harness — "bounded `await*` / `settle()`
only", with the `runTest` ceiling as a wedge backstop and never a load-bearing assertion. The same
applies here: the roster wait wants a bounded helper that, on expiry, fails with a named
`AssertionError` quoting the roster it actually observed.

Sites: every `roster.first { … }` / `events.filterIsInstance<…>().first()` in
`kuilt-conformance/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/conformance/RoomConformanceSuite.kt`.

`verifyDocCitations` enforces `<!-- verbatim from <path>#<symbol> -->` and `<!-- condensed from … -->`. It does **not** see a plain line-range comment of the form:

title: Apple targets: PeerId/PlyId/Principal are value classes, so they erase to Any on the Swift boundary
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Measured while investigating #1418. Independent of that issue's outcome — this is a kuilt-side gap that no consumer-side tooling fixes.

## The gap

`PeerId`, `PlyId` and `Principal` are `@JvmInline value class`es. Across the Kotlin/Native → Objective-C boundary they erase, so a Swift consumer sees `Any` rather than a distinct type. Verified by building a real `iosSimulatorArm64` framework exporting `:kuilt-core` and typechecking Swift probes against the generated header.

The erasure is **not** something a consumer can tool their way out of — it is present with and without the Swift-interop layer #1418 evaluates, because it happens when the ObjC header is generated, upstream of anything a consumer applies in their own module.

## Why it matters

These are identity types — the whole point is that a `PeerId` is not interchangeable with a `PlyId` or a bare `String`. On the Swift side that distinction is gone: `seam.peers` hands back a set of `Any`, and nothing stops a caller passing the wrong one. Every guarantee the Kotlin type system gives is dropped exactly at the boundary where an unfamiliar consumer needs it most.

This lands now rather than hypothetically: `:kuilt-nw` is real appleMain surface, so Swift consumers are imminent.

## What to work out

No settled design — hence no prescribed fix. The options worth costing:

1. Accept it and document the Swift-side shape in `docs/usage.md`, so a consumer at least knows what they will see.
2. Expose Apple-facing wrapper types (a real `class`/`data class` per identity) on the appleMain surface, and convert at the edge.
3. Change the identity types themselves — almost certainly not worth it; the value-class representation is right for every other target.

title: A mutation receipt that adds a module reds on the BOM, not on the guard under test
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while proving `verifyModuleTable` (#2265). Not specific to that guard — it bites any receipt of the same shape.

**Fixed in #2296.** The receipt shape is now a flag, not an edit:

```
./gradlew <theGuardUnderTest> -PguardProbeModule=:kuilt-zzz-probe
```

`settings.gradle.kts` includes the probe against a directory under `build/`; `kuilt-bom` exempts the same property, so configuration succeeds and the guard under test is the only thing left that can fail. No tracked file is edited, so there is nothing to revert and a probe cannot be committed. Full receipts, and two corrections to what this body originally said, are in [the fix comment](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2272#issuecomment-5274643136).

**The hazard.** The natural way to prove a guard notices a new module is "add one to `settings.gradle.kts`, watch the build go red". It does go red. It reds on the **wrong thing** — and the red *names your probe*, which is what makes it so easy to tick off. Two things pre-empt the guard, in this order:

1. **Gradle refuses to configure a project whose directory does not exist** — `Configuring project ':kuilt-zzz-probe' without an existing directory is not allowed` (Gradle 9.4.1). *This body originally missed this one, and so its prescribed workaround below was insufficient.*
2. Then `kuilt-bom/build.gradle.kts`'s `check(unaccounted.isEmpty())` fails at **configuration time**, before any task executes: `Modules neither published (apply kuilt.publish / kuilt.kmp-library) nor listed as deliberatelyUnpublished …: [:kuilt-zzz-probe]`.

Either way: zero evidence about the guard under test. That is the "read a red's **shape**, not just its presence" failure `CLAUDE.md`'s fixture-configuration section war

title: kuilt-nw/module.md points at the internal NwNativeLib.jvmAvailability; there is no public JVM availability probe
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while reviewing #2261's `:kuilt-nw` module-table row, which had faithfully copied the error.

[`kuilt-nw/module.md:69`](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/kuilt-nw/module.md#L69) tells a reader to "Probe `NwNativeLib.jvmAvailability()`" before using the desktop-JVM bridge off macOS. That symbol is not reachable:

- `internal interface NwNativeLib : Library` (`kuilt-nw/src/jvmMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/nw/NwNativeLib.kt:35`), so its companion's `jvmAvailability()` is internal too;
- `public class BridgeNwApi internal constructor(…)` (`BridgeNwApi.kt:100`) — the other candidate — cannot be constructed from outside either.

So there is **no public JVM-side availability probe at all**. A consumer following the doc gets an unresolved reference; a consumer who wants to branch gracefully rather than catch has nothing to call. `nwHost`/`nwJoin` do fail fast with an actionable `IllegalStateException` off macOS, which is why this is not urgent.

**Why `needs-design` rather than a doc fix.** Two defensible resolutions and they are not the same decision:

1. **Expose a public probe** — e.g. `public fun nwJvmAvailability(): FabricAvailability` delegating to the existing internal one. This is the shape the doc already promises, and it matches `Loom.availability()`'s role elsewhere in the contract. But it is new public API on a pre-1.0 fabric, and it publishes a capability — per the in-tree lesson, publishing a capability value subscribes you to every conformance case selected on it.
2. **Correct the doc** to describe the fail-fast contract instead, and say plainly that graceful branching is not available on the JVM bridge.

#2261 took the third, narrowest option for its own row — dropped the parenthetica

title: build/core: promote freshPeerId() into :kuilt-core and add a LoomDefaults home (#1430 slice 1)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

First slice of #1430 (uniform Loom construction, option (b) — [decision](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1430#issuecomment-5263468214)). **Blocks every per-fabric slice**, so it lands alone and first.

## Why

`#1430`'s survey found `freshPeerId()` privately duplicated in **three** modules, and no shared home for the universal defaults each fabric factory is about to reference. Both have to exist in `:kuilt-core` before any fabric can adopt the convention, or the seven per-fabric PRs each invent their own.

## Scope

1. Promote `freshPeerId()` to `:kuilt-core` as `public`, and delete the three private copies, repointing their callers.
2. Add a `LoomDefaults` constants home in `:kuilt-core` carrying at least `WEAVE_TIMEOUT: Duration`. KDoc the value with its rationale — per this repo's convention a bare number in prose rots the moment the constant moves.

Nothing else. No fabric factories in this PR.

## Watch out

- `:kuilt-core` must stay free of fabric-specific imports — the dependency arrow never points back into it.
- `explicitApi()` is enforced: the promoted declarations need explicit `public`.
- `freshPeerId()` is randomness. It is a *seam-identity* mint rather than an injected simulation input, so promoting it as-is is fine, but do **not** widen it into a general-purpose RNG helper, and do not let it become the excuse for an un-injected `Random` elsewhere.
- Three copies may have drifted. Diff them before collapsing; if they differ, say which behaviour won and why.

## Done when

One `public` `freshPeerId()` and one `LoomDefaults` in `:kuilt-core`, zero private copies remaining (`git grep freshPeerId` proves it), and a full `./gradlew build` green.

Part of #1430.

title: kuilt-bolt: BoltDecorator's dot frontier is not persisted across a restart — the trade, and when to revisit
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. Split out of #2254, which decided it rather than deferring it silently.

## The decision, and why it is written down

`BoltDecorator`'s `DotFrontier` — which suppressed inserts move from — is **not persisted**. A new
process starts with an empty frontier, exactly as it already starts with an empty removal window,
because "nothing is rebuilt on open" is the rule a bolt's unbounded archive forces.

The cost is the same bounded one-off the shipped design already accepts: **one extra copy of each
peer's live log per process start**, after which the frontier has re-learned everything it needs and
suppression is total again. It does not compound, and it does not scale with the archive.

Persisting it is cheap to *write* — the frontier is small and trivially serialisable, a few thousand
`(replica, first, last)` triples — and that cheapness is the trap. What it actually buys is a second
durable thing sitting beside the archive that has to stay consistent with it **across a crash**. A
frontier flushed after an append that did not land claims dots the archive does not hold, and those
inserts are then suppressed forever: a lost record, which is the one error direction this module
does not allow itself. Getting that right means ordering the two writes, or reconciling them on
open, which is a durability design — not a serialisation one.

## Reopen trigger

Revisit if any of these becomes true:

- a deployment restarts its archive process often enough that "one extra copy of every peer's log per
  start" is a measurable share of archive growth (a supervisor crash-looping, a serverless-style
  lifecycle, a phone-side archive killed by the OS);
- the per-start cost stops being bounded — e.g. a peer's offered l

title: kuilt-bolt: promote 'a resume from beyond a hole still reports it' into BoltConformanceSuite
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`BoltConformanceSuite.resumingFromTheHoleReachesTheSameVerdictRatherThanACleanTail`
drives one cursor: the **start** of the hole, i.e. the offset the `All` verdict
just handed back. Its own KDoc lists what it cannot reach, and one of those is
now known to be a real cross-backend agreement:

**A consumer that resumes from the FAR side of a lost segment.** The retention
shape — it read those records, then the segment holding them was swept — not an
exotic corruption. All three backends answer `Truncated(holeStart, MissingRegion)`
today, and each for a different reason:

- `InMemoryBolt` prunes on its own exact extent, so the pre-hole segment is
  prunable and the minus-one boundary read is what catches it;
- `PosixMappedBolt` prunes on a **derived** extent, inflated by the hole;
- `MappedBolt` (after #2236) prunes on the **successor's** `baseOffset`, which is
  inflated the same way.

So the property holds on all three but is pinned on **one** — `MappedBoltPruningTest.aResumeFromBeyondAHoleStillReportsIt`,
added in #2264 because promoting it needs a fixture hook every subclass
implements and that did not belong in a perf PR.

**What to do:** lift it into `BoltConformanceSuite`, reusing `newDiscontinuousBolt`
plus a way for the suite to learn the offset just past the hole (the fixture
already knows it; the suite does not). Then drop the JVM-only copy.

**Why it is worth the hook:** the three backends reach the same answer by three
different mechanisms, only one of which is checked. That is the exact shape #2240
was — three backends, three reasons, one of them wrong.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while writing #2217's `kuilt-bolt/module.md`.

`verifyDocCitations` builds its `mdFiles` list by walking **only** `docs/` and `Writerside/`:

```kotlin
val mdFiles = docRoots.flatMap { root -> root.walkTopDown().filter { … it.extension == "md" … } }

Two things to fix together, since either alone still leaves a silent pass:

1. Add each subproject's `module.md` to `mdFiles`.
2. Add those files to the task's **inputs**, or a drifted citation stays `UP-TO-DATE` green. `srcRoots` covers `<module>/src`, not `<module>/module.md`.
