title: kuilt-bolt: suppress archived inserts from an O(authors) dot frontier, not a bounded identity window
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. Follow-up from #2252 (task #2216), where the option below was named and deliberately not built.

## The residual

`BoltDecorator` suppresses already-archived operations with a **bounded, LRU** window of `LogOp` identities (`dedupWindow`, default 65,536). LRU means a working set that fits in the window yields zero duplicates however long gossip runs. It does not bound the case where the **aggregate offered working set exceeds the window**: past that point the archive grows by roughly `ΣM_p − dedupWindow` operations per anti-entropy round, forever.

The window is shared across every peer *and* the local export stream, so the operative quantity is the aggregate, not any one peer's log. At `DEFAULT_MAX_LOG_RECORDS = 10_000` a phone's live log sits near 10k–20k ops, so the default is exceeded at roughly 4–7 gossiping phones. Raising `dedupWindow` moves the cliff; it does not remove it, and it is memory sized against an archive that is unbounded by construction.

## The option not taken

**Inserts — the bulk of any log — can be suppressed completely in O(authors), with no per-op memory at all.** An insert mints exactly one causal `Dot`, so "have I archived this insert?" is answerable from a frontier the decorator accumulates itself as it appends:

- a `VersionVector` high-water of archived dots per author, plus
- a small above-floor gap set for dots received out of order, which drains into the high-water as the gaps fill.

That is the same shape `Quilter` already folds and that `Rga` exposes as `causalFloor()` / `causalDots()` — cited as prior art for the *structure*, not as an API the decorator would call. `BoltDecorator` must not reach for a live CRDT: `forbidBoltRejoiningTheLattice` bans the token

title: crdt: DotContextTest's witnessing-equivalence generator can never produce duplicate dots
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`DotContextTest`'s randomised equivalence test (`witnessing` vs folding `add`) builds its input with `List(...).shuffled(random).toSet()`. The `.toSet()` guarantees **distinct** seqs in every trial.

With distinct sorted seqs, `witnessing`'s guard `seqs[index] <= frontier + 1` degenerates to `== frontier + 1`, and the `maxOf(frontier, seqs[index])` is a no-op. So the duplicate-absorbing arm — the code the inline comment says exists for duplicates — is **dead in every trial**.

Duplicate input is expressible and reachable: `witnessing` takes a `Collection<Dot>`, `ORSet.removeAllPatch` feeds it via `flatMap`, and `DotContext.of(vararg)` is public.

The existing non-vacuity floor (`cloudyCases > 190`) measures **gaps**, which is the right property for the cloud arm but structurally cannot see this one — a clean example of a floor being satisfied while the interesting case is missed.

**Fix:** drop the `.toSet()` (the fold is duplicate-safe — `add` is idempotent), or add one deterministic trial with a duplicated dot.

Found by a Fable review of the #2208 arc. The implementation is correct — I verified `[1,1,3]`, `[1,2,2,3]` by hand against the fold — this is a test-coverage gap, not a defect.

title: Audit every conformance suite for properties the in-memory reference satisfies for free
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Generalises the finding in #2240, which is about to close with #2244 and would otherwise take the question with it.

## The shape

> **A conformance property is only as strong as the weakest failure the REFERENCE implementation can reach.**

When the in-memory reference makes a failure structurally impossible, nobody writes the property for it — the suite goes green, and **every real backend then has to invent the check on its own.**

The evidence in #2240 is unusually strong, because it is a controlled experiment nobody designed. #2213 and #2214 were implemented **in parallel, by two workers who never saw each other's code**, from the same plan and the same `BoltConformanceSuite`. Adversarial review found the *identical* defect in both: a replay crossing from one segment to the next never checked that the next segment's `baseOffset` continued where the previous one stopped, so a missing segment yielded a history with a silent hole, offsets that jumped, and a **`CleanTail` verdict**. Two out of two independent implementers missed it, because `InMemoryBolt`'s segments are an in-process list that cannot lose an element.

Investigating #2244 turned up the sharper version: `InMemoryBolt` does not merely fail to *reach* that failure, it would not **detect** it either. Its `check(header.baseOffset == snapshot.baseOffset)` compares a header against its own bookkeeping, so both sides jump together when a segment is lost. The reference implementation carried the same bug, invisibly, as the thing it was the reference for.

## What to do

Audit each suite by asking one question per property: **which branch of this property does the reference implementation reach for free, and which failure can it not construct at all?**

title: kuilt-bolt: a failed msync is invisible — both mmap backends degrade to async silently
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Both mmap backends (#2213 JVM/Android, #2214 Apple) agree — deliberately, and correctly — that a
failed `msync` returns `AppendResult.Written` rather than `Failed`. The frame **is** in the archive:
whole, CRC-valid, and visible to every reader of the file. `Failed` means "the ops are lost" and its
remedy is to re-feed them, which would write a second copy of a record already on disk.

What neither backend does is tell anyone the flush failed. A `forceOnAppend`/`synchronous` bolt
whose volume refuses to flush **silently degrades to the asynchronous guarantee**, and the consumer
that asked for durability has no way to find out. Today the failure is caught and dropped in both
implementations.

That is a gap rather than a decision, and it is the same gap in both, so it wants one answer:

- `AppendResult` has no "written, but not durable" shape. A fourth variant is a public API change.
- `BoltAvailability` has `Unknown(reason)` — documented for exactly "the backend cannot report
  ground truth right now" — but `availability()` is not consulted after an append, so a consumer
  would have to poll it to notice.
- A flush failure is also *sticky* in a way an append failure is not: on Linux an `EIO` from
  `msync`/`fsync` may be reported once and then cleared, so a backend that drops it has destroyed
  the only notification that will ever arrive.

Whatever shape is chosen must land on **both** backends together, which is why this is filed rather
than answered in either PR. Both carry a comment at the swallow site pointing here.

Related: #2240 (the other cross-backend contract question left open by the same pair of PRs).
lastComment:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Decided: the signal is sticky state on the bolt, and it reports deviation from the level *this backend* promised — not absolute durability.**

### Why not on `AppendResult` (options 1 and 2 in the body)

title: kuilt-bolt: decide whether a mapped bolt's append should block its caller
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. Raised by the adversarial review of #2234 (`PosixMappedBolt`), deferred rather than
changed blind because it alters `append`'s back-pressure semantics.

## What happens today

`PosixMappedBolt.append` is `suspend`, but every syscall on its path runs **on the caller's thread,
under an atomicfu `reentrantLock`**:

- rolling a segment does a real `write(2)` of up to `segmentFrameBytes` zeroes (1 MiB at the shipped
  default) — deliberately, because `ftruncate` would defer the allocation to a page-touch that is a
  `SIGBUS` on a full volume;
- a synchronous bolt then does an `msync(MS_SYNC)` per append.

`limitedParallelism(1)` confinement as a mutex, and nothing inside the locked section suspends), and
a single writer is the correct shape for an append-only file.

Moving the syscalls off the caller's thread by adding an injected dispatcher would not change the
serialization — the lock would still be the bottleneck — it would only change *which* thread waits.
The change that actually helps is the other one CLAUDE.md explicitly allows: **a single dedicated
writer coroutine draining a `Channel`**. That is a real design change, because it decides what
`append` does when the writer falls behind — suspend the caller, drop, or grow unboundedly — and
each answer is a different contract for a *best-effort* archive.

title: kuilt-bolt: MappedBolt.replay reads the whole archive even for a FromOffset resume
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`MappedBolt.replay` (#2213) reads **every** segment file, whatever the scope. For
`ReplayScope.FromOffset` — the documented resume cursor — that makes a poll-and-resume
consumer O(whole archive) per round, so a decorator that resumes after each batch is
quadratic in the archive's size.

`InMemoryBolt` prunes at segment granularity because it holds each segment's `baseOffset`
and frame extent in memory. `MappedBolt` does not: on reopen it deliberately scans only the
newest segment, so the earlier segments' base offsets are on disk and nowhere else.

The fix is cheap and already available in the format: every segment header carries an
absolute `baseOffset`, and the header is a **fixed size** for a given `BoltArchiveFormat`.
So a `FromOffset` replay can read `headerBytes` from each file — not the file — and skip
any segment whose successor's `baseOffset` is at or below the cursor. That is the same
predicate `InMemoryBolt.skippable` applies, computed from the bytes rather than from memory.

Two things to get right:

- **Only the last segment has no successor**, so it is never prunable — which is correct, its
  extent is not knowable from a header alone.
- Pruning must stay scope-gated. For `ReplayScope.All` the header pass is pure overhead, and
  for `Arrived`/`InsertsAbove` no offset predicate applies.

Not urgent while the only consumer is a test: v1 is correct, just not cheap. It becomes
load-bearing when Task 6's decorator starts resuming from a stored cursor.

Deferred deliberately in #2213; see `MappedBolt`'s class KDoc.

title: kuilt-bolt: a chunked-IndexedDB backend for wasmJs
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. The deferred alternative from #2215, filed in the same turn as the decision to defer it.

## Why this is more tractable than #2215 implies

#2215 frames wasm as "no filesystem exists". True — but wasm does have durable storage, and **this repo already ships a working adapter for it**: [`IndexedDbDurableStore`](../blob/main/kuilt-otel/src/wasmJsMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/otel/IndexedDbDurableStore.kt), landed by #801, 239 lines and tested in `wasmJsTest`. It has a real durability point — `write` suspends until the IDB transaction fires `complete`, not until the `put` request succeeds.

So a wasm bolt is not blocked on inventing a storage layer. Scoping it out of v1 is an effort call, not a capability one.

## The design questions

1. **Segments → IDB keys.** The mmap backends chunk into fixed-size segments so a mapped window stays fixed-size and eager pre-allocation stays affordable (one allocation per segment, not per append). IndexedDB has neither constraint. Does a bolt segment survive as the storage unit — one `Uint8Array` value per segment, keyed by `baseOffset` — or does the chunking exist only to serve mmap?

2. **Pre-allocation has no analogue, and that is a simplification, not a gap.** The SIGBUS hazard driving eager physical pre-allocation on both mmap backends does not exist here: IDB either stores the value or rejects the transaction. That removes the zero-filled-region hazard too — but the frame codec's defences against it (CRC over the length prefix, `MINIMUM_BODY_BYTES`) are shared and stay.

3. **Quota is the exhaustion mode**, and it is the one `BoltAvailability.Unavailable` was written for. `QuotaExceededError` on a transaction is the natural `newExhaustedBolt` fixture, and i

title: otel: WarpMetricExporter has no write mutex — two concurrent increments can lose one durably
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`WarpMetricExporter` encodes under `lock` and then persists **outside** it, with no mutex anywhere in the class:

```kotlin
public suspend fun incrementSum(key: MetricKey, by: Long = 1L): MetricExportResult {
    val encoded = lock.withLock { … ; encodeSums() }   // snapshot taken here
    return persistSums(encoded, key)                    // …written here, unserialized
}
```

Two concurrent `incrementSum` calls therefore encode in one order and land in another. A encodes `{k:1}`, B encodes `{k:2}`, B's write lands, then A's — and the store holds `{k:1}`. B's increment is durably lost while `incrementSum` returned `MetricExportResult.Success`, which its KDoc defines as "durably written to the local store".

**This is the third instance of one defect class**, and the only one still open:

- `WarpSpanExporter` — fixed in #1053 with a narrow `ioMutex` over the durable section, which is sound there *because* it re-encodes inside the section.
- `WarpLogRecordExporter` — fixed in #2187 with `writeMutex` over the whole write turn, because its bytes are encoded from already-mutated fields before `commit` is called.
- `WarpMetricExporter` — **unfixed.** Its shape matches the span exporter's (one key, one encode, one write), so the narrow form is likely the right fix, but the encode must move inside the mutex.

`WarpLogRecordExporter`'s `writeMutex` KDoc already sets out which form applies when; this is the same analysis applied to the third exporter.

## How it was found

Planning [#2208](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2208)'s `clear()`. A metric `clear()` deletes the five keys, and a concurrent `incrementSum` can rewrite one straight afterwards — so the clear is racy for the same reason increments are. T

title: Seam has no way to await delivery — send() returns on acceptance, so a frame sent during shutdown is silently lost
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`Seam.broadcast` (and everything layered on it) returns once the bytes are **accepted**, not once they are **delivered**. There is no `flush` / `awaitDelivered` / `drain` anywhere in kuilt-core, so a caller that must guarantee a frame reached the peer *before* tearing the transport down has no way to express that.

### Where it bites

Fireworks' clean-shutdown contract (ADR-037 §3) says the server emits `server.goingAway` to every connected peer **before** the socket closes. The implementation is:

```
LiveLeaderImpl.broadcastGoingAway → LiveSessionRoster.broadcast → LiveChannel.send → Seam.broadcast
```

`LiveChannel.send`'s own contract already concedes the gap — *"Suspends until the bytes are accepted by the underlying transport."* So the shutdown path returns, Ktor proceeds to close the transport, and kuilt's pump is cancelled with the frame still in it. The frame is silently lost: `send` reported success, nothing threw, and no drop was recorded.

Root-caused in tractat-us/fireworks-compose#4073. Evidence, from a deterministic reproducer (`-Pflaky.repro.dispatcherThreads=2`, which pins `Dispatchers.Default` to 2 threads):

```

53.647 [worker-2 @coroutine#110] PROBE roster.broadcast sent  sessionId=session-c61e92c1-…   ← send() returned cleanly
53.658 [worker-1 @coroutine#52]  action=detached
```

…and **no** corresponding `Sending Frame BINARY` anywhere in the run — the bytes never reached the WebSocket layer. On an unloaded box the pump wins the race and it passes, which is why this only ever showed up under CI contention.

`WebSocketVoterMeshFormationTimeoutTest.formationTimeoutCancelsPumpsAndClosesPartialSeams` failed during a full local `./gradlew build detektAll --max-workers=6`. **Not a timeout and not a hang** — it failed in **0.654 s** with the wrong exception type.

```
java.lang.AssertionError: Expected an exception of class kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException
to be thrown, but was io.ktor.utils.io.ClosedReadChannelException:
Failed to parse HTTP response: the server prematurely closed the connection
	at us.tractat.kuilt.cluster.WebSocketVoterMeshFormationTimeoutTest$…$1.invokeSuspend(WebSocketVoterMeshFormationTimeoutTest.kt:111)

The test asserts a *specific exception type* around a **real** WebSocket dial:

```kotlin
assertFailsWith<TimeoutCancellationException> {
    scope.voterMeshOverWebSockets(voters = voters, httpClient = client, …, formationTimeout = formationTimeout)
}
```

The intended path is: the higher voter's `NeverYieldingSource` never completes the roster, so formation exceeds `formationTimeout` and `withTimeout` throws. That is a **race against the real network stack**. When the box is saturated, the lower voter's dial to `ws://localhost:$port/higher` can fail at the **HTTP upgrade** — the server closes before the client parses the response — and that exception escapes the block first. The assertion then reports a type mismatch, which describes the *symptom* and hides the *cause*.

So the failure is not "the formation timeout didn't work". It is "the connection never got far enough for the timeout to be the thing that fired", reported as though the timeout logic were at fault.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #2193's Phase 3B (PR #2224), found in review of that PR. **Not a correctness problem — unclaimed value.** The KDoc that overclaimed it is corrected on #2224; this issue is the fix itself.

## The hole

`Rga.threadedSequence` is `cache?.sequence` — it reports only a **cache-threaded** order. It returns `null` for an instance whose `sequence` lazy has already been forced by a *plain read*. So `insertAfter` / `insertAllAfter` pass `base = null` and thread nothing, on the archetypal shape:

```kotlin
log = log.insertAfter(a, tail, v).first
render(log.toList())      // forces `sequence` — Θ(N) computeSequence
// next turn: threadedSequence == null, nothing threads, Θ(N) again, forever
```

Only chains warmed via `removeAt` / `removeFirst` / `insertAt` benefit. `WarpLogRecordExporter` is one of those, so #2193's measured ~20% win is real — but nothing else in the library gets it.

**Why it is sound to widen:** the guard's premise is `base == computeSequence()` of the *current* state. A forced lazy satisfies that exactly as a threaded one does.

Read the lazy without forcing it, via `kotlin.Lazy.isInitialized()` (common stdlib, KMP-safe):

public val sequence: List<RgaId> get() = sequenceLazy.value

title: crdt: Rga.compactedIds is public, Fugue.compactedIds is private — the same concept, two visibilities
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while writing #2211's `OpLogCrdt` contract test, which needed to reach the compacted-id set on both CRDTs and could only do it on one.

`Rga.compactedIds` is `public`. `Fugue.compactedIds` is `private`. They are the same concept — the ids a `Compact` has suppressed — on the two op-log CRDTs that are meant to be interchangeable behind `OpLogCrdt`.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

`explicitApi()` means each visibility is a deliberate declaration, so this reads as an intentional asymmetry when it is almost certainly drift. A consumer that writes against `Rga` and then swaps in `Fugue` — exactly the swap `OpLogCrdt` (#2211) exists to enable — hits a wall with no stated reason for it.

It also cuts against #2211's own argument. That issue settled on a shared contract precisely so per-type ad-hoc access stops being the way to inspect an op-log; a public field on one type and a private one on the other is the shape that argument rejects.

## The decision this needs

Not obviously "make `Fugue.compactedIds` public". Three options, and the right one depends on who actually needs it:

1. **Promote `Fugue.compactedIds` to `public`** — symmetric, smallest diff, but adds permanent public surface to close a gap no consumer has yet asked for.
2. **Demote `Rga.compactedIds` to `internal`** — if nothing outside `:kuilt-crdt` reads it, this is the cheaper symmetry and *removes* a commitment. Check consumers first; `:kuilt-quilter`'s `WindowPolicy` reaches for `Rga.tombstones` and may reach for this too.
3. **Put it on `OpLogCrdt`** — if an archive or a window policy genuinely needs it for both types, the contract is where it belongs, not on the concrete classes.

title: otel: evictLeading materialises the whole buffer to read its head — ~0.18 ms/record at the production cap
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`WarpLogRecordExporter.evictLeading` (`WarpLogRecordExporter.kt:1127`) does:

```kotlin
val evicted = log.entries().take(count)
```

`Rga.entries()` is `sequence.filter { … }.map { … }` — **two eager Θ(N) lists**, built in full, before `take(128)` throws almost all of it away.

## Measured

**≈0.18 ms per record at 10,000 ops** on an iPhone XS, Debug K/N ([#2193 comment](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2193#issuecomment-5229084972)) — the third-largest term in the export path, and **fixed by neither of #2193's two candidate tracks**. It is a plain bug, not an algorithmic tradeoff.

## Provenance

Mine, introduced in #2199 (#2194's Task 3) and waved through in planning as "O(N) once per turn, acceptable". It *is* once per turn. It was still the third-largest term.

## The fix, and the API step it needs

Read the leading `count` **visible** ids off `log.sequence` directly and resolve values by id. `insertsById` backs that in O(1) — but it is `internal` to `:kuilt-crdt`, so `:kuilt-otel` cannot reach it. **`Rga.valueAt(id): V` must therefore be added as `public` API**, with the KDoc/`@sample` obligations this repo attaches to public API changes. Budget that step.

**There is no useful fallback.** `log.entries().asSequence().take(count).toList()` looks like one and is not — `entries()` has already built both eager lists before `asSequence()` sees anything, so it recovers ~0%. If the accessor is rejected, drop the change rather than ship a form that buys nothing.

## Plan

Task 2 of `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-otel-export-path-residual.md`.

title: otel: the exporter logs a WARN per evicted record — at the production cap that is one per exported record
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`WarpLogRecordExporter` emits one `logger.warn` per evicted record. At `DEFAULT_MAX_LOG_RECORDS = 10_000` the buffer is full essentially always, so **every exported record evicts one** — the exporter narrates a ring buffer behaving exactly as configured, forever, on the export hot path.

The line was written when eviction was an exceptional event. #2194's batching made it the steady state, and it is an idea that has outlived its purpose.

## Measured

On device (iPhone XS, Debug K/N, post-#2194, 10,000 ops — [#2193 comment](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2193#issuecomment-5229084972)), the whole export path is 3.34 ms/record and the CRDT is only ~51% of it. This logging sits inside the remaining **~58%** alongside the CBOR encode, the two file writes and the amortised window pass. At a 128-record turn that is **128 WARN lines per turn**.

## Do not simply delete it

Silent loss is the inversion #1860 was about. The class KDoc promises "**Every drop is logged** with enough detail to correlate against a backend's log index", and that promise has to be replaced rather than dropped:

- exact counters on `ExporterHealth` — `dropped` and `refused`, kept separate because they are different events (an eviction means the buffer recycled; a refusal means this replica declined to author anything at all, which is what keeps its contribution a downward-closed prefix, #2127);

Rate-limit by **count, not by a clock** — this type owns no `Clock`, and a wall-clock read per eviction is the cost being removed. The counter must start at `-1` so the *first* drop reports: starting at `0` means an exporter that drops fewer th

title: kuilt-bolt 6/7: the decorator — and the gossip path, which is the headline scenario
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt-design.md`. Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt.md`.

 Blocked on #2212.

**This is the task the Fable review saved.** A decorator over the op stream: the CRDT owner publishes the ops it applied, the decorator consumes them. The exporter stays ignorant of archiving and the bolt ignorant of telemetry, so the same decorator serves any `Rga`/`Fugue` owner.

## There are TWO paths and the second is the one that matters

`export()` holds its ops already, returned from `insertAllAfter`/`removeFirst` — a straightforward tee.

**`merge()` produces no op stream.** It is `log = log.piece(remote)` (`mergeTurn`), a state join. **Gossip is how a phone's records reach a server**, so a decorator teeing only `export()` gives a server-side bolt holding the server's own telemetry and **zero phone records** — the exact capability #2210 opens by calling impossible. Teeing only the local path leaves it impossible.

The merge path must publish too, by enumerating `remote`'s operations through `OpLogCrdt.operations()`.

**A conformance test that drives a bare `Rga` stays green while this fails.** The asymmetric-retention property must be exercised through a gossiping exporter.

## Which raises deduplication, and append-only does not give it for free

Anti-entropy re-merges the same remote log repeatedly, so appending `remote`'s ops per round writes **one full copy of the peer's log per round**. The frame's dots cannot dedup a `Remove` (it mints none), so identity needs an `Insert`/`Remove` discriminator on the same id. Cheapest sound design: an in-memory set of appended op identities, rebuilt from the archive's tail on open.

body:

Part of #2210. Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt-design.md`. Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt.md`.

 Blocked on #2212.

`platform.posix` mmap. The interop path is proven in-tree — `NSFileManagerDurableStore` already imports `memcpy`, `rename`, `errno`.

## This backend is not the default on Apple, and the KDoc must say why

- **SIGBUS on page-touch**, as in #2213 — and worse here: a full iOS device is a routine state, not an edge case. Eager physical pre-allocation per segment is **mandatory** on this backend, not advisory.
- **Jetsam.** Mapped dirty pages count against an iOS app's memory footprint; a growing mapped archive on a phone is a way to get the app killed. A phone should retain least anyway — the server is this backend's customer.
- **Data Protection.** A file's protection class can make it unreadable while the device is locked. A background-writing archive needs one chosen deliberately, and this fails only on real hardware.

## Review discipline

**`detektAll` lints nothing in `appleMain`** — detekt's type resolution is JVM-only. Do not cite a green `detektAll` as coverage for this code; review it by eye.

title: kuilt-bolt 3/7: mmap backend — JVM / Android
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt-design.md`. Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt.md`.

 Blocked on #2212.

`FileChannel.map()` → `MappedByteBuffer`. **Synchronous and asynchronous are one mechanism and a flag**: `force()` per append is synchronous, omitting it is asynchronous. Two implementations would be two things to keep in agreement.

## Hazards, all of which belong in KDoc

- **Disk-full under mmap is SIGBUS, not an exception — and unhandled it makes the module's stated failure posture unachievable.** Extending a mapped file, or `ftruncate`ing to segment size (which allocates **sparsely**), defers physical allocation to first page-touch. On a full disk that touch is a SIGBUS on POSIX and an unspecified VM error on the JVM: the process dies, taking the application's logging with it — the one outcome "best-effort" promises to avoid. **Eagerly, physically pre-allocate each segment at roll time — a real write, not `ftruncate`.** External truncation of a mapped file is the same class.
- **Remapping.** A `MappedByteBuffer` is a fixed-size window. Chunk into fixed-size segments rather than remapping one growing file — which is also what makes eager pre-allocation affordable, one allocation per segment rather than per append.
- **Durability is `force()`, not `write()`.** Bytes in a mapped buffer are not durable until msync; the synchronous contract *is* this call.
- **Torn frames.** A crash mid-append leaves a partial frame. Length prefix plus checksum; replay stops at the first frame that does not validate and reports how far it got. **A truncated archive must not throw** — same reasoning as `WarpLogRecordExporter.recover()`.

title: kuilt-bolt 2/7: the module, the Bolt SPI, the frame format, and the conformance suite
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Part of #2210. Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt-design.md`. Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-kuilt-bolt.md`.

## The task

Create `:kuilt-bolt`, the `Bolt<Op>` SPI, the frame format, an `InMemoryBolt`, and the `BoltConformanceSuite` every backend subclasses (per the `SeamConformanceSuite` precedent).

Blocked on #2211 (the op-log surface).

## The format is fixed here and is expensive to change

Each **segment** opens with a magic number, a **format version**, and a self-description of what the archive holds. A format justified by "read by future versions of the code that wrote it" must be able to say which version wrote it.

Each **frame**: append offset · arrival timestamp · **insert-only** dots · a reserved key slot.

**Dots are informational; the append offset is the resume cursor.** A `Remove` mints no dot — it reuses its target `Insert`'s id — so a frame of removes either claims its targets' *old* dots, in which case a resume-from-dot cursor skips it and **replays a removed record as live**, or claims nothing. Dot-scoped replay is therefore **inserts only**.

**Arrival time is not event time.** A delta merged from a peer arrives long after it happened; the KDoc must say so.

**The clock is injected** — never `Clock.System` reached for directly.

## The conformance suite is where the invariant lives

1. Round-trip — appended ops replay identically, in order.
2. **The firewall** — a bolt fed ops including a `Compact` **retains** the ops it suppresses. *Mutation-check it: remove the discard and this must redden.* The safety property of the whole module.

title: epic: :kuilt-bolt — a write-only archive so a server can outlive a phone's forgetting
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

A phone can only keep so much. It holds the last few thousand log lines, and when it runs out of room it forgets the oldest — the right trade on a small disk with a battery. A server has no such problem and could happily keep a year.

**Today it cannot, and the reason is not storage.** When the phone drops a record it also records *that it dropped it*, and that decision travels with the data. The moment the server syncs with the phone, the server forgets the same records. **Retention is a property of the group, not of each machine.**

`:kuilt-bolt` is a bolt of cloth — a rolled-up store of everything woven, kept *beside* the live replica rather than inside it. Operations flow in and never out. Because nothing flows back, its retention is nobody else's business.

## Why the obvious approach does not work

Not "make a second replica with a bigger `maxRecords`". That is defeated by the first sync. `Rga.piece` (`Rga.kt:782`):

```kotlin
val mergedFloor = compactedBelow.ceilWith(other.compactedBelow)   // elementwise MAX
val mergedCompactedIds = compactedIds + other.compactedIds        // UNION
val mergedOps = purgeBelow(purge(rawUnion, mergedCompactedIds), mergedFloor)
```

Suppression is **monotone and contagious**. And it is load-bearing for the phone — it is exactly what stops a peer that still holds the raw `Insert` pushing a forgotten record back in. **Asymmetric retention and "windowing is safe without a causal-stability barrier" are the same knob pulled in opposite directions.** Anything that wants the first must stop being a replica.

## The invariant

> **A bolt consumes operations, never states, and never joins the lattice.**

1. **Fed ops, not deltas.** A `Patch<S>` is a state fragment of the same latt

title: otel: no supported way to reset a WarpTelemetry's persisted log — segment keys are unenumerable and a live buffer rewrites whatever you delete
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

There is no supported way for a consumer to reset a `WarpTelemetry`'s persisted log. Three gaps compose into "you must delete the app."

## 1. Segment keys cannot be enumerated

The exporter keeps its op-log under `otel.logs.idx`, `otel.logs.seg.<n>`, and the legacy `otel.logs`. `DurableStore` offers `read` / `write` / `delete(key)` and nothing else — and `LogSegmentIndex`'s own KDoc states the constraint plainly:

> There is no key-enumeration API, so a segment the index simply forgets is unreachable and unsweepable forever.

A consumer holding a `DurableStore` therefore cannot discover which segment numbers exist, so it cannot `delete` them. `LogSegmentIndex` is `internal`, so it cannot read the index to find out either.

## 2. There is no clear/reset on the exporter

`WarpTelemetry` exposes `spans`, `metrics`, `logs`, and `recover()`. Nothing drops in-memory op-log state.

## 3. Deleting the files out-of-band does not work either

This is the part that makes the first two more than an inconvenience. Removing the directory behind a **live** buffer clears nothing durable: the in-memory op-log still holds every record, and the next captured record rewrites the whole log back to disk. In an app that logs continuously, that race is lost immediately.

So the only reliable consumer-side reset today is: delete the platform directory **and** restart the process, so the deletion lands before `recover()`. That is a startup-flag dance in every consumer that wants it.

## Ask

A supported reset — shape open, but something like `WarpLogRecordExporter.clear()` (or `WarpTelemetry.clear()`) that:

- drops in-memory op-log state, and
- deletes all of its persisted keys — **index-driven, so it knows the segment numbers**, in

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Capturing one log line currently costs **one Θ(N) CRDT append + one CBOR encode of the active segment + two durable file writes**. Every record, synchronously. That is per-record durability, and telemetry does not need it.

`CapturingAppender`'s drain is one record at a time:

```kotlin
scope.launch {
    for (event in events) {          // CapturingAppender.kt:96 — one export() per record
```

and `WarpLogRecordExporter` offers no bulk entry point — `export(record: LogRecord)` is the only door. ("Batch" in that class's KDoc means the store-action list for a *single* record's turn, not a batch of records.)

## Measured on the field hardware

iPhone XS (`iPhone11,2`), iOS 18.7.9, **Debug** Kotlin/Native, real `NSFileManagerDurableStore` — via [`OtelStallProbe`](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/probe/1860-device-insertafter/spike/src/appleMain/kotlin/spike/otel/OtelStallProbe.kt) on branch `probe/1860-device-insertafter`. | ops in log | `insertAfter` | whole `export()` | everything else |
|---|---|---|---|
| 250 | ~0.5 ms | 9.5 ms | **9.0 ms** |
| 7,000 | 12.2 ms | 24.9 ms | 12.7 ms |

> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The problem

`build-jvm` runs long enough that a PR touching a core module reliably risks its own timeout. Three PRs in the #2127 series were **cancelled at ~30 minutes** and went green on a re-run of identical code:

| Run | PR | Elapsed |
|---|---|---|
| 31068319363 | #2171 | cancelled at 30m, still in `:kuilt-scale` tests |

- **Timeline** — what is actually on the critical path, and how much is serialized behind one task.
- **Performance → Task execution** — the biggest *executed* tasks, and the split between `EXECUTED`, `FROM-CACHE` and `UP-TO-DATE`.

title: adoptRemoteSegment moves the layout at build time — a refused segment write leaves a permanently pinned phantom segment
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The defect

`WarpLogRecordExporter.adoptRemoteSegment` mutates the segment layout **while the batch is being built**, before the write that publishes it has been confirmed durable:

```kotlin
val number = nextSegmentNumber++
sealedSegments += number
sealedContents[number] = contentOf(remote, number)
// … then returns Put(segmentKey(number), <the remote log>) and the index write
```

If the (large) segment write is refused while the (small) index write lands, **the index permanently names a key that was never written.** On every subsequent start `readSegment` returns `null` → `SegmentContent.Pinned` → never retirable. The phantom segment costs one index entry and one wasted read per start, forever, after a single transient failure.

That is reachable: `IndexedDbDurableStore` under quota pressure fails large writes while accepting small ones — a segment blob is ~123 KB at `DEFAULT_LOG_SEGMENT_OPS`, an index is tiny.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed in #2127

#2127's PR 4 established exactly this rule for two other layout changes:

- **retirement** — `StoreAction.CommitRetirement` → `applyRetirement`, applied after the ledger write returns;
- **the roll** — `StoreAction.CommitRoll` → `applyRoll`, applied after the covering write returns.

`adoptRemoteSegment` is the remaining one, and it is **pre-existing** — byte-for-byte the same shape on `origin/main`. The PR's fix was deliberately scoped to the mutation its own change had made newly harmful; widening it to a third path during a final fix wave would have been scope creep on a delete-adjacent code path.

title: crdt-test: a RetirementReAssertion.shows predicate written against the other samples satisfies the guard while proving nothing
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Residual from [#2157](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2157), noticed while reviewing [#2165](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2165) and not covered by it. **Latent, not present today** — filed so it is recorded rather than carried in someone's head.

## The gap

#2157's fix is right: ordering cannot express retirement, so the binding supplies `shows: (S) -> Boolean` and `samplesReAssertAfterRetirement` checks it reads **true → false → true** across the three states (plus `!shows(retired.piece(asserted))`, which evaluates it on a freshly joined equal instance to prove it reads the value rather than object identity).

But nothing constrains `shows` to be **about a subject**. A predicate defined in terms of the other samples satisfies every assertion while carrying no information:

```kotlin
shows = { it != retired }                      // true, false, true — passes, proves nothing
shows = { it == asserted || it == reAsserted } // same
```

Both are functions of the *value*, so they satisfy the KDoc's stated contract ("Must be a function of the *value*, not of object identity") — and the freshly-joined check passes too, since `retired.piece(asserted) == retired` by the ascent the guard already established.

## Why it is worth recording

**This is #2157's own shape one level up.** #2157's lesson was that *naming the three states* is not evidence. The residual is that *naming a predicate* is not evidence either, unless the predicate is about a subject rather than about the states. title: A high-export-count :kuilt-otel test fails wasmJsBrowserTest with a misleading 'did not discover any tests'
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The trap

A `:kuilt-otel` test that drives a large number of exports can fail `:kuilt-otel:wasmJsBrowserTest` with:

```
did not discover any tests
```

That message is **misleading**. Tests were discovered and ran. The real cause is log volume: `WarpLogRecordExporter` emits a line per eviction, so a test doing ~10,000 exports emits **more than 1 MB inside a single teamcity service message**, and the task fails while reporting a discovery problem.

## How it was found

Hit while writing byte-measurement tests for #2127. A first draft ran 10,000 exports and broke the wasmJs browser task; a control run at 1,200 exports passed. Same test, same assertions — only the export count differed.

## Why it deserves an issue rather than a note

1. **The error names the wrong thing.** "Did not discover any tests" points at test infrastructure, source-set wiring, or a Karma/browser problem. Nobody reading it would suspect log volume, and the cost of chasing the wrong lead is high — this is a browser task, so the local reproduction loop is slow.
2. **It is silent on other targets.** JVM, Android and native swallow the volume without complaint, so a test can be written, reviewed, and merged, and only red on the wasmJs browser task — often in CI rather than locally.
3. **It scales with a number tests legitimately want to raise.** Bound-checking and byte-measurement tests naturally push export counts up; that is the point of them.

- Cap or throttle the per-eviction log in the exporter (it is `logger.warn` on a path that fires once per record past the cap — arguably too chatty regardless of the test problem).
- Reduce log verbosity under test configuration.

title: WarpMetricExporter encodes under lock and writes outside it — concurrent metric updates can silently drop one another
body:

## The defect

`WarpMetricExporter` encodes under a lock and then **writes outside it**, with no serialization between the encode and the write.

1. an `ioMutex` spanning the durable section, and
2. **re-encoding the latest state *inside* that section** (`lock.withLock { cbor.encodeToByteArray(...) }` nested within `ioMutex.withLock`), with an inline comment saying it is so "no concurrent add is dropped by a stale

title: WarpLogRecordExporter.adoptNumberingOnly has no test coverage — and it is the only producer of unknown segment content
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The gap

`WarpLogRecordExporter.adoptNumberingOnly` has **no test coverage at all** — not a partial gap, not a weak assertion. Nothing in the repo reaches it.

Found while mutation-testing #2127's segment-retirement work: two mutations of a newly-added invariant came back GREEN, and the reason was not that the invariant was unpinnable but that **the only path that can violate it is never executed by any test**.

## Why it matters more than an ordinary coverage hole

`adoptNumberingOnly` is a **recovery** path — it runs when the exporter adopts a peer's segment numbering without adopting its contents. Two properties now depend on it:

- It **clears `sealedContents` while keeping `sealedSegments`**, which is precisely the asymmetry that makes "a segment number with no content entry" representable. #2127's retirement logic must treat unknown content as *keep*; `adoptNumberingOnly` is the one producer of unknown content, and nothing exercises it.
- It is reached only in a recovery/adoption scenario — i.e. exactly the situation where a mistake is least likely to be noticed in normal operation and most likely to cost data.

So the module's most safety-sensitive invariant has its only violating path untested. A future edit to `adoptNumberingOnly` cannot break any test.

## What a test would need to do

Drive an exporter into the adopt-numbering-only branch (a peer's index adopted without its segment contents), then assert:

- every number in `sealedSegments` has a content entry, and unreadable ones are recorded as pinned rather than absent;
- no segment reachable that way is judged retirable;
- a subsequent recovery does not delete anything it could still read.

## Scope

Not blocking #2127 — the retirement cod

title: Test the multi-peer floor-absorption path before #2127's exporter PR lands
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The untested path

#2127's PR 3 teaches `Quilter`'s contiguous-frontier walk to start at `Quilted.causalFloor()`, so a compaction floor no longer collapses an author's delivered frontier to zero and stalls tombstone GC.

Its wiring test is **single-replica**. The path it does *not* exercise is the one the feature exists for:

**A peer that never held the floored ops, absorbing the floor through a delta `piece`, and then `Rga.compact()`'s stability condition becoming satisfiable again end-to-end across a real 2-peer session.**

## Why this is filed rather than blocking PR 3

It is **sound by derivation**, in three steps:

1. **Mint.** A floor entry for author `a` can only originate at `a` — `Rga.dropWindow` filters `dropped` to `it.replicaId == self` before the contiguity walk, and advances only from `compactedBelow[self]` across a contiguous own run. So a floor is always a downward-closed prefix of seqs that author genuinely minted.
2. **Propagate.** `Rga.piece` merges via `compactedBelow.ceilWith(other.compactedBelow)` — a monotone join that invents no entries.
3. **Absorb.** On a floor rise, `cacheAfterFloor` purges `insertsById`/`tombstones` at-or-below it, and `applyInsert`/`applyRemove` both return `this` when `compactedBelow.contains(op.id.dot)`. Absorption is **permanent suppression**, not merely deletion.

So a peer absorbing `{a:5}` without ever seeing `(a,1..5)` is entitled to report `delivered[a] ≥ 5`: "delivered" in the causal-stability barrier means *no op at-or-below this seq will ever be applied here later*, and the floor guarantees that **more strongly** than having applied them — a late raw `(a,3)` is suppressed rather than resurrected.

Also, **no shipped path calls `dropWindow` today**

title: ORMap and Causal don't aggregate causalDots of nested Quilted values — a nested Rga gets an empty frontier and never GCs
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The gap

`ORMap<K, S : Quilted<S>>` and `Causal<S : DotStore<S>>` both hold **nested `Quilted` values** and override **neither** `causalDots()` nor `causalFloor()`.

So a consumer writing `ORMap<String, Rga<X>>` gets an **empty** causal frontier — today, floor or no floor. `Quilter.contiguousFrontier` then computes zero for every author, and `Rga.compact()`'s stability condition can never be satisfied, so tombstone GC never runs for anything held in an `ORMap`.

## Why this is filed separately from #2127

#2127's PR 2 added `causalFloor()` aggregation to the four types that already aggregate `causalDots()` — `LatticeProduct`, `JsonNode.Object`, `JsonNode.Array`, `JsonCrdt`. `ORMap` and `Causal` were correctly left alone by that work, because the hole there is **symmetric and pre-existing**: their `causalDots()` doesn't aggregate either, so adding only a floor aggregation would have been incoherent.

The tell that this is a real gap rather than a design choice: `JsonNode.Object` exists precisely to do **by hand** what `ORMap` does not do generically. Both are string-keyed maps of nested `Quilted` values; one aggregates, the other doesn't.

Aggregating in `ORMap` means deciding what a **removed** key contributes. `ORMap`'s removed entries still carry causal metadata, and whether their nested dots remain "delivered" for frontier purposes determines whether a remove can strand a peer's GC. `Causal` has the same question for its dot-store contents.

title: Quilted.causalDots KDoc has Remove and Compact backwards
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The defect

`Quilted.causalDots`' KDoc describes `Rga`'s implementation as:

> returns its `Insert`/`Remove` op dots and **excludes** `Compact` ops

The code does the opposite on **both** counts. `OpLogEngine.deliveredDots`:

- yields **nothing** for a `Remove` — a tombstone carries no new dot, so `Remove` contributes no delivered dot at all;
- yields the `compactedIds`' dots **for** a `Compact` — the exact opposite of "excludes".

So a reader trying to reason about what a replica reports as delivered gets both halves of the sentence backwards.

## Why it matters now

Pre-existing — present identically on `origin/main`, not introduced by #2127. But #2174 added a paragraph to `Rga.dropWindow` that describes the *correct* behaviour (a floor records no id set, unlike `Compact`, so floored dots vanish from `causalDots()` and the author's contiguous frontier collapses to zero).

The two now visibly contradict each other in the same module. The `dropWindow` paragraph is the accurate one. A reader reconciling them will trust the older, wronger text on the interface, and conclude a `Compact` is invisible to the delivered surface when in fact it is the thing that keeps those dots visible.

That distinction is load-bearing: it is precisely why a *floor* stalls GC where a `Compact` does not.

Correct the `Quilted.causalDots` KDoc to say what `OpLogEngine.deliveredDots` actually does — `Insert` dots plus a `Compact`'s compacted ids; `Remove` contributes nothing — and consider cross-referencing `dropWindow`'s paragraph so the floor case is reachable from the interface doc.

title: CanonicalGoldenVectorTest: the 'regenerate every vector together' rule is destructive for RGA_PRE_FLOOR
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The contradiction

`CanonicalGoldenVectorTest`'s class KDoc carries a blanket rule:

> Regenerate only on a deliberate encoding change, and expect every vector to move together.

`RGA_PRE_FLOOR` (added in #2174) is the one constant for which that instruction is **destructive**. It is a byte-for-byte copy of the pre-#2127 `RGA` vector, and its entire value is that it does **not** move when the encoding moves — it is the only pre-floor blob left in the repo, and the receipt that a pre-#2127 `Rga` frame still decodes.

Regenerating it would launder a real backward-compatibility guarantee into a tautology: the test would compare today's encoder against today's encoder and pass forever, while proving nothing. That is the same laundering failure `constructionsStillHaveTheShapeTheyClaim` exists to catch elsewhere in this same file.

Two things are currently unstated:

1. `RGA_PRE_FLOOR`'s own KDoc records where the bytes came from but **not** that they must never be re-recorded. On a future format change the correct action is to update the *re-encode* assertion (`assertEquals(RGA, hex(ser, decoded))`), leaving the constant itself frozen.
2. `RGA_PRE_FLOOR` is not part of `everyVectorMatchesOnEveryTarget`, so "every vector" already has an unnamed exception.

## Fix

Two sentences, no code change:

- On `RGA_PRE_FLOOR`: state that it is frozen, that it must never be regenerated, and that a format change updates the re-encode assertion instead.
- On the class KDoc's blanket rule: a parenthetical naming `RGA_PRE_FLOOR` as the exception.

title: Rga: a compaction floor discards the lamport high-water it swallows
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The defect

`Rga` carries a per-author compaction floor (`compactedBelow`, added in #2127's PR 1) that purges every op at-or-below it. The floor records **seqs**, not lamports — so raising it discards the lamport high-water of the ids it swallows.

That is fine while anything survives the window, because `lamport` is carried as its own field and stays above every purged id. It stops being fine if the window drains **entirely**:

1. A merge inflates this replica's `lamport` above its own `seq` (lamports advance on every observed op, seqs only on own mints).
2. The window drains — every op is purged, `ops` is empty, only the floor remains.
3. A wire round-trip decodes the state. `RgaSerializer`'s format is `{ "ops": [...] }` and `lamport` is **derived on decode** from the surviving ops, so with no ops it comes back as `lamport = seq`.
4. Re-minting now climbs back up through lamport values the purged ids already used.

Two distinct same-author ids then share a lamport, and `RgaId.compareTo` tiebreaks on `(lamport, replicaId)` only — so it returns `0` for ids that are not equal. That breaks the total order the RGA sequence is built from.

## Reachability

**Not reachable through `WarpLogRecordExporter`** — its window never drains; `dropWindow` only ever removes a strict prefix and the visible window survives by construction.

But `dropWindow` and `withCompactedBelow` are **public API** on a published CRDT module, and nothing in either signature or KDoc tells a caller that draining the window fully is unsafe. A consumer windowing to zero gets a silently corrupted total order.

## Why this is `needs-design`, not a fix

The obvious repair — carry a lamport high-water beside the floor — has real design question

title: otel: BufferPolicy documents two meanings for DROP_NEWEST — consider splitting the enum
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Raised independently by both the implementer and the reviewer on #2161 (#2127's PR 0).

`BufferPolicy` is shared by `WarpLogRecordExporter` and `WarpSpanExporter`, and after #2161 its `DROP_NEWEST` constant means two different things:

- **`WarpSpanExporter`** evicts the newest *buffered* span and admits the arrival (`WarpSpanExporter.kt:226-239`).

The alternative is a separate `LogBufferPolicy`, which costs a public type and a migration for anyone constructing the log exporter explicitly, and buys a name that means one thing.

Not urgent, and deliberately not grown into #2161 — but it should be a decision rather than something that just stays that way. Worth resolving before 1.0, since both types are public API.

`WarpLogRecordExporter.evictOldest` opens with:

The repo's fail-loud rule wants `requireNotNull` with a message naming both quantities, so a cache desync surfaces as a diagnosable throw instead of a silent cap breach.

title: kuilt-raft: @ByteString would halve the wire cost of every Raft payload
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kotlinx-serialization`'s CBOR renders a `ByteArray` as an **array of integers**, not as a CBOR byte string. Each element costs one byte inside CBOR's short range (`0..23`, or `-1..-24` — Kotlin's `Byte` is signed) and **two** bytes outside it. For typical payloads that is a flat 2× on the wire.

Measured in `:kuilt-raft` commonTest against `raftCbor`: a 768 B array of `0x7F` encodes to **1538 B** (ratio 2.0026); the same length of `0x00` or `0xFF` encodes to 770 B.

This is paid by every opaque payload Raft carries — `LogEntry.command` and `RaftMessage.InstallSnapshot.data`, i.e. all application state and all snapshot bytes.

## What #2150 did about it

Nothing that changes the wire — it made the *sizing* honest instead. `RaftEngine` now measures the encoding where it can (`boundedBatch`, `checkProposeFitsTransport`) and pays the worst case where it cannot (`chunkBytes`, which must choose a slice size before there are bytes to measure). The constant is `RaftEngine.CBOR_BYTE_EXPANSION`.

The cost of that correctness is real: on a budgeted transport, roughly half the usable payload is reserved against an expansion that a byte-string encoding would not incur at all.

## The change

Annotate the payload fields `@ByteString` so CBOR emits a byte string (1:1, plus a short header). Then `CBOR_BYTE_EXPANSION` becomes 1 and `chunkBytes` stops halving.

**This changes the wire format**, so it is breaking: a peer on the old encoding cannot decode the new one. That is why it is not folded into #2150. It wants the usual treatment for a Raft wire change — a version gate or a coordinated release — plus a golden-vector test pinning the new encoding, in the style of the SRA wire vectors.

## Worth checking at the same time

title: kuilt-raft: HEADER_BUDGET's 256 B reserve is unenforced against an unbounded consumer-supplied ClientId
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RaftEngine.HEADER_BUDGET` is a fixed 256 B reserve for the CBOR envelope around an opaque payload. Since #2154 it is spent in two places: sizing an `InstallSnapshot` chunk (`chunkBytes`) and deriving the propose-time bound (`checkProposeFitsTransport`, `limit = budget - HEADER_BUDGET`).

**256 B does not cover the `AppendEntries` envelope, and no bound on `ClientId` can make it.** Measured, not estimated — full receipts in [this comment](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2156#issuecomment-5560009002).

## What the reserve actually covers

The envelope carries **eight** `Long`s — `term`, `prevLogIndex`, `prevLogTerm`, `leaderCommit`, `round`, the entry's own `index` / `term`, and `dedupKey.requestId` — and CBOR widens each from 1 B to 9 B as the log grows. The headroom left for a `ClientId` is therefore **not a constant**:

| log state | envelope overhead at `ClientId` length 0 | max `ClientId` length 256 B covers |
|---|---|---|
| fresh (`index`/`term` ≈ 1) | 174 B | 81 |
| mature (1e9 entries, term 1e4) | 207 B | 48 |
| long-lived (1e12 entries, term 1e6) | 225 B | 30 |
| `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_INDEX`/`TERM` = 2^60 | 245 B | **11** |

## Reachability — revised

This issue originally said the id "would need roughly 200+ characters to overrun" and called the defect latent. **Both were wrong.** The real threshold is 81 characters on a fresh log and 30 on a long-lived one, so a plain 36-character UUID durable id costs 262 B — already over. And at the plausibility ceiling a 23-character **auto-minted** id costs 268 B: the library's own default identity does not fit the reserve, with no consumer-supplied value involved at all.

Observed on the canonical harness (`RaftSimulation`, 3 voters, `maxPayloadBytes = 1

title: kuilt-raft: a FORWARDED propose bypasses the propose-time payload bound — and ForwardOutcome.Failed surfaces as a retryable exception
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2154 added a propose-time payload bound (`RaftEngine.checkProposeFitsTransport`) so an over-budget command is refused before it can enter the log. It is wired into `proposeWithRequestId` — the **local** propose entry point. The leader-side **forwarded** entry point bypasses it:

https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/kuilt-raft/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/raft/internal/RaftEngine.kt#L3258

`onForward` calls `onPropose(m.command, m.dedupKey, d)` directly, so a forwarded command is appended with no budget check against **this** node's transport.

## When the forwarder's check is not enough

A non-leader's `propose` is gated by its *own* transport budget, which is not the leader's. Where they differ, the unsafe direction is a forwarder with the **larger** budget: it accepts, forwards, and the leader appends an entry it cannot replicate — the same permanent wedge #2154 closes for local proposes. `MeshSeam` reports the minimum across its live links, so two nodes routinely differ: a node with one tight link publishes a smaller budget than a peer with only fast ones.

## Why this is not a five-line fix

The obvious shape — check in `onForward`, reply `ForwardOutcome.Failed` — collides with an existing inconsistency. `ForwardOutcome.Failed` is documented "The proposal failed for a non-retryable reason" (`RaftMessage.kt:298`), but the originator maps it to a **retryable** exception:

https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/kuilt-raft/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/raft/internal/RaftEngine.kt#L3313

```kotlin
ForwardOutcome.NotLeader, ForwardOutcome.Failed ->
    pf.deferred.completeExceptionally(LeadershipLostException("forwarded proposal was not committed; retry"))

title: crdt-test: a wider alphabet silently drops the exhaustive-small bound below the shape it exists to find
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`LatticeLawHarness`'s exhaustive-small pass enumerates every word of length `1..L` and returns the
shortest failing one. `L` starts at `EXHAUSTIVE_WORD_LENGTH = 4` and is then **reduced by whole
lengths** until the ordered-triple count fits `EXHAUSTIVE_TRIPLE_BUDGET = 15_000`:

```kotlin
private val exhaustiveWordLength: Int =
    (EXHAUSTIVE_WORD_LENGTH downTo 2).firstOrNull { triplesUpTo(it) <= EXHAUSTIVE_TRIPLE_BUDGET } ?: 1
```

Cost is `|A|ᴸ`, so the reduction is driven by how wide the binding's alphabet is:

| `\|A\|` | L chosen | triples | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 12,120 | |
| 4 | 3 | 4,560 | |
| 5 | 3 | 8,715 | |
| **6** | **3** | **14,844** | ← `JsonCrdt`, **1% under the budget** |
| **7** | **2** | **1,379** | ← **loses the 3-op shape** |

**The problem.** The pass exists to find the `assert · retire · re-assert` word, which is **three ops
long**. At `|A| = 7` the bound silently becomes 2, and the enumeration can no longer *contain* that
word — the suite keeps passing, and its headline guarantee ("the shortest counterexample, full stop")
quietly becomes vacuous for that binding. `JsonCrdt` is at `|A| = 6` today, so **one added op** is all
it takes.

**Why it will not be noticed.** The drop makes the pass ~10× **cheaper** (14,844 → 1,379 triples), so
wall-clock watching gives the opposite signal. And `EXHAUSTIVE_WORD_LENGTH`'s KDoc asserts the
property in prose — "Every live alphabet keeps `L ≥ 3`, which is the length the assert/retire/
re-assert shape needs, so no binding loses the shape it exists to catch" — which is true today and
enforced by nothing.

**Proposed fix.** Have the harness fail when `exhaustiveWordLength` falls below the longest declared
critical shape (floor 3), naming the alph

title: kuilt-raft: AppendEntries batches the whole un-replicated tail unbounded — a lagging follower wedges permanently on a budgeted transport
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`sendAppendEntries` batches the **entire un-replicated tail** into one frame with no size bound:

https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/blob/main/kuilt-raft/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/raft/internal/RaftLogMath.kt#L179

`logSliceFrom` returns `log.subList(offset, log.size)` — every entry from the follower's `nextIndex` to the end. Nothing caps the count or the cumulative bytes, and `RaftConfig` has no batch parameter.

## Why it wedges

On a transport that publishes and enforces a payload budget, an over-budget `AppendEntries` is dropped at the sender (`SeamRaftTransport.sendTo` catches `PayloadTooLarge` and warns; it must, because `RaftEngine.send` invokes it unguarded). The follower therefore never sees the frame, so it never rejects it, so `nextIndex` never decrements — and it never succeeds, so `nextIndex` never advances. Every heartbeat re-sends the same oversize frame. **That follower is permanently stuck, and nothing self-heals it.** Enough stuck followers and the leader loses commit quorum entirely.

The §7 divert at `RaftEngine.kt:1760` (`ni <= snapshotIndex` → `InstallSnapshot`, which *is* chunked) bounds the batch only to the **live log window** — and compaction is consumer-driven (the `snapshots` flow at `RaftEngine.kt:668`), so a consumer that does not compact has an unbounded window.

## Distinct from the propose-time bound

The one-oversize-*entry* case is being fixed under #2069 by refusing an over-budget `propose()` before it enters the log. That does **not** cover this: N ordinary in-bound entries still sum past the budget. Per-entry and per-batch are separate bounds.

## Shape of the fix

Cap the slice by cumulative encoded size (not just count) inside `sendAppendEntries`, always

title: NSFileManagerDurableStore does not flush the temp file before renaming, so power loss can lose a committed record
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`NSFileManagerDurableStore.write` never flushes the temp file before renaming it, so a **power loss** can commit the directory entry while the new bytes were never written to stable storage — leaving the destination present but empty, with the previously committed record already gone.

Found reviewing #2139 (which fixes #2120's unlink-before-rename window). #2139 is a strict improvement and closes the process-crash window; this is the residual, weaker window it does not buy.

## The gap

`kuilt-otel/src/appleMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/otel/NSFileManagerDurableStore.kt`:

```kotlin
bytes.toNSData().writeToFile(tmp, options = 0uL, error = writeError.ptr)
…
platform.posix.rename(tmp, dest)
```

`writeToFile` with `options = 0` does not flush, and there is no `fsync`/`F_FULLFSYNC` anywhere in the file. `rename(2)` guarantees the **namespace** transition is atomic — `man 2 rename`: "an instance of new will always exist, even if the system should crash in the middle of the operation" — but that says nothing about the file's *data* extents. After `rename` returns, the bytes are still only in the buffer cache.

So the failure ordering under power loss is: directory entry committed → extents never written → `dest` exists, is empty or torn, and the prior version is unlinked. That is a lost committed record, which is the property the class KDoc otherwise promises.

Process termination (crash, jetsam, force-quit) is **not** affected — the buffer cache belongs to the kernel and survives. This is power-loss / kernel-panic only, which is why it is a follow-up rather than part of #2139.

## Why it is worth closing

The sibling implementation behind the same `DurableStore` contract already pays for this. `kuilt-otel/src/jvm

title: kuilt-nw silently DROPS received bytes under burst — a large frame never completes and the stream desynchronizes
body:
> **Resolved by #2140** — real backpressure on both `NwApi` impls, and `NwSeam` now publishes `maxPayloadBytes`. No bridge ABI change was required; see [the settled sub-questions](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/2134#issuecomment-5194450175). The analysis below is the original report.

> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Both `NwApi` implementations publish received bytes through a **bounded, lossy** hand-off. A frame large enough to arrive as more chunks than the buffer holds loses chunks silently — the frame never completes, and because a length-prefixed stream cannot resynchronize after a gap, **every subsequent byte on that connection is misparsed**.

This is a byte stream. It is not drop-tolerant, and unlike the lifecycle signals it sits next to (#1539's drop-tolerant `connectionStates`), nothing reconstructs it.

## The two sites

- `BridgeNwApi` (JVM) — `bytesReceivedStaging = Channel(BYTES_BUFFER = 64, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)`, fed by `trySend` from the JNA callback thread.
- `RealNwApi` (iOS/macOS, **the shipping Apple path**) — `_bytesReceived.tryEmit(...)` onto a `MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = BYTES_BUFFER)`. `tryEmit` on a full buffer drops the emission.

`RECEIVE_MAX_LENGTH` is 64 KiB and `RECEIVE_MIN_LENGTH` is 1, so a 16 MiB frame arrives as **at least 256 chunks** against a 64-slot buffer. The drop happens whenever the drain coroutine falls momentarily behind the native callback thread.

Surfaced by #2069's `payloadOfExactlyTheBudgetIsCarried` once `NwSeam` published its 16 MiB ceiling (#2130). On an **idle** box (load 2.4), `NwBridgeLoopbackConformanceTest.payloadOfExactlyTheBudgetIsCarried` run alone:

title: kuilt-raft: decide whether a sustained run of undecodable frames deserves a RaftMetric, not just a trace event
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2051's fix (PR #2128) makes an undecodable inbound frame a **drop plus a `RaftTraceEvent.FrameUndecodable`**, rather than node death. That closes the safety hole. It deliberately leaves one thing open, recorded here rather than in a code comment that nobody re-reads.

## The gap

`trace` is a `MutableSharedFlow` with `DROP_OLDEST` — **evidence, not a ledger**, and documented as such on both `FrameRefused` and `FrameUndecodable`. That is precisely what makes it safe to emit on a remote-frame-controlled path, and precisely why it is the wrong thing for a production consumer to watch for a *sustained condition*.

The sustained condition here is real and operationally distinct: a peer that cannot be decoded at all is a peer this node will never hear from, which presents **identically to a partition**. Version skew across a rolling upgrade is the ordinary cause. Today the only way to notice is to be collecting `trace` and counting — which a slow consumer's dropped events silently defeat.

## Why it was not folded into #2051

`RaftMetric.WedgeSuspected` is the existing sustained-condition surface, and this cannot ride on it. Its counter (`noteRefusedLeaderFrame`) is keyed to *leader→peer* frames at or above this node's term, and **neither the sender's role nor the frame's term is knowable without the decode that just failed**. Reaching for it would mean either inventing a term for a frame that never had one — the forgery-laundering shape #1817 rejected — or loosening what the metric counts, which weakens it everywhere it is currently exact.

> default policy and the one the field incident is on. `Rga.compact`'s condition 4 ("no

#2126 bounded `WarpLogRecordExporter`'s **per-export write** by moving the op-log into segments. It deliberately did **not** bound the **total**: segments are never dropped, so bytes on disk still grow with the number of records ever exported, and the store gains roughly one key per `segmentOps` operations.

It also left a **startup-latency cost that compounds**, which is the second reason to do this. With nothing dropped, the segment count grows forever, so `recover()` performs a number of `store.read` calls proportional to the whole history rather than one. At `segmentOps = 256`, a 100,000-record log means ~390 sequential reads on every launch, each a separate file open on `NSFileManagerDurableStore` / `FileChannelDurableStore`. It was an accepted trade in #2126 against taking the per-export write from 3.9 MB to ~3 KB, but it does not stop growing, and bounding the total is exactly what bounds it.

title: RgaCache omits the `sequence` field, so every mutated Rga re-derives it — O(n log n) per op for append-then-read consumers
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RgaCache` carries five derived fields but **not `sequence`**, so the `Rga` instance returned by `insertAfter` always re-derives it. Every consumer that mutates an `Rga` and then reads its order pays a full `computeSequence()` per mutation.

```kotlin
// kuilt-crdt/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/crdt/Rga.kt:117
internal data class RgaCache<V>(
    val insertsById: Map<RgaId, RgaOp.Insert<V>>,
    val maxSeqByReplica: Map<ReplicaId, Long>,
    val tombstones: Set<RgaId>,
    val compactedIds: Set<RgaId>,
    val compactPositions: Map<RgaId, RgaId>,
)
```

`sequence` is `by lazy { computeSequence() }` — a `groupBy` over all inserts plus a `sortedDescending()` per sibling group. Because `Rga` is immutable and every mutator returns a **new** instance, that lazy is cold again after each op: the caching is real, but in an append-then-read access pattern it never gets used.

## Measured

From the #1860 investigation, timing the phases of an append-then-read loop against a 7,917-record `Rga` on Kotlin/Native:

| | call #1 (inherits a warm `sequence`) | calls #2+ | jump |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Release | 0.17 ms | ~2.0 ms | **12×** |
| Debug | 2.05 ms | ~15.5 ms | **7.6×** |

title: CapturingAppender's unbounded channel grows without limit when the drain is slower than the producer
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`CapturingAppender` queues every captured log event into an **unbounded** channel. If the drain cannot keep up with the producer, the queue grows without bound — a memory leak during *normal operation*, not just at teardown.

```kotlin
// kuilt-otel-logging/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/otel/logging/CapturingAppender.kt:35
private val events = Channel<NormalizedLogEvent>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
```

## The file already knows about this failure mode — in the other context

Its own KDoc names the hazard for teardown:

> Without it, uninstalling by cancelling the drain's scope alone would leave this appender wired into the global logging config, `trySend`-ing into an unbounded channel nobody drains — **an unbounded memory leak**.

`close()` handles exactly that case. What is unhandled is the case where the drain **is** running and is simply **slower than the producer**. `log()` is `trySend`, which on an `UNLIMITED` channel never fails and never blocks, so there is no backpressure and no drop — the queue just grows.

From the #1860 investigation, on the field's 7,917-record store, per completed `export()`:

|---|---:|---:|---|
| Release | 27.9 ms | 84–140 ms | drains comfortably |
| **Debug** | 230.6 ms | **692–1153 ms** | **at or past break-even** |

A Debug build on an A12 at that store size structurally cannot sustain one log line per second — and the failure mode is not "telemetry lags", it is **unbounded heap growth in the host application**, because the producer is the app's own logging call and it is never throttled or dropped. title: NSFileManagerDurableStore.write deletes the destination before renaming, so a failed rename loses committed data
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`NSFileManagerDurableStore.write` deletes the destination **before** the rename, so there is a window — and a reachable failure path — in which previously committed data is lost. This contradicts the contract the same file documents.

## The code

`kuilt-otel/src/appleMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/otel/NSFileManagerDurableStore.kt`:

```kotlin
check(fm.createFileAtPath(tmp, contents = bytes.toNSData(), attributes = null)) { ... }
// Step 2: atomically rename temp to dest (POSIX rename(2) under the hood).
// Remove dest first so moveItem does not fail when dest already exists.
fm.removeItemAtPath(dest, error = null)
check(fm.moveItemAtPath(tmp, toPath = dest, error = null)) { ... }
```

## What the KDoc promises

> Writes use an atomic write-temp-then-rename strategy … **A crash before step 2 leaves only the `.tmp` file, which is ignored on the next open.**

That sentence is only true if the destination survives until the rename commits. It does not: `removeItemAtPath(dest)` runs first.

## Two ways it loses committed data

1. **Crash between the remove and the move.** The destination is already gone and the replacement has not landed. The next `read` returns `null` — every previously persisted record is lost, and the caller is told the store is simply empty.
2. **`moveItemAtPath` returns `false`.** The `check` throws *after* the destination has been deleted. Same loss, no crash required. In `WarpLogRecordExporter` this surfaces as an `ExportResult.Failure` that every caller discards (see #1860), so the loss is silent.

`moveItemAtPath:toPath:error:` fails when the destination exists — which is exactly why the `removeItemAtPath` was added. So the remove is not incidental; the sequence is load-bearing and wrong.

title: test: kotlin.assert is -ea-gated, so it is a launcher property not a code property — 3 sites left, and nothing forbids it
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kotlin.assert` is **not** an assertion primitive a test can rely on. On the JVM it is `-ea`-gated, so
whether it checks anything is a property of **the launcher, not the code**. It works today only because
Gradle's `Test` task defaults `enableAssertions = true`.

## How this surfaced

Migrating `:kuilt-raft`'s pure Raft model check off jqwik ([#2112](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2112))
found **all five Raft safety invariants** — Election Safety, Log Matching, State Machine Safety, Leader
Completeness, Compaction Completeness — written with `kotlin.assert`. They passed only by launcher grace,
and the migration to `commonTest` would have made that a live hazard on precisely the platforms it added.
#2112 replaced them with an unconditional throw.

## What is left — three sites, in a load-bearing test

Surveyed on `main` at `c97f5b8b` (post-#2112), `kotlin.assert` survives in exactly one file:

:223
    assert(betaEntry1.index > 0) { "beta phase-1 commit index must be positive" }

"no double-apply" property is load-bearing — and three of its checks currently evaporate if anyone sets

title: AdmitMessage.Hello.protocolVersion defaults to the value that gets you rejected — and the safe-looking fix would silently defeat the gate
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`AdmitMessage.Hello.protocolVersion` defaults to `null`, and since #2026 `null` is a **rejection**
(`MIN_SUPPORTED = 2`). So the default value of a field that gates admission is the value that gets
you refused: a caller who constructs a `Hello` and simply doesn't think about the version is locked
out of every room, with the symptom arriving as a **silent admit timeout**, not a `ProtocolMismatch`
the caller can read.

This bit `fireworks-compose` on the dev.1169 bump: two server tests that hand-roll a spoke `Hello`
(kuilt's `Connection` adapter and `NamedFrame` are `internal`, so they re-derive the handshake) both
hung waiting on a roster that would never seat them. Fixed consumer-side by stamping
`ProtocolVersion.CURRENT`, but the API invited the mistake.

## Why the obvious fix is wrong

Changing the default to `ProtocolVersion.CURRENT` would be **worse than the bug**. The single
defaulted field is doing double duty, and the two roles want opposite defaults:

| role | wants | why |
|---|---|---|
| **constructor default** (senders) | `CURRENT` | a peer built by *this* build speaks *this* version |
| **missing-key default** (decoder) | `null` | a pre-#1569 frame has no `protocolVersion` key at all |

The KDoc leans on the second explicitly — *"kotlinx omits the defaulted null, so a version-less
`Hello` is byte-identical to the pre-#1569 wire form."* Flip the default and a genuine legacy peer's
frame decodes as `CURRENT`, silently admitting precisely the population #2026 exists to exclude. The
gate would still compile, still look present, and no longer gate.

## Suggested shape

Separate *constructing* a `Hello` from *decoding* one, so the wire default stays `null` while no
sender can accidentally inherit it:
