title: kuilt-raft: the pure model cannot reach §5.4.2 — the Figure-8 mutation is structurally unkillable without bounded AppendEntries batches
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`:kuilt-raft`'s pure model check ([#2112](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2112)) reddens on §5.4.1
and §5.2 but **cannot** redden on §5.4.2 (the Figure-8 prior-term commit restriction). That is not a budget
problem. It is structural, and the mutation is **unkillable by construction** in the current model.

## Mechanism — why no trajectory can reach the state

In `PureRaftModel.kt`:

- `becomeLeader` appends a **current-term no-op** and points `nextIndex` past it.
- `appendEntriesMsgs` always ships the **entire suffix** — there is no max-entries-per-message bound.
- `matchIndex` resets to 0 per term.

So the first heartbeat's `prev` is the new no-op, every follower rejects, fast-backup resends the **whole
log**, and every successful ack in a term therefore covers the leader's entire log *including* the
current-term no-op. The quorum-th `matchIndex` consequently always lands at or above the no-op index,
where every entry is current-term — so `entry.term == r.term` at the commit-advance site is **always
true**, and deleting that guard changes nothing observable.

## Evidence

- Instrumented probe: **0 prior-term majority-commit states in 450,000 trajectories across 100 root seeds.**
- The §5.4.2 mutation also survived the shipped budget *and* 100× it (300,000 / 150,000 trajectories)
  during #2112's implementation.

That experiment has now been run twice, by two independent agents, and can never succeed. This issue
exists so it is not run a third time.

## What would actually close it

**Bounded AppendEntries batches** — a max-entries-per-message knob, so a follower can ack a *prefix* that
stops short of the current-term no-op. Only then does a quorum-th `matchIndex` land on a prior-term entry,

Found while landing Task 7 of #2044 (PR #2110).

`ORSet`, `ORMap` and `LWWMap` now return a `Patch` from every mutator, so one write puts one
element/key/cell on the wire. `JsonCrdt` — which is a thin wrapper over `ORMap<String, JsonNode>` —
still returns a whole new document:

```kotlin
public fun set(key: String, node: JsonNode): JsonCrdt =
    JsonCrdt(root.piece(root.put(replica, key, node)), replica)
```

`Quilter.apply` broadcasts a patch's delta verbatim, so `Patch(doc.set(k, v))` puts the entire
document on the wire on every write — the exact cost #2044 measured for `ORSet` (138x a minimal
delta at 400 entries, growing linearly with entry count).

The underlying delta already exists: `root.put(replica, key, node)` **is** the minimal delta, and
Task 7 wrapped it in a local `piece` only to preserve `JsonCrdt`'s existing signature. So the fix is
mechanical for the top level:

- `JsonCrdt.set(key, node): Patch<JsonCrdt>` returning `Patch(JsonCrdt(root.put(…).delta, replica))`
- `JsonCrdt.remove(key): Patch<JsonCrdt>` likewise

Two things to settle before implementing, which is why this is not folded into #2110:

1. **The nested case is the interesting one.** A write deep inside `JsonNode.Object`/`Array` is

title: crdt: ORMap.putDelta is O(the sender's own contribution to the key), so a single-writer append key costs O(n²) cumulative
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`ORMap.putDelta`'s frame is flat in the size of the map and flat in *other* replicas' contributions to the key — #2044's headline properties, both still pinned. It is **not** flat in the **sending replica's own running contribution to that key**, and for a single-writer append workload that term is the whole stored value.

This is a **confirmed trade from #2086, not a defect.** Recording it so it lives somewhere a reader will find it, rather than only in a KDoc on the method.

## Mechanism

A put supersedes the putting replica's own tag on the key and folds that tag's write into the fresh one (`ORMap.foldOwn`). The fold is what keeps a put additive over the value lattice while leaving a replica one tag per key — and it is what the delta has to carry, because the dot the delta names and the dot `put` mints must agree on their payload or a peer taking the delta and a peer taking the whole state end up holding one dot with two values.

## The workload that hurts

A key one replica grows alone — `ORMap<K, GSet<LogLine>>`, `ORMap<K, ORSet<X>>` used as an append log:

```
put #1  ships 1 element
put #2  ships 2 elements
…
put #n  ships n elements     →  O(n²) cumulative
```

**Measured: ~400× frame growth across 1000 puts**, pinned as a floor by `ORMapDeltaMutatorLawTest.aPutDeltaCarriesTheSendersOwnRunningContributionToTheKey` (the assertion is deliberately one-way — it fails if the frame goes *flat*, which is the tell that the supersession term was dropped).

Multi-writer keys are unaffected: each replica ships only its own share, and a replica with no prior tag on the key ships exactly what it passed.

## Why the obvious alternative is worse

Supersede nothing. Every delta then stays at O(the value you passed) —

title: crdt-test: consolidate the four overlapping lattice-law surfaces — each has a different blind spot, and all four passed on a broken ORMap
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

> **RESOLVED 2026-08-05.** Rewritten to lead with what is now true. The four-surface table this body
> carried for two revisions described the tree *before* any of this landed, and a closed issue whose
> body describes a tree that no longer exists is the thing that gets quoted forever. The measured
> verdicts, and the eight places the plan turned out to be wrong, are in the closing comment.

**There is one randomised lattice-law suite now.** `:kuilt-conformance`'s **`LatticeLawSuite`** —
renamed from `CrdtConvergenceSuite`, package `conformance.lattice` — runs on **every target** over
**19 bindings**, and it is where a lattice defect in the CRDT zoo is expected to be caught.

## What it asserts

- **All four laws** over a causal-ancestor pool: associativity in both bracketings, commutativity,
  idempotence, least-upper-bound — plus **byte** equality wherever two states compare equal, because
  `Quilter`'s root-hash gate (#1955) compares digests rather than values.
- **A named-op alphabet per binding** (`LatticeOp`, `OpKind`), driving both the randomised pool and
  an **exhaustive-small** pass that enumerates every word up to a bounded length and returns the
  **shortest** failing one — the replacement for jqwik's shrinking, alongside an op log that prints
  the word which built each operand.
- **Constructed critical shapes.** The `assert · retire · re-assert` word is applied as a pool prefix
  rather than waited for, so the defect class this suite exists for is reached on **every** seed. The
  harness fails a shape whose step did not change the state, so a shape cannot rot into decoration.
- **Vacuity floors** (`VacuityFloors`): strict-ancestor pairs, concurrent pairs, effective retiring
  steps, and a no-op

title: kuilt-quilter: Quilter.mutate cannot decline, so every conditional read-modify-write hand-rolls an identity patch
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Two production call sites now express "read the state, decide, and *maybe* write" on top of
`Quilter.mutate {}` — the atomic read-modify-write entry point (#1270) — and both have to invent
the same workaround, because `mutate`'s transform is `(S) -> Patch<S>` and cannot decline:

- `HeddleNode.applyIfPresent` returns `Patch(EntitlementLedger.ZERO)` when the op refuses.
- `GamePresence.declareIf` returns `Patch(EphemeralMap.empty())` when the declaration refuses
  (added in the #2083 fix).

The identity patch is correct — every `piece` returns the receiver unchanged — but it is not free:
it bumps `nextSeq`, buffers a pending delta, and broadcasts an empty `Delta` frame to every peer.
So each site then has to decide whether to pay that or add a fast-refuse read *ahead* of the lock,
and the two sites answered differently for good local reasons (`HeddleNode`'s refusal is on a hot
path and is not a postcondition; `GamePresence.declareAdmissionOpen`'s is a postcondition, so it
cannot refuse on a read nothing holds still). Neither answer is satisfying — the primitive is
missing.

## Shape

A declining variant, e.g.

```kotlin
public fun mutateOrSkip(transform: (S) -> Patch<S>?): Boolean
```

returning whether a patch was published, so the transform's own refusal branch stays inside the
lock and no frame is emitted. Both call sites collapse onto it and both lose a hand-rolled
`var applied = false` / identity-patch constant.

Public API on `:kuilt-quilter`, so it wants the usual: KDoc, a `@sample`, and an
`docs/agent-cookbook.md` entry if it is something a consumer would reach for.

Not urgent — both current sites are correct as written. Filed so the third site does not
re-derive the workaround a third time.

title: crdt: ORMap.piece is not associative on the value axis (and the law test hides it)
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`ORMap.piece` is **not associative on the value axis**. Found while implementing the `ORMap` delta
mutators (part of #2044); reproducible with **no delta code at all**, on `main` today:

```kotlin
val start   = ORMap.empty<String, GSet<String>>().put(a, "k", GSet.of("v1"))
val removed = start.remove("k")                                // a peer that removed k
val rePut   = start.remove("k").put(b, "k", GSet.of("v2"))     // a peer that removed, then re-put

start.piece(removed).piece(rePut)["k"]   // → {v2}
start.piece(removed.piece(rePut))["k"]   // → {v1, v2}     ← diverged
```

`ORMapEntry.join` merges the two values whenever both sides hold the key, but `remove` discards the
value along with the tags. So whether `v1` survives depends on whether the remove was applied before
or after the concurrent put — an ordering the lattice is supposed to make irrelevant. `ORSet`, whose
entries carry no payload, is unaffected (checked).

**Why `ORMapLawsPropertyTest.pieceIsAssociative` passes anyway.** Its generator puts
`GCounter.of(replica to 1L)` — the *same* value for every put by a given replica — so a lost value is
indistinguishable from a kept one. The law is being asserted vacuously on the axis where it fails.
Any generator that varies the value per put reproduces it immediately.

**Why it matters more now.** Reaching the bad state used to require a peer to do remove-then-put
locally. With the `ORMap` delta mutators landing in #2044, a delta carries the *supplied* value
rather than the sender's locally merged one (deliberately — that is where the O(change) saving
lives), so **any** `remove` racing a `putDelta` on the same key hits it. Two peers applying the same
two deltas in different orders end up with diff

`GamePresence.declare`

title: crdt: decide per type whether MVRegister and EphemeralMap want delta mutators — O(replicas), not O(entries)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of **#2044** during its design pass ([#2076](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2076)).
`MVRegister` and `EphemeralMap` have the same full-state-mutator shape as `ORSet`/`ORMap`/`LWWMap`, but
the term is a **different order of magnitude**, so they are tracked separately rather than bundled.

## Why separate rather than folded into #2044

Measured during #2076's design pass:

| type | full-state cost | measured overhead vs a minimal delta |
|---|---|---|
| `ORSet` / `ORMap` | **O(entries)** | 3,926× |
| `LWWMap` | **O(keys)** | 9,184× at 10k keys |
| **`MVRegister`** | **O(replicas)** | **11.3× at R=64** |
| **`EphemeralMap`** | O(replicas)-ish | 194× |

The in-scope #2044 types are O(n) in *data size* — unbounded, and the reason a single write can cost 9
full states. `MVRegister`'s whole state is O(#writers), which is bounded by the mesh and small: at R=64
the entire register is only 11.3× a minimal delta, and its full state genuinely *is* close to minimal.

Bundling them would **dilute #2044's before/after measurement** — the headline is "flat in state size",
and mixing in a type whose state was never a function of state size muddies exactly the claim being made.

Decide, per type, whether a delta mutator is worth it at all — and **write the answer down either way**.
That is #739's framing: *the answer should be recorded per type rather than assumed*. A measured "no,
the full state is already effectively minimal for this type" is a valid and useful outcome here, and is
the likelier one for `MVRegister`.

`EphemeralMap` at 194× is the more plausible candidate of the two and should be measured first.

title: kuilt-warp: WarpNode.enqueue(Coordinated) mutates outside the lock — two concurrent enqueues mint the same dot and BOTH are annihilated
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`WarpNode.enqueue(taskId, CoordinationKind.Coordinated)` performs a read-modify-write on a dot-based
CRDT **outside the lock every sibling mutator holds**. Two concurrent coordinated enqueues mint the
**same dot** from the same snapshot, and the causal join then **annihilates both writes** — the tasks are
silently lost, not merely reordered.

Found while designing #2044 (delta mutators); it is **pre-existing and independent of that work**, so it
is filed separately rather than folded into a performance PR.

## The asymmetry

`WarpNode.enqueue(taskId, descriptor)` — the free-path sibling — guards its read-modify-write:

```kotlin
lock.withLock {
    val ts = ++timestampCounter
    queueQuilter.apply(Patch(queueQuilter.state.value.put(replica = replica, key = taskId, …)))
}
```

`WarpNode.enqueue(taskId, kind)`'s `Coordinated` branch does not:

```kotlin
CoordinationKind.Coordinated -> {
    checkNotNull(raftNode) { … }
    coordQueueQuilter.apply(Patch(coordQueueQuilter.state.value.add(replica, taskId)))
}
```

`state.value` is read, `add` mints `context.nextDot(replica)` from *that snapshot*, and `apply` writes
back — three steps, no mutual exclusion.

## Why the result is loss, not just a race

Two threads read the same snapshot `(S, C)` and enqueue tasks `A` and `B`. Both mint
`nextDot(replica)` from the same `C`, so **both get the same dot `d`**:

- patch₁ = store `{A → {d}}`, context `C ∪ {d}`
- patch₂ = store `{B → {d}}`, context `C ∪ {d}`

Under the causal join, a dot present in the other side's **context** but absent from its **store** reads
as *retired*. Each patch witnesses `d` and does not carry the other's key, so each retires the other's
only dot: `A` drops, and `B` drops. **Both enqueues vanish.*

title: Nothing bounds a joiner-asserted PeerId at admission — one long id breaks the payload budget for every other member
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`AdmitMessage.Hello` carries the joiner's **self-chosen** `PeerId`, and the admit path applies no length bound. `PeerId` itself is a bare `@JvmInline value class PeerId(val value: String)` with no validation, so an admitted member's id can be arbitrarily long.

Contrast `PlyInboundGate` in `:kuilt-core`, which explicitly analyses the 1 MiB-`originId` attack for composite frames. The same shape reaches the room admit path with no gate at all.

## Why it matters now

#2047 landed `Room.maxPayloadBytes`, which reserves `RELAY_ENVELOPE_BUDGET` (256 B) for the relay envelope. The envelope's size is ~42 B of structure plus the **two peer ids** it carries (`origin`, and `RelayDest.One(peer)`). Measured: 114 B for a uuid pair, 242 B for two 100-byte ids.

So one admitted member with a multi-KB id makes every `RelayDest.One(thatPeer)` envelope exceed the reservation — and the damage lands on **everybody else**. A member running a perfectly budget-faithful chunker, sized to the number the library published, gets `PayloadTooLarge` on every chunk addressed to that peer. The published promise is broken for honest callers by a third party's id choice, and nothing they can do at their end fixes it.

It also inflates roster-bearing `Welcome` frames, which are size-checked nowhere.

#2047 documents this as a residual ("the reservation covers ids of about 107 bytes each"). Documenting it was the right call for that PR — its refusal is measured on the encoded frame, so the failure is a typed `PayloadTooLarge` rather than a torn seam — but a documented hole an untrusted peer can drive through is still a hole.

## Proposed

- Bound the id in the host's admit gate: reject a `Hello` whose id exceeds a limit sized so **two** max-len

title: Neither fan-out send budget is pinned by a test after per-recipient lanes
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`relaySendBudget` (`HeartbeatConfig.interval`) and `fanOutSendBudget` (`reconnectWindow + timeout`) are deliberately different magnitudes, and after #2048 **no test pins either one**.

## What changed

`StarRelayTest` §T15 (`a relay forward to a wedged spoke does not delay one to a healthy spoke`) was the pin. It was written against a single shared writer, where a healthy spoke waited one budget behind each wedged item — so allowing five relay budgets (200 ms each) while forbidding a membership-sized one (10.6 s) discriminated the two.

Per-recipient lanes (#2048) make that inert: the healthy spoke has its own writer and is served **at the instant its forward is enqueued**, whatever the budget is. §T15 passes on a build that sets `relaySendBudget = heartbeatConfig.reconnectWindow + heartbeatConfig.timeout`. Its KDoc was relabelled to say so rather than left claiming a pin it no longer provides.

The same is true of the admit budget: nothing distinguishes `reconnectWindow + timeout` from any other value now that a wedged recipient delays only itself.

## What the budgets still do

Narrower than before, and still worth having. A lane's budget bounds how long **that recipient's own** next frame waits behind a black hole, and with it the lane's backlog — which is what keeps an `UNLIMITED` admit lane's growth analysis true, and what keeps a relay lane from sitting at its 64-frame ceiling indefinitely.

## Shape of a real test

Assert on a *second* frame to the *same* wedged peer:

1. wedge B; enqueue frame 1 (parks in `sendTo` for the budget);
2. unwedge B;
3. enqueue frame 2, and assert B receives it after ~one budget and **not** materially before or after.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## ⚠️ Corrected 2026-08-05 — the premise below was wrong, and the property changed

**Mutating this guard does not livelock and does not hang.** `nextIndexAfterFailure` clamps its result to `maxOf(1, minOf(proposed, currentNextIndex - 1))` — #1829's **exclusive** ceiling — which forbids the fixed point on the *leader* side no matter what the follower replies. Under the mutation the backup loop still terminates; it just **crawls one index per round** instead of closing the gap in one.

title: Seam decorators drop the payload budget they could pass on (Mux / Tiered / Composite / Gossip)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#2047 added `Seam.maxPayloadBytes` and wired the two fabric seams (`LinkSeam`, `MeshSeam`) plus `SeamRoom`/`RoomChannelSeam`. Every other `Seam` **decorator** still inherits the `null` default.

That is *safe* — `null` means "unknown", so nobody is misled — but it is lossy: a decorator over a bounded fabric discards a bound it could have passed on, and a consumer sitting above one gets no guidance where guidance exists.

The sites, and what each owes:

| Decorator | Should report |
|---|---|
| `MuxBase.ChannelView` (`:kuilt-core`) | delegate's, less its channel framing |
| `TieredSeam` | the tightest of the two tiers (one payload may take either) |
| `CompositeSeam` | the tightest across attached plies, recomputed as plies attach/detach |
| `MuxClientLoom.ResumableChannel` | the current underlying channel's |
| `RoomHubSeam` | its delegate's |
| `GossipSeam` / `GossipView` (`:kuilt-gossip`) | delegate's unchanged — neither adds bytes |
| `InMemoryLoom`'s seam | `null` is correct (no ceiling); no change needed |

Not urgent: none of these is the #2047 failure mode, which was a decorator that *added bytes* without reserving them. This is the completeness pass.

The rule to apply is on `Seam.maxPayloadBytes`'s KDoc: subtract your own overhead unconditionally, floor at zero, `inner.maxPayloadBytes?.let { (it - cost).coerceAtLeast(0) }`. `CompositeSeam` is the only one needing thought — its ply set is live.

Part of #2047.

title: kuilt-raft: DenyReason is reconstructed by a priority-ordered when, so a second failing conjunct is masked — attribution shadows itself
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`onRequestVote` and `onPreVote` compute the grant as a conjunction and then **reconstruct** the deny
reason with a priority-ordered `when`. The reconstruction reports only the *first* arm that matches,
so when two conjuncts fail together the second is invisible in the field that exists to attribute it.

`RaftEngine.kt:1337-1348`:

```kotlin
val grant = m.term == state.currentTerm && logOk && (state.votedFor == null || state.votedFor == from)
…
val reason = when {
    m.term < state.currentTerm -> DenyReason.StaleTerm
    state.votedFor != null && state.votedFor != from -> DenyReason.AlreadyVoted
    else -> DenyReason.LogNotUpToDate
}
```

A candidate that has *both* already lost our vote *and* fails the §5.4.1 log check reports
`AlreadyVoted`. A mutation that weakens `isLogUpToDate` is therefore shadowed **inside the attribution
mechanism itself** on every such trajectory — the exact #1980 shadowing pattern, one level up from
where that survey has been looking. `onPreVote` (`RaftEngine.kt:1369-1378`) has the same shape with
`leaderAlive` first and `StaleTerm` as the fallthrough.

Found by the #2033 sweep, whose brief listed the pre-vote/vote deny paths as *"already carry a
`DenyReason`, so they may be fine"*. They are not — the premise was mine and it was wrong.

evaluating `logOk`**. Today that is sound, but only by an argument: `m.term > state.currentTerm` was
already resolved by the `stepDown` on line 1334, so a false `grant` past the first two arms does imply
`!logOk`. The soundness rests on a step-down two lines away and on the three con

title: kuilt-raft: an undecodable inbound frame kills the node — the decode in transport.incoming.collect catches only ClosedSendChannelException
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RaftEngine`'s inbound pump decodes every frame inside a `try` that catches **only**
`ClosedSendChannelException` (`RaftEngine.kt:640-648`):

```kotlin
launch {
    transport.incoming.collect {
        try {
            cmd.send(EngineCommand.IncomingMessage(it.from, raftCbor.decodeFromByteArray(it.bytes)))
        } catch (_: ClosedSendChannelException) {
            return@collect // channel closed — node is shutting down
        }
    }
}
```

A frame that fails to decode throws `SerializationException` out of `collect`, out of this `launch`,
and into `scope` — the **constructor-injected caller scope** (`RaftEngine.kt:101`). There is no
`SupervisorJob` and no `CoroutineExceptionHandler` on the path, so one undecodable frame cancels the
node and everything else structured under the consumer's scope.

That is precisely the failure mode #1818 established the "never `throw` on a remote-frame-controlled
path" rule for — *"a `require` on this path would convert one hostile frame into permanent node
death"*, as `refuseFrame`'s own KDoc puts it (`RaftEngine.kt:1058`). The rule is honoured everywhere
downstream of dispatch and skipped at the one point upstream of it, where the frame is still bytes.

**This is not a refusal site with weak attribution — it is a refusal site that does not exist.** It
came out of the #2033 sweep as the one entry that fell outside that issue's scope, which is why it is
filed separately.

## Reachability

`raftCbor` is `Cbor { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }` (`RaftEngine.kt:70`). `ignoreUnknownKeys` tolerates
an unknown *field*; it does not cover an unknown sealed-class **discriminator**, nor truncated or
corrupt bytes. So the honest trigger is **version skew**: a peer on a newer kuilt sends

title: Fan-out queues are global FIFOs — one wedged recipient starves healthy ones; key them per PeerId
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Both of `SeamRoom`'s fan-out queues are **global FIFOs drained by a single serial writer**, so one wedged recipient delays every healthy one behind it by up to one per-recipient budget each. `runAdmitFanOutWriter`'s KDoc already names this as a follow-up; the star relay (#1994) strengthens the case considerably.

## What the relay changed

`relayForwards` is a second such queue (bounded 64, `DROP_OLDEST`, per-recipient budget `heartbeatConfig.interval`). Two things make its version sharper than the admit queue's:

1. **The production budget is 5 s**, not the "~seconds" the design's table implies — `HeartbeatConfig.interval` defaults to 5 s. With a single serial writer, one black-holed spoke throttles the room's whole relayed data plane to roughly **0.2 fan-outs/second**, after which the 64-deep `DROP_OLDEST` queue sheds frames aimed at **healthy** recipients.
2. **The trigger is ordinary.** Routing flips to the relay when `rosterPeers ⊄ seam.peers`. On a flat mesh the dominant cause of that is a single member sitting in its reconnect window — exactly the #1557/#1614 state. So one transiently-partitioned peer can route *every* other peer's traffic through the host, for the whole reconnect window, on a topology that has no star in it.

The design's rule I2 (once any divergence exists, relay everything) is sound — it keeps hop counts consistent so a `Quilter`'s ack cannot overtake the delta it acknowledges. What is undocumented is the interaction above.

## Shape

Key the fan-out by `PeerId` — one queue and writer per recipient — so a wedged peer's backlog cannot delay or evict frames destined for healthy ones. Applies to both `admitFanOuts` and `relayForwards`; they have different capacity/overflow policies and

title: The relay envelope is unbudgeted — a payload that fits unrelayed can overflow the fabric once wrapped
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

The star relay (#1994) wraps an application payload in a `RelayEnvelope` before sending it to the host. **Nothing reserves room for that wrapper.**

A payload that fits when sent directly can exceed the fabric's frame limit once wrapped — surfacing as `FrameTooLargeException` from `:kuilt-stream`, at the moment the roster diverges and routing flips to the relay. So the same payload succeeds on a mesh and fails on a star, with no surface warning the caller.

The envelope costs roughly **40–60 bytes** (origin `PeerId`, a `RelayDest` discriminator plus its optional peer, and the CBOR framing).

## Why there is no budget today

The design's revision 1 claimed "the `RELAY_HEADER_BUDGET` reservation is honoured". That is **false**, and it is recorded as spec correction I7: that constant is `internal` to `:kuilt-cluster` and invisible from `:kuilt-session`. There is no payload-limit surface at the Room layer at all.

## Shape

Either expose a max-payload surface on `Room`/`Seam` that the relay can subtract its header from, or have the relay fail fast with a typed error naming the overflow rather than letting a fabric-level `FrameTooLargeException` escape from a send the caller thought was in-budget.

Named as a non-goal in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-03-star-relay-design.md`; only meaningful now that the relay has landed.

title: crdt: dot-based payloads carry a flat 47-78% per-entry causal tax that scale never dilutes
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced by #1986's Phase 0 measurement ([#2036](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2036),
[analysis](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1986#issuecomment-5173689349)). Recording the cost
because the measurement found it while looking for something else, and #1986 closed without anywhere to
put it.

## The finding

Dot-based CRDT payloads carry a **flat per-entry causal tax** that scale never dilutes:

| naming | causal metadata as % of `ORSet` full-state frame |
|---|---|
| 28-char element ids | **47%** |
| 8-char element ids | **78%** |

`ORSet` costs **65.9 b/entry** against a `GSet` baseline of 35.0 b/entry — **≈1.9× at every size**
measured, from n=1 to n=100k. `ORMap` is 130.8 b/entry. A UUID replica id roughly **triples** the
per-entry tax.

**This is not the `DotContext`.** The context itself *vanishes* with scale — 18.4% of the frame at n=1,
0.00% at n=100k (under 1% past n=100 at R≤2, n=1,000 at R≤16, n=10,000 at R=256). #1986 expected the
context to be the problem and it is not. The cost is the **per-entry dot**, one per element, and it is
paid on every full-state frame forever.

## Why this is being recorded rather than fixed

#1986 proposed a version-vector gate and it was rejected as **unsound** — `ORSet.remove` drops store
entries while passing `causal.context` through untouched, so equal contexts do not imply converged
states. A gate is the wrong lever for this cost regardless: #1955's shipped `RootDigest` already removes
essentially all *quiescent* egress (63,960× at 100k entries; egress 109.8 KB/s → 1.72 B/s). The tax is
paid on the frames that **do** ship — real divergence, and initial sync for a joining peer.

So the question is payload encoding, not anti-entropy scheduling.

title: crdt: canonical sort encodes keys with an empty SerializersModule, so a @Contextual key throws
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`CanonicalMapSerializer` and `CanonicalSetSerializer` sort by running each key/element through
`PrimitiveLeafEncoder`, whose `serializersModule` is `EmptySerializersModule()`
(`crdt/internal/SerialKeyComparator.kt`). So a `@Contextual` or open-polymorphic key that the
**format's** module would have resolved throws at encode time inside the sort instead — a key type
that serializes fine through the format on its own becomes un-encodable the moment it is wrapped in
a canonical collection.

Both classes' KDoc already documents this as a precondition; it is a latent gap, not a live bug —
no in-tree key type is contextual or polymorphic.

## Why this is being filed now

Both KDocs said "Threading the real module through is tracked as **#1964**". That is a
misattribution: [#1964](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1964) is about collapsing the
three `Dot` serializers onto the shared canonical sort and its constant factor, and says nothing
about `SerializersModule`. #1964 is being closed by
[#2034](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2034), which would have left two KDoc comments
pointing a reader at a closed issue for a concern it never tracked. Both now cite this issue.

## Fix

`Encoder.serializersModule` is available at `serialize` time, so the sort can thread it into
`PrimitiveLeafEncoder` rather than defaulting to empty. That means passing the module down through
`sortedByCanonicalKey` → `serialLeaves` → `PrimitiveLeafEncoder`.

Byte-parity caveat: for every key type in the tree today the module is irrelevant to the leaves, so
`CanonicalGoldenVectorTest` must stay byte-identical. If any vector moves, the change is wrong.

title: kuilt-raft: frame refusals outside the dispatch boundary still carry no RefusalGate, and everyRefusalGateIsReachable is blind to it
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1998 shipped `RaftTraceEvent.FrameRefused(clock, node, from, messageType, gate)` so a refused frame
names the guard that refused it. It was wired to the **dispatch-boundary** guards: the term-jump
bound's two arms, the §5.2/§8 leader-authority gate, and each of `onTimeoutNow`'s five guards.

**Frame refusals elsewhere in the engine still have no attribution**, and the guard `everyRefusalGateIsReachable`
cannot see the gap — it compares the observed set against `RefusalGate.entries`, i.e. it proves every
*declared* gate has an emit site. It says nothing about a refusal site that declares no gate at all.
The check is sound in the direction it was built for and blind in the other.

## The instance that found it

`isWellFormedBatch` (`onAppendEntries`' batch validator) refuses with a bare `debug { }` and emits
**nothing**. Found writing #2031, which had to pin its bounds using
`AppendEntriesAccepted`/`AppendEntriesRejected` plus response emission instead.

That worked, but the region shows exactly why attribution is the better instrument — from #2031's
receipts:

- Deleting the implausible-`prevLogIndex` clause produces **no log effect whatsoever**. The frame is
  processed and answered, then rejected by the §5.3 consistency check a screen later
  (`AppendEntriesRejected(conflictIndex = 8)`) and never touches the log. A log-based assertion there
  is not ambiguous, it is **blind** — the exact failure mode #1989 was filed about.
- The validator turned out to hold **five independently-deletable clauses**, not the three
  `return false` statements it appears to (see #2022). Attribution scales to that; hand-built
  "was it processed at all" probes do not, because each new clause needs a fresh trajectory argument.

title: kuilt-raft: local command refusals have no attribution — onChangeMembership's two in-progress guards are indistinguishable, so the subsumed one is unmeasurable
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1998 gave every **frame** refusal an attribution event —
`RaftTraceEvent.FrameRefused(clock, node, from, messageType, gate)`, with `RefusalGate` exhaustively
`when`-ed at one site. **Local command refusals got no equivalent**, and #2030 found the first place
that costs something concrete.

## The gap, with a worked instance

`onChangeMembership` refuses a caller for several distinct reasons. Two of them —
`pendingConfigChange != null` and the uncommitted-last-config check — both surface as
`MembershipChangeInProgressException`, which carries **no discriminator**. On the leader the second
*subsumes* the first (`RaftEngine.kt:2751` says so: "a superset of the in-memory `pendingConfigChange`
guard above"), so:

- deleting `pendingConfigChange` alone is behaviour-preserving, and
- **no test can ever be red under that mutation** — the guard is dead *as a refusal*, though it is
  still live as the machinery holding the caller's `CompletableDeferred`.

This is exactly the shape #1989 diagnosed for frames: *a refusal observable only as the absence of a
state change carries no attribution, so a downstream guard silently un-pins its upstream.* #1998 fixed
it for frames by making the refusal an **event that names the gate**. The command path never got that,
so #2030 could pin the superset guard but had to report the subsumed one as unmeasurable-by-construction.

## Why it is worth closing rather than shrugging at

The argument for subsumption is a **three-step proof** about when `pendingConfigChange != null` implies
an uncommitted last config entry — spanning `appendConfigEntry`, `advanceCommit` → `onConfigCommitted`
(both Simple and Joint branches), and `onInstallSnapshot`'s finalize ordering. It is currently correct.

title: build: enforce forbidUnlintedModule's allowlist citation format, and document kuilt.detekt-jvm
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Two small follow-ups from #2011 (the `forbidUnlintedModule` guard, closing #2005). Neither is
urgent; both are one-sitting changes.

### 1. The allowlist's "must cite an issue" rule is a comment, not a mechanism

`forbidUnlintedModule`'s allowlist in the root `build.gradle.kts` carries:

> An entry MUST cite an issue — a bare exclusion turns this guard back into the silence it exists to
> break.

and its failure message repeats the requirement. But nothing checks it: the value is a free-form
`String`, so `":foo" to ""` or `":foo" to "TODO"` is accepted silently.

That is the same shape as the defect the guard exists to end — a convention held by asking rather
than by construction. The guard's whole thesis is that "compiled but unlinted" should be a build
failure instead of a comment; its own allowlist should meet that bar.

**Fix:** validate each entry against `Regex("#\\d+")` at task-configuration time and fail with the
offending module path. Three lines, and it makes the rule the guard already states actually true.

Modest, and worth doing precisely *because* it is modest: the escape hatch is where a guard rots.

### 2. `kuilt.detekt-jvm` isn't mentioned in `CLAUDE.md`

`CLAUDE.md`'s "Build logic is centralized in `build-logic/`" bullet names `kuilt.kmp-library` and
`kuilt.publish`. #2011 added a third convention plugin, `kuilt.detekt-jvm`, which is now the
required one-line answer for any plain Kotlin/JVM module. A reader of that bullet would not know it
exists.

One line in that bullet. Note the repo convention that **CLAUDE.md changes go in their own PR** —
don't fold this into a code change.

The counter-argument, which is fair and why this is filed rather than fixed inline: the guard's
failure message

title: build: :demo-shared and :demo-web are plain KMP modules with no detekt wiring
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`:demo-shared` and `:demo-web` are plain KMP modules (deliberately not
`kuilt.kmp-library` — no `explicitApi`, no publishing, a reduced target set). Detekt is
registered only by `kuilt.kmp-library`, so neither module is linted at all.

Found by `forbidUnlintedModule` (#2005), which now fails the build on any module with
Kotlin source and no detekt task. Both are in its allowlist, citing this issue.

### Why they weren't fixed with the others

#2005 shipped `kuilt.detekt-jvm`, a one-line convention plugin covering every plain
**Kotlin/JVM** module (`:kuilt-scale`, `:examples`, `:kuilt-warp-ksp`, `:demo-cli`,
`:demo-relay`, `:demo-tap`). The KMP case is not a one-liner:

- `:demo-shared` has `commonMain`/`commonTest` over jvm + wasmJs. Type-resolved analysis
  of `commonMain` needs the source-set folding `kuilt.kmp-library` does in ~70 lines
  (fold `commonMain` into `detektJvmMain`, which carries the jvm compile classpath).
  Doing this right means extracting that block into a shared convention plugin — a
  refactor touching the detekt coverage of all ~40 KMP modules.
- `:demo-web` is **wasmJs-only**. It has no JVM target, so there is no type-resolved
  detekt task to fold anything into; only a metadata task, which runs without type
  resolution and therefore fires none of `detekt.yml`'s four rules.

`:spike` is the same shape and is tracked separately by #1863.

### Suggested shape

Extract the KMP detekt wiring out of `kuilt.kmp-library` into a `kuilt.detekt-kmp`
convention plugin, apply it to both demo modules, then drop them from
`forbidUnlintedModule`'s allowlist. `:demo-web` additionally needs a decision on what
"linted" means for a target with no type resolution available.

title: crdt: VersionVector.entries encodes non-canonically — merge-order dependent, and it is on the wire
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`VersionVector.entries` is a plain `@Serializable` `Map<ReplicaId, Long>` with no canonical
serializer, and it rides the wire as `QuiltMessage.Delivered.vector`. Two peers at the **same
logical vector** reached by different merge orders encode to **different bytes**.

Same defect class as #1957 / #1978 — but unlike the `HashMap` cases in #1979, this one reproduces
on **JVM**, because the offending order is deliberate insertion order, not hash order.

## Reproduced, not predicted

`VersionVector.combine` builds the result as `authors.associateWith { … }` where
`authors = entries.keys + other.entries.keys` — a `LinkedHashSet` in **merge order**
(`VersionVector.kt`, `combine`). `VersionVector` is a `data class`, so `equals` is order-insensitive
over the map and every equality test stays green.

Probe on JVM, `:kuilt-crdt:jvmTest`:

```kotlin
val left  = va.ceilWith(vz).ceilWith(vm)   // alpha=3, zulu=5, mike=7
val right = vm.ceilWith(vz).ceilWith(va)   // same three, merged the other way

assertEquals(left, right)                  // PASSES — they are the same value
```

```
left  keys=[alpha, zulu, mike]  bytes=bf67656e7472696573bf65616c70686103647a756c7505646d696b6507ffff
right keys=[mike, zulu, alpha]  bytes=bf67656e7472696573bf646d696b6507647a756c750565616c70686103ffff
                                            ^^ same three pairs, three different orders
```

Both existing canonical-suite uses of `VersionVector` are **single-entry**
(`VersionVector.of(mapOf(replica to 4L))`, in `CanonicalSerializationTest` and
`CanonicalGoldenVectorTest`). A one-entry map has exactly one order, so neither pins the property.

title: Room frame discriminators are five loose constants in four packages, two of them not even the same kind — reserve the byte space in one registry before 1.0
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`SeamRoom.dispatchIncoming` classifies every inbound room frame by calling four independent
`isXFrame(bytes)` predicates. Each owns its own discriminator, declared `public` in a different
package, with nothing but prose keeping them from colliding:

| Discriminator | Declared in | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| `0x61` | `session.admit.AdmitMessage.PREFIX_BYTE` | byte |
| `0x63` | `session.RoomChannel.CHANNEL_PREFIX` | byte |
| `0x65` | `session.election.LobbyMessage.PREFIX_BYTE` | byte |
| `0x6b` | `liveness.HeartbeatPartitionDetector.PING_PREFIX` / `PONG_PREFIX` | **String** (`"kuilt.heartbeat.ping"`) |

Two problems, not one:

1. **No registry.** Nothing makes a collision a compile error. The reserved ranges are documented
   only in `RoomChannel`'s KDoc — and that documentation is **wrong**: it names CBOR major-type-7
   (`0xe0`–`0xff`) as the hazard band. The real band is `0x60..0x7f`, because CBOR text-string
   headers are `0x60|len` and therefore collide with *all five* claimed prefixes (len 1 → `0x61`,
   3 → `0x63`, 5 → `0x65`, 11 → `0x6b`, 18 → `0x72`). A registry can assert distinctness; it
   cannot assert safety, and must not pretend to.
2. **Heterogeneous kinds.** Three are bytes; heartbeat is a *string* prefix whose first byte
   happens to be `0x6b`. So the byte space is partly claimed by something that does not declare a
   byte at all, and a reader surveying "which bytes are taken" has to know to go look at a String.

These are all `public const val`, so centralising them is source-breaking. **Pre-1.0 is the window.**

## Shape

title: quilter: a new peer's anti-entropy digest is silently dropped by an old peer — no signal, no fallback
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Recorded as the deliberately-accepted limitation of the root-hash anti-entropy gate (see #1955).

### What happens

The anti-entropy tick now sends `QuiltMessage.RootDigest`. A peer running a build that predates it hits the unknown-variant path in `Quilter.dispatch` and **drops the frame**. There is no error, no log, no negotiation — anti-entropy from the new peer toward the old one simply stops.

### Why it was accepted rather than fixed

Uniform peer versions are already an implicit precondition: `QuiltMessage` has **no version handshake** at all, so this is not a new class of exposure. And the pair does still converge — the *old* peer's own `FullState` ticks continue, and `onFullState`'s push-back heals both directions. The cost is reduced rate and one-sided initiation, not divergence.

So this is a real gap with a bounded consequence, not a correctness bug.

### The rejected alternative, recorded so it isn't re-derived

**Reply-always fallback:** have the digest sender fall back to `FullState` for a peer that never answers a digest. Rejected for now because it needs a way to distinguish "old peer" from "converged peer" — and a *converged* peer legitimately answers a matched digest with nothing at all, which is the entire point of the change. Distinguishing them requires either an explicit ack on the match branch (undoing part of the saving) or a per-peer "has ever answered a digest" heuristic with its own false-positive mode on a peer that joins mid-round.

A version handshake on `QuiltMessage` would subsume this and is probably the better shape, but it is a larger decision than this issue.

### Worth deciding

1. Is silent one-directional degradation acceptable, given uniform versions are already assumed

title: :kuilt-scale is compiled but entirely unlinted — detekt is registered only by kuilt.kmp-library
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`:kuilt-scale` applies plain `kotlinJvm`, not the `kuilt.kmp-library` convention plugin — and that convention plugin is what registers detekt. So the module is **not linted at all**.

Evidence: root `./gradlew detektAll --dry-run` schedules ~250 tasks, **zero** of them in `:kuilt-scale`.

Found while adding measured acceptance tests to `:kuilt-scale` under #1955 — the new code had to be held to the repo's conventions by hand, because nothing would have caught a violation.

### This is the third instance of one cause

Detekt coverage is a side effect of applying `kuilt.kmp-library`. Any module that doesn't gets silent zero coverage:

- #1863 — `spike/` is compiled but unlinted
- #1960 — detekt never scans `commonTest`
- this one — `:kuilt-scale`

The per-module fix is easy (register detekt for the module). The more useful fix is structural: make "compiled but unlinted" **impossible to reach** rather than fixing instances as they're noticed — e.g. a root-level check that every module contributing Kotlin source to the build also contributes a detekt task, failing on a module that doesn't. That would have caught all three at once and will catch the fourth.

Worth deciding which of those two this issue is before picking it up.

title: kuilt-raft: the init restore seeds leaderForTerm raw, so a pin above currentTerm arms itself once the node campaigns — the restore's own argument doesn't cover that
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while documenting `onTimeoutNow`'s guard 2 for #1980 (PR #1999). **No live bug** — the guard
that would be needed is present. What is wrong is the *argument* recorded at the restore site, and
that argument is load-bearing for reasoning elsewhere.

## The site

`RaftEngine.kt:558-560`, in the `init` restore:

```kotlin
storage.leaderForTerm()?.let { restored ->
    leaderForTermTerm = restored.term
    leaderForTermId = restored.leaderId
}
```

Seeded **raw**. The KDoc above it defends that, and explicitly contemplates the awkward input: a
record for a term this node has not reached "can only come from storage that lost the accompanying
term write."

## What the argument misses

It reasons only about the term the node restores *at*. Its stated worst case is bounded and benign:

> a wrong pin costs *liveness* for the remainder of one term (this node refuses the real leader's
> AppendEntries and campaigns at the next term)

But `leaderForTerm` decides relevance by **equality** with `currentTerm`. So a pin restored at
`(T+1, L)` while `currentTerm = T` is invisible at first — and then the node campaigns, reaches
`T+1`, and the pin **becomes live for the term the node is now a Candidate in**. The window isn't
"the remainder of one term"; the record lies dormant and arms itself at a term the node reaches by
its own election.

arguments assume cannot happen. `startRealElection` is the only site assigning `Candidate`, and it
runs `persistTermAndVote(currentTerm + 1, …)` first, which is precisely why a Candidate normally holds
no pin for its own term. PR #1999 records that chain as the reason `onTimeoutNow`'s `||

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

A `[symbol]` KDoc link written in a **test** source that resolves to nothing is caught by nothing in
this build.

- **Dokka doesn't run on test sources**, so its unresolved-link warning never sees them.
- **`verifyDocCitations` only reads markdown** — it checks `<!-- verbatim from … -->` /
  `<!-- condensed from … -->` blocks in `docs/` and `Writerside/`, not KDoc in `*.kt`.
- Nothing else looks.

## How it surfaced

Writing #1996, the author reached for `[noteRefusedLeaderFrame]` in a KDoc in
`kuilt-raft/src/commonTest/…/WedgeDetectionTest.kt`. It cannot resolve — the function is `private` in
`RaftEngine` — and they caught it by reasoning, not by any signal. The full gate

each guard exists — `TermJumpBoundTest` and `WedgeDetectionTest` both open with several paragraphs of
spec reasoning, and #1980's whole method depends on a reader trusting them. A link that silently

title: otel-logging: timestampEpochNanos is stamped on the drain coroutine, so it is a flush time, not an event time
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`LogRecord.timestampEpochNanos` is documented and consumed as the **event** time, but it is currently
stamped on the **drain coroutine**, so it is really a second copy of the observed/flush time.

`CapturingAppender.log()` runs synchronously on the thread that logged, and hands the event off:

```kotlin
// CapturingAppender.kt
events.trySend(normalized.copy(activeTrace = capture.resolveTrace()))
```

It resolves the **trace** at the edge — that is #1034's fix, and the KDoc explains exactly why the
drain is too late for ambient context. The **time** was left behind. `LogCapture.capture()` then runs
off the drain and does:

```kotlin
// LogCapture.kt — drain-side
val now = clock.now()
val epochNanos = now.epochSeconds * NANOS_PER_SECOND + now.nanosecondsOfSecond
val record = LogRecord(
    …,
    timestampEpochNanos = epochNanos,
    observedEpochNanos = epochNanos,
)
```

Both OTLP fields get the same drain instant. Per the OTLP spec they are distinct: `timeUnixNano` is
when the event occurred, `observedTimeUnixNano` is when the collector saw it.

## Observed impact

Records recovered from an iPhone's durable store come out **near-uniformly spaced regardless of when
anything happened** — ~150 ms on one device and ~560 ms on another in the same two-device capture.
Every consumer that prints or sorts by `timestampEpochNanos` therefore shows flush cadence, not
event timing:

- `fireworks tools-log-puller --mode merge-wallclock` (the ADR-068 cross-device timeline)
- the `ios-app-logs.sh` decoder

Two wrong headline claims came out of this on tractat-us/fireworks-compose#3972 / #1637 — a joiner
reported as going terminal 250 ms after a blip had actually dwelled the full 60 s window. The error
is not detectable from

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Deliberately scoped out of #1984 (PR #1990), which validated the two *relations* between the timing
fields. This is a different failure in a different field, and #1990's new `require` does not prevent it.

## The defect

`RaftEngine.kt:1341`, the leader's heartbeat loop:

```kotlin
while (true) {
    cmd.trySend(EngineCommand.HeartbeatTick)
    delay(raftConfig.heartbeatInterval.inWholeMilliseconds)
}
```

`inWholeMilliseconds` **truncates**. Any `heartbeatInterval` under 1 ms becomes `delay(0)`, and the loop
spins as fast as the dispatcher will schedule it.

#1990's `require(heartbeatInterval < electionTimeoutMin)` does not catch this — `heartbeatInterval =
500.microseconds` with `electionTimeoutMin = 5.milliseconds` satisfies the relation and still truncates
to zero. The two are independent: #1990 bounds the field from *above*, this is a missing bound from
*below*.

Under `StandardTestDispatcher` the raft suite runs on **virtual time**, and a `delay(0)` loop never
yields the virtual clock. That is the documented signature of the worst diagnostic in this repo: the
test does not fail, it **hangs**, and `runTest` eventually reports `UncompletedCoroutinesError` with no
state dump — the failure mode `CLAUDE.md` calls a stop-and-re-plan signal, and which is also
indistinguishable at a glance from #1739's load-sensitive false reds. So a sub-millisecond
`heartbeatInterval` in a test config would present as "a flaky timeout", and the actual cause is a
config value the constructor accepted.

In production it is an unbounded hot loop on the leader.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Falls out of #1980's mutation survey. That survey keeps finding the same shape, and the per-finding
fix it prescribes does not scale — this is the structural version.

## The problem

Every dispatch-boundary guard in `RaftEngine` refuses a frame by `return`ing. A refusal is therefore
observable only as **the absence of a state change** — and absences do not carry attribution. As soon

which one did it, and the upstream guard's coverage silently drops to zero.

## What the measurement found

**1. The quiescent win already shipped — this issue's premise is stale.** `Quilter.stateRoot()` hashes

state it replaced — **133×**, already banked. At 100k entries the shipped digest round is **63,960×**
cheaper than full state; egress went 109.8 KB/s → **1.72 B/s**.

`ORSet(Causal(DotMap(causal.store.entries - element), causal.context))` — it shrinks the store and

three ordinary ops (A adds, B absorbs, A removes and the delta is lost) leave **byte-identical
`DotContext`s (18 b vs 18 b) with divergent states (74 b vs 95 b)**. A context/vector gate reports
"converged" and skips the heal — *permanently*, since nothing changes between two quiescent peers. The
shipped root hash catches

title: crdt-test: pin canonicalDigest's absolute value with a golden vector
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by the final review of #1981. This is the one literal ask of #1957 that PR did not ship.

#1957 asks for *"Golden vectors pinning **the digest** of a known state, run per target."* #1981
pins the **encodings** (`CanonicalGoldenVectorTest`, ten checked-in CBOR byte strings on every
target) but all three `CanonicalDigestTest` cases are **relative** — equal-to-each-other,
not-equal-to-each-other, equal-to-itself. Nothing pins an absolute `Long`.

Three consequences:

1. A change to `FNV_PRIME`, `FNV_OFFSET_BASIS`, or the file-private `Cbor { }` config in
   `CanonicalDigest.kt` is undetected by the entire suite.
2. The tests never establish that JVM and wasmJs compute the *same* `Long` — each target only checks
   its own internal consistency, which is exactly the blind spot golden vectors exist to remove. The
   encoding vectors subsume this *by argument* (equal bytes ⇒ equal FNV), but the digest function
   itself is unpinned.
3. The KDoc advertises the digest as a divergence alarm between live peers, which makes its absolute
   value a compatibility surface between peers on different kuilt versions.

Worth doing because the risk is demonstrated, not theoretical: while verifying #1981, a mutation
that made the digest **order-independent but platform-dependent** passed every test the helper had.

Fix is one line in `CanonicalDigestTest`:

```kotlin
assertEquals(<captured>, canonicalDigest(GSet.serializer(String.serializer()), GSet.of("alpha", "beta")),
    "digest is pinned across targets and versions")
```

Capture on JVM, then confirm it holds on macOS, wasmJs and iOS — a per-target mismatch would be a
real defect, not a reason to record per-target values.

best-tested thing in the function. **Work item 2 below is answered: no.**

The defect is what that guard *shadows*. `leaderForTerm` is by construction a fact about `currentTerm`
(`leaderForTermId.takeIf { leaderForTermTerm == state.currentTerm }`), so in any state where it reads
`null`, `if (from != established)` refuses **every** sender — producing exactly the state effects an
earlier guard would have produced. Any upstream guard whose tests assert only state effects therefore
goes vacuous, silently. Two confirmed victims:

1. The founding instance — the §5.2 gate's `TimeoutNow` membership (#1889). Fixed by #1977.
2. **New and unfixed: `onTimeoutNow`'s own higher-term guard** (#1889's other half). Mutation
   [D3](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1980#issuecomment-5167048914) deletes
   `if (m.term > state.currentTerm) return` and `:kuilt-raft` stays green, 442/0.

So the fix shape is **not** "test that guard harder". It is: **every guard upstream of a total refuser
needs attribution, not state effects.**

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found during the #1957 Task 5 review. #1957 enumerated and fixed nine non-canonical zoo types. Three
more have the same root cause and were not in that set — **and, unlike the nine, they have no
`CrdtConvergenceSuite` binding at all**, so the byte-equality enforcement #1957 added will never see
them.

## The three

| Type | Field | Merged at |
|---|---|---|
| `Histogram.kt:56` | `buckets: Map<Int, GCounter>` | `:117` via `mergeValues` → `HashMap` |
| `DDSketch.kt:79-80` | `positive` / `negative: Map<Int, GCounter>` | `:202-203` via `mergeValues` |
| `GCounterDouble.kt:26` | `counts: Map<ReplicaId, Double>` | `:46` via `mergeMax` |

All three are `public`, `@Serializable`, `Quilted`, and reach a `HashMap` through `MapMerge` — root
cause A from #1957, visible on Kotlin/Native and wasm (and invisible on JVM, where `HashMap`
iteration is permutation-invariant for a fixed key set).

The missing convergence bindings matter more than the missing annotations. #1957's design doc
already names the risk — that the enforcement is "a strong net, not a complete one" — and this is
that risk instantiated: a zoo type with no suite binding is invisible to the very check that is
supposed to make this class of bug unable to regress.

Three one-line `@Serializable(with = CanonicalMapSerializer::class)` annotations, plus three
`CrdtConvergenceSuite` bindings so the enforcement covers them.

Worth also auditing for a fourth: the general question is "which `public` `Quilted` types have no
convergence binding?", and answering it once is cheaper than rediscovering this a third time.

Blocks a complete answer to #1955 (Merkle anti-entropy).

Found during the #1957 Task 5 review. Same defect class as #1957, in two types that work did not
reach — and here it is converged **state**, not a transient patch.

## The defect

- `kuilt-crdt/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/crdt/Rga.kt:97` — `RgaOp.Compact.positions:
  Map<RgaId, RgaId>`, encoded by a plain `MapSerializer` (`RgaOpSerializer.kt:38,62`).
- `kuilt-crdt/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/crdt/Fugue.kt:125` — `FugueOp.Compact.positions:

the wire. This is exactly the situation #1957 hit with `MovableTree.compactedDots`, which was fixed
there with a dedicated public-API test after a negative control proved the convergence suite could
not see the field.

title: kuilt-raft: the §5.2 leader-authority gate hand-rolls the leader→peer type list that isLeaderToPeer now derives exhaustively
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Noticed while reviewing #1971. Trivial, behaviour-identical, and only possible now that #1971 has landed the helper.

#1971 added `RaftMessage.isLeaderToPeer` (`RaftMessage.kt`) — an extension property over the three RPCs only a leader sends to a peer, written as an **exhaustive `when` with no `else`**, so a new `RaftMessage` variant fails to compile until someone decides which side of the distinction it is on.

The §5.2/§8 leader-authority gate in `RaftEngine.onMessage` still enumerates the same three types by hand:

```kotlin
if ((m is RaftMessage.AppendEntries || m is RaftMessage.InstallSnapshot || m is RaftMessage.TimeoutNow) &&
    voters.isNotEmpty() && from !in voters
```

That was correct to leave alone in #1971 — its brief required the gate be byte-for-byte unchanged, and it was. But the set is now written in two places, and **only one of them forces a decision**: add a new leader→peer RPC and `isLeaderToPeer` will not compile, while the gate will silently fail to guard it. That is the same shape as #1889, which existed because `TimeoutNow` had been left out of exactly this list.

## Change

Replace the hand-rolled triple with `m.isLeaderToPeer`. Behaviour-identical by construction — the property's `true` branches are those three types and nothing else — so this is a readability-and-safety refactor, not a behaviour change.

Worth pinning with a test that the two agree, or better, deleting the duplicate so there is nothing to disagree.

**Prefer check-at-use over maintain-at-write:** an invariant restated at a second site is worse than one derived where it is used, even when the second site is provably correct today.

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by an adversarial review of #1965, immediately after #1897 merged (`9c3fc2b7`).

`RaftConfig.maxTermJump` is unvalidated — `RaftConfig.kt` performs no `require`/`init` checking on any parameter — and two values silently undo the fix that introduced it:

- **`Long.MAX_VALUE` (or any value large enough) reinstates the one-frame cluster-wide wedge #1897 removed.** `onMessage`'s guard becomes vacuous, a single frame carrying an arbitrary term is adopted again, and #1833's original symptom returns in full.

title: kuilt-session: a joiner's resume-refusal loop burns its whole reconnect budget silently
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

A joiner whose `Resume` is refused (e.g. `ResumeWindowNotYetOpen`) retries every `heartbeatConfig.interval` for the whole 60 s `reconnectWindow` and **logs nothing at all** while it happens.

On `origin/main`:
- `SeamRoom.kt`, `is AdmitMessage.Reject ->` (~L1167) has no logging — it just calls `resumeMachine.rejectFlight(msg.reason, msg.code)`.
- `JoinerResumeMachine` has exactly three `logger.info` calls: `resume.terminal`, `resume.ok`, `resume.no-op`.

So the only observable of an episode is a terminal `HostLost` 60 s later, by which point the mechanism that produced it is gone. That invisibility caused a real hardware capture to be misdiagnosed twice — see https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1637#issuecomment-5154399035.

**Want:** one log pull from one device answers *was this joiner being refused, by whom, with what code, how many times, and how far through its budget and its dwell did it get?* Identities and state, not sizes: the host `PeerId`, the `RejectCode`, the room id, the attempt index, elapsed against the reconnect budget, and elapsed-in-dwell against the dwell target.

**Constraints:** follow the existing `resume.*` naming; `logger.info` (the on-device captures collect INFO, so DEBUG is invisible on the hardware this exists to diagnose); bounded volume — one line per retry interval at most, and a healthy session must add none.

Diagnostics only; no behaviour change. Part of #1637.

The costly case is reachable.

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1957 added `CanonicalMapSerializer` / `CanonicalSetSerializer` to `:kuilt-crdt`. Three
pre-existing serializers now hand-roll the same sort-then-delegate logic:

- `DotSetSerializer.kt:31-33`
- `DotFunSerializer.kt:34-39`
- `DotMapSerializer.kt:42-47`

Collapsing them onto the shared pair is a net-negative diff and removes three places the sort
can drift independently.

The same change fixes a measured inefficiency. `serialKeyComparator` runs a full
`KSerializer.serialize` into a fresh `PrimitiveLeafEncoder` + list for **both** operands of
**every** comparison, so sorting N keys costs ~2·N·log₂N key serializations instead of N.
Measured within one JVM process (relative, so host-load-independent): a 2000-entry
`Map<Dot, Long>` over 20 post-warm-up iterations took **20.2 ms** through `serialKeyComparator`
vs **14.2 ms** sorting the already-`Comparable` `Dot` — **1.42×** on the whole CBOR encode.

Fix both at once: expose `serialLeaves` plus the leaf-list comparator from
`internal/SerialKeyComparator.kt`, add a shared `sortedByCanonicalKey` helper doing
decorate-sort-undecorate (each key serialized once), and route all five serializers through it.

Why this is worth doing rather than leaving: the motivating consumer for canonical encoding is
#1955 (Merkle anti-entropy), which is a *repeated full-state-encode* workload — exactly the
shape that pays this cost on every round.

Not urgent — canonicality is correct today, this is duplication plus a constant factor.

title: crdt-test: cross-target convergence digest — prove a wasm/Native/JVM replica converges byte-identically
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Add a canonical state digest for CRDTs so convergence can be asserted **across runtimes and processes**, where direct object comparison isn't available.

### Why not just compare the states

In-process, `assertEquals(a.state, b.state)` is strictly better — exact, no collision risk, better failure output. A digest earns its place only where direct comparison is impossible:

- **Cross-target.** Does an `ORSet` replicated between a JVM peer and a wasmJs or Kotlin/Native peer converge to *byte-identical* state? Nothing checks this today. A serialization asymmetry across targets would converge "successfully" while the encodings differ — the same bug class `:kuilt-deal` pins with golden vectors for SRA byte-parity.
- **Cross-process / real-socket tests** — compare one small value instead of shipping whole states back for assertion.
- **Divergence alarm.** A cheap periodic equality check between live peers, in test harnesses or in production diagnostics.

### It dodges #1955's hardest constraint

A **test-side** digest can live in `:kuilt-test` / `:kuilt-conformance` and use whatever hash it likes, so it never touches `:kuilt-crdt`'s depends-only-on-kotlinx-serialization rule.

It still needs canonical encoding and stable key ordering, and pinning those with golden vectors is most of the work — which is exactly the machinery a wire-side digest (#1955) would need later. Doing this first de-risks that one.

### Suggested shape

- A digest over the canonical serialized form — either `Quilted<S>.digest()` or a conformance-suite helper, whichever keeps `:kuilt-crdt` clean.
- Extend the CRDT conformance suite: after convergence, assert equal digests as well as equal states.
- Golden vectors pinning the digest of a known s

title: spike: REAPI execution backend over :kuilt-warp, with :kuilt-heddle multi-tenant admission
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Investigate implementing the **Remote Execution API** (`build.bazel.remote.execution.v2`, [spec](https://github.com/bazelbuild/remote-apis)) as an execution backend over `:kuilt-warp`, with `:kuilt-heddle` as the multi-tenant admission layer.

### Why this fits warp better than the orchestrator framings

REAPI actions are **hermetic and deterministic by construction** — that is the premise making `digest(Action)` a valid cache key. So duplicate execution is harmless, which means warp's optimistic `CoordinationKind.Free` ring path is **correct with zero consensus**.

That inverts the problem with CI/agent orchestration, where every task is effectful and must ride the Raft-coordinated path — making warp's coordination-free design, its whole point, irrelevant. Build execution is the workload warp was actually designed for.

### The mapping mostly already exists

| REAPI | kuilt |
|---|---|
| `Platform` properties (worker constraints) | `Affinity` / `CapSet` — the same design, independently arrived at |
| ContentAddressableStorage | the bobbin/creel content-addressed store |
| worker selection | `TaskRing` consistent hashing over the eligible roster |
| queue admission / priority | `AdmissionControl` + `:kuilt-warp-heddle` |
| ActionCache (`digest(Action)` → `ActionResult`) | **missing** — an `ORMap<Digest, ActionResult>` |

### Why heddle is the differentiator

Multi-tenant fairness on a shared remote-execution farm is under-served — the established servers offer priority queues, not hierarchical weighted fair-share with conserved entitlement that survives a partition. *"Team A gets 3× the farm, interactive builds preempt CI batch, and the accounting balances after a netsplit"* is heddle's exact shape, and it is

title: crdt: investigate Merkle state digests for the non-causal CRDTs (LWWMap/GSet/Rga) — anti-entropy still ships full state
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Anti-entropy used to ship the whole state every round. It now ships a 64-bit root hash, and state moves only when two peers' hashes disagree.

### Where this stands — SHIPPED

Root-hash gating landed in [#2008](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/2008). Measured on the wire, not modelled:

| | converged 100k-entry `GSet` node |
|---|---|
| before | 3.49 MB every 60 s — **58.1 KB/s**, ≈5 GB/day |
| after | **~1.7 B/s** (~34,000×) |

A converged round is **94–103 bytes** — the digest out, plus the `Ack` back that the match branch still owes for the #1266 cursor resync. The real claim is flatness rather than the ratio: a converged round costs **1880 bytes at 200 entries and 1880 bytes at 20,000**, byte-identical across a 100× state-size difference. Figures are rounded so the saving is understated, and come from an in-memory metered seam (they exclude transport framing and TLS).

Two predictions along the way were wrong, both caught by measuring rather than by review — Phase 0's **0.52 B/s** (its model omitted `upThrough` and priced `root` as `-1L`, one CBOR byte where a real 64-bit hash costs nine), and a first measurement of **~1 B/s** taken against a harness whose replicas had never mutated, so no `Ack` was ever emitted.

All four original open questions are resolved:

- ✅ **Canonical serialization** — #1957.
- ✅ **Hash dependency** — moot; a 64-bit FNV-1a was written in-tree, no new dependency.
- ✅ **Incremental maintenance vs O(n) rehash** — **rehash.** 1.59 ms per 100k-entry round against a 60 s interval.
- ✅ **Measure first** — #1985, then re-measured against the shipped code.

### What was deliberately NOT built

title: kuilt-game: GameReplacementTest's tail awaitVoterCount samples a transient, but its comment claims the spectator never takes a seat
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Same class as #1856 and #1929, in `kuilt-game`: a comment claiming a property the await cannot check.

`GameReplacementTest`'s spectator test ends with

```kotlin
// Voter count must be exactly 2 (host + j1): the final Simple config entry
// commits host+j1 as voters. Await it to confirm the spectator never took a seat.
awaitVoterCount(host.node, expectedCount = 2)
```

`awaitVoterCount` resolves on the **first** instant the voter count equals 2 — i.e. the moment j1 is
admitted. "The spectator never took a seat" is a claim about the whole remaining trajectory, and a
first-match await cannot establish it: a spectator promoted *after* that instant leaves the test green.
The comment describes a stable property; the code samples a transient one.

This is **pre-existing** and not introduced by #1947 — the previous implementation scanned
`committedFrom(1)` for the first Simple config entry carrying two voters and had the same
first-match shape. #1947 only made the helper read `RaftNode.membership`, which is why it surfaced.

Disposition, with the #1856 discipline: **establish first whether the property is unpinned** — mutate
the promotion path so a learner *does* get promoted after the count reaches 2, and confirm the test
stays green. If it does, the fix is to assert the stable property (the spectator's role remains
`Learner`, and the voter set still excludes it, after the cluster has quiesced), not to reword the
comment. The test already asserts `assertIs<RaftRole.Learner>(spectator.node.role.value)` earlier, so
the tail await is currently the weaker of the two.

Related: #1856, #1929, #1947.

title: kuilt-raft: RaftNode.membership KDoc claims 'latest committed config entry' but the flow is adopt-on-append
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`RaftNode.membership`'s KDoc states the flow reflects "the effective cluster membership **as of the
latest committed config entry**" (`RaftNode.kt:124`). The implementation does not wait for commit:
`recomputeMembership` resolves from `state.log.lastOrNull { it.config != null }` — **adopt-on-append**,
§6's actual rule. An *uncommitted* config entry already moves this flow.

This is the same imprecision #1898 found in the §5.2 leader-authority gate's KDoc ("live committed
voter set"), in a different place — and this one is on **public API**, so a consumer can reasonably act
on it. The gap that matters: an appended-but-uncommitted config can still be truncated by a new leader
(§5.3), so a consumer that treats this flow as committed can observe a membership that never existed in
the committed log and never gets a correcting event for the value it acted on.

Two candidate dispositions, and the choice is a real one:

- **Fix the doc.** Say adopt-on-append, name the truncation window, and point a consumer that needs
  committed membership at `committedFrom` + `Committed.Internal` (#1718 makes config commits
  observable as markers, though without payload — see #1946).
- **Fix the behaviour** — publish only committed configs. Safer for consumers, but it changes what
  every current reader sees and the engine itself needs the adopt-on-append value internally, so this
  would mean two surfaces rather than one.

The doc fix is almost certainly right; filing rather than assuming, because the flow is public and
`WarpNode`'s roster feed is named in its own KDoc as a consumer.

Found while reviewing #1947 (#1718), which touches an adjacent claim in `kuilt-game`'s test helper.

Related: #1898, #1718, #1946.

title: kuilt-game: TurnSequencer.events drops Committed.Internal, so a game consumer cannot build an applied index comparable to readIndex()
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1718 added `Committed.Internal(index)` so a state machine folding `RaftNode.committed` / `committedFrom` can advance its applied prefix across the entries raft withholds (the §5.4.2 election no-op, §6 config entries) and therefore reach a `readIndex()` fence.

`TurnSequencer.events` **drops** those markers (`mapNotNull { … is Committed.Internal -> null }`). That is right for the stream's own meaning — a marker is not a turn, and `TurnEvent`'s two variants are the game facade's vocabulary — but it means a consumer that only ever sees `TurnEvent` cannot build an applied index comparable to `RaftNode.readIndex()`. It re-opens the #1718 trap one layer up, for anyone who reaches for a freshness gate over the game facade.

Today nothing in `kuilt-game` calls `readIndex()`/`awaitRead`, so nothing is broken; the KDoc on `TurnSequencer.events` says to fold `RaftNode.committed` directly if you need the index. This issue is to decide whether that stays the answer.

Options:
- **Leave it, document harder.** Cheapest. A game consumer needing a linearizable read reaches past the facade to the `RaftNode` it was handed.
- **`TurnEvent.Internal(index)`.** Makes the facade index-complete and the fold uniform, at the cost of a third variant every exhaustive `when` over `TurnEvent` must handle (`SpeculativeSequencer`, plus consumers).
- **An `appliedIndex: StateFlow<Long>` on `TurnSequencer`.** The facade folds the whole `Committed` stream itself and publishes the index, leaving `TurnEvent` alone. Pairs directly with `awaitRead(applied)`.

Deferred out of #1718's PR deliberately: that PR's consumer changes were mechanical, and picking between these is a game-facade API decision.

title: Decorator Looms (MuxClientLoom, FaultyLoom, FlakyLifecycleLoom) discard their delegate's capability() and substitute the confident default
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by the #1746 `Loom.capability()` audit. Splitting it out because it is a **different defect class** from #1746: that issue is about looms whose *own* default verdict is an un-established `Available`. This is about looms that **discard a delegate's correctly-established verdict** and substitute the confident default.

## The defect

Three decorator `Loom`s wrap an arbitrary delegate `Loom`, forward the weave surface, and silently do **not** forward `capability()`:

| decorator | file |
|---|---|
| `MuxClientLoom(private val base: Loom, …)` | `kuilt-core/src/commonMain/…/MuxClientLoom.kt:63` |
| `FaultyLoom(private val delegate: Loom, …)` | `kuilt-test/src/commonMain/…/FaultySeam.kt:178` |

```kotlin
override suspend fun join(tag: Tag): FaultySeam               = wrap(delegate.join(tag))
// no capability() override → inherits Loom's roleless `Available`
```

`MuxClientLoom` is the same shape and is **production `commonMain` in `:kuilt-core`**.

title: TieredSeam.sendTo silently drops a frame addressed to a peer in neither tier — Seam.sendTo requires PeerNotConnected
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by binding the `SeamConformanceSuite` harness for `TieredSeam` (option (1) of #1871). It is the *first* thing the new harness reports, and nothing in-tree could see it before.

### The violation

`Seam.sendTo`'s contract is explicit:

> `sendTo` when the addressed peer is absent from `peers`: throws `PeerNotConnected`.

`TieredSeam.sendTo` instead returns normally:

```kotlin
when {
    peer in localTier.peers.value -> localTier.sendTo(peer, payload)
    peer in peerTier.peers.value  -> peerTier.sendTo(peer, payload)
    else -> Unit          // ← silent drop
}
```

`SeamConformanceSuite.sendToAbsentPeerThrowsPeerNotConnected` is **ungated core** — no `SeamCapabilities` flag can excuse it — so the new `TieredSeamConformanceTest` is red on it:

```
sendToAbsentPeerThrowsPeerNotConnected[jvm] FAILED
  java.lang.AssertionError: Expected an exception of class us.tractat.kuilt.core.PeerNotConnected
  to be thrown, but was completed successfully.
```

The drop is documented (`TieredSeam` KDoc) and pinned (`TieredSeamTest.sendToUnknownPeerIsDroppedNothingSent`), so a behaviour-preservation review would pass it — the spec-conformance dimension is what catches it.

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while reviewing #1933 (the #1329 guard). Same defect class as #1329, one rule over — and this one is documented in the config file itself, which makes it worse.

`ForbiddenMethodCall` **is not configured anywhere.** It appears in neither `config/detekt/detekt.yml` nor `config/detekt/detekt-test.yml` as a rule. #1329 established why: detekt cannot resolve a callee descriptor for kotlin-stdlib functions in this KMP setup, so `ForbiddenMethodCall` silently no-ops on them even with type resolution demonstrably active.
