title: Surface elapsed-vs-ceiling on timeout failures — the data is already in the results XML, just not where the reader looks
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

> **⚠ CORRECTED 2026-07-31, before the fix landed (PR #1941).** The framing below is wrong in its
> central claim and is kept only for the record — read this box first.
>
> This issue asserted that the `time=` attribute next to the declared ceiling is *"the **entire**
> discriminator between slow box and genuinely wedged"*. **It is not.** For a `runTest` ceiling trip,
> elapsed is always within a second of the ceiling, so the ratio is ~100% **by construction** and
> carries almost no information. Measured, not argued: JVM 2.193 s/2 s (110%), Kotlin/Native
> 1.333 s/2 s (67%), 5.267 s/6 s (88%), 11.233 s/12 s (94%).
>
> **What actually discriminates is the exception *message* variant** — `completed, but only after the
> timeout` (slow box) · `did not run to completion` (wedge) · `active child jobs` (leak). Gradle's
> console drops the message on both platforms, rendering only `<class> at <file>:<line>`, which is
> the real reporting gap.
>
> Elapsed still earns its place, but on a **different axis** than claimed: it separates a genuine
> ceiling trip from a **teardown-leak** `UncompletedCoroutinesError`, where elapsed ≪ ceiling and the
> message carries no ceiling at all.
>
> Two further things measurement produced that the text below would have got wrong:
> - one ceiling shape is a ***virtual*-time** budget (`Timed out after 750ms of _virtual_ … time`),
>   which trips in ~4 ms of wall clock — a percentage there is a category error, not a datum;
> - Kotlin/Native under-reports elapsed by a roughly constant ~0.7 s, so it approaches 100% from
>   *below* while the JVM sits just above. Same understated value Gradle writes into the XML `time=`.
>
> The premise that the data already exists and is merely unsurfaced

title: kuilt-raft: CheckQuorumTest.healAfterStepDown_nodeRejoinsAsFollower_noTermInflation asserts neither of the two properties its docstring claims
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while landing #1856 (PR #1928), in the same file and of the same class: a test docstring asserting a property the test body does not check.

`CheckQuorumTest.healAfterStepDown_nodeRejoinsAsFollower_noTermInflation` makes two claims in prose, neither of which has a matching assertion:

| Docstring claims | Body actually asserts |
|---|---|
| "the old leader's term … must match the final cluster term" | only `term > 0` |
| "the cluster term must not have inflated past the original term+1" | only that *a* leader exists |

Both are real properties worth pinning — term inflation after a heal is exactly the failure a check-quorum step-down is supposed to avoid — so the likely disposition is to add the assertions, not to reword. But that is the determination to make first, with evidence, exactly as #1856 required: **establish whether the property is unpinned (→ assert it) or whether the prose is stale (→ reword it)**, and do not reword a genuinely unpinned property. #1856's method works here — mutate the mechanism the docstring names and confirm the test does *not* go red.

The other three fixtures in the file were checked during #1856 and are reachable states; this is the only remaining one.

## Why file it separately

#1928 is scoped to the property #1856 named, and its own gate is clean. Folding a second unpinned-property fix into it would blur which mutation pinned which test — the receipt discipline that made #1856 decidable.

## Related

#1856 / PR #1928 (the sibling case, same file), #1846 (the fixture the file's other test regressed on), #1832.

title: kuilt-raft: a snapshot rejected by snapshotTotalCeiling stalls the follower with only a debug log — emit a RaftMetric
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #1881 (PR #1925), filed against the one trade-off that fix deliberately accepts.

## The gap

`SnapshotReceiver` now returns `ChunkOutcome.TooLarge` when a reassembly would exceed
`RaftConfig.snapshotTotalCeiling`, and `RaftEngine.onInstallSnapshot` discards the buffer and
re-advertises offset `0`. For the attacker case (a peer feeding `done = false` chunks forever) that is
exactly right — the buffer never grows past the ceiling.

For the **honest** case it is a silent non-convergent loop. A legitimate leader whose snapshot genuinely
exceeds the follower's ceiling restarts from `0`, hits the ceiling again, and repeats indefinitely. PR
#1925's own KDoc says so plainly:

> If its snapshot is genuinely above the ceiling the transfer will not converge; that is the intended
> loud, configurable failure in place of an OOM.

The disposition is right — a knob to raise beats an OOM kill — but **the failure is not actually loud**.
The only signal is a `debug { }` line, so an operator sees a follower that never catches up, with nothing
above debug level explaining why, and the fix (raise `snapshotTotalCeiling`) is not discoverable from the
symptom.

## Shape

Emit a `RaftMetric` on the `TooLarge` arm. The precedent is exact: `RaftMetric.ElectionSuppressedTermCeiling(term, ceiling)`
(`RaftMetric.kt:98`) already covers "a configured ceiling suppressed an operation" — this is the same
shape for the snapshot lane, e.g. `SnapshotRejectedSizeCeiling(attemptedTotal: Long, ceiling: Int)`.
`ChunkOutcome.TooLarge` already carries both values, so nothing new has to be plumbed.

Worth considering alongside it: whether a repeated `TooLarge` from the *same* peer for the *same*
`SnapshotMeta` should escalate above debug o

title: kuilt-conformance: RaftStorageConformanceSuite does not pin the field ranges and log contiguity the engine now refuses to start on
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #1887, where it was deliberately scoped out: #1887 makes the **engine** refuse to start on
corrupt durable state, which is the safety fix. This issue is the complementary move — catching the adapter
bug at the *adapter's own test time* rather than at a consumer's startup.

## The gap

kuilt ships **no** durable `RaftStorage` — `InMemoryRaftStorage` is the only implementation in the library,
so every persistent adapter is consumer code. `RaftStorageConformanceSuite` is the contract those adapters
are verified against, and it currently constrains none of the fields #1887 has to defend against: it checks
that entries round-trip and that `truncateFrom` / `entries(fromIndex)` filter correctly, and nothing about
ranges or contiguity.

So an adapter can pass the whole TCK and still hand the engine a `lastIncludedTerm` of `Long.MAX_VALUE`, a
log with a gap in it, or entries whose indices do not start at `snapshotIndex + 1`. After #1887 the engine
refuses to start on those — which is the right outcome, but the consumer learns about it at **startup in
production**, not when running the conformance suite they were given for exactly this purpose.

Extend `RaftStorageConformanceSuite` so a conforming adapter must faithfully round-trip the values the
engine now validates:

- `SnapshotMeta.lastIncludedIndex` / `lastIncludedTerm` at edge values (`0`, and at the `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_*`
  ceilings) — a lossy numeric column (e.g. an adapter persisting a `Long` through a `Double`, or a schema
  with a 32-bit integer column) corrupts these silently today.
- `LogEntry.index` / `term` at the same edges.

title: kuilt-heddle: confirm or refute — a re-homed child may be STARVED because committedService counts issuedRelocIn (unproven code reading)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Surfaced as a **hedged side observation** during the #1752 design pass. Filing it separately because if it holds it is a live fairness defect on shipped code, and because the observer explicitly did **not** trace the full reparent flow — so per this repo's discipline it is a **code reading, UNPROVEN**, and step one is to confirm or refute it, not to fix it.

## The claim

A re-homed child may be **starved**, not over-served — the opposite direction from every relocation bug found so far.

The chain, as read:

1. `EdgeSummary.issued` is `effIssuedTotal` (`EntitlementLedger.kt:232`).
2. `committedService` therefore includes `issuedRelocIn` (`EdgeSummary.kt:41`).
3. A fresh edge's frozen neutral seat was the front **at prepare** time.
4. So after a shipped #1760 re-home, `ev(t)` should sit roughly `strand / w` **above** the front — and an edge above the front does not get picked.

Magnitude scales with the relocated strand, so a large re-home would starve the child for correspondingly long.

- It is on **`main`**, in machinery that shipped in #1760 (slice 3).
- Every other relocation finding has been in the over-service direction (#1783, #1916), so a starvation-direction bug would not be caught by any conservation or supply check — the identity is untouched. Nothing currently looks for it.
- **#1894** already records that the randomized conservation property test never exercises RELOCATION, which is the family real breaks keep appearing in. This would be a second reason to close that gap, and a starvation assertion is a different oracle from a conservation one.

title: jvmMain MDNSServiceDiscoverer.departures() never emits: serviceRemoved's ServiceInfo carries no TXT records
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kuilt-mdns`'s **jvmMain** `MDNSServiceDiscoverer.departures()` is a real `callbackFlow` over JmDNS's
`serviceRemoved` — but it emits **nothing**, ever, because it reads the peer id from a TXT record the
removal event does not carry:

```kotlin
override fun serviceRemoved(event: ServiceEvent) {
    val peerId = event.info?.getPropertyString(MDNSAdvertisement.TXT_KEY_PEER_ID)
    if (peerId != null) trySend(peerId)   // peerId is always null here
}
```

So JVM has the *same* ghost-peer symptom as Android (#1903), for a different reason: Android never
implements the signal, JVM implements it against data that isn't there.

## Evidence — real multicast, JmDNS 3.6.3, pinned `0.7.0-dev.1027`

Two `JmDNS` instances on one non-loopback multicast interface. Advertiser registers
`ServiceInfo.create("_fireworks._tcp.local.", "probe-service", 19099, 0, 0, txt)` — the exact shape
`MDNSServiceAdvertiser.buildServiceInfo()` builds — then unregisters. A raw `ServiceListener` on the
browser logs what each callback receives:

```
PROBE registered
PROBE added    name=probe-service infoNull=false
PROBE resolved name=probe-service peerId=null
PROBE resolved name=probe-service peerId=probe-peer
PROBE unregistered
PROBE removed  name=probe-service infoNull=false peerId=null textLen=37 \
               props=[probe-service._fireworks._tcp.local.]
```

`serviceRemoved` **does** fire, and `event.info` is non-null — but its text is the qualified service

title: kuilt-heddle: reconcile does not require the live and retired edges to share a parent — honest acks double the mint (no crash needed)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by an adversarial design pass on #1783, and **verified by execution** against the production derivation shape. **This is more severe than #1783**: it needs no crash, no restart, no incarnation gap, and no dishonest participant. Every party behaves correctly and the mint is still doubled.

## The hole

Neither `Activate` (`ControlPlane.kt:589-618`) nor `reconcile` (`ControlPlane.kt:766-794`) checks that **the live edge's parent matches the retired edge's parent.**

The §5.2 telescoping proof that makes reconciliation conservation-safe silently assumes the retired edge `s` and the live edge `t` share a parent. The implementation never enforces it.

## Reproduction (executed)

1. Raced-retire `e1 (a → g)`.
2. Reparent `g` under `b` via `e2 (b → g)` — a legal reparent.
3. Complete the quiesce/ack fence **honestly**. Every ack is truthful.
4. `reconcile`.

The drain credits **`a`** with the full 10 — its `netInflow(e1)` subtraction vanishes — while `issuedRelocIn(e2)` debits **`b`**:

```
a = 10,  b = -10,  g = 10        Σ holdings + Σ effLeafSpent = 10  (identity INTACT)
```

Then `a` and `g` both spend their apparent 10:

```
ConservationViolation(20, 10)    →  20 units of real service from a 10-unit mint
```

The identity holds at every intermediate state because `b`'s unenforceable −10 pocket arithmetically offsets `a`'s phantom credit — so **no identity check catches this**. `b` simply never delegates again, and the phantom supply at `a` is fully spendable.

## Fix — one gate

Refuse the reconcile when the parents differ:

```kotlin
require(recordOf(s).parent == recordOf(t).parent)   // in reconcile, refuse otherwise
```

title: build: re-enable Kotlin/Wasm incremental compilation once a stable Kotlin carries the upstream ICE fix
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Removal trigger for the `kotlin.incremental.wasm=false` line #1909 added to
`gradle.properties` to fix #1893.

## Why it is off

The Kotlin/Wasm backend ICEs out of `DefinedDeclarationsResolver.resolve` with
`NoSuchElementException: Key ic#NN:kotlin.text/… is missing in the map` when a
stdlib call is removed from test code and the wasm link runs against the retained
incremental cache. Reproduced deterministically here: 3/3 with wasm IC on, 0/6 with
it off (see #1909).

## Why it should come back on

Measured cost of having it off, on this repo: a one-line `:kuilt-core` commonMain
edit that ripples to all 37 wasm test-executable links relinks in **~26 s** with IC
off vs **~6.5 s** with IC on — roughly 4x. (Ratio measured within one session on a
box at load ~6, so treat the ratio as the trustworthy figure, not the absolutes.)
That is a real everyday-iteration tax for anyone editing shared code with the wasm
target in their loop.

## Blocked on

An upstream Kotlin release that carries the fix. This is a compiler bug, not a
kuilt one: it is tracked upstream as `KT-85270` ("K/Wasm: incremental compilation
fails with NoSuchElementException when a stdlib call is removed"), state **Fixed**,
subsystem *Backend. Wasm*, **available in 2.4.20-Beta1**. As of 2026-07-30 the
latest *stable* Kotlin is **2.4.10** (2.4.20 exists only as Beta2), so there is no
stable version to bump to yet. Kotlin/Wasm incremental compilation only became
stable-and-default in 2.4.0, which is why this surfaced now.

title: build: make `--rerun-tasks` actually invalidate Kotlin's incremental-compilation caches, so the mandated pre-merge gate means what it says
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #1893 / #1909. `#1893` was fixed by turning Kotlin/Wasm incremental
compilation off, which removes the one cache that was actually biting. The hole it
exposed is structural and still open.

## The promise vs. what happens

`CLAUDE.md` mandates a cache-disabled build before auto-merge:

```
./gradlew :<module>:build detektAll --rerun-tasks
```

`--rerun-tasks` forces every task to re-execute. It does **not** clear Kotlin's
incremental-compilation state, because that state is not a tracked task *output*.
So the task re-runs "from scratch" while still reading caches written by an
earlier, differently-shaped execution — the exact condition that produced #1893's
ICE. "Cache-disabled" is not true of the thing the gate is supposed to disable.

## Where the state actually lives

#1893 guessed `build/kotlin/`. Measured on this repo (Kotlin 2.4.10):

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `<module>/build/klib/cache/<target>/<compilation>/version.<hash>/` | the real JS/Wasm IR link IC caches — one subdirectory per input klib (`kotlin-stdlib-wasm-js-2.4.10.klib.<hash>`, `main.<hash>`, …). 22 MB for `:kuilt-core` alone; **37** such dirs across the repo |
| `<module>/build/kotlin/<task>/{local-state,cacheable}/` | present but **empty** for the wasm link tasks |

So a fix keyed to `build/kotlin/` would have missed it entirely.

## Why it is worth closing even though #1893 no longer bites

Kotlin/Native incremental compilation of klib artifacts is **enabled by default**
from Kotlin 2.4.20-Beta2. The moment this repo bumps past 2.4.10, the native lane
acquires its own retained-IC-state-across-`--rerun-tasks` surface, and the next
instance of this class will look like a fresh mystery rather than a known one.

title: kuilt-raft: delete the redundant sender-identity wire fields (leaderId/candidateId) and read `from` — five forgeable inputs, one structural fix
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Structural fix for a category found by an adversarial audit of the `_leader` lane (#1906). **Survey found
five instances of one defect shape; this makes it impossible rather than checking it five times.**

## The shape

A `RaftMessage` carries a **sender-identity field that must equal `from`**, nobody compares the two, and
the field is then read as *authority*:

| Field | Read as | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `AppendEntries.leaderId` | `_leader.value = m.leaderId` (`RaftEngine.kt:1338`) | #1906 |
| `InstallSnapshot.leaderId` | `_leader.value = m.leaderId` (`:1159`) | #1906 |
| `RequestVote.candidateId` | **persisted as `votedFor`** (`:680-682`) | below |
| `PreVote.candidateId` | same shape (`:711`) | below |
| `TimeoutNow.leaderId` | **written and never read by anyone** (`RaftMessage.kt:161`) | dead field |

`from` is already the true origin — `SeamRaftTransport` / `RoutedRaftTransport` / `RaftRelayHub` unwrap the
relay envelope — and every honest sender sets the field to its own `selfId`. So each field is **redundant
with `from` on every honest frame and forgeable on every hostile one.** `TimeoutNow.leaderId` already
models the correct pattern by accident: it is written, never read, and nothing is worse for it.

term with `AlreadyVoted`.

its vote cannot stop the other two members of a 3-voter cluster electing each other

title: kuilt-raft: ForwardResponse has no provenance check — a forged receipt makes propose() report a commit that never happened, and the consumer marks the write done
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by an adversarial audit of the `_leader` provenance lane (#1906). **Pre-existing. Executed, not
reasoned** — a two-frame chain with zero network faults. This is the most severe finding of that audit:
the outcome is a **silently lost write that the consumer's exactly-once bookkeeping marks as done.**

## Mechanism

`onForwardResponse` never checks who sent it:

```kotlin
private suspend fun onForwardResponse(from: NodeId, m: RaftMessage.ForwardResponse) {
```
`RaftEngine.kt:2133` — **`from` is an unused parameter.**

`ProposalForwarder.onResponse` keys solely on a per-node counter starting at `0`
(`ProposalForwarder.kt:102`), and `PendingForward` never records **which peer the `Forward` was sent to**.
So there is no state to check against even if the handler wanted to. `ForwardResponse` is also outside the
§5.2 gate, so the sender need not be a voter.

## The chain (executed)

1. Forge `leaderId = ghost` in an ordinary `AppendEntries` (#1906) → the victim's `_leader` becomes a peer
   that does not exist.
2. The victim's `propose()` sends `Forward(0, …)` into the void — no one receives it.
3. Forge `ForwardResponse(0, Committed(7, 1))` from **any** peer.
4. `propose()` returns `LogEntry(index = 7)`. Probe reports `commandPresentInAnyLog=false`.

The caller is told its command committed at index 7. It did not commit anywhere. The consumer then marks
that `DedupKey` complete, so **the write is lost permanently** — the retry that exactly-once semantics
exist to provide never happens. Ongaro §8 (client interaction) is the section violated: a client must
never observe a committed result for a command that was not committed.

title: kuilt-raft: InstallSnapshot's lastIncludedTerm is not checked against the recipient's own committed term — a locally-available floor nobody enforces
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Rescoped 2026-07-31.** This issue was originally filed as "the snapshot lane's Log-Matching analogue
fails open — a mismatch (incl. past-the-tail `null`) discards the whole log instead of rejecting (§7
rule 8)". **That framing was wrong and its prescribed fix would have caused a severe regression** —
refutation in [this comment](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1910#issuecomment-5140670859),
kept because the reasoning error is instructive. What survives is the check below, which is genuinely
separable and genuinely unchecked.

## The check

`RaftEngine.finalizeInstalledSnapshot` accepts any `lastIncludedTerm` that clears
`isWellFormedSnapshotChunk`'s shape bound (`0..min(m.term, MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM)`). But there is a tighter
bound available from state the recipient already holds:

> **`m.lastIncludedTerm` must be `>=` the term of our own entry at `commitIndex`.**

Soundness: if the snapshot legitimately covers an index above our commit frontier `C`, then by Leader
Completeness it *contains* our committed entry at `C`, and terms are non-decreasing along a log, so its
`lastIncludedTerm` is at or above `C`'s term. Rejecting below that floor therefore never rejects a
legitimate snapshot.

```kotlin
val floor = state.entryAt(state.currentCommitIndex)?.term ?: state.snapshotTerm
```

**The floor must be the term at `commitIndex`, NOT `state.lastLogTerm`.** Uncommitted entries can
legitimately be overwritten by a snapshot carrying a *lower* term — a node holding an uncommitted term-7
entry can be caught up by a legitimate term-8 leader whose log has term 5 at that index. Keying to
`lastLogTerm` would reject honest snapshots. `entryAt(commitIndex)` returns `null` exactly when
`commitIndex == snapshotIndex`

The threat model records three unauthenticated exposures on the snapshot path, all of them accepted

what the frame asserts.**

title: androidMain MDNSServiceDiscoverer never implements departures(), so NSD consumers accumulate ghost peers
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kuilt-mdns`'s **androidMain** `MDNSServiceDiscoverer` never implements
`PeerDiscoverySource.departures()`, so it silently takes the interface default `emptyFlow()`. Any
consumer folding it through `discoveryRoster` accumulates ghost peers forever on Android.

The jvmMain implementation *does* implement it (`callbackFlow` at
`kuilt-mdns/src/jvmMain/.../MDNSServiceDiscoverer.kt:92`). androidMain has no `departures` token at
all. Confirmed against the published artifact too: in `kuilt-mdns-release.aar` (`0.7.0-dev.1027`)
`MDNSServiceDiscoverer.departures()` is a one-line bridge to the interface default, whereas the jvm
jar's is a real `callbackFlow`.

So the same API on the same class behaves differently per platform, and the difference is invisible
at the call site — a consumer that correctly handles departures on desktop gets none on Android with
no error and no log.

## Failure scenario

Android LAN lobby browsing over NSD. A desktop host stops advertising → Android NSD fires
`serviceLost` → nothing reaches the roster → the dead host stays listed indefinitely and remains
dialable. The user taps a host that is gone.

## Why it's an upstream fix

Android's `NsdManager.DiscoveryListener` already delivers `onServiceLost(NsdServiceInfo)`, so the
signal exists and is simply not forwarded. A consumer cannot fix this without reimplementing the
discoverer, and `discoveryRoster`'s KDoc explicitly tells callers not to hand-roll the merge.

Found while consolidating a hand-rolled roster onto `discoveryRoster` in fireworks-compose
([#3870](https://github.com/tractat-us/fireworks-compose/pull/3870)); tracked downstream as
[#3871](https://github.com/tractat-us/fireworks-compose/issues/3871).

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Noticed while tracing #1880's scenario 4. **Pre-existing, independent of #1880.**

**Status: CONFIRMED — driven and mutation-verified 2026-07-31** ([finding](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1898#issuecomment-5141025484),
[mutation check](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/issues/1898#issuecomment-5141034029)). The
reachability question this body was filed to raise is **answered: the wedge is reachable**, through five
legal §6 joint-consensus changes past an absent voter, each retaining dual majorities among the live
nodes with headroom at every step. The victim was *crashed*, not partitioned, so the persistence claim is
exercised too — it survives two restarts. Observed: 500 `AppendEntries` from the current leader dropped
over 1 s of virtual time, victim pinned at `membership={a,b,x}`, `leader=null`, `commit=0` while the
leader is at 12. Disabling one clause of the gate makes the same trajectory recover fully, so it is not a
harness, quorum, or election-churn artefact.

**Two corrections to what is written below, both from the executed run:**

1. **It is not the *committed* voter set.** `recomputeMembership` resolves from
   `state.log.lastOrNull { it.config != null }` — adopt-on-append — so an **uncommitted** config entry

title: kuilt-raft: replace the absolute term ceiling with a relative jump bound — an absolute ceiling cannot avoid a boundary that wedges the cluster
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Split out of #1886, which established that **no absolute term ceiling can avoid a boundary pathology**:
for an adoption ceiling `A` you need `T ≤ A ⟹ T + 1 ≤ A`, true only for `A = ∞`. Whatever constant is
chosen, a frame at `A` (or `A - 1` for an exclusive bound) is admitted, propagates on ordinary traffic,
and then every election proposes a term every peer drops — #1833's symptom, reached through the one
value the filter lets past. Making the bound exclusive moves the boundary; it does not remove it.
#1886 ships loud containment, which makes the failure diagnosable but not survivable.

## The shape that removes it

Bound the **jump**, not the value:

```kotlin
if (m.term > state.currentTerm + MAX_TERM_JUMP) return   // instead of: m.term > MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM
```

`currentTerm + 1` is then admissible at every term, so there is no boundary at all. And the attack
becomes infeasible rather than one-shot: reaching `2^60` costs `2^60 / MAX_TERM_JUMP` frames instead
of a single frame. It also subsumes what the absolute ceiling was actually for — an implausible term is
implausible *relative to what this node has seen*, which is the stronger and more local test.

## Why it needs design, not a patch

A relative bound rejects legitimate large jumps, and Raft has real ones:

- a node absent across more than `MAX_TERM_JUMP` elections (long partition, crashed for a while) must
  still be able to adopt the cluster's current term to rejoin;
- a node restored from durable state that is far behind (interacts with `checkedRestoredTerm`, #1855);
- a learner/spoke catching up from a snapshot.

So it needs a catch-up path for the rejected-but-honest case — plausibly "reject the jump, but let
`InstallSnapshot`/`AppendEntries` f

> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

## The defect

Slice 3's re-home moves only the **charge** half of the conserving move onto the live edge at charge time. The **credit** half (`issuedRelocIn`) arrives only with a later committed `Reconcile` — §6.3's ownership discipline is why the data plane cannot write the credit itself. body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while verifying #1886 with an executed probe.

The §5.2/§8 leader-authority gate (#1383) drops `AppendEntries` and `InstallSnapshot` whose sender is not a current voter, and covers nothing else:

```kotlin
if ((m is RaftMessage.AppendEntries || m is RaftMessage.InstallSnapshot) &&
    voters.isNotEmpty() && from !in voters
) {
```
`RaftEngine.kt:2151-2154`

`RaftMessage.TimeoutNow` belongs to the same class. It is a **leader→peer** RPC: `sendTimeoutNow` is only ever called from the §3.10 graceful-transfer path, by a leader, at `RaftEngine.kt:1941` and `:1421`, and its effect on the recipient is to **bypass the election timeout and start an election immediately** (`RaftEngine.kt:546` — `TimeoutNow` is the one trigger that marks an election as transfer-driven).

Nothing validates that the sender is the leader, or even a voter. So any peer that can address the node can force it to start an election at any in-range term, repeatedly — a disruption primitive that PreVote exists specifically to deny.

Measured, in a healthy 3-voter cluster on `origin/main`: a **non-leader** sending one `TimeoutNow` moved the victim's durable term from `1` to `2^60 + 1`.

```
PROBE3 victim=v2 spoofedFrom=nonLeader termBefore=1 termAfter=1152921504606846977
```

(That particular escalation is #1886's inclusive-ceiling bug and is fixed there. This issue is the residual: even with the ceiling closed, an ungated `TimeoutNow` still lets any peer force elections at will.)

## Fix

Add `TimeoutNow` to the gate's type test. It is a one-line change to the same condition; the empty-voters carve-out should apply unchanged, since a node with no known voters is not a voter and has no leadership to transfer.

title: kuilt-raft: restored log entries and snapshot metadata are unvalidated on init-restore — the §5.4.1 domination of #1832/#1868, reached from storage instead of the wire
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Scope boundary of the #1855 fix, deliberately not fixed there.

#1855 bounds the **term** restored by `state.currentTerm = checkedRestoredTerm(storage.term())`. Everything else the init-restore reads from `RaftStorage` is still adopted verbatim (`RaftEngine.kt:306-335`):

```kotlin
state.snapshotIndex = stored.meta.lastIncludedIndex   // unbounded
state.snapshotTerm  = stored.meta.lastIncludedTerm    // unbounded
state.log.addAll(storage.entries(state.snapshotIndex + 1))   // entry index/term unbounded, contiguity unchecked
```

## Why it matters

The same §5.4.1 Leader Completeness violation #1832 (AppendEntries) and #1868 (InstallSnapshot) closed on the wire is reachable here. §5.4.1 orders log positions by `(term, index)` lexicographically, so a node whose restored `lastLogTerm` is huge is **unbeatable in every election**: `isLogUpToDate` says every honest peer's log is less current, so every peer grants it the vote. It then becomes leader carrying a corrupt log and overwrites the cluster's.

Note the term bound added in #1855 does **not** cover this: a `RequestVote`'s `wireTerm` is the *candidate's term*, not its `lastLogTerm`, so a node with a perfectly plausible term and a poisoned entry term passes every existing check. Unbounded `lastIncludedIndex` is the index-half of the same lever — see `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_INDEX`'s KDoc on why bounding only the term half is insufficient.

Non-contiguous restored entries are a separate corruption: `RaftLogMath` reads positionally (`log[index - snapshotIndex - 1]`), so a gap silently returns the wrong entry for every lookup — the failure mode `nodeRestart_filtersCompactedPrefix_whenLogDiscardCrashedMidWay` already guards against for the compacted-prefix case.

title: kuilt-raft: the term ceiling is inclusive but leaves no headroom for `+ 1` — one frame at exactly MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM reproduces #1833 cluster-wide
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while closing #1855. This is a residual hole in #1846's own fix for #1833, on the wire path — **not** the restore path, and more severe than #1855 (cluster-wide, not single-node).

## Mechanism

`onMessage` rejects `wireTerm > MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM` (`RaftEngine.kt:2189`), so a term of **exactly** `2^60` is **admitted**. But the election increment is `currentTerm + 1`, which then proposes `2^60 + 1` — a term the same bound rejects on every recipient.

1. One `RequestVote` (or any term-carrying frame) at `term = 2^60` is adopted: `m.term > currentTerm` → `stepDown(2^60)`. The §5.2 leader-authority gate does not cover RequestVote/PreVote, so any peer can send it.
2. The victim's own responses carry `state.currentTerm = 2^60`, which is *also* inside the bound, so **every peer adopts it in turn on ordinary traffic** — the identical propagation step #1833 described.
3. Every node now sits at `2^60`. The next election proposes `2^60 + 1`. Every recipient drops it as implausible.
4. **No leader can ever be elected again, cluster-wide**, surviving restart because `currentTerm` is persisted.

That is #1833 verbatim, reached through the one value the fix leaves open. The wrap to `Long.MIN_VALUE` no longer happens, but the observable outcome — permanent, silent, cluster-wide election failure — is the same.

## Fix

The **adoption** ceiling must sit strictly below the **emission** ceiling, so a term that was admissible to adopt is still admissible to increment. The minimal change is to make the check exclusive:

```kotlin
if (wireTerm != null && (wireTerm < 0L || wireTerm >= MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM)) return
```

title: Release flow: the README version-bump PR is opened by GITHUB_TOKEN, so its CI is withheld as action_required and the PR wedges
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

The `maven-central` job ends by opening a README version-bump PR. That PR is created with
`GITHUB_TOKEN`, and GitHub **withholds workflow runs on PRs opened by `GITHUB_TOKEN`** (recursion
prevention). So its `ci` run is created with `conclusion = action_required` and never starts.

Observed on **v0.7.2** (2026-07-28): PR #1883, run `30343814639` — `completed/action_required`,
`statusCheckRollup` empty, `mergeStateStatus` BLOCKED. It does not self-resolve. I unwedged it with
`gh api repos/tractat-us/kuilt/actions/runs/30343814639/approve -X POST`, after which `detect` correctly
classified it docs-only, the build jobs skipped, `ci-required` went green in ~1 min, and it merged.

### Why this is worth fixing rather than remembering

The release flow has a final step that **silently requires a human to notice a PR is stuck**. The
failure mode is indistinguishable from "CI is slow" — an empty `statusCheckRollup` reads the same as
not-yet-started (see the existing note about `ci-required` being an aggregator that is absent until its
deps finish). Left alone, the README keeps advertising the previous version while the release is live,
which is the one place a concrete version number is allowed *because* it is release-managed.

It will recur on **every** release.

### Options

1. **Open the PR with a PAT** (or a GitHub App token) instead of `GITHUB_TOKEN` — workflows then trigger
   normally. Costs a secret to maintain.
2. **Don't open a PR at all** — commit the README bump directly to `main` from the release job. It is a
   release-managed file and `main` requires only `ci-required`; a docs-only push runs the cheap path.
   Simplest, and removes the step rather than fixing it.
3. **Auto-approve within the workflow**

title: kuilt-raft: SnapshotReceiver reassembles into an uncapped ArrayList<Byte> — attacker-driven done=false chunks OOM the follower
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by adversarial spec review of #1872 (#1868's fix). **Pre-existing; #1872 neither introduces nor covers it.** A resource-exhaustion hole rather than a safety one.

`SnapshotReceiver.onChunk` accumulates into an unbounded `ArrayList<Byte>`:

```kotlin
private class SnapshotReassembly(val meta: SnapshotMeta, val buffer: ArrayList<Byte> = ArrayList())
…
r.buffer.addAll(data.asList())
```

There is no cap on the reassembled total. The sender chooses `done`, so a peer that keeps sending `done = false` chunks with matching `meta` and correctly-advancing offsets grows the buffer without limit until the follower OOMs. The transport's `maxPayloadBytes` caps a *single* chunk, not the sum.

The multiplier makes it much cheaper than it looks: `ArrayList<Byte>` stores **boxed** `java.lang.Byte`, so on a 64-bit JVM each wire byte costs roughly 16 bytes of heap plus 4–8 for the backing array slot — call it ~16–24×. A few hundred MB on the wire is several GB of heap.

Note the §5.2 leader-authority gate (#1383) means the sender must be a current voter, so this is a Byzantine-voter / spoofing threat, the same model as #1868 and #1876 — not something an unauthenticated stranger can do.

### Directions

1. **Cap the reassembly at a configurable maximum** (`RaftConfig`), dropping and resetting past it. Needs a sane default: it must exceed any legitimate snapshot, which is application state and therefore unbounded in principle.
2. **Have the leader declare the total size up front** in the first chunk and validate each chunk against it — closes it properly, but changes the wire format.
3. **Store the buffer as a `ByteArray`/growable byte buffer rather than `ArrayList<Byte>`** — removes the ~16× boxing multiplier and is wort

title: kuilt-nearby: NearbySeam._state is an unguarded MutableStateFlow — rosterWatcher's check-then-act can stamp Woven over a terminal Torn (reasoning-only)
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**Reasoning-only — NOT executed.** This is a read of the code, not a reproduced failure. It is
not demonstrable under `runTest`: the test dispatchers serialise everything, so the interleaving
below cannot occur there. Treat the claim as unproven until a real-thread harness shows it.

`NearbySeam._state` is a bare `MutableStateFlow<SeamState>` with no guard, and `rosterWatcher`
performs a check-then-act on it *outside* `peersLock`:

```kotlin
sharedPeers.collect { session ->
    peersLock.withReentrantLock { if (!collapsed) _peers.value = session + selfId }
    if (_state.value is SeamState.Weaving && session.any { it != selfId }) {
        _state.value = SeamState.Woven          // ← read and write are not atomic
    }
}
```

The interleaving: the watcher reads `_state.value` and sees `Weaving` → another thread runs
`latchTorn` to completion (CAS, `collapseRoster`, `_state.value = Torn`, scope cancel, spool
close) → the watcher's in-flight write stamps `Woven` over the terminal `Torn`.

Scope cancellation does not prevent it. Cancellation is **cooperative**: it takes effect at a
suspension point, and there is none between the `_state` read and the `_state` write. A
cancelled-but-not-yet-suspended coroutine still completes a plain field write.

The resulting state is contract-impossible and permanent — `closed == true`, `incoming`
completed, `peers == { selfId }`, and `state` reporting `Woven` forever, with no further
`sharedPeers` emission able to correct it (the collector is gone). A consumer waiting on
`state.first { it is Torn }` never wakes.

**The asymmetry worth noting:** the two impls #1873 mirrored — `TieredSeam` and `RoomHubSeam`
(#1869) — route every lifecycle write through `SeamStateGate`, whose `u

title: kuilt-nearby: NearbyLoom's session-wide roster is never pruned, so a reused loom seeds the next seam with a phantom roster and false-latches Woven
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`NearbyLoom` keeps one loom-wide `sharedPeers` `MutableStateFlow` for the lifetime of the
loom and never prunes it when a seam tears. Nothing removes a *local* seam's own id from it,
so the residue of a finished weave seeds the next one.

Demonstrated by execution at `265e7197` (PR #1873's head): weave seam A (`selfId = a`,
remote `b`), close A → the loom-wide roster stays `{a, b}` **forever**. A's `disconnectLoop`
is the only thing that would evict `b`, and it is closed and cancelled; `close()` no longer
writes the flow at all. A later `weave` on the same loom seeds its mirror from that residue,
so a fresh seam with **zero connections** reports `peers == {a, b, c}` and false-latches
`Woven` — its roster watcher sees a non-self id and flips `Weaving → Woven` immediately.

**The class is pre-existing, not introduced by #1873.** Pre-fix the same probe leaves
stale-remote residue too: the old `sharedPeers.update { it - selfId }` in `close()` only
cleaned up `a`, leaving `{b}`. #1873 changes *which* id lingers, not *whether* one does.
Filing it separately because the fix is a `NearbyLoom` lifecycle change (per-weave roster,
or a seam-scoped eviction on tear), not a `NearbySeam` one, and it wants its own TDD cycle.

This is squarely the #1854 blind spot: the TCK matrix enumerates "seams a `Loom` produces",
one weave at a time, so **sequential weaves on one loom** are outside it. No conformance
obligation covers "a fresh seam from a reused loom starts at `{ selfId }` and `Weaving`",
which is why a false-`Woven` seam with a phantom roster passes everything today.

Worth deciding as part of the fix: whether `sharedPeers` should be per-weave rather than
per-loom. The single-flow design is what made the #1850 cross-pee

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Structural follow-up from #1869 / #1854. Not a bug — a **gap in how we know we have coverage**.

**Status (updated 2026-08-16): candidate fix (1) has landed; this issue now tracks (2) only.**

[#1937](https://github.com/tractat-us/kuilt/pull/1937) (`c82e39a6`) bound the two missing harnesses — `MuxServerLoomConformanceTest` and `TieredSeamConformanceTest` — closing today's concrete gap. Verified on `main`; the suite is now at **21** `: SeamConformanceSuite` subclasses.

**What remains is the part that generalises:** nothing tells us when a production `Seam` has *no* harness. The blind spot is intact for every future obligation.

## What happened

#1859 added `SeamConformanceSuite.peersCollapseToSelfIdWhenTorn` and measured its blast radius across all 16 harnesses. `SeamConformanceSuite` drives seams **through a `Loom`**, and the coverage story rests on enumerating the harnesses. body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found by adversarial spec review of #1846, which closed the AppendEntries lane of this hole. **This is the other lane, and it is strictly worse than the #1832 witness.** Pre-existing; #1846 neither introduces nor covers it.

`isWellFormedBatch` guards only `AppendEntries`. `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM` guards only `m.wireTerm` — the frame's **own** `term` field. `InstallSnapshot.lastIncludedTerm` / `lastIncludedIndex` (`RaftMessage.kt:98-99`) are inspected by neither.

### The frame

```kotlin
InstallSnapshot(
  term              = <victim's currentTerm>,   // honest: passes the #1833 bound AND the stale-term check
  leaderId          = <the real leader>,         // passes the §5.2 leader-authority gate
  lastIncludedIndex = Long.MAX_VALUE - 1,
  lastIncludedTerm  = Long.MAX_VALUE,
  offset = 0, data = <any bytes>, done = true,
)

1. `m.lastIncludedIndex <= state.currentCommitIndex` is false → the etcd-style guard does not fire.

title: Tap admission MACs a counterparty-chosen nonce — the challenge carries no prover-contributed freshness, so the harvest path is precomputable and the TTL still bounds nothing
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Follow-up to #1820, filed while fixing it. #1820 enforces `Challenge.nonce` at `NONCE_BYTES` — a real wire-invariant fix, and it lands. It does **not** close the attack its title describes, and this issue records the residual honestly.

## What survives the width fix

`TokenGatedSeam.respondToChallenge` MACs a nonce chosen **entirely by the sender**:

```kotlin
val tag = ByteString(hmacSha256(prover.code.encodeToByteArray(), challenge.nonce.toByteArray()))
```

Enforcing the width makes the nonce **well-formed**, not **fresh**. An attacker that previously sent `Challenge(ByteString())` now sends `Challenge(ByteString(ByteArray(16)))` — sixteen zero bytes, a legal challenge — and harvests `HMAC(code, 0x00^16)`. That value is precomputable against the ~2⁴⁰ code space *before the token is ever minted*, so recovery on harvest is a table lookup. The TTL bounds nothing on this path either way; the width check does not change the attacker's cost by a single HMAC.

## Where this bites

Only where the **prover** hosts — the `installLogTapJoining` topology (device joins, puller hosts), which is a shipped public entry point. There the sole control is `TokenGatedSeam.boundHost`: the prover answers the *first* peer that challenges it and ignores the rest. So the attack is a race, not a certainty — but winning the race once is enough, and it also denies the legitimate host.

Where the **verifier** hosts, the nonce is the verifier's own `random.nextBytes`, precomputation is impossible, and the "Entropy ↔ TTL" argument on `LogTapJoinToken` holds exactly as written.

title: kuilt-core: CompositeSeam.close's per-ply close loop is unguarded — one ply's throw skips every remaining ply, and a minted cancellation makes the composite violate the obligation #1859 states
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Pre-existing; surfaced by the adversarial review of #1859. Not caused by that PR, but squarely in its thematic blast radius.

`CompositeSeam.kt:1083`:

```kotlin
toClose.forEach { it.seam.close(reason) }
```

Completely unguarded. Two consequences:

1. **One ply throwing skips every remaining ply's close** — a plain exception is enough; the rest of the plies leak.
2. **A minted `CancellationException` escaping makes the *composite* violate the very `Seam.close` obligation #1859 just added to the contract** — "must not report failure as cancellation." The decorator breaks the rule it now enforces on its members.

It passes the new TCK only because every in-tree member conforms. That is precisely the shape #1826 was filed about: a guard (or the absence of one) that is correct only by convention.

### The right shape

Per #1847, this is an **unshielded** best-effort loop, so the correct guard is per-item `try` / `catch (_: Throwable)` + `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` — **not** `runCatchingCancellable` (rethrows a callee-minted CE and strands the rest) and **not** a bare swallow (loses a genuine caller cancellation). `MeshSeam.closeBestEffort`, landing in #1845, is the exemplar.

### Note on the sibling site

The same review flagged `MeshSeam.close:529` (`runCatchingCancellable { conn.close() }`) for the identical exposure. That one is **already being fixed in #1845** — the review read `main`, which predates it. Only the `CompositeSeam` site needs work here.

Sequence after #1845 and #1859 land, since it touches `CompositeSeam.kt` (the #1788 / #1811 / #1815 cluster). Related: #1847, #1826, #1834, #1803.

title: Cookbook's resume sample branches on a ResumeResult a joiner can never receive — and sends the reachable case to the opposite action
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**The published cookbook tells consumers to branch on a `ResumeResult` case `room.resume()` can never
return, and routes the case that *does* occur to the opposite action.**

Found while reviewing the #1637 fix (#1848).

## The two contracts on one type

`ResumeResult` is returned by two different callers with **different reachable subsets**:

| Caller | Can return |
|---|---|
| **host-side** `JoinerReconnectController.tryResume` | `Success`, `WindowNotYetOpen`, `WindowClosed`, `TokenInvalid` |
| **joiner-side** `Room.resume(token)` | `Success`, `WindowClosed`, `TimedOut`, `TokenInvalid` — **never `WindowNotYetOpen`** |

The joiner never sees it because `JoinerResumeMachine` resolves **any** host `Reject` as
`ResumeResult.WindowClosed` (`JoinerResumeMachine.kt:239`, and its KDoc at 221–228 says so); the
specific code is carried separately in `refusal` as a `RejectCode`.

## The defect

#1846 added `MAX_PLAUSIBLE_TERM = 2^60` at the `onMessage` dispatch boundary, so an implausible term arriving **on the wire** is now dropped rather than adopted. That closes the live attack.

title: kuilt-webrtc: WebRTCPeerLink.close does not collapse peers (the remote-tear path does) — fails the #1816 TCK obligation
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1816 put the collapse obligation on `Seam.peers` (a `Torn` seam's `peers` must be exactly
`{ selfId }`) and asserted it in `SeamConformanceSuite.peersCollapseToSelfIdWhenTorn`.
**`WebRTCPeerLink` fails it on the local-`close` path only.**

The remote-tear path is exemplary — `WebRTCPeerLink.kt:94-95` collapses *then* tears:

```kotlin
_peers.value = setOf(selfId)
_state.value = SeamState.Torn(CloseReason.RemoteRequested)
```

`close()` (`:134-144`) does not, so a locally-closed data channel reports its pre-close
roster forever. Receipt (with the flag forced `true`):

```

  - a Torn seam must advertise NO reachable remote peer … Expected <[]>, actual <[PeerId(value=peer-kwcwfrug)]>
```

Should be a two-line fix — hoist the collapse the remote path already performs into the
shared teardown, so both paths reach `{ selfId }`.

title: kuilt-multipeer: MCSessionLink/BridgePeerLink tearDown never collapses peers on local close (fails the #1816 TCK obligation)
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1816 put the collapse obligation on `Seam.peers` (a `Torn` seam's `peers` must be exactly
`{ selfId }`) and asserted it in `SeamConformanceSuite.peersCollapseToSelfIdWhenTorn`.
**Both Multipeer link implementations fail it on the local-`close` path.**

`MCSessionLink.tearDown()` (`kuilt-multipeer/src/appleMain/…/MCSessionLink.kt:192-198`) and
`BridgePeerLink.tearDown()` (`…/jvmMain/…/BridgePeerLink.kt:218-224`) write `_state`, the
bridge handle, the spool and the scope — and never touch `_peers`. So a closed link reports
its pre-close roster forever.

Receipt (with the flag forced `true`):

```
MultipeerConformanceTest.peersCollapseToSelfIdWhenTorn[jvm]
  - a Torn seam must advertise NO reachable remote peer … expected:<[]> but was:<[PeerId(value=conformance-joiner)]>
```

The **remote-drop** paths are already correct — `MCSessionLink.kt:246,255-257` and
`BridgePeerLink.kt:131,140-141` reach `{ selfId }` before tearing. The local `close()` only
gets there if a post-cancel ObjC/JNA `.notConnected` callback happens to land, which is not
a guarantee. The fix is to collapse `_peers` in `tearDown()` itself, matching
`LinkSeam.tearDown` / `MeshSeam.tearDown`.

title: kuilt-nearby: NearbySeam.close removes selfId from the SHARED roster instead of collapsing its own peers (fails the #1816 TCK obligation)
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1816 put the collapse obligation on `Seam.peers` (a `Torn` seam's `peers` must be exactly
`{ selfId }`) and asserted it in `SeamConformanceSuite.peersCollapseToSelfIdWhenTorn`.
**`NearbySeam` fails it** — and unlike the reference `InMemoryLoom` (#1849), this is a
production transport.

`NearbySeam.peers` is `sharedPeers`, a session-wide `MutableStateFlow` every seam in the
session holds (`NearbySeam.kt:66`). `close()` latches `Torn` first and then removes *itself*
from that shared flow (`NearbySeam.kt:190-197`):

```kotlin
if (!latchTorn(reason)) return          // :190
…
sharedPeers.update { it - selfId }      // :197
```

So a host closing a 2-peer Nearby session ends with its own `peers.value == { joiner }` —
a remote peer still advertised as reachable through a dead seam, and `selfId` dropped — and
the same write mutates the *joiner's* view of the roster.

Receipt (with the flag forced `true`):

```
NearbyConformanceTest.peersCollapseToSelfIdWhenTorn[jvm]
  - a Torn seam must advertise NO reachable remote peer … expected:<[]> but was:<[PeerId(value=810de7f9-…)]>
  - a Torn seam's collapsed roster is { selfId }, not empty …
```

The **remote** path is already correct: `NearbySeam.kt:141` removes the departing peer before
tearing at `:146-147`, leaving `{ selfId }`. Only the local-`close` path deviates.

Declares `collapsesPeersOnTear = false` with this issue as the gap URL until fixed.

Part of #1816.

title: The #1835 carve-out covers only the SHIELDED case — an unshielded best-effort loop still gets advice that produces the #1834 bug
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

#1839 closed #1835 by adding a carve-out to `CLAUDE.md`'s exception-discipline rule for code **inside a `withContext(NonCancellable)` shield**. That carve-out is correct, but its justification is explicitly shield-scoped:

> The shield exists so cleanup completes *despite* outer cancellation, so your own job is never cancelled there — which makes every `CancellationException` reachable inside it necessarily callee-minted…

**#1834's two sites are deliberately NOT shielded** (see #1845). There, your own job *can* be cancelled, so the carve-out's premise does not hold and its advice does not apply — yet the general rule immediately above it is still wrong for them. Following `if (e is CancellationException) throw e` literally in an unshielded best-effort loop is exactly how the rest of the roster gets stranded, which is #1834.

The #1845 worker put it precisely, having hit it:

> The prose has no notion of a *callee-minted* cancellation, so it gives no way to reach the correct `ensureActive()` discriminator.

### There are three cases; the doc describes two

| Context | Correct shape |
|---|---|
| Best-effort **single** send, cancellable context | `runCatchingCancellable { … }` — the general rule |
| Inside a `NonCancellable` shield | plain `try` / `catch (Throwable)` + log — the #1839 carve-out |
| **Unshielded best-effort loop over N items** | `try { … } catch (_: Throwable) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); log }` — **undocumented** |

### The better framing

The axis that actually matters is not *shielded vs unshielded*. It is **whose cancellation is this — mine, or the callee's?** `ensureActive()` is the universal discriminator: it rethrows only if *we* were cancelled, and a callee's `withTimeo

title: docs/extending-fabrics.md teaches the TOCTOU port-probe that forbidPortProbeRebind rejects — a doc that invites the file the guard refuses
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Same class as #1835, found while fixing it.

`docs/extending-fabrics.md:373` presents this as **"the copy-paste template"** for a new fabric's conformance test:

```kotlin
port = JvmServerSocket(0).use { it.localPort }
serverSocket = aSocket(selector).tcp().bind("127.0.0.1", port)
```

That is verbatim the probe-then-rebind TOCTOU `forbidPortProbeRebind` exists to reject (#1590). The guard's own allowlist comment in the root `build.gradle.kts` says of the file such a snippet would produce: *"do NOT add a new file here; bind 0 instead."*

So a contributor following the tutorial writes the exact file the `check`-wired guard refuses — and the guard cannot warn them, because it scans `src/**/*.kt` and never sees the doc. **The prose is the only enforcement at that surface, and it points the wrong way.**

### Why this was not fixed in #1839

The snippet quotes `TcpConformanceTest.kt`, which is still on the guard's allowlist. Rewriting the doc first would falsify the quote until the source lands — so the doc edit should ship **with** the source conversion, which #1749 already owns for the `TcpLoom` half.

### Fix

When #1749 converts the `TcpLoom` sites to bind-0, update this snippet in the same PR and re-verify the quote. If #1749 lands without it, this issue stands alone.

Related: #1835 (the same failure mode in `CLAUDE.md`), #1749, #1590.

title: NearbySeam.receiveLoop has no corrupt-inbound backstop — any throw under assembleFrame kills receiveJob without latching Torn
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kuilt-nearby/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/nearby/NearbySeam.kt:99-111`

`receiveLoop` collects `api.payloadReceived` with no guard around the per-event work:

```kotlin
val frame = endpointPeersMutex.withLock {
    ...
    assembleFrame(event.endpointId, event.bytes, remotePeerId)
} ?: return@collect
```

Any throw from `assembleFrame` escapes the collector and kills `receiveJob`. `disconnectLoop` is a **sibling** under the seam scope's `SupervisorJob`, so it keeps running and `_state` never latches `Torn`: the seam goes permanently deaf with no `CloseReason` and no reconnect trigger. The consumer sees a live seam that has stopped delivering.

#1819 was one instance of this (`ChunkCodec` indexed past a bound array). That fix made the codec **total** — it can no longer throw on any input — so there is no known live path today. This issue is about the *structural* gap: nothing stops the next throw introduced anywhere under `assembleFrame` from reproducing the same silent-deafness shape.

## Precedent

`NwSeam.bytesReceivedLoop` (#1528 finding 1) already does the corresponding hardening: it wraps the decode, re-throws `CancellationException`, and routes any other failure through `evictCorruptConn` — a *signalled* outcome rather than a dead loop.

The Nearby side has no `evictCorruptConn` equivalent, so the fix needs a decision, not just a `try`:

1. **Drop the frame and log** — cheapest, but silently swallows a real defect.
2. **Disconnect the endpoint** (`api.disconnect(endpointId)`), letting `disconnectLoop` produce the normal roster update and, on the last endpoint, `Torn`. Closest to the `NwSeam` precedent.

title: A disconnected host renders "Player left the game", blaming the peer — and saves a replay that does too
body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

**A host that loses its own network tells the user the _other_ player left the game** — and writes a replay blaming them. Found on hardware 2026-07-26 (`main` @ `efaf6be33`, kuilt dev.964, 2 USB-wired iPhones).

## Evidence

The iPhone XS (host) was put into airplane mode. Its own log:

```
13:58:13.657  nw.path.update status=Unsatisfied interfaces=[] reason=NotAvailable
13:58:14.024  nw.path.self-loss device-path unsatisfied → setViability(false)
13:58:29      presence.overlay Paused(reason=PeerPartitioned, displayName=iPhone (7e84))
13:59:27      presence.overlay Terminal(reason=PeerDeparted, displayName=iPhone (7e84))
```

On screen: **"Player left the game"** — shown to the person who actually dropped, naming the peer who did not. `LiveGameScreen`'s one-shot `launchPartialSave` then fires on that terminal, so a saved replay records the innocent peer as having abandoned the game.

The host keeps running its own presence pipeline while partitioned, so `PauseOverlayReducer.project` takes the `peer is PeerPresence.Departed && endsGameOnDeparture && !isHostSeat` branch. Nothing in that path asks whether *this* device is the one that went offline.

## Why it wasn't caught

A mesh partition is **symmetric** — both devices log the other as unresponsive — so membership events alone never identify which radio died. The only discriminator is `nw.path.update` / `nw.path.self-loss`, which appears solely on the dropped device. Any two-phone trace that doesn't check it can be read backwards; this one initially was.

## The fix is now available

body:
> 🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Reproduced on hardware (iPhone XS, iOS 18.7.9) with `Join · S4 only`, captured via `devicectl --console`:

```
[4] Teardown+reconnect     FAIL   21.1s  torn=false reconnect peers=2
    leg1 wove state=Woven peers=[2e5609c1,1fa4e56a] t=746ms
    awaiting terminal Torn after host drop t=746ms
    torn=false stateA=Weaving t=20752ms
    leg2 wove state=Woven peersImmediate=2 peersAfter5s=2 woven5s=true in 435ms
```

**Everything the library did was correct.** leg1 wove in 746 ms; the host dropped; the joiner re-formed; leg2 re-wove in 435 ms with both peers. The fabric log shows the contract being honoured exactly:

```
nw.api.receive-transient id=nw-1 domain=1 code=96 → retry 1..8 … budget (8, ~2750ms) exhausted → escalateClose
nw.seam.closed connId=nw-1 … evicted peer=1fa4e56a… → peers=[2e5609c1…] state=Weaving (reform, not tear)
```

The only thing that failed is the **assertion**. `ConnectivitySuite.kt:357-361`:

```kotlin
} else {
    hop("awaiting terminal Torn after host drop t=${ms()}ms")
    val torn = withTimeoutOrNull(TORN_TIMEOUT) { seamA.state.first { it is SeamState.Torn } }

```

Per `NwSeam`'s contract (#1513) a joiner losing its last remote is **not** terminal: the seam goes `Woven → Weaving`, resets `peers` to `{selfId}`, keeps `incoming` open and waits for a redial. `Torn` latches only on an explicit consumer `close()` or the initial weave timeout — it "is never a consequence of peer loss". > 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`CLAUDE.md`'s exception-discipline rule, followed literally, **reintroduces the #1803 bug that #1824 just
fixed — in a form the new build guard cannot see.**

## The collision

`CLAUDE.md:218-224` states, with no carve-out:

> A `catch (e: Exception)`/`catch (e: Throwable)` that should tolerate failure must
> `if (e is CancellationException) throw e` (or a leading `catch (CancellationException) { throw e }`)
> before swallowing.

That rule is correct essentially everywhere. It is **wrong inside a `withContext(NonCancellable)` shield**,
which is exactly what #1824 established: inside the shield our own job is never cancelled, so every
`CancellationException` reachable there is necessarily *callee-minted*, and rethrowing it aborts the very
cleanup the shield exists to guarantee.

#1824 converted nine sites to precisely the shape this rule tells you to "fix":

```kotlin
withContext(NonCancellable) {
    seams.forEach {
        try {
            it.close()
        } catch (_: Throwable) {   // CLAUDE.md says: add `if (e is CancellationException) throw e`
        }
    }
}
```

## Why this is the dangerous one

#1824's guard (`forbidRunCatchingCancellableUnderNonCancellable`, wired into `check`) greps for the
**`runCatchingCancellable` token**. An agent following `CLAUDE.md` would not reintroduce that token — it
would hand-write `if (e is CancellationException) throw e` inside the `catch`. Same defect, **zero signal**:
the guard stays green, CI stays green, and the regression is invisible.

In an agent-heavy repo this is not hypothetical. The documentation is the more likely regression path than a
human re-adding `runCatchingCancellable`, and it points straight down it.

## Fix

One sentence appended to the exis

title: MeshSeam's two unshielded best-effort close loops abort on the first callee-minted cancellation, leaking the rest of the roster
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Two multi-item best-effort close loops in `MeshSeam` abort at the first callee-minted
`CancellationException`, leaking every remaining connection. They are the siblings of the nine sites fixed
in #1824 — same failure, but **outside** a `NonCancellable` shield, so #1824's guard cannot flag them.

## The two sites

| Site | Loop | Bounded by |
|---|---|---|
| `MeshSeam.kt:529` (`close()`) | `toClose.forEach { conn -> runCatchingCancellable { conn.close() } }` | **The full roster** — `tearDown()` snapshots `links.values.map { it.conn }`. **Unbounded in count**: a `hubMesh` accepts arbitrarily many spokes. |
| `MeshSeam.kt:332` (construction dedup) | `losers.forEach { runCatchingCancellable { it.conn.close() } }` | Duplicate links in the caller-supplied initial connection set. Unbounded in principle, small in practice. |

`:529` is the one that matters. It is the **public `Seam.close`** path for every mesh fabric, and one wedged
or timing-out peer means every remaining connection in the roster is never closed — the exact half-open leak
that `MeshSeam`'s drain-latch shield (fixed in #1824) exists to prevent, reachable through the ordinary
close path instead.

#1824 enforces *"no `runCatchingCancellable` lexically inside `withContext(NonCancellable)`"*. That rule is

`CancellationException` reachable inside it is necessarily callee-minted.

title: term adoption has no sanity bound and currentTerm + 1 overflows — one Long.MAX_VALUE frame permanently prevents any future election, cluster-wide
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found in the adversarial sweep around #1817 / #1818 (PR #1828). Fifth instance of the unvalidated-wire-field class. This one takes down the **whole cluster, permanently, with no crash and no diagnostic** — arguably the worst failure mode of the set, because there is nothing to look at afterwards.

## Mechanism

Term adoption has no upper sanity bound. Any message carrying a higher term is adopted wholesale via `stepDown(m.term, StepDownReason.HigherTermObserved)`, and the term increment on election is a bare `+ 1`:

- `RaftEngine.kt:529` — `val proposed = state.currentTerm + 1` (pre-vote)
- `RaftEngine.kt:557` — `persistTermAndVote(state.currentTerm + 1, transport.selfId)` (real election)

Kotlin `Long` arithmetic wraps silently. So:

1. One message anywhere carrying `term = Long.MAX_VALUE` is adopted by its recipient.
2. The victim's own responses now carry `term = Long.MAX_VALUE`, so **every peer adopts it** in turn — the poison propagates through the cluster on normal traffic, no further malice needed.
3. The next election computes `Long.MAX_VALUE + 1`, which wraps to `Long.MIN_VALUE`.
4. Every `RequestVote` / `PreVote` now proposes a hugely **negative** term. Every recipient compares it against its stored `Long.MAX_VALUE` and sees a stale term, so it denies the vote and replies with its own higher term.
5. **No leader can ever be elected again.** Not for a timeout, not after restart — `currentTerm` is persisted, so it survives process death.

There is no exception, no log line, and no crashed node. The cluster simply stops making progress forever while every node reports itself healthy.

## Fix

Honest terms cannot approach 2^63 — they increment once per election, so a real deployment stays many orders

title: AppendEntries entries are appended with unvalidated indices — a non-contiguous batch breaks log contiguity and wins every election (Leader Completeness violation)
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found in the adversarial sweep around #1817 / #1818 (PR #1828). Fourth instance of the unvalidated-wire-field class, and the most serious: it is a **Leader Completeness (§5.4) violation**, not merely a crash or a stale read.

## Mechanism

`RaftEngine.onAppendEntries`, `RaftEngine.kt:1184-1212`, walks `m.entries` and appends the suffix from the first divergence:

```kotlin
for ((i, entry) in m.entries.withIndex()) {
    if (entry.index <= state.snapshotIndex) continue
    val existing = state.entryAt(entry.index)
    if (existing == null) { appendFrom = i; break }   // first index past our tail
    …
}
…
state.log.addAll(toAdd)
```

`LogEntry.index` and `LogEntry.term` arrive off the wire and are never checked against the batch's own frame. The protocol implies `entries[i].index == prevLogIndex + 1 + i` — contiguous, ascending, starting immediately after the probed position — but nothing enforces it. `entryAt` returns null for any index past the tail, so the `existing == null` branch appends **whatever index the sender supplied**, at any distance from the real tail.

A single AppendEntries with a matching `prevLogIndex` and one entry at `index = Long.MAX_VALUE - 1, term = Long.MAX_VALUE` is therefore appended directly onto the victim's log.

## Two consequences

**Contiguity break (correctness).** `logEntryAt` (`RaftLogMath.kt:99`) computes its offset as `index - (snapshotIndex + 1)`, valid only because "indices are monotonically increasing and there are no gaps" — its own KDoc states the assumption. A log holding `[… 7, MAX-1]` violates it, so subsequent lookups index into the wrong slot or out of range.

**Election Safety (the safety half).** `RequestVote.lastLogPosition` is built from the node's last ent

title: AppendEntries stale-term rejection echoes the old request's round into the current term — a foreign echo with no forgery, confirming a stale read
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found in the adversarial sweep around #1817 / #1818 (PR #1828). This one needs **no forgery** — two honest, correct nodes produce a foreign echo on their own, so it fires in the plain crash-fault async model.

## Mechanism

`RaftEngine.kt:1088`, the stale-term AppendEntries rejection:

```kotlin
if (m.term < state.currentTerm) {
    send(from, RaftMessage.AppendEntriesResponse(state.currentTerm, false, echoedRound = m.round))
    return
}
```

It pairs the **current** term with the **old request's** round. `ReadIndexTracker.round` resets to 0 on every `becomeLeader` (`ReadIndexTracker.reset()`, called at `RaftEngine.kt:688`), so a round from an earlier leadership can be arbitrarily larger than the current one.

Sequence:

1. Leader L at term 2 reaches round 1000. One AppendEntries (`term = 2, round = 1000`) is delayed in the network.
2. L loses and regains leadership; it is now leader at term 4, and its round counter has reset and climbed only a little.
3. The delayed AE finally reaches follower F, which is now at term 4. `m.term (2) < currentTerm (4)` ⇒ the stale-term branch fires.
4. F replies `AppendEntriesResponse(term = 4, success = false, echoedRound = 1000)`.
5. At L, `m.term == state.currentTerm` (both 4) passes the guard at `:1247`, and the response reaches `recordAck(from, 1000)`.

In a 3-voter cluster, `lastAckRound[F] = 1000` beats any plausible `sinceRound`, so self + F is a freshness quorum and a read is confirmed even though F answered nothing in the current round — **a stale read served as linearizable** during a CheckQuorum deposal window.

## Why this is a bug rather than a deliberate choice

The sibling stale-term path already does the right thing. `RaftEngine.kt:998`, the InstallSnapshot

body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

Found while fixing #1817 / #1818 (PR #1828) and surveying the same class — an unvalidated numeric wire field stored into safety-critical leader state. This is the third instance, and it is the most interesting one: **it reaches the exact `error(...)` that #1175's clamp was added to prevent, by taking the branch that clamp does not cover.**

## Mechanism

`RaftEngine.onAppendEntriesResponse` handles the two branches asymmetrically:

```kotlin
if (m.success) {
    // #1175: clamped
    state.matchIndex[from] = maxOf(state.matchIndex[from] ?: 0L, minOf(m.matchIndex, state.lastLogIndex))
    …
} else {
    // NOT clamped
    state.nextIndex[from] = nextIndexAfterFailure(state.nextIndex[from] ?: 1L, m, state.log)
    sendAppendEntries(from)
}

…
return response.conflictIndex ?: maxOf(1L, currentNextIndex - 1L)

- `prevIndex == snapshotIndex` is false, so it falls through to (`:894`)
- `state.entryAt(prevIndex)` returns null (out of window) ⇒ **`error("prevTerm for in-window index $prevIndex missing …")`** (`:898`)

title: The three forbid* verification tasks declare no output, so they re-run on every build
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`forbidUnboundedSwatchDelivery`, `forbidSourcelessKmpTarget`, and `forbidPortProbeRebind` (root `build.gradle.kts`) all declare **inputs but no outputs**, so Gradle has no basis to mark them `UP-TO-DATE` and re-runs them on every build.

Individually cheap, but this is how a verification task earns a reputation for slowing the build down and then gets deleted — which is exactly the outcome these guards exist to prevent.

#1824's `forbidRunCatchingCancellableUnderNonCancellable` added a stamp-file output for this reason and reports `UP-TO-DATE` on a second run. The brief for that task told the author to follow the siblings' structure; the author correctly pushed back that the siblings are the ones that need retrofitting, not the model to copy.

The retrofit is a few lines each — a `layout.buildDirectory.file("<name>/verified.txt")` output plus `outputs.cacheIf { true }`, matching #1824's shape. Worth doing in one PR across all three so the four guards are uniform, and worth a one-line comment on each saying why the stamp exists, so a future reader doesn't remove it as dead weight.

title: Seam.close carries no 'must not report failure as cancellation' obligation, so every best-effort close guard is defending against conforming code
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kuilt-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/core/Seam.kt:101-102` is the whole contract:

```kotlin
/** Disconnect from the session. Idempotent. */
public suspend fun close(reason: CloseReason = CloseReason.Normal)
```

#1800 put the *"a send failure must not be reported as a cancellation"* obligation on `sendTo`, with a pointer from `broadcast`, mirroring the one `Loom.weave` already carried — and named the reason: a caller cannot distinguish its own cancellation from a callee-minted one, so a `CancellationException` out of a foreign call **cancels** rather than fails the caller, with no handler and no stack trace.

**`close` never got the same obligation** — and all **nine** sites fixed in #1824 guard a `close()`. So that entire class of defect is reachable through *conforming* consumer code: an implementor who reads the contract and wraps their teardown in `withTimeout` has done nothing wrong, and every caller's best-effort cleanup silently stops at the first such peer.

The trap is identical to the one #1800 documented: `withTimeout(closeTimeout) { … }` throws `TimeoutCancellationException` — which **is** a `CancellationException` — to its caller without cancelling that caller's job.

## Why this is the right place to fix it

#1824 hardens the nine call sites, which is necessary regardless — a library cannot trust a consumer. But the sites are defending against something the contract permits, so new call sites will keep needing the same guard and new fabric implementations will keep being free to break them. Stating the obligation converts "every caller must defend" into "an implementation that does this is non-conforming".

title: verifyDocCitations: support an elision marker so "class shell with members elided" can be verified
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`verifyDocCitations` (#1792, PR #1799) matches a `verbatim from` block against the cited
declaration, its body, or a **contiguous** run of either. That leaves one common doc shape
unverifiable: **a class shell with some members elided.**

The clearest case is `InMemoryLoomConformanceTest`, quoted in both
`Writerside/topics/testing.md` and `docs/testing.md`:

```kotlin
class InMemoryLoomConformanceTest : SeamConformanceSuite() {
    private val loom = InMemoryLoom()
    override fun newLoomPair(): Pair<Loom, Loom> = loom to loom
}
```

Every line is verbatim, but the real class has four more overrides between
`newLoomPair()` and the closing brace, so the block is two slices plus a synthesised `}` —
not contiguous. Both citations were therefore relabelled `condensed from` in #1799, which
means their content is now **never checked again**, even though they are ~0.99 identical to
the source. That is the weakest outcome available: the drift these blocks are most likely to
suffer (a member is renamed, the class shell changes) is exactly what went unenforced.

## Suggested fix

Support an explicit elision marker — a bare `// …` line in the block — matched as an
**ordered multi-slice**: split the block on elision lines, then require each part to appear
in the source in order, non-overlapping. That would let the shape above be checked properly:

```kotlin
class InMemoryLoomConformanceTest : SeamConformanceSuite() {
    private val loom = InMemoryLoom()
    override fun newLoomPair(): Pair<Loom, Loom> = loom to loom
    // …
}
```

Two things to get right:

- **The trailing `}`.** The doc closes a brace the elided region also closes. Either treat a
  final closing-brace line as satisfied by the declaration's own last

title: single()/getValue() inside an assertAll lambda masks every sibling assertion — exactly in the failing state where the diagnosis matters
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`assertAll` (`kuilt-test/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/test/Assertions.kt:8-24`) catches **only** `AssertionError` — its own KDoc says so at `:6`:

> Non-assertion throwables propagate immediately.

So a lambda that calls `list.single()` on an **empty** list throws `NoSuchElementException`, which is not an `AssertionError`, and the whole `assertAll` aborts at that lambda — skipping every assertion after it. The list is empty precisely in the broken state, so the mechanism deletes the diagnosis exactly when it is needed. What the developer sees is `NoSuchElementException: List is empty.` instead of the named failure they wrote.

Found during #1809, where the first draft of a new pump test reported a bare `NoSuchElementException` and hid two named assertions. Rewriting them list-shaped (`assertEquals(listOf(expected), actual)` rather than `actual.single().field`) is what made the real reds legible:

```
2 assertion(s) failed:
  - a consumer flow's own throw must be reported, not escape the pump's launch
      expected:<[(PlyId(value=only), INBOUND)]> but was:<[]>
  - the cause must be the flow's own expected:<[this consumer's incoming flow threw]> but was:<[]>
```

Each of these calls `.single()` on a collection inside an `assertAll` lambda, so an empty collection masks its siblings:

title: ChunkCodec binds an array from the first chunk's chunkCount but validates it per-chunk — 16 bytes from a peer make a NearbySeam permanently deaf
body:
> 🤖 This comment was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`kuilt-nearby/src/commonMain/kotlin/us/tractat/kuilt/nearby/ChunkCodec.kt`

The KDoc at `:50-51` promises the header check is whole:

> Returns null if `bytes` is shorter than `HEADER_SIZE` **or the header is internally inconsistent** (e.g. chunkIndex ≥ chunkCount, chunkCount = 0)

`decodeChunk` (`:58`) checks `chunkIndex >= chunkCount` **within one chunk only**. `Reassembler.feed` (`:124`) binds the array size from whichever chunk arrived *first* — `pending.getOrPut(chunk.msgId) { Assembly(chunk.chunkCount) }` — and never re-checks it against later chunks for the same `msgId`. `:141-142` then does an unchecked `slots[index]`.

## The input — two payloads, 16 bytes total

```
00 00 00 07 │ 00 00 │ 00 02 │ <1 byte>    → Assembly(2), incomplete
00 00 00 07 │ 00 05 │ 00 06 │ <1 byte>    → passes decodeChunk (5 < 6) → slots[5] on a size-2 array
```

## Consequence — deaf, not torn

`IndexOutOfBoundsException` from `NearbySeam`'s `assembleFrame` (`reassembler.feed`), which runs **inside** `endpointPeersMutex.withLock` in `receiveLoop`.
